
10 May
1
Election of Speaker
WEDNESDAY, 10 MAY 1978
Parliament was prorogued on 19 December 1977 and met again for the dispatch of
business on 10 May 1978 at 3 p.m.
The Clerk at the table (Mr Littlejohn) informed the House that the office of Speaker
was vacant.
ELECTION OF SPEAKER
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I am commanded by His Excellency the
Governor-General to inform the House that it is His Excellency's desire that the House
should proceed forthwith to the choice of a new Speaker.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That Mr J. R. Harrison, member of Parliament for
Hawke's Bay, do take the chair of this House as Speaker. As has been said many times
before, the Speakership is a most high, honourable, and onerous office. Those qualities are
reflected in its official status and privileges. They are best summed up in Erskine May's
Parliamentary Practice: "The Speaker is the representative of the House itself, in its powers,
proceedings, and dignity. Mr Speaker derives his authority from the House." History shows
that the Speakership has evolved in the House of Commons-slowly, naturally, and
unsystematically-over 600 years. In the New Zealand Parliament the Speakership follows
the procedures of the Commons, but has been adapted to meet our constitutional conditions
and political style. The choice of Speaker is one of the most important decisions taken by this
House. Once in the chair, the Speaker is very much on his own as he deals with the problems
and the excitements of conflicts and party battles. Whatever may be his personal technique
as occupant of the chair, the Speaker has to be aware of the powers and authorities which the
Standing Orders and practices of the House confer upon him. Although the Speaker is the
servant of the House, the House appoints him as the executor of its authority. Mr Harrison
was elected to Parliament in 1963. He served as Chairman of Committees and Deputy
Speaker in 1972 and again over the past 2 years. In the absence of Sir Roy Jack last year Mr
Harrison was Acting Speaker. No other parliamentarian here today is more experienced and
able to carry out the task of Speaker. He has proved his qualities of firmness, fairness, and
good judgment. I ask the House to offer its full support for my motion.
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): It gives me great pleasure to second the nomination
of the member for Hawke's Bay, Mr J. R. Harrison, as Speaker of the House. Honourable
members are fortunate in having had the opportunity to serve under the chairmanship of Mr
Harrison, both as Chairman of Committees and as Acting Speaker. Mr Harrison will come
to this distinguished office with experience and knowledge of the intricacies of presiding over
the House of Representatives which exceeds that of any present sitting member. On his
election as Chairman of Committees on 24 June 1976 Mr Harrison gave the following
undertaking I quote from Hansard: "I shall do my best to maintain order with impartiality,
so that members may take a proper part in debate; and also try to adjudicate as fairly as I can
on the conflicting rights of the minority to be heard and of the majority to be heeded." Mr
Harrison has carried out that undertaking. He has proved his ability and impartiality and has
upheld the traditions and the debating rights and privileges of all members of the House. It is
proper on this somewhat traditional occasion to mention the service given by Mr Harrison in
the New Zealand armed services, both overseas and also as Commanding Officer of the
Hawke's Bay Regiment between 1956 and 1959-a position he held 3 years before his
election as member for Hawke's Bay. Mr Harrison is proud of the traditions and disciplines
of the armed services, and he has carried this background through to maintain fair and
orderly debate in the House during his term as Chairman of Committees and as Acting
Speaker. Mr Harrison is now Vice-President of the Commonwealth Parliamentary
Association. Next year, as Speaker of the House of Representatives, he will have the honour
and the responsibility of presiding over the annual conference of Commonwealth
parliamentarians, which will be held in Wellington. His involvement in and influence on
parliamentary democracy will therefore extend beyond New Zealand's shores. I am sure
honourable members will agree that Mr Harrison's background and experience make him
the logical and outstanding choice for the distinguished position of Speaker in New
Zealand's House of Representatives. I have very much pleasure in seconding the motion

moved by the honourable member for Franklin.
Mr HARRISON (Hawke's Bay): Centuries ago in England there arose a tradition of
reluctance on the part of a member to accept office as Speaker. The reasons then were fairly
obvious. In the turbulent politics of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries more than
characters were assassinated. One Speaker lost his life in battle, some were murdered by the
mobs, and several lost their heads to the King's axeman. I am happy to report that those
customs seem to have been discontinued; I certainly hope so anyway. There is another cause
for a candidate's reluctance to accept the office of Speaker, and that is his doubt about his
fitness to preside to their satisfaction over the deliberations of his fellow colleagues, his
fellow members. Knowing my own limitations, it is certainly not undue modesty that inspires
my doubts about my ability to fill this high office. For that reason my reluctance is not merely
conventional, it is genuine. However, I realise that there must be a Speaker, and I am
encouraged by the generous comments of the honourable member for Franklin and the
honourable member for South Canterbury. I thank them for the unduly kind words they
spoke in nominating me, and I now submit myself to the judgment of my colleagues in the
hope that they will not weigh my merits too carefully and will pardon my offences.
[The House then having unanimously called Mr Harrison to the chair, he was taken out of
his place and conducted to the chair by his proposer and his seconder.]
Mr SPEAKER-ELECT: Honourable members, I feel deeply moved by your action this
afternoon, partly for the cause of it-the death of the Hon. Sir Roy Jack-and partly for the
effect of it, your election of me as your Speaker. My emotion is a mixture of pride because of
the honour you have conferred on me, and humility because of my frailty in occupying this
high office. I am conscious that, as Speaker, you have entrusted me with the dignity of this,
the nation's representative assembly. You have made me the master of the members but the
servant of the House, higher than anyone but lower than all. My task is to preside impartially
over your deliberations, somehow reconciling the conflicting right of individual members
and minority groups to be heard with the legitimate need of the Government to ensure that
its business proceeds. I hope, therefore, to be seen by you as independent-to be
Parliament's man, not that of the Crown, although, of course, I have a responsibility to both.
I am supposed to be impartial on all party issues, and that I shall try to be. A daunting array
of qualities is expected of a Speaker, qualities such as patience, tolerance, dignity, and good
humour, and I leave it to honourable members to decide in what measure I possess these. I
hope I may exercise enough of them to meet with your approval. One quality which I do not
possess in full is that of a legal training. I am no solicitor.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: A jolly good thing, too.
Mr SPEAKER-ELECT: I have always thought of myself as a simple, honest soul.
Hon. Members: Ha, ha!
Mr SPEAKER-ELECT: But, if it will help, I must admit I am partly compromised in
that at one time I sat at the feet of the late Sir Kenneth Gresson, then Dean of the Law
Faculty at Canterbury University College, and read, of all things, jurisprudence. However, I
am sure he never thought I would one day wear that sort of wig. It is generally agreed that it
is more important that the Speaker should have experience of Parliament than a knowledge
of the law, and should understand the problems of members and the moods and foibles of
the House, and I hope I do. I certainly have a reverence for Parliament as an institution and
a faith in parliamentary democratic government. It grieves me that, although most New
Zealanders I am sure share my reverence and my faith, many apparently do not believe that
our Parliament is as proper in its conduct and as relevant in its deliberations as they would
wish.
There has been much criticism about procedures and practices, and there have been
various calls for a revision of our Standing Orders. While I must concede that there are some
rules I would like to amend—such as those governing the lodging of notices of motion-by
and large I consider that it is their general application that is in need of change. In 1961 Sir
Ronald Algie, in much the same position as I am now, referred to this question of the public
standing of Parliament. He observed that people enjoy a fight, but considered that in
Parliament the people wanted it to be a battle of ideas, of wit and argument, not an
irrelevant slanging match bedevilled with personalities. I think all members agree that the
problems of the nation are far more important and relevant for our deliberations than the
personalities of their colleagues. Mr Speaker Selwyn Lloyd tried to draw a distinction
between an attack on a member personally-that is, on his personal character—and an
attack on him for his political statement or opinion. He recounted how, when one member


## p. 3 (#11) ###############################################

10 May
3
Election of Speaker
shouted at his opposite number, "humbug"-I omit the epithet which was in Australian-he
ruled that it was out of order if it was meant to apply to the member but acceptable if it
applied to his argument.
If Parliament at times has been irrelevant in these ways, in others it has appeared
tedious and repetitious, and that, of course, is another tendency for which I would be
grateful for the co-operation of honourable members in limiting. As your impartial presiding
officer, I see it as one of my duties to bring members together outside the Chamber in order
to reduce personal tensions that have led, on occasion, to unfortunate words and incidents
within it. I aim, also, to administer the buildings and grounds of Parliament for the benefit of
members. These are not the House and grounds of the people, but of you, the
representatives of the people-the House of Representatives. As the spokesman of
Parliament I aim to liaise not only with the Crown but with the people and their
institutions—the church, the professions, commerce, industry, the trade unions, and local
government-and I hope honourable members will help me in that task.
Finally, I have your rules to guide me, supplemented by the wisdom of former Speakers,
the ancient practices of Parliament, and, such as they are—and you permit-my own wits.
With your co-operation I shall do what I can to uphold the best traditions of this House, its
rights and its privileges, with dignity and relevance. Mistakes I shall make, but to err is
human and to forgive divine. Therefore, in anticipation of my errors I beg your forgiveness.
Once again I thank you, honourable members, for your trust in promoting me your
Speaker, and therefore the third man in the land. In so promoting me you have also made
my wife the third lady in the land. For that I thank you, for I believe she deserves it. I have
more confidence in assuring you that she will perform her tasks with distinction. For myself I
can only pray for God's guidance that I shall not fail you.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Mr Speaker-Elect -and this is one of the
rare occasions when we can use that term-I congratulate you on the assumption of this high
office. I can speak for the members on this side of the House in saying that we believe there
is no better member of this Parliament than yourself to become our Speaker. I have had the
privilege of sitting with you in the National Party caucus since you entered Parliament at the
end of 1963, and I, together with your colleagues, know that you are a man of quiet
intelligence and very great wisdom who speaks rather less than some of us but never without
considerable deliberation. When you have spoken in our caucus you have been listened to.
Through the sad events of last year we have had the experience of seeing you in the chair as
Acting Speaker for a considerable time and through that part of the session when difficulties
arise as members become involved with the more difficult subjects and gradually grow a little
more tired. It is not customary to comment on the activities or rulings of a Speaker. This may
be the rare occasion when, for a moment, it is permitted. I, and I am sure my colleagues on
both sides of the House, felt confident when you were in the chair that we would receive
carefully considered, totally impartial, and firm rulings. I would add to the growing volume
of comment and advice on behaviour in the House that is coming from so many quarters.
One of the most important things to ensure that this House is more ruly-and, of course, it is
less unruly than most parliaments in other countries, although most people here do not
realise that is firmness from the Chair; immediate firmness at the starting point of any kind
of disruption. I believe that in you we have a Speaker who will adopt that approach, and I am
sure Parliament will be the better for it. There are many things one could say in
congratulation, but I do not propose to say much more. I just want to assure you that you
will have the total support of your former colleagues on this side of the House in carrying out
the task that members of the House have given you.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Mr Speaker-Elect, I join the
Prime Minister in offering my congratulations, and those of my colleagues, on your
appointment and also on the modesty with which you accepted this extremely critical office.
I know, too, that your wife will play a very vital role at the many functions that you will
attend outside the immediate dealings of this Chamber, and I extend to her, also, the
Opposition's good wishes. I particularly applaud your commitment to the restoration of
Parliament's public image. I fear that it has fallen to an all-time low in the public's eyes and
that there is considerable disenchantment among the young and a feeling that Parliament no
longer has any real relevance to the problems of their everyday lives; that it is a tired old
talking shop occasionally jolted out of its rut by some personal exchange or vilification-and
we all suffer from that. Respect for law is undermined, respect for the democratic process is
undermined, and respect for members of Parliament and their life and work in this

institution is undermined, so we all have a great responsibility in our hands.
As leader of the parliamentary Labour Party I welcome and share the public
commitment you have made. This session will be hard, but I hope it will be fought on issues
that concern the people, and I hope also that members will heed your comments of a few
days ago to the effect that people cannot hold Parliament in real esteem if the members

Parliament.

Opening of Parliament
THURSDAY, 11 May 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
OPENING OF PARLIAMENT
A message from His Excellency the Governor-General, desiring the immediate
attendance of honourable members in the Council Chamber, was delivered by the
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod.
Accordingly, Mr Speaker, accompanied by honourable members, and preceded by the
Serjeant-at-Arms, proceeded to the Council Chamber, and, after a short absence, returned.
MR SPEAKER
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I have to report that, accompanied by my
proposer and seconder, I waited upon His Excellency the Governor-General and I addressed
His Excellency as follows:
"May it please Your Excellency:
"In obedience to Your Excellency's command, the members of the House of
Representatives, in the exercise of their undoubted rights and privileges, have proceeded to
the election of a Speaker, and as the subject of their choice, I now present myself for Your
Excellency's approbation."
To which His Excellency replied as follows:
"Mr Speaker, it is with much pleasure that, on behalf of the Queen, I approve and
confirm the choice that the House of Representatives has made in your person.
"I congratulate you on your election to this distinguished office, marking as it does the
appreciation of the House of Representatives of your impartiality and ability."
I desire to repeat my respectful acknowledgment to the House of the high honour
members have done me in electing me to the Speaker's chair.
"Honourable members, I have received the following commission from His Excellency
the Governor-General authorising me to administer the oath or affirmation prescribed by
law to be taken or made by members of the House:
"To all to whom these presents shall come and to John Richard Harrison, Speaker of
the House of Representatives, greeting. Pursuant to the authority in me vested in that behalf
I, Sir Keith Jacka Holyoake, the Governor-General of New Zealand, do hereby authorise
you, the said John Richard Harrison, to administer to all or any members or member of the
House of Representatives the oath or affirmation of allegiance to Her Majesty the Queen
required by law to be taken or made and subscribed by every such member before he shall be
permitted to sit or vote in the said House. Given under the hand of His Excellency the
Governor-General and issued under the Seal of New Zealand this tenth day of May 1978."
MEMBER SWORN
Mr SPEAKER administered the oath of allegiance to Mr Bruce Craig Beetham, who
then took his seat in the Chamber.
EXPIRING LAWS CONTINUANCE BILL
This Bill was read a first time pro forma.
GOVERNOR-GENERAL'S SPEECH
Mr SPEAKER: I desire to report that when the House did attend upon His Excellency
the Governor-General this day in the Council Chamber, His Excellency was pleased to make
a speech, the text of which speech was handed to me by His Excellency. The text of this
speech is:
HONOURABLE MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
It is a great privilege for me to exercise for the first time the prerogative of Her Majesty
The Queen in opening this fourth Session of the Thirty-eighth Parliament. My wife and I are


## p. 6 (#14) ###############################################

6
11 May
Governor-General's Speech
deeply conscious of the obligations of Vice-Regal office and share with all members that high
privilege of serving our people to whom we both have a responsibility.
Today we are reminded sadly of the absence from this place of the Honourable Sir Roy
Jack who died on 24 December 1977. He faithfully served Parliament for 23 years as a
member, as a minister and twice as Speaker of the House. We shall miss his humanity,
culture, and wit.
Honourable members, earlier this year the New Zealand Planning Council published
Planning Perspectives 1978-1983. This document, which I would remind you is addressed to
all New Zealanders, reiterates some basic truths which often tend to be ignored—they are:
that old attitudes must be changed if we are to achieve the social and economic goals
which we deem important
that we must re-examine carefully the inefficient and wasteful use of limited
resources.
As a nation we have to live within our income over the longer run-the remedies are in
our own hands.
The New Zealand economy continues to face difficulties. These result from the slowness
of the world's recovery from depression since 1975 and from continuing international
inflation which, together, have caused a major deterioration in our terms of trade. As a
consequence we have suffered a large drop in national income, which is now having an effect
on the domestic economy.
The Government has acted to solve the country's economic problems. The high balance
of payments deficit has been reduced and the growth of expenditure on imports has been
retarded considerably. With the balance of payments on current account still in deficit the
Government will be obliged to continue to control tightly the total quantum of imports.
Imported inflation and domestic wage and price increases have developed a strong
momentum. The Government has therefore applied a wide range of policies to cope with the
problem including price regulation and fiscal and monetary restraint. It is now clear that
these policies are succeeding. While still high, the rate of inflation is falling and further
improvement is expected. The Government regards a higher rate of productivity as an
important means of reducing inflation and will continue to encourage efforts in this
direction.
The Government is firmly committed to a policy of controlling inflation and reducing
the balance of payments deficit. These are the priorities. Without them a permanent
strengthening of the economy cannot be achieved.
Over recent months a major difficulty has been the drop in domestic activity and
increased unemployment. The Government has moved promptly to minimise the effects of
this cyclical downturn. Policies are now in train which have increased the money supply and
have boosted direct Government spending in the weaker sectors of the economy. The
business community can now look forward to improved demand and can take confidence
from the Government's preparedness to sustain activity.
While unemployment has become a growing problem the policies of economic
stimulation pursued by the Government have been instrumental in controlling its growth. In
addition the Government has made special work available and assisted local authorities and
private employers to take on additional workers. The emphasis is on retraining to diversify
and improve the skills of the labour force. This is a necessary part of the economic
restructuring.
The Government has successfully introduced a system of free wage bargaining, and the
round of wage negotiations through the summer was the first for several years. Difficulties
which might have occurred were largely avoided and in general reasonable settlements were
reached.
The integrated system of wage settlement tribunals which was enacted at the last session
is now in place. While the main emphasis in wage determination will remain on conciliation,
the Government trusts that the new Arbitration Court and its associated tribunals will
quickly gain the respect of all parties in cases where it becomes necessary to resort to
arbitration. It is essential that restraint should continue in wage negotiations. New Zealand
cannot afford excessive wage rises or industrial stoppages.
Farming continues to be the main source of our overseas income. Despite the
deteriorating net incomes for farmers shown in the Agriculture Review Committee's report,
the Government is committed to ensuring the continued viability and productivity of farming
enterprises.
The Rural Banking and Finance Corporation will continue to give a high priority to


## p. 7 (#15) ###############################################

11 May
7
Governor-General's Speech
finance for development and it will maintain its functions of granting loans for the settlement
of young farmers, for the purchase of stock, and for the restructuring of essential debt.
Policies which encourage the development of remaining areas of unproductive and under-
utilised land capable of contributing to export earnings, and the establishment of holdings
suitable for intensive horticultural production will be maintained.
Among the Bills affecting the agricultural sector, which will be submitted for your
consideration, will be a Pesticides Bill to revise the Agricultural Chemicals Act 1959, and an
amendment to the Meat Act to allow for more effective appeal rights against decisions of the
Meat Industry Authority. The Noxious Plants Bill and the Milk Amendment Bill which are
at present before a select committee wil be further considered.
The Government's main activities in the international field will be designed to
strengthen the economy at home. It will place special emphasis on moves to improve access
to traditional markets and to open new export opportunities. It will engage in bilateral
discussions on access and will also play an active part in the current multilateral negotiations
under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Relations with the European Economic
Community will be of continuing importance, particularly for the dairy industry and for our
lamb export trade, which is faced with the prospect of a Community sheepmeats regime. The
Government will spare no effort to protect New Zealand's vital interests.
The year 1978 has been designated Export Year. Steps are being taken to help with the
establishment of markets overseas for our manufactured exports. The strengthening of the
trade commissioner service will be of material assistance.
Special efforts are being directed towards developing markets in North America and
South-east Asia. However, this market diversification is not proceeding at the expense of
strengthening our trading links with our more traditional partners. The consolidation of our
NAFTA relationship with Australia will continue to receive high priority.
In fostering new projects which make the maximum use of our limited resources in
economic and social terms, the emphasis will continue to be on the establishment of export-
oriented industries which are soundly based on natural resources and can use the skills of
New Zealanders.
Consideration of a draft Treaty on the Law of the Sea will be resumed this year. The
Government attaches the greatest importance to achieving international agreement on this
matter which would not only protect New Zealand's rights in the Exclusive Economic Zone
but also represent a major step towards world order. In granting approval for foreign fishing
vessels to fish in New Zealand's 200-mile economic zone, care will be taken to ensure that
our own fishing industry is given every opportunity to expand and to realise its growing
export potential.
The Fisheries Act 1908 will be amended to provide for joint fishing ventures within the
200-mile economic zone. To give a practical effect to the growing international concern over
the depletion of marine mammals the Government will introduce a Marine Mammals Bill to
protect these animals found in New Zealand waters.
Special encouragement will be given through regional development measures, which
have been extended recently to provide incentives to the primary and tourism sectors, as well
as to manufacturing. Participation by local communities in the planning of their region's
future will be encouraged through the resources survey work being undertaken by regional
development councils in the eleven priority regions.
Major steps in rationalising energy planning, development and utilisation were taken
recently with the establishment of the Ministry of Energy and the creation of a separate
group of petroleum exploration and production companies. The programmes of exploration
for petroleum, coal and geothermal resources will continue to be accelerated and the
campaign to encourage energy conservation intensified.
The Government is determined to improve the co-ordination and full utilisation of all
transport services and equipment. A number of Bills will be introduced for your
consideration. They will provide for the amalgamation of the National Airways Corporation
and Air New Zealand, measures relating to the maritime field, the reorganisation and
financing of urban transport and a number of measures to improve safety on the roads.
The Government, in furtherance of its general policy that legislation should reflect the
needs of the community, will promote a number of meaures covering a wide spectrum of the
law. Major Bills in commercial law will deal with credit contracts and contractual remedies.
In the criminal justice system a new sentence, a sentence of community service- is proposed
and the Police Offences Act will be reviewed.
There will also be reforms in the administration of deceased estates, evidence and


## p. 8 (#16) ###############################################

8
11 May
Governor-General's Speech
property law including amendments to the Unit Titles Act.
Reforms in family law will include the revision of the law on divorce, separation,
maintenance, and paternity. The problem of the trans-Tasman abduction of children will
also receive attention.
The importance of the family unit continues to be recognised by the Government, and
an expansion of existing policies in this area will be announced in the near future.
The Government will continue to give full attention to meeting the special needs of the
Maori people. Maori housing, land development, and trade training schemes for young
people will continue to receive special consideration. The active involvement of Maori
owners in the control and management of their land will be further encouraged by the
continuing transfer of Maori reserved lands to the control of incorporations or trustees.
Pacific Island peoples living in New Zealand will receive further assistance in housing
and social welfare fields. A new emphasis in community and youth development are
activities that will also be supported.
The Government is continuing its efforts to improve the quality of housing and housing
finance in New Zealand. As a result of its policies accommodation is now much more readily
available in all parts of the country. Increased attention in this coming year will continue to
be given to the housing of the elderly and the rehabilitation and renewal of obsolescent
housing.
The Government intends to introduce a Toxic Substances Bill which will strengthen the
law relating to the production, importation and distribution of toxic substances. It is also
intended to introduce a Bill which will provide for the organisation of post-graduate medical
education.
The Government will continue to implement its stated policy of developing a
comprehensive health service, with emphasis on community based health measures and
preventive services. These innovations are being introduced after consultation with local and
professional interests and voluntary organisations.
The Accident Compensation Commission is presently in the course of reviewing and
reappraising accident compensation legislation. Anomalies have become apparent in the
scheme and it is proposed to introduce legislation in this Session to deal with some of these.
Several amendments are proposed to the Education Act 1964. The principal
amendment will seek enabling powers for local controlling authorities who agree to a
reorganised form of district administration of education. A major consolidation of the Act is
in the course of preparation and it is hoped to be able to introduce this measure for recess
study.
The Government intends to introduce at this session the final Bill to complete the
lengthy and complex task of revising and consolidating the Municipal Corporations Act and
the Counties Act into a single major piece of local government legislation.
A thorough revision and consolidation of the Public Works Act 1928 has been
undertaken by a review committee whose report has recently been published. The comments
of interested parties will be carefully studied before the Bill is drafted. It will be introduced
late in the coming Session for reference to a select committee and recess study.
A Bill establishing a film commission will be introduced to promote the making of New
Zealand films. This will represent an important step in developing an industry which last
year clearly demonstrated its capacity to provide good entertainment for both local and
overseas audiences.
In furtherance of the Government's policy, provisions now before the House to set up a
council for traditional Maori and Polynesian arts will be resubmitted for your consideration.
Progress towards improving and rationalising immigration procedures and legislation
will continue in 1978. The Immigration Amendment Bill currently before a select committee
will be resubmitted for your consideration.
Relations with New Zealand's traditional friends in Europe, North America, Australia,
and the Pacific will continue to be given the highest priority. The Government will play an
active part in the economic development of New Zealand's close friends and neighbours,
particularly through its programme of assistance to the smaller Pacific states, including the
Solomon Islands and Tuvalu which will shortly become independent.
The Government will continue to lend its strong support for the United Nations. It will
oppose racial discrimination in all its forms wherever it occurs. It will work to achieve greater
universal respect for human rights. The necessary steps will be taken to ratify this year the
International Covenants on Human Rights. At the forthcoming special session of the United
Nations it will press for substantive disarmament and arms control measures.

Business of the House
FRIDAY, 12 MAY 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): As is usual, the House will meet at 7.30
p.m. next Tuesday, when the Address in Reply will be moved by the member for Palmerston
North and seconded by the member for Invercargill. That will be the only business for that
day. On Wednesday, formal business will be followed by private members' notices of
motion, and, in the evening, the resumption of the Address in Reply debate, which will carry
on for the remainder of next week.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): There has been a good deal of

DEATH OF THE HONOURABLE SIR ROY JACK
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That this House records its high
sense of the devoted and distinguished services rendered to New Zealand by the late Hon. Sir
Roy Emile Jack, member of Parliament and Speaker of this House, and respectfully tenders to
his family the assurance of its sincere and deepest sympathy with them in their sad
bereavement.
Sir Roy was born in New Plymouth in January 1914. He was educated at Wanganui
Collegiate School, and at the Victoria University of Wellington, graduating LL. B. He was a
judge's associate in Wellington from 1935 to 1938, and served in the Royal New Zealand Air


## p. 11 (#19) ##############################################

12 May
11
Death of the Honourable Sir Roy Jack
Force from 1939 to 1945. In 1946 he went into practice as a barrister and solicitor in
Wanganui. He quickly entered public life, serving on the Wanganui City Council from 1946
to 1955, and was deputy mayor for 8 years. He was elected member for Patea late in 1954.
On a change of boundaries in 1963 he was elected member for Waimarino, and on a further
change member for Rangitikei in 1972. In all he was a member of Parliament continuously
from November 1954, a record of service surpassed on his death by one other member. He
was Chairman of Committees from 1961 to 1966, and Speaker from April 1967 to February
1972, when he was appointed Attorney-General and Minister of Justice. He held those
portfolios until the change of Government in December 1972. In June 1976 he was again
elected Speaker. He was created a Knight Bachelor in the Queen's Birthday List in 1970.
That brief recital of the public service of the late Sir Roy Jack utterly fails to give a true
impression of the man, the human being. Sir Roy Jack was an ornament in this Parliament.
He was a rare example of a man who kept the virtues of an earlier age in the modern world.
He had the grace, wit, and the culture of a professional man of earlier times, something that
to a very large extent has disappeared from today's scene. He was one of those who believed
that to be a professional man you did not simply have to have the tools of trade of your
profession; you had to have certain standards of conduct that went with them. Sir Roy, along
with one other former member in my time in this House, the late Dan Riddiford, brought
those virtues into a world which lacks them sadly. He was a man of principle and a man of
integrity. He loved Parliament. He was totally devoted to the precision and excellence of
chairmanship. If occasionally that got him into difficulties in the chair, nevertheless it was a
rigid principle that has a great deal to commend it. I recall that in comparatively recent
times, when not in good health, he sat up until after 2 a.m. battling with a finely reasoned
ruling which many another chairman would have dealt with quite quickly, and possibly even
crudely, and in the morning he was too exhausted to read it to the House. He was a kind
man, and a wonderful host who played a full role in bringing members together socially in
the building with members of the outside community.
In some ways he was an unworldly man. I well remember, as I am sure do those who
were with me, the travels of a party of parliamentary innocents through South-east Asia in
1963. That was the first of many trips, and I do not think that any of the six members of that
party had been abroad since World War II. The party comprised three members from each
side of the House, and we travelled through Singapore, Malayasia, Thailand, the
Philippines, Vietnam, and finally back home in 6 weeks. The anecdotes from that trip will be
told for as long as any member of that party remains in Parliament. I should like to record
one in the Journals of the House. The party travelled by train from Penang to Bangkok-a
24-hour, not very comfortable, journey. We decided in our innocence that we would not
trust any of the local food and would eat nothing but chocolate and drink nothing but canned
English beer, which we thought would be safe.
The Minister of Social Welfare, Sir Roy, and I were sitting in a compartment in the train
and had just had a bar of chocolate and a can of beer. We were in the middle of the jungles of
southern Thailand, and the nearest sign of life for about 100 miles was probably a tiger. The
Minister of Social Welfare and I threw our beer cans and chocolate wrappers out of the
window. However, Sir Roy sat looking pensive, and when we asked what the matter was he
said he had a dislike for litter and thought that one should keep one's principles in all
circumstances. He realised it was a bit silly, but did not think he should throw his beer can
out the window. When we said that there was nothing within miles but tigers, he replied that
there must be another way of disposing of litter. I called the cabin attendant, and Sir Roy
asked him what one did with one's litter. The reply came back, "Out the window, sir." Sir
Roy then said that he did not like to throw it out the window, and the cabin attendant—
thinking Sir Roy was a very superior VIP above disposing of his own litter said he would fix
it. He then picked up the litter and threw it out the window. We have all seen Sir Roy look
sad when something like that happens, and on this occasion he looked sad. But that was Roy
Jack as we knew him. He did not and would not compromise his principles.
At the end of the 1975 session he used the word "prevarication". That was not too
heinous a crime when compared with the reports from the Mother of Parliaments we have
seen during the last week. Sir Roy's sense of precision was offended when the word was
ruled out of order, because he felt he would not have made such a ruling. Although he
withdrew the word, he did not do it adequately and he was asked to withdraw from the
Chamber. Last year an unfortunate reference to this incident caused me to utter some words
which I sincerely regret. Coincidentally, it was the day Sir Roy told me his illness was


## p. 12 (#20) ##############################################

12
12 May
Death of the Honourable Sir Roy Jack
terminal. I knew that he was listening to the proceedings of the House in the Speaker's
quarters. I saw him later that morning, and although he had heard the incident he was not
angry. Those members who knew him would not have expected him to be angry. He was sad.
He said, "Why did they raise the matter?" That was Sir Roy and his relationship to the
things members do in the House from time to time, and, I hope, later regret. His reaction
was not of anger, but of sadness.
The first sign of his fatal illness came when he was skiing. As members know skiing,
gliding, and jogging were among his activities almost to the time of his death. He was an
extremely fit man for his age, and that is what made watching his health and strength go
down in a few months so tragic. I saw him go down week by week, and as his strength left
him he would say to me and to others that he would be like the Cheshire cat-when
everything else was gone the smile would still be there. To the date of his death that was
true; when his strength had left him his smile was there. He worried that his death would
precipitate a by-election, which would be inconvenient for his colleagues. Sir Roy was a
remarkable man. The last tribute I want to pay is to his great courage. Members have the
deepest sympathy for his lovely wife and daughter. We shall long remember our former
Speaker.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I second the motion moved by
the Prime Minister, and join with him in the sentiments and sympathy he has expressed. He
well documented for Parliament and the people the life of Sir Roy, which in his
parliamentary career was very substantial-as Chairman of Committees, as a Minister, and
twice as Speaker of the House. He was a member of Parliament for 23 years, which is a big
part of a man's working life. Most people who aspire to be a member of Parliament would
envy that record. The Prime Minister said that Sir Roy had great respect for the institution of
Parliament. He showed that frequently with the admonitions he dealt out to members who
were from time to time delinquent in some way. I recall one occasion when he had to deal
with a succession of breach of privilege charges. He took that opportunity to remind
members that they were depreciating the important privilege that they have. One always felt
when he spoke to Parliament on issues of that kind that if someone had done something
hurtful to the institution it was something he felt personally, too. Whatever the member
thought about the ruling, he could not escape that feeling.
Sir Roy had a different side. He was a very sensitive and cultured person. He was well
read and an interesting conversationalist. As the Prime Minister has said, he was a good host
to all from time to time. He was an accomplished musician-one could say his violin was
almost as much a symbol of his character as was his Speaker's wig. On many occasions
members heard the strains from his violin when they left the Chamber in the evening. His
real sign of strength came during the first part of his illness when he made a tremendous
effort to carry on. The Prime Minister alluded to one incident that all of us will remember.
He surrendered physically only when it was impossible for him to continue the task that he
had been set by the House. Even from his sickbed he kept very close contact with what was
happening. I know that from a letter I have under my hand as I speak here this morning. He
discussed with me, through the pen, the announced retirement of one of our colleagues, and
made his comments. He showed how determined he was to keep his mind active and alert by
reading a great deal, even by going back to the study of French.
During his term of office, as Hansard will reveal, we did not always agree. That is the
nature of politics. He is now lost to us, and, more importantly, he is lost to his family.
Parliament has been robbed of a very colourful figure and we are all much the poorer for
that. There is not really much I can add to what the Prime Minister has said, except to say on
behalf of my colleagues that we feel a very great sympathy for Lady Jack and her daughter.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): It is nearly 5 months since Sir Roy
Jack died, and memories really crowd one's vision. For me, those memories go back to pre-
war days in Wanganui. Sir Roy died here in Parliament Buildings, and on the occasions that I
visited him I recall his saying that he knew he was right in staying. I know there were many
who thought he should perhaps have gone to hospital, but he said he was right in staying
because his friends and colleagues were here, and I believe he was right.
As Bishop Norman remarked in his funeral address, it would have been so easy for Roy
Jack to become full of self pity and bitter at the cruel injustice of falling ill after the
announcement of his retirement. Having made the decision to retire, he believed that not
only was he doing the right thing in a political sense, but he was opening a new door that
would give him and his wife the opportunity to travel. He looked forward, I know, to

Death of the Honourable Sir Roy Jack
exercising his knowledge of French, and was going to enjoy his retirement with his wife and
Amanda. But there was no bitterness.
Whatever recollections I have of Sir Roy Jack's earlier life—and I shall remember him
with affection-1 remember the courage and grace with which he died. It showed another
facet of the character of a truly notable man. He was a lawyer, an economist, an historian, a
student of English, and a student of international affairs. Roy Jack's wide-ranging interests
encompassed an enormous appreciation of the arts. One recalls his links with the National
Orchestra, his interest in its works, his association with musical groups, and, of course, his
violin playing, to which reference has been made. Heaven knows, I remember when first I
came into the House in 1958 the times when the House sat late at night, and after it rose the
strains of that violin echoing through the library wing. There are some quite delightful stories
associated with that, but I shall not recall them now. Those interests bubbled through his
personality, and from time to time the lines crossed and confronted what I can only describe
as a very robust sense of humour.
To say that he was a conservative is to underestimate his devotion to and respect for
tradition, and for the rights, privileges, and responsibilities of parliamentary office-and
perhaps he was even over-respectful of those rights and privileges. He was a lawyer, and had
a consuming interest in fact; but he was a lawyer who won for himself the admiration, and
perhaps even the affection, of clients, because I know that he was always prepared to go that
second mile in search of equity for a client. While a vigorous and penetrating debater who
caused considerable discomfort to his political foes, he was an outstanding chairman, judicial
in his impartiality. He had a considerable grasp of the rules, and expected others to share his
appreciation of those rules and the reasons for them. As the Prime Minister has suggested,
sometimes in sadness Sir Roy perhaps expected too much.
In this place, so concerned with the affairs of men, he was one who constantly pressed
the case for the arts, and he pressed the case by example and by argument. He had foresight,
and a clarity of thought that led him to recognise the need to listen to the voice of the
minority, even in the midst of seeming certainty. I recall that, as his parliamentary colleagues
on both sides of the House argued for greater effort to encourage the development of
Manapouri, he said, “On the one hand, it may lead to the setting up of a very large and a
very welcome industry. On the other, it may presage the unwarranted and unnecessary
destruction of part of our fast-reducing heritage of national beauty." He also said, "We
should beware of acquiescing too readily in the permanent impairment of our heritage of
beauty." At the time he saw further than many others.
He was a city councillor, and deputy mayor of Wanganui. From his earlier days he was a
student of the works of Major Douglas, as I remember clearly. Roy Jack died listening to
Mozart and the words of Stevenson's Requiem. Those who knew him have lost a friend, and
the House has lost one of its most notable servants.

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Roy Emile Jack was in many ways not

Roy Emile Jack, Knight, would have graced any British Parliament of the last 4 or 5

another century. Perhaps it was the precision and the range of his use of the English
language, matched by an unusual formality and insistence on etiquette, that could quite
easily have placed him in a former age. Perhaps it was the bite of those same words that
reminded us of the political satires and the cartoons of past eras, or it might have been the

Some of these qualities were evident even when I first met him as a law undergraduate
at Victoria University College. They showed in the grace of address and the manner that
many judged to be artificial, but which was the natural expression of a profound inner
courtesy, the mark of a truly civilised man, who, as many of us recall, on a very solemn

It was the same with his love of music, which I shared with him. It was a pleasure and an
honour to do so, though at no stage would I pretend to equal his competence and the high
standard with which he played his own beloved fiddle. We had many private lunches
together in the House when we listened to some of our favourite music in silence, the same
silence with which he would send me an invitation asking me whether I would "care to join
him in a Trappist lunch". Many of his particular and dearest friends had close associations
through a common love of music. I remember many occasions, as will other members, when
we listened to music in his company in his own suite. Some of us also attended the luncheon
concerts presented by the Victoria University department of music. We remember his
unobtrusive Christian conviction and his deep family affection, which were manifested so
strongly in those last months. Some of us who were privileged to be near him at that time
experienced a humour, an honesty, a courage, and a selflessness we will never forget. In
those quiet rooms along the corridor, tended by his brave and gentle wife whom we console
today, and solaced by his beloved Mozart or Vivaldi, he nevertheless continued to think of
others. Some of us who thought we knew him realised we had not known him as well as we
should have. We had not known the essential man, we had not known such a warmth and
humility, and, for those of us who were very close to him, a greatness, revealed by his
frankness in the face of death, which he knew was imminent.
Roy Jack had his critics-and who has not-in the House, and in his electorate. He was
judged by many to be too rarified for the political scene. His perennial difficulty in
remembering names was often taken as a lack of interest, even of rudeness. As a friend of 40
years, I recall rising in my place in the House, and he could not remember my name. Many
of us know how hard he worked at this difficulty, almost to the end, without success; but we
cannot hold that against him. Because of his father's long connection with the Maori Land
Court Sir Roy's interest in the Maori people was deep and sincere. Having seen his life
completed, with its moving end, we honour him, not only as a distinguished parliamentarian,
but as a rare man and, for me, a real friend.

When I entered the House, the Government had a majority of one and the atmosphere
was tense. The debates were long and there was a great deal of Committee work, sometimes
late into the night. We did not have the process we have now whereby the Whips run a very
orderly ship and, on both sides of the House, even in the 5-minute speeches, give speakers
their order of speaking: "You are No. 18; make sure you are in your seat when it comes up."
In those days we had some great characters in the House. I think of Jimmy Maher, Jimmy
Kent, and others who would not take kindly to that sort of order.
From time to time members all round the House sprang up, and Sir Roy introduced a
'new weapon in which I, as the newest member in the House, was very interested. At that
time I sat on the other side of the House, in the place now occupied by the member for
Nelson, and Sir Roy sat next to me, in the seat now occupied by the member for Auckland
Central. He used what I can best describe as a stop-watch alarm clock to help him with the 5-
minute debates. We were very interested to see how it worked. When he received the call
the first problem he had was to press the button, which took a moment before he was able to
speak. The next problem was that the alarm clock had a very loud bell, which somewhat
disturbed the Chairman of Committees. Shortly after that time the Government changed,
and Sir Roy found himself Chairman of Committees. I often wished that another member
would introduce a similar device just so that I could have seen Sir Roy's reaction to the
sound of the alarm bell, but that did not happen.
I should like to make further reference to the comment made by my colleague the

argument. I listened, learned, and was stimulated by their often somewhat pungent

debate was raging.
Over the years as a member of the members' services committee-and I have served on

was exacting and meticulous in his demands, but he always exhibited a great personal
interest in their well-being, as he did in the well-being of members.

Sir Roy loved music, and so the words of Shakespeare could not apply to him. In fact, it
was the reverse. If Shakespeare's words are true, then the reverse applied to our late
colleague the Hon. Sir Roy Jack. He could be trusted. There was no treason or malice in his

I came to know him particularly well during his illness, and could see that he was a man

ADDRESS IN REPLY
[With the leave of the House, it was agreed that the speaking time of the mover and
seconder be extended.]
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North): I move, That a respectful address be presented to
His Excellency the Governor-General in reply to His Excellency's speech. In moving this
motion I am deeply conscious of the privilege and responsibility accorded me, and the
honour accorded my electorate of Palmerston North. On this occasion the time-honoured
custom of sending an address from the House of Representatives to the Governor-General
of New Zealand is a particularly significant event. For the first time in our history the Crown
has appointed as its representative, in Sir Keith Holyoake, a fourth-generation New
Zealander who has given most of his working life to serving the people of this country. Sir
Keith has earned the respect of people from all walks of life, regardless of their political
persuasion. It is fitting tonight that we pay tribute to Sir Keith and Lady Holyoake and
assure them of the support and regard of all loyal New Zealanders. We wish them well in the
distinguished vice-regal position they hold, and through them continue to acknowledge our
allegiance to Her Majesty the Queen.
Mr Speaker, may I now congratulate you on your election to the high and honourable
office of Speaker of the House of Representatives. Your ready sense of good humour was
apparent at the time of your election in the House last week. I have no doubt that all
members share with me the confidence that you will carry out the duties required of you in a
fair and patient manner. I should also like to congratulate Lincoln Agricultural College for
passing its first centenary as a tertiary education establishment. Lincoln College has made a
major contribution to the improvement of New Zealand agriculture, farm management, and
marketing of New Zealand agricultural products, domestically and throughout the world, in
its first 100 years. I am sure my six colleagues on this side of the House who passed through
Lincoln will wish to add further comment on the achievements of New Zealand's and the
Southern Hemisphere's first agricultural college.
I should like to direct the main theme of this address into the areas of commerce and
export, education relating to commerce, the stock exchange and share registry, alcohol,
hospital expenses, and driving. My electorate and the city of Palmerston North will
frequently be used as a reference point for all subjects. From 1971 our manufactured export
sales figures have risen, in round figures, from $150 million to $770 million. I quote from
New Zealand at the Turning Point: "Our size and isolation, our dependence and
vulnerability, particularly in economic terms, and the fact that in world terms we belong to a
minority-the Western-type affluent society-all these factors point up the simple fact that
we are expendable as far as the power centres of the outside world are concerned." The
affluent Western World does not owe us a living. The affluent Western World can live well
without our products. Obviously there are markets for our products among countries which
cannot or will not pay the prices we want. It appears to have escaped the minds of many New
Zealanders that, if we are forced to trade extensively away from countries that have a similar
or better standard of living, our sales value will drop and our standard will drop. For New
Zealand to survive we must learn to trade effectively, market well and sell harder, produce
efficiently, and recognise delivery times.
Much has been made of the strong line taken by the Prime Minister over trading
relations between Japan and New Zealand. The New Zealand press and other media were
quick to give coverage to the Australian Deputy Prime Minister's statements that he, Mr
Anthony, was dissociating himself from our Prime Minister's appeal for a concerted effort by
all of Japan's trading partners to tell the Japanese Government it was having things too much
its way. The Auckland Star on 1 April was one of the few newspapers to feature the facts. Mr
Anthony returned from Japan empty handed. Far from obtaining an improvement in raw
material sales, Australia could now expect a reduction of $300 million in sales of coal and


## p. 20 (#28) ##############################################

20
16 May
Address in Reply
iron ore. Observers in Canberra are wondering whether Australia should have been so keen
to give away its exclusive economic fishing zone with nothing in return. New Zealand has not
done so, and I am confident that the majority of people in this country support the Prime
Minister's stand. We have very few bargaining points, and we must make them work to our
utmost advantage.
I turn now to the Opposition's attitude to exports. To use our export efforts as a political
football is totally abhorrent to me. The Leader of the Opposition did so in Nelson earlier this
year. A heading in the Christchurch Press read, "Export year a farce, says Mr Rowling". The
article went on to say that Export Year "would stagger on for a few months, occasionally
mentioned in ministerial speeches, and lie forgotten".
Mr Courtney: Like the member for Palmerston North.
Mr LITHGOW: The Opposition leader exposed his weak commercial flank when he
made that statement to the Society of Industrial Designers, and the member for Nelson
would know that. The Leader of the Opposition had no idea of the amount of work and
planning that was already in top gear. The Opposition gave little attention to mail from the
Auckland Export Institute, because by 6 February it would have received two news flashes
which gave full details of the exporters' fair to take place between 11 and 14 April. The
Opposition and its candidates have consistently avoided the theme of Export Year. The
negative attitude of its leader towards exports would destroy the enthusiasm of both
production staff and management of any export-orientated company.
Let us now look briefly at the export incentives the Government has made possible since
it came into office. The opportunity for more pay in the hand motivates many workers, but,
let me hasten to add, not all. The profit motive for management and company investors
needs to be present to venture into an export programme. The National Government has
been quick to recognise the need for such incentive in the export field. Even in the 1976
Budget export investment allowances were made for new plant and machinery, and
machinery bought for export production was granted exemption from sales tax. In the 1977
Budget we saw further review and improvement. The incentive was then based on the net
foreign exchange earnings, and was applied to total exports rather than just to the increase.
The export guarantee office increased its guarantee to trading banks for loans on export
transactions from 85 to 100 percent. The stage was set for significant progress in
manufactured export sales. It has happened, and this is well confirmed by the enthusiasm
with which firms have tackled export business.
Even further incentives with Development Finance Corporation loans for small
companies were announced last October. It has always been a feature of the National
Government to look after and encourage small businesses. Greater processing of our
primary products within New Zealand also received tax incentives. Last year trade posts
were strengthened in Vancouver, San Francisco, and Singapore, where business is
increasing. More export liaison officers were appointed for companies new to exporting.
Acting as an official contact within New Zealand for the would-be exporter, export liaison
officers have already created and generated confidence.
The National Government has done much to see that the taxpayers get full value from
their trade commissioners. They are recognised by this Government as being a valuable aid
to the exporter. In several seminars I have already attended the praises of trade
commissioners have been sung loud and clear. May I take this opportunity of congratulating
the Department of Trade and Industry for bringing the commissioners back to attend the
export fair in Auckland. This was a constructive and well appreciated move by the overseas
buyers who came to the export fair. The exporters' fair in Auckland was a culmination of 2
years of hard work and planning. It was done by a dedicated group of young businessmen
who made up the organising committee for the fair. They gave hundreds of hours of unpaid
effort, quite apart from their normal work requirements. Breakfast sessions, lunch or tea
sessions, were all part of their time structure and New Zealand owes much to this new breed
of marketer.
These are the men who realise that, to survive, this country must upgrade its marketing
methods. We must make more contacts, service our products, package them safely and
attractively, and deliver on time. Jim Fletcher, David Donaldson, Mark Sainsbury and Ross
Southcombe are just a few who are part of a high-power team that planned New Zealand's
most successful ever export fair. Government support and recognition of the fair gave
overseas buyers an added degree of confidence that this country is in tune with its
manufacturers and exporters. The 260 companies who both manufactured and displayed the

15 000 products proved that the spirit of Kiwi ingenuity and private enterprise is not only

New Zealand has a long record in the field of agricultural bulk food, such as meat and
butter, throughout many countries in the world. It is almost an inheritance we have to bear.
Only in this last decade have we really entered into the true value-added products. Value
adding to historic products not only provides more employment for New Zealanders, but
also helps to overcome the high relative freight costs from this country. Freight costs,
increasing with every oil price rise, are accelerating the change from conventional bulk
products to higher-value export products. The most expensive stretch of water in the world is
across the Tasman. The products we sell to Australia must have a high basic value if we are
to avoid being uncompetitive through the freight factor. Ask any businessman trying to
freight frozen food to Australia. It costs more in freight for only 3 days on ship to Australia
than it does for 18 days on ship to Japan.
The displays at the export fair illustrated great advances being made in the value-added
foodstuffs field. Raw milk value-added products include cheese cake, cheese powder and
reduced cream, being marketed by Premi Foods, a division of the Rangitaiki Plains Dairy
Company. The outlets for their products are already included in Australia, the Gulf States,
the Pacific Basin, and South-east Asia. Sheepmeat and beef have had considerable room for
value adding before export.
Shipping a full carcass increases the freight percentage of the landed protein value.
Expensive freighting requires continuous reviewing without damaging long-held markets.
Close examination of the various meat companies' displays showed that vast sums are being
spent to cut and package meat more effectively. The rise in local popularity of smallgoods
and salamis has meant that, with a sound domestic market, we have a base for high-value
exports. Certainly, overseas buyer inquiry was directed to the high-value, well packaged
products. The groups of 36 Palmerston North businessmen and manufacturers who travelled
to the export fair were highly complimentary of the excellent quality of the displays.
Palmerston North itself was well represented at the fair by its own manufacturers, with
companies such as Winstone Plastics, that produces plastic pipe and fittings. It was successful
in opening up a new market in Tasmania, competing against the tough Australian mainland
producers. Palmerston North-based Glaxo Laboratories is another company that has worked
hard and responsibly to establish overseas markets. Its food lines and pharmaceuticals are
excellent examples of value adding to our basic agricultural products. Prepared Foods made
sales of its total range of canned products to Hong Kong. A special sale of canned eel is now
on its way to Holland.
Mr Courtney: Ha, ha!
Mr LITHGOW: Perhaps we can export some of the Opposition as well. Inquiries from
new outlets were a feature of their period at the fair. Trackweld, a Palmerston North drain
machinery company, is now opening up swamps and markets in the South Pacific Basin,
thanks to its display at the fair. More than 1200 buyers from at least 40 countries throughout
the world spent 4 days at the fair and firm-ordered much more than $5 million worth of
products from the fair.
I get extremely angry when I think of the Leader of the Opposition calling Export Year
a farce. It is quite obvious that Opposition members will still call it a farce, and I get angry
when I think of the hundreds of New Zealand people who have spent so much time and
effort in producing such a successful fair. These are the people who are prepared to do
something positive about earning our way out of our overseas balance of payments problem.
They deserve the utmost credit for their drive and enthusiasm because it will be them, and
not the knockers, who will put New Zealand in front again.
A "designmark" award went to Tullen Industries for its scissor-type cutter for
household use. As a result of carefully planned marketing this consumer product finds 95
percent of its outlet overseas. The product is one of the finest examples of a New Zealand
company breaking into the tough, but rewarding, world consumer market. What do the
workers of Tullen Industries think when they strive and battle to get their product made and
delivered on time and earn overseas funds for New Zealand, while the militant strikers at
Kawerau throw away overseas dollars 100 times faster than Tullen Industries could ever
hope to make them? This is where the attitude to exporting must change. All New Zealand
men and women are in exporting together. No one can stand aloof and say, "That's not our
problem." Clearly, however, the Opposition is trying to do so. If any company or producer
board loses an export sale, each one of us loses, and until that attitude is understood by

everyone we cannot hope to compete continuously on the world market. Few people realise

Mr Rogers: That's in my electorate.
Mr LITHGOW: Perhaps the member for Onehunga might care to make some

The National Government has made a full commitment to Export Year. Let us look at
the careful planning that went into the whole concept of Export Year. A nine-man Export
Year committee, headed by Mr Alan Hellaby, was put together to relate every aspect: the
work force, management, farming, industry, production, marketing, and freighting.
Initially, four export seminars were held in the main metropolitan centres in February and
March, with manufacturers from those centres invited to participate and contribute with
their suggestions and recommendations. Regional problems and advantages were identified,
such as the freight factor from Dunedin to the South Pacific. Conversely, Dunedin's and
Southland's excellent delivery service into Melbourne makes this outlet important to them.
In Palmerston North two export seminars have already been held. Such interest in
regional meetings indicates the latent enthusiasm waiting to be tapped when government,
education, and commerce work in harmony. The theme of one seminar in Palmerston North,
"You are never too small to export", drew 46 manufacturers together for a full weekend.
There was ample evidence of the small manufacturers present learning about the
Government's incentives. They had the opportunity to gain a wider appreciation of the vast
number of market research services that are available free, both from the Government and
from their own banking organisations, before they invest even one dollar of their own in
market research. Such points need wide coverage to every manufacturer, particularly the
small businessman who tends to carry so much of the decision-making load himself, and
often overlooks the free information so readily available.
The continuity of Export Year has been well planned, with a first-ever, all-New-
Zealand trade fair in the United States of America being held in Los Angeles. One hundred
companies have already booked more than 3000 square metres of display space for the fair in
October. A further trade fair is planned for Kuala Lumpur in November, confirming that the
Export Year theme will be operated over the full 1978 trading year.
A new breed of New Zealander has emerged this decade, born of the greatest driving
forces of all-necessity and survival. This man is the true marketer. He is not a salesman. He
is not a producer. He is not a promotions man. He is a marketer. The marketer does not
make a product and then look around to find a place to unload it. The marketer finds out
first what the consumer wants, either domestically or overseas. He finds out the needs of that
consumer-and, going on the actions of the Opposition, we would not find any of the needs
over there. He researches the total sales. The marketer then designs an article or modifies
his present product to suit the potential or compete with an established demand.
New Zealand has developed from a production-orientated society because, in short, our
farmers have produced milk, meat, and wool-and expected people around the world to
want them. Twenty years ago they did. The brutal facts are that now they do not. What
happened to wool when synthetics arrived? What happened to butter when Britain entered
the European Economic Community? What could happen to meat now that textured
vegetable protein is established? This and other products have already made inroads into the
hamburger and smallgoods markets, which are now serviced with more than 70 percent of
New Zealand beef. The change from selling-or should I say order-taking—to marketing by
our producer boards has been apparent over the last two decades, and the process must
continue. The export fair showed that our manufacturers are either already, or rapidly
becoming, consumer orientated by studying or researching what the consumer wants. Most
of the manufacturers displaying at the fair had researched the market. Their products will
sell. Re-orders are not necessarily assured.

Delivery is an item every New Zealander has a responsibility for, and a stake in. Each
one of us has a part in the production and delivery chain. Failure to deliver an overseas order
on time affects everyone from the school child to the superannuitant. The striking unions
could well become more caring towards all New Zealanders instead of displaying some of the
greedy and selfish attitudes we have seen recently. Failure to deliver, as happened at
Kawerau, means the loss of established markets, and long-term damage to all market
outlets. The development of a real sense of pride in our exports has been slow in New
Zealand, and is a follow-on from the days of bulk selling when we shipped out by the ton and
let our overseas buyers break the product down and repackage it, or cut it up. This still
happens with our lamb in the 30 000 butchers' shops throughout Britain. The lamb markets,
however, may still demand this. Today, many products could be developed further, and our
people have the opportunity to add greater value. Every New Zealander has a part to play in
knowing about our products.
I encourage the media and press to do more in their Dominion-wide education
programmes, which are already helping New Zealanders to develop that sense of pride in
New Zealand-made and exported products. The articles to date have been excellent, and
both the press and the media are to be congratulated. With the right knowledge and the right
attitude, each of us can be a marketer.
With the movement towards commerce and exports, greater attention is being paid to
school leavers who have a commercial and production-orientated education. In discussions
with many business leaders I have found that some school leavers applying for a position
have very little training or preparation for an interview. There appears to be an increasing
shortage of teachers fully trained in commerce and mathematics. The number of pupils
taking commerce, marketing, sales and management courses at technical institutes is
increasing because school leavers are quickly becoming aware that they need more training.
My strong stand for a new technical institute at Palmerston North is well known in the
electorate, and the Minister of Education has had ample contact from me to know that a new
institute is vital to the needs of students from Palmerston North and the region. I intend to
maintain pressure until the institute is completed.
The marketers of the next two decades are leaving school now. A delegation of
responsible and dedicated teachers at my home recently mentioned their growing concern at
the lack of discipline in school children, and the "could not care less" attitude of an
increasing number of parents. The disturbing influence of only one child in the classroom
could easily downgrade the quality of education for the other 29. Are the parents of the 29
aware? Such added pressure on teachers who are dedicated to their positions did not seem to
be getting through to the public by normal channels. Even the teachers' strike left the
reaction that it was for money only. Conditions were an equal factor, if not the dominant
factor, in some cases. A greater requirement for parental discipline is necessary, for which
no cash settlement can be a real compensation, and I am sure that basically the teachers
recognise this. A shortage of teachers in commercially aligned subjects is a factor we are
living with now.
The shift of commercial education from schools to technical institutes, after school
leavers have entered the work force, shows that the individual becomes very aware of his or
her lack of training immediately he or she is faced with the need to earn a living. The core or
heart of New Zealand commerce is the stock exchange. I am not convinced that the stock
exchange and the share registry offices are doing their utmost for all present or potential
investors. What percentage of people under the age of 30 buy shares? For that matter, what
percentage of the people buy shares? Surely, the greatest interest in company performance is
shown by those who have a stake in the company.
Recent legislation that became effective from 1 April this year must help reduce share
scrip delays. Until now it has taken anything from 6 to 16 weeks to deliver a share scrip. I am
fully aware that there can be a combination of factors-a slow seller, a slow lawyer, a slow
stockbroker, and an overworked share registry office. Nothing is more disappointing to a
new investor than to have to wait 10 weeks or so for a share scrip. When it eventually arrives
it turns out to be a large sheet of high-quality paper containing information that could quite
easily be compressed into the size of a pocket cheque form. There is no need for fancy,
ornate share scrips, which are a page out of a previous era when companies had to convince
their stockholders of their solidarity by the quality of their scrip. There are much more
convincing ways today, such as the quality of the company report, which has a far greater
impact on the shareholder.
