Why does the New Zealand Stock Exchange see fit to close down over Christmas, and
even up to 10 January, while its Australian counterpart takes only the statutory holidays? I
am informed that many sharebrokers work over that period, so it must be logical that the
exchange could, also. It would set an excellent example for overcoming the "great New
Zealand Christmas shutdown" syndrome. Such a move could well steer commerce towards
staggered holidays and avoid the crippling overheads of plant gathering dust over New
Zealand's extended holiday period. New Zealand lawyers do little to break down the
"shutdown syndrome", and the country could well look to the legal fraternity to set
improved standards and take a closer look at staggered holidays.
The Stock Exchange could and should set the standard for commerce as the mecca of
private enterprise. I am aware that at the Auckland Stock Exchange much is already done to
educate school leavers, including inter-school share-buying games over a school term. The
opportunity to present a whole new attitude to commerce lies with the Stock Exchange,
share registry offices, and the listed companies. There is a great deal of ground to be made
up with such training in provincial cities, where so much of New Zealand's latent potential
lies. A closer examination could also be made of the method and number of multiple
appointments of directorships. Several weak directors with a network of multiple
appointments can have a similar stagnant effect on a group of companies. Commercial
vitality is essential at all levels of a company, and no more so than at the top.
In summarising the commercial section of this address, I confirm again the atmosphere
of enthusiasm towards exports amongst manufacturers throughout the country. Export
seminars that I have attended have explained the Government's incentives to potential
exporters well. The export institutes, the Department of Trade and Industry, and the
Manufacturers Federation have worked together with a purpose and a harmony that can
only strengthen ties and further boost the export drive. That is only the base. It must go
further still.
When 102 manufacturers from the Palmerston North region pack into a half-day
seminar, and similar situations are repeated throughout the country, the mood of enthusiasm
is plain to see. I am convinced also that management needs to keep staff well informed of the
importance of export business. A new export order provides a unique opportunity to
develop a sense of pride in one's product and company. I have already spent time on the
factory floors with staff in export-orientated Palmerston North companies, both large and
small. The attitude of staff to delivery times, overtime, and their contribution to the product
itself, changes completely when they understand that it is an important export order. Both
job security and job satisfaction result. There is a greater sense of purpose.
There is a need for co-operation and a closer relationship between commerce and the
total political scene-and I underline "the total political scene". The strongly negative
reaction from the Manufacturers Federation President, Mr Gemmel, to the Leader of the
Opposition's "export year farce" statements was natural. Because of his petty political
knocking attitude the Leader of the Opposition successfully widened the gap between
commerce and politicians. Commerce has responded to the Government's theme of Export
Year, and New Zealand will benefit. There are unlimited challenges ahead to prove our
ability to harmonise politics and commerce. The Government will continue to put every
effort into making these two sections of society work in the country's interests.
I move now to an issue that not only concerns constituents in my electorate, but which is
urgent throughout New Zealand—alcohol and driving. I believe I speak for the vast majority
of responsible New Zealanders when I express my concern about this serious problem in our
society. The death toll itself is convincing enough. Alcohol-related accidents simply confirm

I should like to turn to education and make some general observations on what I believe
is a definite correlation between the increasing numbers of ill-mannered, ill-disciplined, and
inattentive students in the classroom and the alarming and increasing juvenile crime rate. My
27 years' experience of teaching in primary and post-primary schools and finally in a
technical institute, and my discussions with post-primary teachers of long experience,
convince me that the main strain felt by teachers today is the emotional one of having to cope
with the changed attitudes of most of today's college students. To put it plainly, in far too
many classrooms today the majority of students are an ill-disciplined, arrogant, and ill-
mannered lot, and many teachers, particularly the younger teachers, are finding it
impossible to cope with those students.
In my opinion, the root cause is that, for the past two decades at least, both parents and
teachers have been fed a lot of collectivised pap by sociologists and educational
psychologists. We have been conned as parents and teachers into believing that we are
failures if we whack our children occasionally to discipline them. I myself have been in staff
rooms and heard principals spell out to the staff that they consider the caning of a pupil is a
mark of failure. So in many of our schools, for at least two decades, bottoms that ought to
have been soundly whacked because they deserved to be-and girls also, who should have
been strapped because they deserved to be-have gone unpunished, and, as a consequence,
a good proportion of what were pampered and indulged teenagers in the home and ill-
mannered and ill-disciplined students in the classroom are now among the statistics for
domestic purposes benefits, broken marriages, early divorces, and juvenile crime.
As a consequence, our community has more guidance counselling, more sociologists,
more criminologists, and more educational psychologists. We also have more patients in
mental hospitals, more alcoholics in alcoholic wards, and more massage parlours in our main
centres-most of them fronts for prostitution-more hard drugs, more hard pornography,
and an increasing juvenile and adult crime rate.
We are all jointly and severally responsible to some degree, but in my view a great deal
of the responsibility and blame should attach to the fact that over the past two decades we
have allowed our individual consciences on discipline and acceptable behaviour and codes to
be collectivised, and this collectivised thinking has been introduced into our educational
system and into our law reform system by faceless echelons of bleeding-heart academic
theorists inside our schools, inside the Department of Education, and inside the Department
of Justice. In our haste to try out their new theories in education and new methods in penal
reform we have almost convinced ourselves as a country that what used to be good is now
bad, and that what used to be bad is no longer bad-in other words, we have thrown the
baby out with the bath water.
I believe that the silent majority in our long-suffering community has had a stomachful
of criminal psychologists and school psychologists who argue ad nauseam about why some
people commit crimes and some do not, about why some students misbehave in classrooms
and others do not. I have even had a guy in Paremoremo telling me he was there because he
was bottle-fed instead of breast-fed as a baby. I saw quite a lot in Paremoremo.

My final burst this evening will be on the economy. In the last election campaign the
main issue was the economy, and all the indications are that it will be the main issue again in
the coming election. If every thoroughbred racehorse in New Zealand was an Uncle Remus
and every standard-bred horse was a Young Quinn, the TAB would go out of business
tomorrow. If there was one simple, practical, solution to inflation, or even two, three, or
more simple, practical, solutions, every economist in the world would go out of business
tomorrow. The fact is that there is no simple, practical, solution to inflation. Certainly, the
Labour Party has never had any solutions to anything; it does not even have any ideas, full
stop. In 1972 it claimed that, if elected to office, it would knock inflation for six. Inflation
was then about 5 percent, and the Labour Government did knock it—it trebled it. Inflation
has not trebled under the National Government. It has not even doubled. In fact, it has not
risen any more than it did during the time of the former Labour Government; it has been
marginally reduced.
National has never claimed to have the answers to inflation; it has claimed only that, as
a Government, it would make a much better job of containing and holding inflation than
would either the Labour Party or the Social Credit Party. That is precisely what the National
Government has done, and the facts speak for themselves. The 2 percent increase in the
consumer price index in the first quarter of 1978 is the lowest quarterly increase since the last
quarter of 1972.

INTRODUCTION OF BILLS-ALLOCATION OF TIME
Mr SPEAKER: Before the introduction of Bills this afternoon I should draw the
attention of the House to a technical problem relating to the introduction of Government
Bills and the inadequacy of the Standing Order relating to it. Standing Order 216 says:
"Debate on introduction-time limits. The debate on the question, That a Bill be
introduced," that is, a Government Bill-"shall not exceed 2 hours. This time shall be
divided equally between the parties and used at their discretion." Now we can have a
discussion about the meaning of the word "between" as relating to a distinction between
only two parties, or we can have a broader interpretation-as some dictionaries would allow
-of that word, which would mean that parties in the House are, at the moment, three.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Four.
Mr SPEAKER: No, three. There is one independent member, and, as I understand the
meaning of the word "independent", he belongs to no party so he is excluded in terms of the
Standing Order from taking part in any debate on the introduction of a Bill. I am sure this
situation was not envisaged by members of the House when they drew up this Standing
Order. I have taken advice on this from my advisers, and there are two courses open to me
from a strict interpretation of the order. One would be to say that as there are now three
parties represented in the House the 2 hours should be divided equally among them, giving a
maximum of 40 minutes to each. That would tend to give a slight edge to the leader of the
smallest party, but I think honourable members could rely on me to protect their interests by
giving close consideration to the matters of relevancy and tedious repetition. I defy any
member to speak for 40 minutes relevantly and without being tediously repetitious on the
limited debate that is allowed on the introduction of Government Bills.
The alternative would be to suggest that the parties as referred to in the Standing Orders

CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion Amendment Bill be introduced. I have, I hope for the assistance of
members, circulated copies of the notes I am using, but I have made some minor
amendments in them to make sure that my language is the language of the Bill wherever that
is possible. This Bill is a practical measure to meet a practical situation. I do not propose to
take up much time in introducing it, and I propose to deal with it in as factual and unemotive
a way as is possible.
Let me explain briefly how the Bill comes to be before the House, and what it does and
does not set out to do. It is common knowledge that the Bill was prepared for and on behalf
of the Abortion Supervisory Committee by parliamentary counsel, whom the Government
made available to the committee. I remind members that this committee is not a
Government committee. It is a committee set up by Parliament and accountable to
Parliament. Thus, when the committee came to the conclusion that certain amendments in
the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act were desirable, it would have been quite
wrong for the Government to refrain from giving Parliament the opportunity to consider
these amendments.
The Bill proposes three minor changes in the Act as passed last year. Two could be
called procedural, and one substantive, but it is essential to appreciate that these
amendments are put forward within the framework and principles of the existing legislation.
They are designed to remove certain frictions and doubts so that the Act may work as the
majority of us wanted to make it work. Very properly, the supervisory committee did not see
its function as being to propose changes in approach or of principle. However, it found from
its early experience in administering the Act that there were certain possible obstacles in its
practical operation. It came to the view that these obstacles could in fact be removed only by
legislation, and it has recommended what it considers are the minimum changes needed to
attain that object.
What are these changes? Let me take the substantive one first. This involves altering the
definition of an unlawful abortion in the new section 187A of the Crimes Act. At present an
abortion is lawful-apart from certain special cases-only if the continuance of the
pregnancy would result in serious danger to the life or to the physical or mental health of a
woman or girl and the danger cannot be averted by any other means. It is this last phrase that
has caused some concern and uncertainty, and the Bill proposes to delete it. I point out that
this particular phrase was added during the Committee stage of the progress of last year's
measure through Parliament. It was not a recommendation from the royal commission set up
by the Labour Government that was reported to us in March last year. As far as I can


## p. 35 (#43) ##############################################

17 May
35
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Amendment Bill
recollect, it was not publicly discussed before it was proposed in the House-I think on 10
October.
Did these words "and the danger cannot be averted by any other means" alter the law? I
do not think that anyone can say for certain. I believe that those of us who supported it
regarded its purpose as simply to clarify the law and to make explicit what had been implicit
previously. This is the view favoured by the Solicitor-General. There are those who disagree,
and many others who are in doubt. Among these are many doctors, and, whether their
doubts are justified or not, the important thing is that they are held by a large body of
medical opinion. The result has been to render the working of the Act more difficult. The
truth seems to be that many doctors are scared of the phrase and are, therefore, reluctant to
play a role under the Act. It does seem that what was meant to make things clear has created
confusion.
The two other amendments are intended to clarify the procedures that are to be
followed when an abortion is at issue. The first clarifies the independent role of the surgeon
who proposes to perform the abortion, by involving him in the decision-making process at an
earlier stage-that is, on reference from the doctor first consulted, and before the certifying
consultants come into the picture.
The second gives the certifying consultants the explicit right to see the woman
concerned before they make up their minds; and here again last year's Act did not follow a
recommendation of the royal commission. The commission had recommended a system of
panels, and there was general acceptance that this would not be workable. The concept of
certifying consultants followed the spirit of the commission's recommendations, but
departed considerably from them in detail. It cannot be said, therefore, that we are dealing
with a provision, the details of which had been considered by the royal commission.
There is one point I should make at the outset. Under the proposed new section 32(2),
the woman's own doctor will have to consider that she may have grounds for an abortion
before referring her on. This is not so under existing law. I am advised that this change
represents the advisory committee's clear intentions, and that it is not considered good
medical practice to require a doctor to refer a patient on without any prior consideration of
the case. I refer specifically to this point because it is not mentioned in the committee's
report to the House. I have also heard it suggested that the new section 32 will remove the
patient's right to choose her own certifying consultants. This right is not spelt out in the new
section, but neither is it in the present section. I am advised that the committee intends to
cover the matter with its own guidelines.
It has been suggested that these changes are not necessary, that the Act already allows
these procedures, and that in any event they could have been brought about administratively
by the supervisory committee issuing appropriate guidelines to the medical profession. In the
abstract this may well be so, and indeed the supervisory committee in its report recognised
that the law may be sufficiently flexible now. None the less, the committee saw the need to
have the situation spelt out in black and white in the statute. The members of the committee
feel that, as matters have gone, nothing less than a further degree of detailed codification
will secure the confidence of a sufficient section of the medical profession to enable the
procedures to work satisfactorily. I remind the House that this sort of consideration is by no
means unknown in legislation that we enact. In the strictest sense a particular provision may
be thought unnecessary by the Government's advisers and by members of Parliament. It may
be thought not to make any difference, but it is put in—in the well-established phrase "for
the avoidance of doubt"-to remove a fear, or an uncertainty, that is genuinely felt.
Let me summarise. The 1977 Act sprang from an undertaking to place before the House
legislation based on the royal commission's report. The present Bill accepts both the
principles and the machinery that Parliament approved last year, and simply attempts to
adjust the details to remove certain frictions that could otherwise seriously impair its
practical working. It does not in any way reopen wider issues, and there is nothing in it that
canvasses or that authorises us to canvass the questions of referendum or repeal. I commend
the Bill to honourable members' consideration.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Mr Speaker, in the light of your

forward, because basically there is little here to quarrel with. In the Minister's own words,

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The honourable member for New Lynn
challenged the next Government speaker to answer a question. I vote in this debate with a
completely free vote, and believe I am one of many members who has demonstrated by the
way he has voted that there is no question of toeing a party line. If the honourable member
for New Lynn, who espouses the liberal cause on this matter, would but think, he would
realise that his blanket opposition to the introduction of this measure might very well deny
the women of New Zealand the opportunity of removing one of the most objectionable
clauses from the Bill.
In light of widespread and understandable public disappointment and disapproval of the
abortion laws passed by Parliament last December, which we are now invited to amend, the
House must ask itself the serious question, do we want this Bill? I make no criticism of the
Minister of Justice in introducing it to the House. He is doing what he must at the request of
the supervisory committee, a body created by this House and charged with an impossible
task-to make an unfair, unwanted, unworkable piece of legislation, workable. The reasons
why it has proved to be unworkable can be canvassed more extensively in later stages of this
debate that is assuming of course that the House agrees to its introduction—but it is
relevant to note at this stage the reasons why the supervisory committee is asking Parliament
to enact these changes. There are three reasons set out in the report of the chairman of the
Abortion Supervisory Committee to the Clerk of the House, dated 18 April. First, the
operating surgeon under the present law is not a major party to the decision making;
secondly, the certifying consultants could be asked to come to a decision without being given
the opportunity to examine or interview the patient; and, thirdly, the supervisory committee
is of opinion that the words "and that the danger cannot be averted by any other means❞—
known widely as the Wall amendment-have created difficulties of interpretation for doctors
which have not been resolved by the opinion from the Solicitor-General.
I have carefully studied these reasons and the draft legislation now before us, designed
to correct these deficiencies, and am convinced that the first two grounds are essentially
superficial and cosmetic, and only the third reason-the removal of the Wall clause--is of
substance. To me, it is important that the Wall clause be removed, and I will vote for the
Bill's introduction as a step towards the achievement of this. Later, I shall vote to remove the
machinery clauses which are no more helpful than telling the distressed woman and her
confused doctors—that is, if she can find approved doctors in her area-that the procedures
will now go anti-clockwise, rather than clockwise, round the abortion mulberry bush. It is
important that Parliament be under no illusions as to what this Bill will or will not do. The
Minister, when replying, might be good enough to correct or confirm the answers to the
following questions. Does the amendment Bill, as at present drafted, meet the minimum
criteria set by the council of the New Zealand Medical Association for their support? The
answer, I can assure him, is no. Does this Bill find the approval of the General Practitioners
Society? Again, the answer is no. Does this Bill meet the wishes of the many thousands who
signed the repeal petition? The answer, clearly, is no. This Bill is no substitute for repeal.

becoming a closed shop for the privileged few. Let us take the supervisory committee's first
reason the need for the operating surgeon to be a major party to the decision making. The
amendment proposed here says the operating doctor may be a certifying consultant, which
he may be under the present law. I know of none presently serving as operating doctors who
are not certifying consultants.
The only additional provision in this amendment is that he may endorse the certificate
of the two certifying consultants to agree to do what he was going to do anyway. If he
chooses not to endorse the certificate it is not invalid, and, of course, under the present law it
was not invalid anyway. The operating surgeon would in future, under the proposed
amendment, submit his authoritative decision for the concurrence of others not necessarily
as well qualified as he, and with no legal liability to the Crimes Act. This change is purely
cosmetic-occasioned, no doubt, by the desperate feelings of the supervisory committee for
the need to grasp at any shadow which might win some support from the medical profession.
Members of the supervisory committee have had to resort to the ignominious course of
personally canvassing and pleading for medical support to fill the empty posts of certifying
consultants and operating doctors. A desperate course for a desperate supervisory
committee-largely unsuccessful,. I regret to say. This provision in the Bill will not help
remedy the present situation in the Auckland area, where there are more holders of
diplomas in tropical medicine than holders of diplomas in obstetrics and gynaecology among
the certifying consultants selected.

Hon. G. F. GAIR: Then I will move to another clause. On the matter of certifying
consultants seeing their patients- the second reason given by the supervisory committee for
this amending legislation-the reasons must again be largely cosmetic. The certifying
consultant can, under the present law, supported by the ethical code of his profession,
decline to accept a referral if the woman does not consent to see him. I have been told of
several certifying consultants who follow this course. The amendment proposed today,
which we are invited to accept, makes additional difficulties for women living in many parts
of New Zealand not at present served, or inadequately served, by certifying consultants.
This procedure is followed by some practitioners now, and no change in the law is required
to achieve it.
Then we come to the most important difference in the proposed procedures, where a
woman would now carry the onus of finding an operating doctor. This is what will happen if
we introduce and pass the clauses in the amendment. In effect, in the future a woman would
need to canvass for herself four separate legally acceptable medical opinions-her own
doctor's, the operating doctor's, and two certifying consultants. This might be reduced to
three if the operating doctor is a certifying consultant, and in some circumstances possibly
increased to five if she must seek the arbitration of a third certifying consultant. The
procedures in the present law, and in this proposed amendment, are in many respects even
less acceptable than the royal commission's panel system, which Parliament unanimously
rejected. I hope the procedural provisions in this amendment Bill will be struck out at the
Committee stage. I remind the member for New Lynn that the test of principle, or test of
response to specifics, in the Bill cannot be established until we come to the Committee stage.
That stage may well, however, give us the opportunity of further amendments which will be
more than cosmetic, but this is not the time to detail those thoughts. On balance, I believe
the Bill is worth introduction, but only to support its provision to remove the Wall
amendment. At least, in this respect, it represents one important step forward, out of the
darkness of last December's dreadful law towards the light of a new day.

Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Amendment Bill
Fundamentally we have had, since the Woolnough case, a situation in which the medical
profession realised that there was no effective legal control of abortion, and it enjoyed an
independence in this matter which its members had never had before. Their attitude was that
everything was fine and that they were controlling their own house, so why let anyone
interfere? That was a widespread opinion within the profession, and, in common with all
professions, it did not want further controls imposed on it. Here we have all seen much
legislation imposing professional control, and the cry by members of the profession
concerned has always been that they want the minimum control. They state that they can do
very well without legal control and can run their own show. That is the attitude we have seen
dominating a large section of the medical profession on this issue.
If this measure does persuade them that they have a greater responsibility to the
community at large than to their own professional organisations, or to their own prestige,
then this part of the legislation will be good. However, the second part has been
misinterpreted, I think intentionally, by those who did not wish to see the Act work because
they thought it was too restrictive. It was pointed out early in the piece by Dr Moody of the
Auckland Hospital Board, in his advice to the board, that this must be interpreted, as we all
know, in the light of the interpretation in the Acts Interpretation Act 1924, which states that
every Act shall receive a fair, large, and liberal construction and interpretation as will best
ensure the attainment of the objective of the Act. As Dr Moody said, that puts a very
different complexion on what appeared to be a hard-line statement.
If it would ease the situation I would not oppose the addition of the word "reasonably"
to the amendment that stood in my name, which would then read ". . . that the danger
cannot reasonably be averted by any other means". In this way the spirit and the intention of
the Acts Interpretation Act would be specifically written into this clause. The argument is
constantly put forward that abortion is something that happens only to a woman, and that
the only way to solve the mother's problem is to kill her child-and an abortion does mean
the death of a child. That hard cold fact brings to light the reality of the problem, and if
members thought about that point during this debate their consideration of the Bill would be
made a great deal easier.

PUBLIC TRUST OFFICE AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): I move, That
the Public Trust Office Amendment Bill be introduced. This short Bill of four clauses proposes
three comparatively minor amendments to the Public Trust Office Act 1957. The first
amendment in clause 2 relates to the power which the Public Trustee already has to advance
money out of his common fund to estates under administration in his office. That authority
can be used for a number of purposes, including, for example, the provision of temporary
finance to meet death duty or other commitments of an estate, thus avoiding forced
realisation of assets. It will also be very useful in estates in which there are business assets-
for example, a farm-and there is a need for development or seasonal finance.
In the case of the estates of deceased persons no problem arises over security for the
money advanced, because the assets of the estate are in the name of the Public Trustee. A
problem could, however, arise when the Public Trustee is acting as agent for a living person,
because in that case the assets are not in the name of the Public Trustee. Clause 2 therefore
provides for a simple form of statutory charge in cases in which the Public Trustee is acting as
agent. It will be of particular advantage in the provision of seasonal finance in those cases, of
which there are a number throughout New Zealand, in which the Public Trustee acts as
agent for a farmer.
The second amendment in clause 3 relates to the administration of small estates. Under
existing legislation, if an estate is valued at less than $7,500 the Public Trustee is empowered
to file in the Supreme Court a short document by which he elects to administer the estate.
This reduces the costs that would otherwise be incurred in obtaining a formal grant of
probate or administration. If it is later found, for example by discovery of another asset, that
the value of an estate in fact exceeds $10,000, the Public Trustee must then apply for a grant
of probate or administration in the ordinary way. Clause 3 proposes that these limits be
brought up to date by increasing them to $15,000 and $20,000 respectively.
The third amendment in clause 4 is similar. The Public Trustee is frequently asked to
complete the administration of estates in which the executor or administrator had died or is
unable to continue. If the assets remaining to be dealt with are valued at less than $7,500 the
Public Trustee can elect to administer them instead of applying to the court for a formal
grant. Again, however, if it is later found that their value in fact exceeds $10,000, the Public
Trustee must apply to the court for a grant of administration. It is proposed that these limits
also be raised to $15,000 and $20,000.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I have just one or two questions to which I should
like answers from the Minister. First, can he indicate whether or not it is his intention to
refer the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee? It seems that there may be a case for
doing so. I do not imagine that the hearings of the committee on the Bill would need to be
very lengthy, but not all members of the House are lawyers and it is difficult to understand
all the implications from a quick perusal of the Bill. Clause 2 is a very long and complicated
provision. The Minister says that the Public Trust Office already has some of the powers
referred to in clause 2, but he indicated that the Public Trustee is taking some additional
powers for himself. I am particularly interested in the reference to the Public Trustee acting
as agent for a living person. It seems to me that there could be cases in which the Public
Trustee might want to act in a way that, in actual practice, would be in conflict with the
wishes of the person for whom he acted as agent. I believe that is one matter that should be
considered by the Statutes Revision Committee before the Bill proceeds. Again, I ask the
Minister to say whether it is his intention to refer it to the Statutes Revision Committee.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert): I ask the Minister, when he replies to the member for
Manukau, to tell us whether the subject-matter of the Bill has been discussed with the Law
Society or whether the request for the measure came purely from within the Public Trust
Office itself.


## p. 50 (#58) ##############################################

50
50
17 May
Public Trust Office Amendment Bill
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): It is not my
intention to refer the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee, mainly because no matters of
great principle are involved. I shall answer first the question raised by the member for Mt
Albert. The matter has not been discussed with the Law Society. It was raised by the Public
Trust Office, but it has been discussed with the president of the Trustee Companies
Association. The honourable member will realise that the Public Trust Office and the trustee
companies are more analogous than are the Public Trust Office and the Law Society, or
lawyers in particular.
The member for Manukau makes a little more of the question of the Public Trustee
acting as agent than will in fact occur as a result of the amendment, which will simply add to
an existing clause in the Act and empower the Public Trust Office to advance money. On the
question of whether an estate is the property of a deceased person or a living person, a
deceased person's estate is in the hands or the name of the Public Trustee, and therefore he
has no need for security against a loan, because he already has security. When he lends as an
agent for the specific purpose of seasonal finance or special circumstances, it is necessary to
protect the loan by taking some form of security, and it is proposed that there should be a
simple statutory charge over the property. Under the amendment there is no question of the
Public Trustee acting in conflict with the principal for whom he is acting as agent.
The amendments are very simple. No principle is at stake. The Public Trustee has those
powers, and I am sure that when the member for Manukau reads the Bill carefully in
conjunction with the principal Act his fears will be dispelled and he will see, as I see, that
there is no real need for the Bill to go to the Statutes Revision Committee and add to that
committee's already very busy schedule, for no real purpose.
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga): The Minister said that there is no need for this Bill to go
before the Statutes Revision Committee. Does he intend to seek an opinion from the Law
Society? How did the Minister arrive at the 100 percent increase in the two amounts, from
$7,500 to $15,000, and from $10,000 to $20,000?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): The answer to
the member's first question is that no change in the law is involved. The proposal concerns
the Public Trust Office and its competitors in the trustee companies field. If the member for
Onehunga had been listening to what I had been saying, he would have realised that. The
answer to his second question is that the legislation is being brought up to date.
Mr Rogers: Well, that is a question of law.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot argue with the member if he does not want to
understand. The amounts of $7,500 and $10,000 were used in about one-third of deceased
estates that came into the Public Trust Office for administration last year. With the increases
to $15,000 and $20,000, the number of deceased estates involved will rise to about 45
percent. In other words, now a greater number of people will not have to apply for probate
in relatively small estates.

fish factories likely to be built in Bluff?

others are in the pipeline, some in the initial stages. It would not be appropriate for me to
give details of specific firms. Among the firms at present under consideration or in the
pipeline, I notice two or three concerned with food processing, and they could well be the
firms to which the honourable member has referred.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: When is approval or final decision likely on these regional
development assistance applications?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: In giving my answer I explained that five applications are being
evaluated, and one application is at present before the council. I cannot speak for the
council. Presumably, when it has finished its studies, it will pass the inquiry on. Of the five
applications under consideration by the department, one is awaiting further details from the
applicant, a report is being drafted on the second, the third is awaiting a DFC report, the
fourth is awaiting a Ministry of Energy comment because there are considerable energy
considerations, and the fifth is under investigation.
Mr W. R. Austin: Could the Minister confirm that the regional development council in
Southland is the most active in the country?
Mr SPEAKER: That is really a matter of opinion, unless the Minister has statistics to
prove it.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I do not have such statistics. However, I assure the member for
Awarua that the Southland Regional Development Council is very active, but I would not
like to suggest that other councils are not active.

Address in Reply
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: At least the honourable member for Rotorua will be going
out gracefully; he is retiring. Some will go much less gracefully. Clearly, the House could
have met much sooner-at least a couple of months ago—but it did not. That delay might
have been forgiven if, when Parliament finally came together, the Government had
produced for the consideration of the people some plan of action-but there has not been a
sign. What we had instead were five pages of political claptrap, an inglorious combination of
fatuous comment and inaccurate assertions.
Shortly I shall deal with some of these areas in more detail, but first I shall draw
attention to a few of the statements in the Speech from the Throne, and then relate them to
the facts of the situation. This is necessary to demonstrate the complete lack of credibility,
both of the document and of the Government that wrote it. The Government certainly goes
to great lengths to find somebody else to blame. Listen to this in the Speech from the
Throne: "The New Zealand economy continues to face difficulties." Everyone can say
"amen" to that. "These result from the slowness of the world's recovery from depression
since 1975 and from continuing international inflation which, together, have caused a major
deterioration in our terms of trade." That is pretty interesting in a way, because for a couple
of years it always used to be the previous Labour Government that was at fault, but now the
National Government is trying someone else, and its excuses are just as feeble and just as
wrong, because the fact is-and I turn to the Government Statistician as my authority—that
the import price index has risen by more than 30 percent since the change of Government in
late 1975.
In the same period the terms of trade, referred to in the Speech from the Throne,
actually improved by almost 6 percent. New Zealand exporters reaped a record export
boom- hardly a major deterioration, as was claimed in the Speech from the Throne.
Indeed, the only major deterioration we have seen is in this Government. Looking at the
question of inflation, mentioned in the speech, it is a fact that every one of the five major
trading partners of New Zealand-the United States, Japan, Germany, the United
Kingdom, and Australia-has succeeded in lowering its inflation, some to an incredible
degree, in the last 2 years. In other words, there has been a declining by rate of international
inflation. That could have been verified by turning to any reputable world publication in the
economic field. I ask the question: Is it that the Government cannot read, or is it that it does
not wish to read the truth?
Let us look at a couple more of the excuses raised in the Speech from the Throne.
"Imported inflation and domestic wage and price increases have developed a strong
momentum." Again, the fact is that inflation in this country at 15.7 percent included 9
percent that came in from overseas; but in 1977, after 2 years of National administration,
when the inflation rate was still at 15.3 percent, only 2.5 percent of that inflation came from
overseas. The rest of it was home grown, most of it as a direct result of this Administration.
Hon. L. W. Gandar: Where did you get those figures?
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: It is momentum all right, for the information of the
Minister of Education, but it is hardly momentum of the type that is claimed in the Speech
from the Throne. These are the facts, along with one other fact,—the Government is again
trying to blame people overseas for its ineptitude. But the real masterpiece and fiction in this
speech is the claim of some success. I note: "The high balance of payments deficit has been
reduced." The Prime Minister often has something to say about this. It so happens he is not
the only one. The New Zealand Insitutute of Economic Research has also made comment
from time to time, and it is rather interesting to note that its estimate is that there will be for
the 1978 financial year an $18 million increase in the balance of payments deficit-in its
estimate, not a reduction, but an increase.
The most serious sentence in this document, because of its human implications, is this
one: "While unemployment has become a growing problem, the policies of economic
stimulation pursued by the Government have been instrumental in controlling its growth."
Again, what are the facts? From November 1975 until April 1978 the registered unemployed
in this country rose by 445 percent, and special work rose by 64 percent-and those mainly
women and the young who were just tipped out of jobs with no recognition at all. Those
packing up and leaving-again they are mainly the young-have risen by tens of thousands,
and the tragedy is that the number continues to rise. If one looks at the trends over recent
years it would not be unreasonable to say-for the information of the Minister of Tourism,
who is trying to interject, and who does not seem to care-that we could well have by the end
of this winter a couple of hundred thousand New Zealanders who want to work-

I congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply. The Leader of the

and I say that without disrespect to those who have gone before. The member for
Palmerston North, in moving the address, gave us a well reasoned, deeply researched,
constructive, and impressive speech on a matter of great public interest as his main theme,

everyone will agree with the member for Invercargill, and he would not expect them to, but

Then we were talking about deficits before borrowing. The Leader of the Opposition
has a rudimentary grasp of Government accounts. He told us what his 1975 Budget had by
way of a deficit before borrowing. In the 1972-73 year, when we went out of office, the
deficit before borrowing-the difference between revenue and government expenditure-
was $206 million, or 2.7 percent of gross national product. Three years later we came back
and found that the deficit was not the $900 million estimated after the supplementary
estimates in 1975; it was heading for $1,200 million. So we made some rapid adjustments,
took off some subsidies, cut back Government spending, and got it down to $1,002 million.
That was not 2.7 percent of the gross national product; it was 9.7 percent of gross national
product-and wildly inflationary.
The reason for it was very simple: in the last year of that National Government,
1972-73, the Government spending was 29 percent of gross national product. The
Government was taking 29 percent, and spending it. Three years later the Government was
taking 42 percent. That was 3 years of Labour. We have got it back now; it is in the thirties.
It is not back to 29 percent, because once you build these things in it takes a while to get
them out. It went from 29 percent to 42 percent in 3 years. Let us have another election issue
on that. Let the Leader of the Opposition say in a simple forthright manner that we will
spend a higher percentage of the gross national product than we are spending today. I will
say that we are not. Let us make an issue of that, and let the people vote on it.

previous National Government; but the $1,000 million worth of reserves were cleaned up by
the Labour Government in 12 months. However, the interesting point about borrowing-
and we have, in fact, borrowed less-is not the amount we have borrowed but the rates at
which we have borrowed it. The former Labour Government, during the time the present
Leader of the Opposition was Minister of Finance, arranged a $400 million revolving credit
through Lloyd's Bank in 1974 at a rate of 1 percent above the London interbank rate for a
term of 5 years.
Last year we had a look at that loan and said, "We think we can do better than that."
The term had not expired; the credit had been current for only about 3 years. We
renegotiated it with the same bank, which added another $100 million. So we arranged the
credit for $500 million, and got it not for a term of 5 years, but for 7 years—a longer term. In
addition the rate for the credit is not 1 percent above the London interbank rate, but five-
eighths of 1 percent above the London interbank rate for 2 years and seven-eighths of 1
percent above it for the balance of the period. Then we had a look at some of the Swiss franc
borrowing arranged by the Leader of the Opposition when he was Minister of Finance in the
former Labour Government. He raised a loan in Switzerland, due in 1979, and paid 9
percent interest. We repaid that loan by borrowing in Swiss francs, not at 9 percent interest
but at 5 percent. We repaid that loan several years before it was due and obtained another
loan with an interest rate 4 percent cheaper. This year we have borrowed from Switzerland
again, at a rate of 3.75 percent. That sounds like pretty good money.
Miss Dewe: For how many years?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It was at 3.75 percent, but I think there are two issues-one
public and one private loan. The terms for each are different, and I do not have them with
me, but the period would be between 5 and 7 years. When I was in Switzerland 2 or 3 weeks
ago I had dinner with some of the people involved in that loan, and they commented on how
high New Zealand's credit rating is under this Government. One of them said, "You know, I
think that was the lowest rate on any loan since World War II." They had a chat among
themselves, and concluded that the New Zealand loan had been arranged at the lowest rate
for an external source loan since World War II. That says something about New Zealand's

QUESTIONS-ORAL
High-Priority Activities Scheme
1. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: How
many firms have made inquiries concerning the high-priority activities scheme recently
introduced by the Government, and what are the criteria for high-priority rating?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I can answer the
first part very briefly, but the second part is more difficult because it involves the criteria.
Interest in the scheme to date has been very encouraging, with 33 firm applications and more
than 250 inquiries having been received. The criteria are that the firm's activity: (1) is
capable of being isolated from other productive activities; (2) must be of a sort that its
production would be eligible for the existing increased exports taxation incentive; (3) must
have in the preceding year, (a) had maximum direct and indirect import content of 25
percent, excluding capital; (b) exported a minimum of 20 percent of its production, based on
factory door value, the minimum rising in annual steps of 2 percent to 30 percent over 5
years; (c) sold the remainder of its production on the New Zealand market for an ex-factory
selling price not more than 10 percent higher than the f.o.b. export price; and finally (d) had
total energy inputs from outside the company not exceeding 7.5 percent of the factory door
value of production.
Mr Lithgow: Has the Minister any plans for future extension of criteria, and, if so,
when?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have no plans now for extending the scheme, but I
have received official representations from the New Zealand Manufacturers Federation, and
I have informed the federation that the Government will give consideration to this after the
scheme has been in operation for some time.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Are the carpet yarn, carpet, and ceramic industries covered by the
scheme?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: All industries that apply are covered by the scheme.
I shall make a further announcement on the scheme at a formal ceremony shortly, and I shall
indicate the firms whose high-priority activities have been approved.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Could the Minister explain why it took 8 months from the
announcement in the Budget for firms to get the forms to send in for the scheme?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It took considerable time for the Government to


## p. 85 (#93) ##############################################

18 May
85
Questions-Oral
discuss the ramifications of the scheme with officials, with the NZ Manufacturers
Federation, and with other interested parties. It is an entirely new scheme. It was announced
by the Prime Minister in an economic package, and at the time I said publicly that it would
take some time to develop the criteria aimed at giving recognition to the highest
performance in terms of exporting and New Zealand content of products.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Will the Minister confirm that the Government announced the
scheme before it had worked out, even with officials, the details of that scheme?
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: No; that was the MRP scheme.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The scheme was properly announced, and proper

time for this to be done. One of the problems in the past was that adequate time was not
given to half-baked schemes of this nature.
Energy-Pricing and Tariffs
2. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Is he able to give an
indication as to the outcome of his proposed talks, which he gave notice of his intention to
undertake in reply to a parliamentary question on 27 July 1977, with the Electrical Supply
Authorities Association and the Gas Association on energy pricing of lower tariffs and
reduced rates for such matters as the heating of swimming pools?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The Gas Association has followed up my
approach by recommending to its members that in considering tariff changes they take
account of my views as to the undesirability of promotional tariffs for swimming pool
heating. Most undertakings, and possibly all, have made the desired adjustments. The
subject had already been discussed with the Electrical Supply Authorities Association, and
there is no special concession for swimming pools. The only reduced rate that is still available
from some supply authorities is the supply tariff available for controlled water and space-
heating. Since 1975 these rates have more than doubled, and this has encouraged the use of
solar panels and heat pumps as an alternative to resistance heating for new installations.
Hon. F. M. Colman: As it would appear that the Minister is getting co-operation from
the respective associations, are Government measures to bring about the desired position
necessary?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I believe that, as a result of the review, the position will be corrected
without any further action from me.

Railways Permanent Way-Christchurch-Picton
5. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Railways: What are the costs of
maintenance and improvements to the permanent way between Picton and Christchurch for
each of the years ended 31 March 1976, 1977, 1978, and what are the estimates for this
current year?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Minister of Railways replies: "Normal
maintenance expenditure on the Christchurch-Picton line was $1.39 million in 1976, $1.6
million in 1977, $1.83 million in 1978, and is estimated to be $2 million in 1979. In addition to
normal maintenance, the department carries out special work such as improvements to track
structures and weatherproofing. During the year ended 31 March 1976, $397,000 was spent
on this type of work; in 1977, $630,000; in 1978, $752,000; and it is estimated that $532,000
will be spent this financial year. In addition, expenditure on capital works such as bridge
renewals and crossing loop extensions totalled $533,000 in 1976, $600,000 in 1977, and $1
million in 1978, and $1,325,000 is programmed for this year.
Mr Latter: Would this expenditure, which appears to exceed $12 million, have had a
beneficial effect on line availability?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The lengthening of the crossing loops and the loop extensions
allows longer trains and more frequent movements, especially under CTC control.
Mr Kirk: Has the rapid increase in expenditure, from $1.39 million in 1976 to a
projected $2 million for next year, occurred since the Rangatira was withdrawn?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I cannot answer that question accurately. That track has had a
marked upgrading, especially as a result of using temporary workers from the labour pool.
The availability of labour has been taken advantage of, and at one stage we proposed to
introduce a holiday camp to try to get workers into the area to upgrade the line. The
availability of labour, more than the theory, probably answers the question.
New Car Prices

introduced into the House.

the Government?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I consider that the present figure is acceptable,
because almost all of the marques are selling at lower prices than those approved by the

Hypertension Drug Charge
1. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Is it a fact that, during World
Hypertension Month, in early April 1978 a charge was levied by the Department of Health
for the first time on a number of drugs which ease hypertension, and, if this is correct, why
was this done?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: On 15 January 1978 it was decided to
place a part charge on one brand of guanethidine, an anti-hypertensive medicine, from 1
April 1978 because a cheaper locally manufactured identical product became available which
was free of charge to patients. Similarly, early in February 1978 a decision was made to place
a part charge on some brands of frusemide, a diuretic substance sometimes used as adjuvant
therapy for hypertension. Another and cheaper brand of the identical substance became
available. It has been the practice, since the inception of the pharmaceutical benefits
scheme, that, in the case of availability of several equal quality brands of the identical
substance, payment by the State will be based on the price of the cheapest brand. This
practice has been accepted by all political parties when in power, and in no way affects the
availability of free treatment for patients.

PUBLIC EXPENDITURE COMMITTEE REPORT-PILLAGING
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Public Expenditure Committee
to present the report of the subcommittee on pillaging. I move, That the report do lie upon the
table. The subcommittee to report on pillaging was set up in 1974, and has met over the past
4 years under two Administrations. It has had to deal with an issue which has for many years
been of major concern to the New Zealand public generally. The subcommittee has made
very comprehensive investigations to establish, as far as possible, the extent of pillaging in
New Zealand. I recognise and commend the work done not only by the present chairman of
the subcommittee, but also by the member for Gisborne and the member for Dunedin
North. They have had to undertake their task without any statistical information, either
current or historical. Bringing this report together was quite a mammoth task.
The subcommittee has reported on the nature and extent of pillaging in New Zealand. I
propose to quote briefly from the report to give some indication of the extent of pillaging in
New Zealand. These interesting statistics may indicate a higher level of pillaging than is
actually the case: goods pillaged before importation in 1976-77, 427 cases; goods pillaged
after importation, 8767 cases; and New Zealand-produced goods subject to excise duty, 658
cases. Without the statistics available in the report, nothing could be done to overcome the
serious problem of pillaging.
The report also deals with the causes and factors contributing to pillaging. We all know
the disturbing and increasing trend in the community's tolerance of crime. This will decline
only when the attitude of society changes. That fact came through very strongly in the
report. I shall not deal in detail with all the subcommittee's recommendations. The major
recommendation is the establishment of an anti-pillaging agency under the auspices of the


## p. 93 (#101) #############################################

18 May
93
Public Expenditure Committee-Pillaging Report
Customs Department, to collect, collate, analyse, and publish information on pillaging on a
New Zealand-wide basis, and to take initiatives to improve the efficiency and effectiveness
of the handling of goods so as to minimise loss.
The report also states that the following benefits can be expected from the
establishment of the anti-pillaging agency: first, the ability to assess accurately the extent and
location of pillaging would indicate more specifically than is possible with existing
information the initial action necessary to reduce pillaging losses; secondly, the monitoring
of trends and pillage losses should suggest where further action may be needed; thirdly, the
statistics so produced should aid the detection and the prevention of pillaging; and, fourthly,
the on-going publication of statistics, by revealing to the industry and the public at large the
scale of pillage losses, should promote more awareness of the problem.
I have mentioned only a few of the conclusions and recommendations to give some idea
of the importance of this comprehensive report. I hope and believe that the work undertaken
by the subcommittee will activate positive action within the transport industry itself. With
the statistics already available and expanded statistics in the future, we can look forward to a
change in attitude and to some positive action towards overcoming this serious problem. I
congratulate the chairmen of the subcommittee, the member for Gisborne and the member
for Dunedin North, on their work.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): In supporting the motion I thank all those
who assisted the subcommittee with its inquiries-the Police Department, the Customs
Department, and commercial and other interested parties who tendered evidence, and also
the members of the committee itself, who worked so hard over a long period to produce this
report before Parliament. The subcommittee's recommendations have the potential to
minimise pillaging, but the effectiveness of those recommendations will depend on the co-
operation of everybody involved in the transportation and storage of goods. If the spirit and
intention of the subcommittee's recommendations are put into effect, the desired results will
be achieved.
The subcommittee established that there was no comprehensive public record of the
type and degree of loss from pillaging or, in fact, where pillaging had occurred. Such
information is a prerequisite to a realistic approach to minimising the problem. We must
know what is happening before we can tackle it. The subcommittee views pillaging as theft,
and sees no difference in principle between the theft of money and the theft of goods that
represent money's worth. Irrespective of whether one distinguishes between pillaging and
theft, the owner of goods is deprived permanently of their use through pillaging. The
subcommittee found that attitudes towards pillaging vary and, in some cases, create an
environment conducive to pillaging. Public tolerance of crime has been increasing. The
subcommittee believes a major factor in the apparent acceptance of pillaging as something
less than theft arises from a lack of factual information on the extent of pillaging. Some
witnesses reported a tendency for employees in the transport industry, including supervisory
staff, to regard pillaging as a perk, and some employers tended to condone it. The
subcommittee strongly condemns this attitude and states that pillaging should have no
greater degree of social acceptance than premeditated theft.
Despite the fact that publicity about pillaging in recent years has tended to place the
blame on waterfront workers, leaving the impression that they alone are responsible, my
impression from the evidence tendered to the committee is that most pillaging occurs either
before the goods arrive in New Zealand waters or after they leave the wharf. The
subcommittee considers that responsibility for goods in transit must lie with the
organisations who benefit financially from the transportation and storage of goods. We
established that, because of a lack of some central or co-ordinating body and the fragmented
nature of security in relation to the transportation of goods, responsibility for adequate
storage at each stage in the handling of goods was not accepted by any one organisation.
Several witnesses believed that the Police should accept substantial responsibility for the
prevention of pillaging. We discussed this matter with the Police, who pointed out that,
while they accept the same degree of responsibility for dealing with theft in relation to
transportation as in other areas, there were limitations to their undertaking a greater role in
the prevention of pillaging for the following reasons: their obligation to meet other priorities
when allocating their manpower and other resources; public sensitivity to a police presence
in a work place and, in particular, the reaction of employees if subjected to a greater degree
of police surveillance than was normal in other places; and the likelihood that the provision
of extra police service in transportation areas might create a demand and a precedent for


## p. 94 (#102) #############################################

94
18 May
Public Expenditure Committee-Pillaging Report
similar services to be expected elsewhere-for instance, in the retail trade to detect
shoplifting and situations of that kind.
The subcommittee came to the conclusion that pillaging can be prevented if effective
measures are taken. Evidence tendered to the subcommittee indicated that this was so in the
air freighting of goods and the handling of goods by the Auckland Harbour Board. In the
case of the Auckland Harbour Board, or in both cases in fact, the principle applied was the
provision of special security staff. We discussed this aspect in particular with the Auckland
Harbour Board, the National Airways Corporation, and Air New Zealand.
The Auckland Harbour Board employs uniformed officers whose duties include the
random patrolling of wharf areas. They operate day and night. On container wharves it has
uniformed gate keepers who check cargo leaving the area or coming in, item by item. The
National Airways Corporation's appointment of a security officer led to major
improvements in that organisation, including a freight education programme and a security
programme that included restrictions on access to certain areas and improved supervision of
freight areas. The result was a reduction in pillaging. It was suggested that the level of
surveillance that would be tolerated by employees was no more than that accepted at present
on the Auckland wharves. It was considered that the means were available to strengthen
security in good handling areas without incurring adverse reaction from the relevant unions.
The validity of this observation was borne out in particular through the experience of the
National Airways Corporation in gaining support from the unions for co-operation in
security designed to reduce losses.
The NAC freight loss reduction programme arose out of consultation and agreement
with the unions, thus enabling a security education programme to be introduced. The same
approach was adopted by Air New Zealand, and the subcommittee recommends the
establishment of an anti-pillaging agency under the auspices of the Customs Department, to
collect, collate, analyse, and publish information about pillaging. That approach is expected
to provide the following benefits: the extent of pillaging could be accurately assessed, thus
enabling initial action to be taken and the monitoring of the effect of the initial action to see
what further action was necessary; information to assist the detection of pillaging would be
published, thus enabling the industry and the public to be made aware of the position and to
promote more effective measures. The availability of that information and the availability of
information as to the extent of losses would enable freighting and other organisations
concerned with costs and improvements to judge the desirability of expenditure of this
nature based on the overall savings that would result. Apart from that, the information
would enable vocational training programmes and education programmes on security within
the industry to be undertaken.
A key recommendation of the subcommittee is that a training council comprising union
and employer representatives should be established to assist in making people aware of the
problems involved, and the steps necessary to eliminate them. The subcommittee
recommends that representatives of industry and labour should go abroad to investigate
activities of an anti-pillaging nature in other countries, and that the cost of this should be
borne by industry. The report contains more, but over all it is forward looking and
progressive, and advocates the improvement of facilities, design, and layout. It also calls for
improvement in the pay and conditions of workers and improvement in the facilities used in
the industry.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): As the Minister primarily concerned
with the pillaging problem I acknowledge the excellent work done by the committee,
although, frankly, it has taken quite some time to conclude its investigations. However, I
accept the reasons given in the report, although I am disappointed that the report does not―
and to be absolutely fair cannot-go further than it does. Apart from the specific
recommendations, the report's main value lies in indicating that there is more work still to be
done if the true dimension of the problem is to be found.
In 1971 my colleague the member for Taupo said that the pillaging problem in New
Zealand was costing the people of this country hundreds of millions of dollars. He has still to
be proved wrong, and closer examination may well prove him right. All the indications I
have suggest that the community is paying a very heavy cost indeed for pillaging, and I
believe that once we confront the public with the real dimensions of the problem, people will
not begrudge the allocation of the extra resources needed for the setting up of the anti-
pillaging agency recommended by the subcommittee, which it very appropriately
recommends should be administered by the Customs Department. The agency's foremost


## p. 95 (#103) #############################################

18 May
95
Public Expenditure Committee-Pillaging Report
responsibility would be the gathering of the necessary statistics. Without these it will not get
very far. Unless the agency has real teeth to pursue that function, we are just wasting our
time.
If I have any criticism of the subcommittee's recommendation, it is that too much
emphasis has been placed on encouragement at the expense of enforcement. Frankly, I have
rather a cynical view of pillaging. Everyone is ready to pay lip service to the necessity for
fighting pillaging, but I question whether many people respond to mere persuasion when it
comes to spending money, or to radically overhauling procedures, or to doing anything
involving great effort or a lot of expense. Certainly, as the subcommittee has pointed out,
some members of the commercial community will respond to suggestions that to minimise
the risk of pillaging they improve their procedures or packaging or the design of freight
holding areas, etc.; but far too many people will still not face up to the fact that the wrong
kind of labelling on liquor, sports goods, transistor radios, or similar products, can be an
open invitation to theft, and be avoided or greatly mitigated. So when, for example, the
subcommittee suggests that freight handlers be encouraged to spend money to employ their
own uniformed personnel, I wonder how realistic its members are being. The more cynical,
but also the more realistic view, is that freight handlers accept as a fact of life that some
goods will always go missing, and that the cost can always be passed on.
It is out of this attitude of resignation that the cycle of apathy and lethargy has grown
that has in turn enabled pillaging to thrive. If we are really serious about pillaging we have to
contemplate a tougher stance than that envisaged by this report. I know that some elements

serious. That is not to denigrate the excellent work of this subcommittee. Before we were

The member for Wigram mentioned the waterfront unions. I think we have to be fair,

furthermore, I am assured that official union policy is not to protect any of its members
caught pillaging. In all fairness those points must be made.
My final point is that anyone who has custody of goods should have the responsibility of
ensuring that the goods are transported and stored safely, but the present law cannot be said
to be rigorous in casting the onus on those people. Under the present law freight forwarders
face a very small liability for the goods they handle, and that should be looked at. I join with
my colleague the member for South Canterbury in thanking members on both sides of the
House who sat on the subcommittee. I intend now to consider carefully the proposals in the
report and marry them with one or two ideas of my own. I shall then present a report to the
Government in an effort to tackle this pernicious problem, the extent of which I suspect is
much wider than many people realise.
Mr BELL (Gisborne): As a member of the subcommittee for the past 2 1/2 years, I

positive and worth-while action towards solving this serious social problem.
