STATUS OF CHILDREN AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Status of Children Amendment Bill. The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. This Bill, which was introduced at the end of last parliamentary session and
referred to the Statutes Revision Committee for recess study, amends the Status of Children
Act of 1969. The principal Act abolished the legal distinction between children born within
and out of wedlock. As a result of that change to the law, ex nuptial children have the same
rights in respect of a deceased's estate as children born in wedlock. This in turn places an
obligation on executors and trustees to make inquiries regarding possible ex nuptial children
who might have a claim against an estate, and, in the case of an intestacy, the court had to
satisfy itself before granting letters of administration to an applicant, that there were no ex
nuptial relatives who had a better claim to administer the estate. This second problem was
dealt with somewhat unsatisfactorily by a Supreme Court Practice Note issued in 1970. The
present Bill is intended to supersede that practice note, and also to clarify the obligations of
trustees who make inquiries regarding ex nuptial relatives.
Understandably, because of the technical nature of the Bill, it attracted only two
submissions, one from the New Zealand Law Society and the other from the New Zealand
Trustees Association. The Law Society, which had liaised closely with the Department of
Justice in the preparation of the Bill, gave almost unqualified support. However, the trustee
companies did express some reservations about the provisions of the Bill and about the
obligations that it would impose on trustees and executors.
It is appropriate that before dealing with the changes proposed by the committee I
should deal briefly with the three major objections raised by the trustee companies. First,
they were concerned that the Bill would impose obligations on them in respect of all the
estates and trusts that have come into existence pursuant to instruments executed since 1
January 1970, the commencement date of the principal Act. That, however, is not the case.


## p. 99 (#107) #############################################

18 May
99
Status of Children Amendment Bill
This Bill comes into force on 1 October 1978, and imposes obligations only in respect of
estates that are administered, or are in the course of administration, from that date. The
committee is satisfied that this is not an onerous requirement. Secondly, companies were
concerned that the Bill laid down a series of steps that had to be followed by trustees, and
that if any one of those steps was omitted, whether inadvertently or otherwise, the
companies would be liable to a potential but unknown beneficiary. The committee will be
recommending certain changes to the Bill which will make it not only easier for inquiries to
be made but will give a measure of protection if one step is inadvertently omitted.
Thirdly, there is concern that until such time as necessary inquiries had been made
trustees would be obliged to refrain from making payments to beneficiaries, including
advances of money to needy dependent families. Again, this is not the case. The committee
is suggesting less onerous inquiries, and these can be made during the ordinary course of the
administration of the estate. The trustee companies also made other specific criticisms of
certain provisions, and some of these have been met by changes proposed by the select
committee. It should be noted that the trustee companies accepted, as a matter of principle,
that trustees are under an obligation to make reasonable inquiries as to persons who might
be entitled to benefit under an estate or trust. Their real concern is how far such inquiries
should go, when they should be made, and what protection should be afforded to trustees
who do make proper inquiries.
This Bill spells out the steps that should be taken by a trustee, giving protection if the
procedures are followed. It should be noted that several of the inquiries required under the
Bill-that is, a search of the register maintained by the Registrar-General of Births, Deaths,
and Marriages and a perusal of the papers of the deceased-were accepted reasonable by
trustee companies. They did not raise objection to inquiries having to be made of the
solicitor known to have last acted for the deceased. They did question whether this would
reveal any information, and asked if the solicitor would be able to disclose material without
breaching professional privilege. The committee had discussions on the latter point with a
representative of the New Zealand Law Society, and is satisfied that a solicitor can, and
should, in a number of circumstances be permitted to give information that could result in
the discovery of ex nuptial relatives.
I turn to the changes proposed by the committee. In its original form the Bill required
that extensive inquiries had to be made before letters of administration were granted in an
estate. This provision did not apply if there was a will-unless the executor had died,—did
not apply to trustee companies, and did not apply where the estate was less than $25,000,
and where there was a surviving spouse. In view of this limited application, and in view of the
fact that the Act also required that similar inquiries to ascertain ex nuptial relatives had to be
made at a later stage in all estates, the committee recommends a change to the proposed
section 5A that would substantially limit the nature of the inquiries to be made at this early
stage.
Secondly, to meet the valid concerns expressed by the trustee companies as to the
nature of the inquiries they were obliged to make before distributing the estate, the
committee recommends substantial changes to the proposed section 6. The committee
considered that the revised list of inquiries that trustees must make before distributing the
estate are more clearly defined, less onerous, and will yield equal information. Furthermore,
it is recommended that the protection to be given to executors, administrators, and trustees
should be extended so that, if it appears to the court that the trustee has acted honestly and
ought fairly to be excused for his failure, the court may relieve him either partly or wholly
from personal liability. Finally, the committee also recommends a number of other changes
to the Bill of a minor technical or drafting nature.
Motion agreed to.
IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Immigration Amendment Bill (No. 2). The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. In the form that the Bill was introduced last year it added 10 new sections or
subsections and 2 new schedules to the Immigration Act 1964. The Bill established a
Deportation Review Tribunal to review deportation orders made in respect of persons
convicted of criminal offences. It empowered the authorities to refuse entry into this country
to a non-New Zealand citizen, and to detain such person pending his or her departure. It


## p. 100 (#108) ############################################

100
18 May
Immigration Amendment Bill (No. 2)
made provision for the deportation of persons involved in offences threatening national
security, and allowed for appeals against certain types of deportation order either to the
Deportation Appeal Tribunal or the Supreme Court. Only three submissions were received
on the Bill: from the Council for Civil Liberties in Wellington, Amnesty Aroha, and the
Wellington Regional Pacific Islands Advisory Council. All these submissions gave qualified
support to the Bill. In fact, the Council for Civil Liberties recommended some of its features.
However, all offered constructive criticism, which was carefully considered by the
committee. As a result of its deliberations, the committee recommends a number of changes
to the Bill.
Clause 3 authorises any policeman to detain a person who has been refused an entry
permit, pending that person's departure from New Zealand. This provision will be
particularly valuable where the person in question cannot leave New Zealand that day, or if
the person is considered likely to commit an offence or to be a threat to public safety if not
held in custody. However, although a person who is refused an entry permit would not
ordinarily be prosecuted, for that reason a court appearance would not be warranted. We
propose an amendment to require that, where a person is detained for more than 24 hours
before leaving the country, a warrant shall be obtained from the registrar of a magistrate's
court authorising that the person be held in a penal institution. I should make two points
about this provision: first, in the vast majority of cases the person concerned would be
detained for less than 24 hours, and accordingly a warrant would not be required; secondly, a
person who believed that he was being improperly held in custody would have access to the
courts through a writ of habeus corpus to challenge his detention.
In the form that it was originally introduced, the Bill would have permitted the
detention only of a person who has been refused a temporary permit to enter New Zealand.
Under section 19 of the Immigration Act, Australians have been granted exemption and are
not required to obtain such a permit. Accordingly, a suspected terrorist, who is an
Australian, would not be detained under this new provision. The committee agreed that this
situation was undesirable, and accordingly proposed in clause 3B an amendment to section
19 that would permit the Minister of Immigration, or an immigration officer authorised by
him, to revoke the exemption for a person, or class of persons, who is suspected of terrorist
activity, or is considered likely to commit an offence against either the Crimes Act or the
Misuse of Drugs Act. It should be noted that, in spite of an agreement that allows for trans-
Tasman travel without a permit, Australians have long had a provision in their Migration
Act permitting the Minister or an authorised officer to prevent a person, or class of persons,
from entering the country if it is considered "undesirable that he be permitted to enter
Australia". The provision proposed by the committee in the Bill is much more limited than
the Australian provision.
The new section 22C, which would be inserted in the Act by clause 4 of the Bill, provides
that any person who is ordered to be deported because he has been convicted of a serious
criminal offence may appeal to the Deportation Review Tribunal established by the Bill. The
Bill required that this appeal be lodged within 14 days, and we recommend that the period be
extended to 28 days. Clause 5 of the Bill inserts a new section, 33B, in the principal Act,
relating to powers of arrest. It protects any police officer who arrests a person, in accordance
with the section, from criminal and civil liability, and makes it clear that, when an
immigration officer calls a policeman to his assistance, that policeman is entitled to enter any
premises if it is necessary to enable him to render such assistance. It was pointed out to the
committee that, until such time as the policeman had actually entered the premises, he could
not be absolutely sure that the person claiming to be an immigration officer was in fact such
an officer. Accordingly, a change is recommended to enable a policeman to rely upon his
belief that the person was an immigration officer.
We also propose some minor amendments, including a new section 22(4), to protect the
position of a permanent New Zealand resident who leaves the country for a short period.
This would be a redraft of the transition provisions of the Bill to ensure that those persons
who had immunity from deportation before the Bill became law will retain that immunity
after it comes into effect. Provisions are recommended to enable the suspension of
deportation orders pending the determination of any appeal. The committee was
considerably assisted in its deliberations on the Bill not only by officials from the
Immigration Division of the Department of Labour but also by the Ministry of Foreign
Affairs, the Department of Justice, and the Police. Members of the committee have already
expressed thanks to the officials concerned, and I repeat the committee's appreciation.
Motion agreed to.

Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
Having travelled the extent of my electorate and consulted approximately 1000 New
Zealanders in an electorate that has a total population of over 77 000, I can say that the
reaction of the people to this Government reflects the concern of expert commentators on
the subject. That the increase in the power of the Executive of this Government has made
considerable inroads into the democratic processes of New Zealand is widely acknowledged.
We have no written constitution, we have a single Chamber, and we have no Bill of Rights,
but, under precedents derived from Britain, Parliament is supposed to be supreme.
Regrettably, that is now more of a nostalgic thought than a current practice. Historically,
political philosophy distinguishes between legislative, executive, and judicial branches of the
Government. Each is supposed to be supreme in its own field and subject to checks and
balances to preserve the stability of the State and the rights of citizens. This is not the New
Zealand situation, where an Executive that is normally more supreme than the other
authorities has now become so supreme that I would say we have an oligarchy ruling New
Zealand.
Parliament should not be used as a vehicle to extend bureaucratic power, as it is in this
country. Parliament, after all, is the key institution of our democracy, but it no longer serves
in that role. Parliament has become a rubber stamp, and has been brought into such
disregard by this Government and by the Leader of the House that there must be a change if
New Zealand is to retrieve democracy. Maintenance of law and order in a community is the
mark of civilised society. There must be rules and laws, and they must be obeyed. Without
the rule of law there is anarchy. I do not believe any member will disagree with that
statement.
As lawmakers, we expect the law to be upheld, but we know that if the people are to
respect and obey the laws we pass, then the Government itself must set an example. Can we
expect the ordinary person to obey the law religiously when the Government on many
occasions has shown its complete contempt for the Acts passed by this House?
The National Government regards law and order as something for the people out there.
It does not apply the same standards to itself. It is prepared to suspend Acts and regulations
by ministerial press statements or by Prime Ministerial press conference statements. I shall
refer to many examples in the course of my speech. One diabolical example of sweeping a
parliamentary statute aside was the merger of Air New Zealand and NAC without reference
to Parliament. There is no doubt it was illegal. I am sure that members in the House would
not contradict that statement.
An Hon. Member: I would.

As the unilateral exercise of power dominates, there is a tendency for inequality to
increase. If there is any one reason more than another why this Government should
surrender its power, on this vote of no confidence, it is its abuse of the processes of
democracy, and its misuse of Parliament and its procedures. Time does not permit me to go
into detail, so I shall merely enumerate a few examples. There has been first, the trivialising

the decisions of the vast majority of the women, 98 percent of whom voted for the

On the other hand, we have the selective use of reports such as that of the Domestic

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): In rising to deliver my maiden speech in this Address in
Reply to the Speech from the Throne, I wish to affirm the loyalty of the movement I
represent through His Excellency to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II. I also add my
congratulations to those which have acknowledged your elevation, Mr Speaker, to your high
office.
A bold, fresh strategy is required for New Zealand-not an extended plan of sterile
socialism with State domination and bureaucratic control, not an economic miracle based
upon economic dogmas from the past which the march of events has discredited and
rendered irrelevant, but a bold new strategy that will attack the fundamental faults in the
economic system and provide the framework of opportunity within which people themselves
can solve their own problems, which is what they would prefer to do, and in so doing solve
many of those of the nation as well.
Unless a bold new strategy of this nature is entered upon, or at the very least unless a


## p. 117 (#125) ############################################

18 May
117
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
start is made with such a strategy, the present economic situation will rapidly assume socially
explosive proportions. For those not completely divorced from the realities of the outside
world by their cloistered seclusion in the rarified and unreal atmosphere of institutional life,
the warning lights are on. To say a social explosion cannot happen in New Zealand under an
intensification of present pressures is to deny the lessons of history. History demonstrates
time and again that economic pressures producing social disruption give rise to either
reactionary government or a new democratic alternative. The people of Rangitikei were the
first to signal the decision that a new democratic alternative is wanted, and it is daily
becoming more apparent that their lead is being increasingly followed by the rest of the
country. The rising level of frustration within our society, coming from the continuing
escalation of pressures against the family and the individual, is the driving force behind this
change.
The marginal drop in the annual inflation rate has been achieved, not with a wand, but
with a cruel economic cudgel and at the enormous social cost of a severely depressed home-
building industry, falling production, a continuous decline in the real incomes of farmers and
workers, and, by normal standards of international measurement, almost 100 000
unemployed. The rapidly rising cost of production, fuelled and sustained by inflation, is
utterly destroying the confidence of farmers. Forced to attempt to handle more and more
stock units to maintain family security and income, they are running harder and faster just to
stand still, and young farm workers and farm managers are expressing growing frustration
and anger at the increased height of the financial hurdles that have to be surmounted as a
condition of individual farm ownership. It is the farmers of New Zealand who produce 75
percent of overseas income, and it is upon their efforts that the rest of the country depends to
import goods and services for the common benefit.
It is the farmers who must accept three-quarters of the responsibility of servicing and
repaying our overseas debt-and it is a massive responsibility, because the annual cost of
servicing it, together with overseas investment, both private and Government, and without
any attempt to repay principal, has risen nearly five-fold since 1972, from $77 million to $366
million, or to the extent of now consuming more than the total export income from the sale
of butter, casein, and cheese. Farmers recognise the challenge and the work that must be
done to solve the country's overseas debt and importing problem. They are prepared to play
their part, but they do not want to have to make continual trips to Wellington, cap in hand,
for politically manipulated favours-the bureaucratic nightmare of a maze of minor subsidies
and handouts.
Fundamentally farmers want to be paid to produce, and they want to be able to plan
their production on a permanent and stable basis. They do not want to be subsidised into
serfdom. They do not want a debilitating high-interest debt burden imposed upon them to
enable them to continue farming or as the condition of individual farm ownership.
Subsidisation and debt will produce only more amalgamations, absentee ownership, and
company farming with its resulting rural depopulation and disastrous social repercussions.
An essential part of the broad strategy required for New Zealand is to give farmers the
capacity and the confidence to produce for export by paying them, as of right, a just price in
New Zealand dollars for the overseas funds they earn for the whole country.
Farmers must be paid the true value of the foreign exchange they earn-namely, its
total New Zealand cost in New Zealand dollars together with a reasonable profit. Only then
will justice to the farmer and the farm worker be done. The mechanism for this should be the
payment of a variable premium over and above the normal return whenever the realisation
in New Zealand dollars from agricultural exports is less than its internal cost of production in
New Zealand dollars. A court of price review should be established to decide on the
premium to be paid on the exchange earned, but generally the basic price paid to the
efficient farmer should cover all legitimate internal costs and provide for a reasonable profit.
The profit level negotiated annually between the representative farmer organisations and the
Government should reflect due consideration of the ability of farmers to pay competitive
rates of pay, the provision of an income equivalent to that of other members of the
community rendering equal service, the right to a reasonable return on invested capital, and
incentives to maintain full use of the land to achieve the highest possible level of production.
A strategy that gives confidence and incentives to farmers to produce, although vitally
important, will be nullified unless that strategy includes measures to solve the critical trading
problem now facing New Zealand.
The economic strength of this country should revolve around the fact that we can


## p. 118 (#126) ############################################

118
18 May
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
produce the cheapest food in a world where two-thirds of its people are suffering from
malnutrition. Because it can produce so efficiently, New Zealand does have a trading future,
but only within a sane and rational trading system. New Zealanders' anger mounts and their
sense of frustration intensifies when they reach out into the world and are told that their food
production is not wanted. They see barriers in the form of levies and quotas erected against
New Zealand exports. They see us continually exposed to the injustice of exporting more
and more and receiving less and less in return, while what they can produce is the vital
ingredient of human sustenance.
Nations such as India, for example-the tenth industrial country on earth-have a
desperate need for the food we can produce. India has the same system-induced problem of
selling her industrial output at fair prices as we have in selling our food products. In a
starving world the present international financial system is not only stupid, but also immoral.
Any system that forces the poor to sell to the rich or borrow from them at interest as a
condition of trading with one another is wrong. What is needed is a new and just financial
arrangement that allows trade to proceed relative to need and not to the dictates of an
obsolete system. New Zealand itself has no trading future and little room to manoeuvre in
solving its internal economic problems until it breaks out of the impasse forced upon it by the
operation of the international monetary system based upon fabricated reserves and
administered by the International Monetary Fund.
The Western World's monetary capacity to trade is today predominantly regulated to
the extent that the United States incurs debt interest free by creating credit to pay for her
excess of imports over exports. These created dollars become the main reserves base for
world trade, and the total now stands at about 300 billion dollars. An international system of
finance based upon the American dollar means that money is available for everybody's
trading needs only to the extent that the United States prints new money to pay for her
excess of imports over exports, and trading money is at present available to countries only to
the extent that they succeed in trading with the exclusive club of countries which hold stocks
of American dollars. The exclusive club of the United States, the European Economic
Comminity countries, Japan, and the Oil States, with large stocks of United States dollars,
want little of what New Zealand offers in trade. The existing system, then, is colonial in
origin, and lingers on when its original purpose is no longer relevant. It is unjust and distorts
world trade against New Zealand's interests and those of the Third World.
In 1977 the United States printed more than 20 billion United States dollars of new
trading money to enable her to pay for oil and other imports. This massive injection of new
American dollars into the international monetary markets just kept world trade going while,
at the same time, threatening to wreck the United States dollar itself as a viable currency.
New Zealand should step outside of it before she becomes part of the rubble upon its fall. An
essential and vital part of the overall strategy required to improve and protect all that is best
in the New Zealand way of life is that we accept the challenge of standing on our own two
feet in the world of trade and develop new markets with new trading partners under a new
system.
It is the trade problem which has caused the growth of New Zealand's overseas debt and
which has been largely responsible for the imposition of massive unemployment and varying
degrees of hardship and economic stress upon sections of our society. There is no light at the
end of the tunnel under the present system, and defensive measures such as import control
and belt tightening offer only temporary relief. It is in New Zealand's interest as well as that
of many economies of the Pacific Basin that we initiate a new trading method-if need be,
country by country-which is not stifled in development and regulated by the availability of
the debt-ridden reserve dollar.
Third World countries, of which New Zealand is rapidly becoming one, cannot remain
inside a trading system which forces them to pay top-shelf prices for imports from the
advanced economies while receiving bar-room returns for their own exports. The new
approach to trade must operate on the simple principle that the backing for trade money
must be the goods available for export and not some fictitious reserve. Trade is nothing but
barter, and money need be used only as a measurement of the terms of bartering. The
national currencies of two or more willing trading partners can be used to allow fair trade to
proceed without introducing the American dollar into the act at all. The only restraint on the
exchange of goods and services should be the actual limitations of manpower and resources
in satisfying mutual needs.
A new trading policy will take considerable courage to implement, but it must be

effected. We will not solve our trading problems by bluster. This approach is negative and
destroys good will. It is an act of desperation by a Government which has no alternative to
offer for what has been lost, and appears as such. We must take our destiny and our future
into our own hands and, by example, show the many countries with problems similar to our
own that there is an alternative strategy which will lead to a more secure, just, and stable
trading future for us all. It will, of course, be resisted, but this is the trade battle we must
fight and win, recognising that the task will not be easy.
Change and adaptation of our economy will also have to occur to meet the differing
needs of the new markets that will become available to us. It must also occur because we
ourselves must replace and produce much of what we import from our traditional trading
partners. The situation with oil poses the greatest challenge. Fossil fuels will run out within
the foreseeable future, and present oil imports for liquid fuels must be replaced from within
New Zealand. Any discovery of oil here will provide only temporary respite from the need to
develop within New Zealand alternative liquid energy sources such as vegetable and alcohol
fuel based on our farmlands and forests and supplemented by coal and shale refinement. The
technology for this is available, and a new industry of liquid fuel production based on organic
material must be developed. Farmers will have to grow the raw material for gas and liquid
fuel. Decentralised industry, co-operatively owned by the workers, farmers, and the public,
must be developed in each region of the country to maximise the use of such liquid fuels. The
challenge of New Zealand growing and processing its own liquid fuel on a permanent basis
will provide us with one of the most exciting battles in the overall strategy for ensuring our
well-being and prosperity in the future. To win we shall have to have unity of purpose and
the co-operation of every New Zealander, and I believe that this will be forthcoming when
the call is made in the right way.
I now turn my attention to internal matters, because increased flexibility and higher
morale must also apply within New Zealand if an overall strategy of reconstruction of our
economy is to succeed. For too long people have been trying to work, farm, or produce their
way out of financial difficulty and anxiety, but have finished up, even with both parents
working, achieving little and merely heightening the tensions under which they live, partly
because the degree of parental absenteeism and child neglect which their efforts have
involved has produced a maze of self-defeating social problems within their own families and
communities. People are becoming more and more angry and frustrated because the
traditional solution of working harder, or at least longer, is no longer solving family financial
and social problems. I could describe these problems, about which I am as concerned as
anyone, in highly emotional terms, but this has already been well done by others who,
lacking solutions, have had nothing but description to offer. Solutions will be possible only
through a thorough reform of the internal financial structure, and this is also the only way in
which what has been best in New Zealand's economic and social life can be maintained and
enhanced.
A necessary prelude to financial reform is the removal of some persistent myths.
Orthodox politicians might be responsible for the appalling social strain and stress being
faced by more and more people today, but academic economists peddling their myths are the
real architects of the social explosion through which it is likely to find expression. The myth
that has caused the most social damage, because of the excessive financial costs it has piled
upon producers and consumers, has been the repeated assertion that there has been a
continuous increase in the money supply relative to the national income it has to generate.
This has given rise to the popular but thoroughly mistaken belief that inflation and all of its
evils have been caused by too much money chasing too few goods. The excessive money
myth has been sustained only on the basis of a redefinition of the money supply to include
savings and fixed deposits, which is totally untenable because it is not possible, and in fact is
highly illegal, for people to pay for goods and services with bank passbooks.
Contrary to commonly held and carefully cultivated belief, the country's supply of
money, or the country's monetary base, as a percentage of the gross national product and the
national income, has not increased continuously, but has actually declined, by more than 50
percent over the past 20 years. In 1957 a money supply of $586 million was generating a gross
national product of $2,061 million. Therefore the money supply as a percentage of gross
national product was 28.4 percent. By 1977 a money supply of $1,690 million was generating
a gross national product of $12,845 million, which meant that the money supply when related
to the gross national product had declined to 13.2 percent. So although the money supply has
increased in absolute terms, it has declined by more than half in real and relative terms, and

consequentially its speed of turnover has more than doubled from 3.52 to 7.57 in 22 years.
It is the increased scarcity value of money which is imposing steady and relentless
pressure on the social well-being of people. The relative scarcity of money has given power,
privilege, and advantage to those who control it. Money manipulators have become the new
elite in our society, and it is what they take from everyone else that leaves everyone else with
most of their financial problems. Money has achieved a scarcity value, which attracts what is
in effect a form of rent which must be paid by everyone for any and all of the uses money is
required for in a modern economy. The basic money rent is now around 12 percent, and this
interest charge must be paid first before interest rates have any effect in rationing scarce
resources. For this reason young people have to pay crippling interest charges for the money
to purchase a family home. It is these costs against the family, as high as $70 a week, which
constitute a major cause of financial anxiety and stress within the family home of young
married people.
Producers and consumers must pay increasingly higher prices through escalating interest
charges for access to this monetary commodity in short supply, for which, with self-induced
inflation and population increase, there has naturally been an inevitably greater
requirement. The increased price of money has had to be built into the prices of all goods
and services. Every producer has to pay the basic rent for money so as to be able to pay for
wages and raw materials and other running expenses. Investment money has to pay the basic
money rent of 12 percent with a 3 percent margin for risk, and it is this financial pressure
which is the most significant of all in driving up prices because it forces manufacturers, after
allowing for company taxation, to cost the selling price of goods at over 30 percent on the
amount of shareholder capital involved in production. These imposed costs are forced on to
the consumer, who is largely the wage and salary earner.
Fruitless attempts to release financial pressure on wage earners through strike action are
accelerating. The process is the major underlying cause of the near collapse in industrial
relations in this country today. To the extent that neither profits in real terms nor the
purchasing power of take-home pay can be maintained, financial hardship is being forced
upon individual people on both sides of the old industrial and political fences, and as the
process of cost-inflation continues the major beneficiary remains the money manipulator and
the tax gatherer. Under both National and Labour financial policies taxation has been
doubling every 4 years, wages only every 7 years, and all this irrespective of productivity.
This trend simply has to be reversed. The combination of increasing taxation and rising
prices has reduced the purchasing power of take-home pay to the levels of 1963, and these
simply cannot meet the commitments of 1978.
The pressure on single-income families is the greatest of all, and should be eased by
increasing exemptions substantially. The single-income family should not be required to pay
tax on an income of less than $100 a week. The tax penalty for working overtime should be
removed by making all overtime taxable at the one flat rate of 20c in the dollar. Double tax
on company profits has meant that small companies have been deprived of both working and
investment capital. The first $10,000 of company profit should be exempt from company tax.
This would give companies the ability to retain funds within the company and give a positive
incentive to modernise and install new plant and machinery to increase production. Smaller
companies would further benefit from the reintroduction of a graduated company tax on
profits above $10,000 a year. Such a taxation policy would reduce the present pressure on
business to borrow at high interest and would increase the financial capacity of independent
and competitive business to resist takeover by monopolies.
Basically, however, New Zealand's urgent need for tax reform must come by way of a
reduction in the level of taxation, not simply through a redistribution of what has become an
impossible burden for even the average income. Total taxation must be reduced and held
below a maximum ceiling of 35 percent of the gross national product. If a reduction in
taxation means a reduction in the burgeoning bureaucracy which is dominating New
Zealand, so much the better, because it is more than time that an effective system of
decentralisation was applied which allowed people themselves to make their own decisions
through having the means of solving their own problems. What is fundamentally needed is
an increase in the relative money supply, a return at least to the situation that applied 20
years ago, and a corresponding reduction in its speed of turnover. This action, taken
together with a policy to move investment money out of financial speculation and back into
production, would enable, in fact would force, a substantial reduction in interest rates and
take much of the thrust out of the cost-inflationary spiral. The pressure on producers,

workers, families, and individuals would be correspondingly eased.
As the monetary system is reformed to meet individual and social needs, so too can it be
used to initiate a policy of decentralisation and regional development, and to remove the
present confrontation and conflict from industry, and rebuild New Zealand's shattered
industrial relations. Why? Because it will provide the means to initiate worker shareholding
and greater worker participation in industry. Not until we get co-operation through a system
of incentives and involvement, based on a system in which people are responsible for their
own actions, will there be any transformation of our present frightening industrial scene.
Any talk of applying any of these policies without fundamental financial reforms is so much
balderdash because there is no way under the present system that worth-while progress can
be made. New Zealand needs a bold new fresh strategy. Let us make a start with it.

shall recognise the first person whom he sees. I shall now speak about the other Parliaments,

states: "In cases not provided for Mr Speaker to decide. In all cases not hereinafter provided

The Standing Orders are the first guidance in the House. Standing Order 165 reads: "Mr
Speaker calls upon member to speak-when two or more members rise together the member
called upon by Mr Speaker shall be entitled to speak." The Standing Order is amplified by
two or three Speaker's rulings which give the Speaker absolute discretion as to which
member he should call to speak next.
Various Speakers' rulings relate to alternating one side of the House and the other. This
is where the doubt has apparently arisen. One honourable member drew my attention to
Speaker's ruling 60/4 given by the Deputy Speaker Mr George in 1969, which states: "After
the twelfth speaker,"—and so far we have had 13 speakers in this debate so that it would be
at about the same stage of the debate—“a Government member, had completed his speech,
Mr Deputy Speaker gave the call to the Leader of the Social Credit Political League and then
to a member of the Labour Party, and a point of order that the last call should have gone to a
Government member was not sustained." I was also invited to consider procedures from
other Parliaments. If it is necessary to consider the procedure of other Parliaments then I am
happy to do so.
I said earlier that the Standing Orders are my first guide. The next guide I look to is our
Speakers' Rulings, based on the Standing Orders of this House. If those guides are
inadequate, then the Standing Orders require me to turn to the practices and procedures of
the House of Commons in Westminster, and I normally go to Erskine May. If Erskine May is
deficient, and I cannot imagine many cases where he is, and if I want further guidance apart
from my own instinct, whatever it might be, then I could go to another Parliament for a
precedent.
The Junior Opposition Whip invited me to consider the position in 1929. At that time
the House had three parties, as there are now, but then each party was fairly substantial. At
present we have two parties that have substantial numbers and one party that is represented
by one member only, so I believe that the present position is slightly different. As I said
earlier, under Standing Order 165 Mr Speaker has the absolute discretion to decide who of
two or more members competing for the call shall be entitled to speak. It has been the
practice of Speakers for many years to alternate the call between members on opposite sides
of the House, that is between the Government party and the Opposition party.
I turn to Mr Speaker Barnard's ruling 60/2: "If two members rise from opposite sides
simultaneously, the Speaker calls on the member from that side of the House opposite to
that from which the last speaker rose." Now, did he mean physically that side or that side, or
did he mean in terms of the political array of the parties-I think he probably meant the

latter. Speaker's ruling 61/1 is a ruling in 1948 by Mr Speaker McKeen: "The Speaker may

Mr Speaker Jack's ruling given in 1969 in that case is further amplified by references to
Hansard.
The maintenance of the principle of the alternation of calls requires that consideration
be given to the effect that the calling of a third party member has on the sequence of
Government and Opposition calls. The position differs according to whether the third party
has a substantial representation, which was the case before 1936, or whether, as in the period
1967 to 1969, the third party consists of only one member. That situation of course applies
today, and will be considered here.
The ruling given by Mr Deputy Speaker George, in effect, disregarded the third party.
for the purpose of calculating the alternation of calls. The sequence in that case ran National,
Social Credit, Labour. It was argued that the third speaker in that sequence should have
been a National speaker to preserve the alternation of Government and Opposition
speakers. The Deputy Speaker did not sustain that point but relied strongly on his absolute
discretion to decide the call under the Standing Orders, and that is what he did. The method
of rotating calls on a Government and official Opposition basis, and ignoring for this purpose
any third party speakers who might be interposed, would be one method of solving the
problem. But it seems that the decision of the Deputy Speaker of that time was not in line
with the practice adopted in the House on other occasions in 1967 to 1969.
If we look to Hansard, Volume 364, we find at pages 3807 to 3811 and 3855 to 3859 the
practice outlined by the then Leader of the Opposition, the late Mr Kirk, in speaking to the
point of order. He said: "The practice has been to alternate the call as though the member
for Hobson"-that was the member for the Social Credit Political League-“was an
Opposition member, although he is not a member of the majority Opposition party.” Mr
Kirk conceded that in these circumstances it would be the turn of the Government member
to be called. In fact, I believe it was the member for Hawke's Bay at that time. Mr Speaker
Jack on the same page confirmed the correctness of this summary of the position, stating that
he had treated the then member for Hobson as a member of the Opposition, though not of
the major Opposition party. I think it can be said that Mr Speaker Jack's practice in 1967 to
1969 in a similar situation to that which has now arisen was notional, to divide the House into
two groups for the purpose of speaking. This does not apply to the special provisions that the
member for Mt Albert referred to, which relate to the Standing Orders-the introduction of
Bills, and one or two other matters. They are different.
Hon. W. W. Freer: They are still a problem.
Mr SPEAKER: They are very much a problem, and I hope the Whips from each side
will come to some amicable arrangement and advise me on it so that I can put it to the House
as a procedure to be followed. Returning to Mr Speaker Jack's ruling, with the Government
party, the official Opposition party, and the third party, the call was alternated among those
groups. As Sir Roy pointed out, there is a certain equity in this solution as it tends to even up
the groups that are to be balanced against each other for the purposes of debate.
It is always open to the Government, with its superior numbers, to prolong a debate
after very member of the Opposition has spoken, and indeed in Address in Reply and
Budget debates when members seek the call, the natural preponderance of Government
members is manifest. Because on many occasions the Government does not seek to assert
this superiority, the official Opposition has tended to assume it will naturally receive an
equal number of calls to that of the Government, but having regard to the disparity of
numbers between the two groups there is no natural equity in that. The members of the
official Opposition party will not always lose the opportunity of speaking, but it is not to be
expected that the third party member would seek the call in every debate, or, if he did, that it
would be granted.

inflexible, and it was incapable of meeting the demands of the trading world.

is a vast improvement on a barter system. It is also interesting that, although the Social

represented the same political persuasion as himself who said in 1967 that demand inflation
was too much money chasing too few goods. If the policy of the new member for Rangitikei
were pursued, we would double the money supply and we would unquestionably have too
much money chasing too few goods. It is as simple as that, and I am sure the honourable
member, even without thinking very hard about it or for very long, will come to that
conclusion. If he does not, I invite him to put together a piece of paper-or his research

Mr HUNT (New Lynn): The New Zealand Parliament has fallen into disrepute, not

listened to when they express their concern.

were passed, some at breakneck speed and some when Parliament was not even being
broadcast. Some Acts were so complex that many members of Parliament had only the
vaguest notion of what they were about. I believe that Parliament should be broadcast not

that there can be no doubt in anyone's mind about what is going on in this place, the highest
court in the land and, one would hope, the place where all persons who have a vote have, by
the process of election, selected members to represent them and to pass laws on their behalf.

be no consideration of legislation after midnight deserves serious consideration. Although
there may be occasion for some debate to continue late right at the end of a session,

legislation should be considered after midnight only by resolution of the House passed by the
unanimous vote of members. In 1977, 337 regulations were passed by the Executive Council.

should be done now. We could invite submissions from all interested members of the public,
and heed should be paid to experts in the field. Parliamentary practices overseas should be
examined and adopted where they have been proven to be superior to those used in New
Zealand. Next, I think the general aim of any Government should be to have legislation
passed unhurriedly. I agree that urgent financial Bills and imprest supply Bills must be
passed as soon as they are introduced into the House, for very obvious reasons. However,
apart from that type of Bill, I believe all measures should be sent to select committees as of
right, even when consideration and scrutiny of the provisions would be minimal.
I shall now discuss briefly parliamentary select committees in general. As was the
practice of the third Labour Government and as is the practice to some extent-although not
to the same extent of the present Government, I feel that select committee hearings should
be open to the news media for the hearing of evidence, except in the most exceptional
circumstances and where not one opposition voice in Parliament is raised in objection. When
people who wish to make submissions are unable to travel, select committees should be able
to do the travelling to meet the people. That, too, is done occasionally, but not often
enough. Far too often we tend to get laws which reflect Government departments in

Wellington and not the wishes of people in Invercargill, Whangarei, or some other area
outside Wellington.
We must examine the whole code of parliamentary privilege. The present system
enables a Government majority to bestow any decision it wishes on any member of
Parliament or member of the public. It would surprise some members if they went through
the present Standing Orders and Acts governing Parliament. A Privileges Committee of this
House, with the support of the House through a simple majority, is able to imprison any
person in New Zealand for any period it may wish. I do not think Parliament should act as a
court in this way. Parliamentary privilege should be determined by a truly independent
committee. This would mean that, before a decision could be arrived at, representatives
from both sides of the House, Government and Opposition-with both a small and a capital
"o"-would need to reach some measure of agreement.
I again advocate fixing, at least 1 year in advance, the days when Parliament meets. In
Australia and I checked this over the weekend with a colleague in the Australian Senate-
every sitting day between now and Christmas is already known to every member of the
Australian House of Representatives and the Australian Senate. In New Zealand we should
introduce the practice of fixing dates so that Parliament would be in session for 3 days a
week, 3 weeks a month, 10 months a year. That would enable select committee work to be
done satisfactorily. By putting two 3-week periods together, we would have occasional 2-
week recesses, 1 week of which could be used for select committee study and the other for
what will become increasingly important in the next 10 years, the work a member is required
to do in his own electorate. At present, members of Parliament are overworked and under-
rewarded in terms of the services they receive from the State. I am referring specifically to
the secretarial service that should be available to every member of Parliament in the
electorate in which he or she serves.
Another major proposal I wish to advance is to take a leaf out of President Jimmy
Carter's book and set up a special select committee of Parliament to examine a "sunset"
proposal and see how best it could be implemented in New Zealand. President Carter's
"sunset" proposal requires every Act and regulation of the United States Government, the
most powerful and wealthiest in the world, to be re-examined on a regular basis. I have
forgotten the exact term, but I think he said that every regulation and every enactment
should be re-examined every 20 years and 40 years respectively. To me that seems a sensible
suggestion. There may have to be modifications to suit New Zealand conditions, but I put
forward the suggestion tonight in the belief that we must take a much closer look at past
parliamentary practices and, if necessary, change old ways when new ones are needed.
Mr Birch: Is that Labour Party policy?
Mr HUNT: Yes, it is Labour Party policy to examine in detail the type of proposal I am
putting forward tonight-that is, the appointment of a select committee of the House, on
which the Senior Government Whip could be represented if his leader chose him. I think it
would be a good idea to have a representative of the Whips from each side on such a
committee. I want to emphasise again that the future conduct of our democracy lies in
Parliament itself.
Parliament is an institution which I hope every member in this House dearly cherishes
as, if not the most perfect this world has thought of yet, at least as an institution which has
made fewer mistakes compared with other systems of government either in communist
countries or capitalist dictatorships. I stress that in future Parliament must be prepared to
take stock of changes that are occurring. We have a more literate population than we had 40
years ago, and we must be prepared to give those people who are highly articulate the
opportunity to express their point of view and opinion within a democratic and non-violent
framework. We can do this without having the kind of disruption seen in other countries,
such as Italy, which has been forced into disruption because its constitution has not kept up
with modern times. We are lucky. We have the British style of constitution which has a great
deal of flexibility, the type of constitution which enables every member of Parliament to
participate in its updating and modernising. I hope we take the opportunity in the time left to
us this year to do something which will be for the good not just of us in this Parliament but of
all New Zealanders; not just for those who are here now but also for those who will come in
the future.

GOVERNMENT RAILWAYS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Railways): I move, That the
Government Railways Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is a short one designed to
introduce to the Railways Department the system of continuous regrading of salaried
positions in line with the system operating in Government departments directly controlled by
the State Services Commission. For the past 50 years the Railways Department has been
obliged under the Act to review the gradings of all salaried division positions every 5 years,
but, following the 1971 regrading, it was decided that it would be more appropriate to adopt
a continuous review of positions as carried out in the State services. The Railway Officers
Institute accepted that the 1976 quinquennial review would be the last of its kind, after which
continuous regrading would be introduced. The Bill gives effect to that agreement, and
follows largely on the recommendations of a working party established by the department
and the Railway Officers Institute.
The system of continuous regrading has proved most worth while in the State services. It
avoids the administrative bottlenecks that arise when all positions are regraded at one time


## p. 136 (#144) ############################################

136
19 May
Government Railways Amendment Bill
by spreading regrading and the hearing of appeals throughout the 5-year period. The
introduction of this system has the full support of the Railway Officers Institute, and I
believe it will provide considerable improvements in the administration of the salaried
division and also considerable benefits to staff, by ensuring that positions are regularly
reviewed and that appeals are not delayed.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): The Minister said that the contents of the Bill had
been discussed with the Railway Officers Instiute. I have not yet had a chance to read the
Bill but I did listen to what the Minister said. This is the first indication that this proposal was
to come before the House. Does this affect only salaried staff of the Railways services? The
Minister referred only to the railway officers. Could he expand on the continual regrading
system? What is meant by continual regrading? He said that the State Service organisations
have this system operating now. Could he clarify the effect this will have on the railway
workers?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Railways): It will affect all people who
were regraded every 5 years. The reclassification was made every 5 years, and in many cases
promotions were held up during that period. The continuous regrading that has been in
operation very successfully throughout the State services means there is no hold-up. Under
the old 5-year period, appeals were delayed for a long time. With the continuous regrading
system they can appeal immediately, with no hold-up. The appeals are spread throughout
the year, whereas under the 5-year system they all came at once, and it took a long time to
process them. The member asked whether the system applied only to salaried staff. It applies
to all graded personnel in the Railways Department; the system merely changes from
operating every 5 years to operating continuously. There is no change at all in the personnel
affected.
Mr KIRK (Sydenham): Although the Minister said that the change would affect all
Railways Department staff, the Bill states that only the salaried division will be affected. Has
this come about because of the diminishing responsibility of the railways in the New Zealand
transport system? Is it necessary to have this reclassification of duties on an annual basis
because some of the duties have diminished as a result of the reduction in rail services? Have
some people lost their jobs because of closures of branch lines and reduced rail services?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Railways): I am at a loss to understand
what the member means, and I do not think he understands either. Nobody mentioned
anything about an annual regrading. I said it was a continuous regrading system rather than a
5-yearly one. It has nothing to do with branch lines closing or anything like that. It is merely
conforming to the same system that applies throughout the State services.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): The Minister has had extensive discussions with the
Railway Officers Institute, which accepts the legislation as proposed. I have had a chance to
read the explanatory note in the Bill, which includes the statement that "section 87A
provides that every member of the salaried division has the right to apply at any time to the
general manager for a review of the position which he occupies". Under the Government
Railways Act the Minister has the final right to decide an appeal; the railway worker can go
direct to the Minister after exhausting every other avenue under the Act if he disagrees with
his grading or conditions. Is the general manager to take over this responsibility from the
Minister? If so, I should be a little concerned. The system over the years under which
Ministers have virtually had the right to determine the ultimate decision on a complaint or a
regrading has been a good one. I do not know of any other State organisation that gives this
right to its Minister, but I have found that it has worked exceedingly well over the years, and
most people have accepted that the Minister is the final appeal authority-if I could use that
term.
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Railways): The right of appeal will be
just as it is now.

QUESTIONS-ORAL
Oil Exploration-Great South Basin
1. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Energy: Following recent publicity
that the Government's "think tank" on energy has poured cold water on exploitation of any


## p. 137 (#145) ############################################

19 May
137
Questions-Oral
oil found in the Great South Basin, will he confirm that no further drilling in this area will
receive Government financial support?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The answer is no. It is true that technology is
not yet available to produce petroleum commercially from water depths in excess of 2 000
feet, but it is equally true that rapid advances are being made. A discovery in very deep
water would present problems at this time, both technically and because of the cost in
establishing production, but it is highly desirable that the search should go on. If New
Zealand has large petroleum reserves, we need to know about them to properly plan our
energy future. The problems and cost of deep water petroleum production could be less
difficult to solve than those associated with the production of energy from non-conventional
sources, at present being extensively investigated.
Mr W. R. Austin: Has there been any indication that substantial quantities of oil exist in
this area, and that the present delay sought by the Government will be useful in advancing
that technology?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The Government has not sought a delay. Over the years it has been

Bastion Point Proposals
3. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) to the Minister of Lands: Can he tell the House what final
land proposals have been reached with the Ngati Whatua elders for Bastion Point, and are
they satisfied that the Government's offer is fair?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): As I announced in a public statement on 27
February, agreement has been reached with representatives of the former beneficial owners
on final land proposals for Bastion Point. These proposals include the addition of
approximately 12 hectares to the Orakei Domain, the reservation of approximately 0.5
hectares for community facilities, a site for the Youthline Trust in Kupe Street, an addition
to the burial ground in Okahu Bay, approximately 2 hectares for high density housing
development, and the balance of approximately 12 hectares to be vested in a trust board
representative of the three Hapu of the Ngati Whatua to be established for this purpose.
These were the basic recommendations of a joint planning study established and conducted
through a steering committee representing the Maori people, the city council, the Auckland
Regional Authority, and the Crown. The Maori people, with their elders, enthusiastically
accepted the Government's proposals, and indicated that the solution represented a fair and
generous decision by the Government.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the Minister's reply that the proposals met with satisfaction,
would he not confirm that a great deal of unnecessary distress has been caused because some
of the proposals have not met with the approval of all the people concerned?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I know there is some unnecessary distress, but only a very small
number of people are involved. Most of the elders accepted with gratitude the decision made
by the joint planning committee and accepted by the Government.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: How many elders concurred with the
agreement, who were they, and where and under what circumstances was the agreement
finally reached?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am unable to identify the elders individually, but I do know that
when the Minister for Maori Affairs returned to New Zealand a meeting was held with as
many of the people with a beneficial interest as possible, the Minister of Maori Affairs, the
Prime Minister, and myself, and the Government accepted in principle the proposals put
forward by the steering committee. When the people were informed of the Government's
acceptance, they stood and sang their appreciation of a decision long sought and finally
made.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the Minister's reply that the Minister of Maori Affairs and he,
as Minister of Lands, met some of those elders, why did the Government find it necessary to
meet on a matter of public moment behind locked doors, with security guards on the doors?

Petrol-Lead Content
14. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister for the Environment: Does the
Government intend to take any steps to reduce the lead content of New Zealand petrol?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): The motor vehicles committee of
the Clean Air Council recommended in 1974 that the lead content in petrol be progressively
reduced to a level of 0.68 g per litre by 1980, pending the expansion of New Zealand's only
oil refinery. It was recommended that the refinery be designed to produce petrol with an
initial maximum lead figure of 0.45 g per litre. New Zealand is dependent for its petrol upon
the Marsden Point refinery, but its present design features limit its technological flexibility.
The planned extensions to the refinery could present the opportunity to provide the
flexibility needed to reduce the level of lead in petrol.
Mr Prebble: As there is now a recommendation to reduce the lead level in New Zealand
petrol, and bearing in mind that the New Zealand level is double that of petrol used in
America and Europe, when will practical steps be taken to reduce the lead content in New
Zealand petrol?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: As I have already indicated, this will depend on proposals to
extend the Marsden Point refinery. The question will be considered then. The octane rating
of petrol is affected by a reduction in the lead content; there is not the same return.
Mr Prebble: Do I take it that the Government has not yet accepted the recommendation
to reduce the lead content level, and is the Minister aware that this is having a serious effect
on pollution in Christchurch, as reported in the New Zealand Herald of 2 May 1978?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That supplementary question contains two questions. The
Minister may answer one if he wishes-if he can.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am not sure which question the member wants me to give priority
to. No firm decision has yet been made on the actual reduction in the level of lead. Any
move on the recommendations of the motor vehicles committee of the Clean Air Council is
tied up with expansion proposals for the Marsden Point refinery.
United Nations-Council for Namibia
15. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Will he inform
the House why the New Zealand representatives to the United Nations did not vote in
favour of the declaration and programme of action proposed by the working group of the
Council for Namibia?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The New Zealand delegation
to the special session of the United Nations on Namibia abstained in the vote on the
declaration and programme of action. This was not so much because of what the document
contained but because of what it did not contain. In particular, it made no reference to the
strenuous efforts by five Western members of the Security Council-Canada, France, the
Federal Republic of Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States-to reach a
negotiated solution to the Namibian question. The vote on the declaration and programme
of action was adopted by 119 votes, with New Zealand and 20 other Western countries
abstaining.
Mr Talbot: Is New Zealand's action in voting against the declaration and the
programme of action the type of responsible action that could lead to an early and
satisfactory solution to this international problem?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: New Zealand abstained in the vote because no
acknowledgment was made of the work done by the five Western countries I mentioned, and
the vote was set in juxtaposition to a promulgation of the idea that the use of force was the
only solution to the problem.
Mr Hunt: Did the five countries mentioned by the Minister also abstain in the vote?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes.
Mr Prebble: As there appears to be some confusion about the word "abstain", could the
Minister of Foreign Affairs explain to his Junior Whip the difference between abstaining and
voting against something?
Mr SPEAKER: That question is too frivolous.

Monetary Base M1
17. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) to the Minister of Finance: What have the increases in the
monetary base M1 been over the past 5 years in New Zealand?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): The monetary base and M1 are
distinct concepts. The monetary base can be defined in a number of ways, but its essential
characteristic is that it comprises certain liabilities of the Reserve Bank and the Government
that perform the function of being reserve assets of the financial system. M1 refers to the
money supply of the public, and consists of those liabilities of the financial system that are in
general use by the public for the settlement of transactions. In New Zealand, M1 comprises
notes and coins held by the public, trading bank demand deposits (excluding Government
deposits and net deposits of the other "selected financial institutions") and savings banks
personal cheque accounts. Annual increases in M1 over the past 5 years have been as
follows. Year ended December 1973, annual change $256.6 million, an increase of 22
percent; 1974, $14.2 million, an increase of 1 percent; 1975, $144.2 million, an increase of 10
percent; 1976, $211.6 million, an increase of 13.4 percent; and 1977, $28.1 million, an
increase of 1.6 percent. This represents an average annual increase of 9.3 percent over the 5-
year period.
Mr Falloon: Has the steadying down of the increase in the M1 figure helped the
economy in the last 12 months?
Mr SPEAKER: That is seeking an opinion.
Mr Falloon: May I rephrase the question? What has been the effect of these changes on
the economy over the last few years?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: As part of the general monetary policy to bring greater
restraint into the economy they have been extremely successful.
Mr Beetham: Notwithstanding that there has been an increase in the monetary base of
the economy M1 over the past 5 years, will the Minister concede that there has been a
contraction in the monetary base M1 as a percentage of national income over the past 5
years, bearing in mind that national income is supply times velocity?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am not sure what the member is getting at. It is clear that
the total monetary supply has contracted as a percentage of national income, but that does
not take into account changes in attitudes to money, the use of money, and the velocity of
circulation-and the member is aware of that.

NAFTA-Apparel Exports
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he seen


## p. 146 (#154) ############################################

146
19 May
Questions-Oral
the comments of the secretary of the Clothing Trades Employees Union, Mr Frank Thorn, in
the Evening Post of 2 May, in which he claimed that the Government under NAFTA,
"allowed the Australians to come over here and sell us everything but the Sydney Harbour
Bridge", and, if so, will he state what arrangements have been agreed to in respect of
apparal exports into the countries under NAFTA, and what sendings of garments have
resulted?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: I did see Mr
Thorn's remarks, which I considered very misleading. The arrangement originally made with
Australia relating to apparel involved the creation of a special quota by Australia for New
Zealand at the level of our best export performance, which was 3 900 000 garments in the
calendar year 1976. The arrangement has since been renewed, and guarantees New Zealand
exporters a share of the Australian market while in addition allowing them to compete for a
share of the global quotas.
The recent renewal gives assurances of the continuation of New Zealand exports during
the life of the Australian global quota system, currently due to expire in mid 1980. In return
New Zealand granted access to the New Zealand market for Australian clothing and reduced
duties to 15 percent. Previously Australia had had to compete for a share of our global
import licences. The new duty structure is more in line with those imposed by Australia on
New Zealand apparel, which vary between 6 and 16 percent. The arrangement creates
special positions for each country's clothing exporters in the other market while at the same
time maintaining control over the quantities traded to ensure that harm is not caused to the
domestic industries. On an annual basis the trade is currently running 20 to 1 in New
Zealand's favour, with exports around 4 000 000 garments and imports around 200,000
garments.

Railways Freight Tonnage
6. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Transport: What was the total
freight tonnage carried by the New Zealand Railways in the financial years ended (a) March
1977, (b) March 1978, and can he express the tonnage for the last financial year as a
percentage increase or decrease in tonnage over the former; and can he confirm that there
has been a marked decrease in tonnage carried since 1 October 1977, when the new 150 km
road-rail competition limits came into effect?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Railways) replied: The total freight
carried by New Zealand Railways for the financial year ended 31 March 1977 amounted to
13 600 000 tonnes. The figures for 1978 have not yet been finalised; however, it is estimated
that the total tonnage conveyed was 12 600 000 tonnes, a decrease of about 1 000 000
tonnes, or 7.3 percent. A decrease in the tonnage being conveyed first became evident
during July 1977. This was evident in all types of traffic and over all distances, and is
attributable to a general decline in demand and to industrial action, including rolling
stoppages, in many industries. The decline did increase after the extension in the road limit
to 150 kilometres but again over all distances.

South Pacific Forum Members-Import Licensing
9. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is the Government making
any endeavour to identify what proportion of exports or potential exports from the Island
members of the South Pacific Forum is subject to tariff or import licensing barriers in New
Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: The
Government has identified that in the year ended June 1977, 8.3 percent of New Zealand's
imports from the Island members of the South Pacific Forum were subject to duty. In
addition, most of the imports subject to duty entered at preferences of up to 20 percent
under New Zealand's generalised system of preferences. Concerning import licensing, 13.3
percent of the imports from these countries in the same period were subject to licensing. A
working party of officials is currently examining the question of access for Island products to
the New Zealand market. This will involve a study of potential exports for Island members
of the South Pacific Forum.

Industrial Mediation Service
11. Mr ELLIOT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Labour: Is he satisfied that the industrial
mediation service is adequately staffed, and is it now in a position to act in cases of incipient
trouble before a dispute arises?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replies: When I assumed office there were two
mediators based in Wellington and one in Auckland. It was clear that this number of
mediators was fully committed in coping with the heavy case load of current disputes
referred to them and this in turn prevented the service from dealing with cases of incipient
trouble which could have led to disputes. Since I assumed office two additional mediators
have been appointed. There are now two mediators in both Auckland and Wellington and
one in Dunedin. The appointment of these additional mediators has enabled the service to
extend its activities into the area of assisting industry to improve industrial relations with the
aim of minimising disruption. The work load of the service is constantly reviewed, and if the
need arises consideration will be given to the appointment of additional mediators.
