Wairarapa has much to commend it. Unfortunately, there has been little to cheer up the
Wairarapa people this year. The area has come through the worst season for primary
production. The farmers have had one disaster after another—a long wet winter swinging
into a long hot summer, with no break for recovery and growth for feedstock. I want
Opposition members to listen to what I have to say.
In the early stages areas north and west of the Wairarapa had enough feed, but soon
that vanished. During the first month donations of hay and grazing from farmers in
unaffected areas, and the spirit behind these gifts, carried local farmers through the difficult
period. I congratulate the Minister of Police, who comes from one of the areas not affected
that gave donations of hay to the farmers in the Wairarapa. By the end of October most
farmers had exhausted their reserves of hay and silage. With pastures severely damaged by
floods and with poor growth conditions the efforts of Wairarapa farmers to cope on their
own was not always enough. The average amount of hay made was between 40 percent and
50 percent of the normal quantity. Many of the worst hit properties were unable to make


## p. 153 (#161) ############################################

19 May
153
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
hay. This meant that farmers had to buy feed for their immediate needs, as well as for the
coming winter. At the same time the exceptionally dry summer wrecked extra feed crops, so
farmers had extremes of weather against them. Butterfat returns from dairy farms seemed to
be better than at first expected but soon they vanished, and, related to the costs of feed and
extra crops, brought in very poor returns.
Hill country and coastal farmers watched their hills turn into mud and slide into the
valleys, and then turn to parched concrete with dead grass and failing water supplies. On
most of the properties the first and only possible action was to reduce stock numbers. The
Wairarapa beef-breeding herds are likely to be reduced by several thousand animals before
the season ends, which is another blow to New Zealand exports as well as to local farmers.
Beef cattle were the first to disappear; because of winter pasture damage and poor hill-
country water supplies, the only option was to reduce the number of cattle. Some were sent
elsewhere for grazing, and are still away, but for most their final destination was the works.
With no significant rain and little grass growth, sheep feed supplies became critical. By mid
February this year in Masterton County about 60 farmers were daily feeding nuts to sheep to
try to hold out, in anticipation of the rain that eventually came.
Members of the industry were not sitting back and waiting for Government handouts.
Wairarapa farmers fought back with every means they had, but the odds this year were too
great for many. Most have pushed ahead with fertiliser applications, so that when the rains
came the grass growth would not be retarded. They have, with the co-operation of local
bodies, even grazed herds on roadsides to make the best possible use of the little grass that
was available. Farmers did not ask for help until they had done all they possibly could
themselves. If we review farming in the Wairarapa, we find pastures damaged by stock trying
to survive in the most prolonged bad weather in the region's history. We find there are too
many animals to be fed by the greatly reduced amount of feed, and the reduced income
prevents farmers from paying their way out of the disaster. Much of the pasture damage is
now under control, and many farmers are geared to cultivation and resowing, or oversowing,
when the weather permits. Many are relying on the Government's regrassing subsidy of 50
percent of the cost up to $40 per acre.
For many farmers the main problem is too much stock, not because of overstocking, but
because the freezing industry has been unable to cope with killing demands in this
unforeseen situation. This is not only a local problem; it is fairly common along the east
coast. While I recognise the need for spreading the efficient use of capital over the year in
the freezing industry, this does not appear to take into account the large amount of capital
tied up in farms. As a guide, the capital tied up in one freezing works would be about the
same as that tied up in 60 farms. In seasons like this latest one, there is not much we can do
to abate the effect of prolonged adverse weather. The only option is to expand and make
more flexible our ability to cull our fat stock when this is made necessary by the weather,
even at comparatively short notice. This is the only way our farmers-and through them our
community and our nation-can survive and progress. When farmers must spend $10,000 or
more-and some of them had to-to buy feed for the stock numbers that the country is
urging them to increase, it is time to look at what co-operation the rest of the community is
giving them.
There is one bright facet here. Government assistance was prompt and willing. The
Minister of Agriculture promised, and gave, immediate help when the scope of the disaster
was known. He visited the Wairarapa to make a first-hand assessment of the problem. After
a little persuasion another colleague, the Minister of Works and Development, was also
convinced the problem was as bad as I had reported, and not merely an exaggeration by a
parochial-minded back-bencher.
Finally, Wairarapa farmers would also want me to thank the climatic relief committee,
which did such an outstandingly successful job on a scale larger than any help we have
needed before. In the short term, our agricultural prospects are dominated by the persistent
effects of last winter's severe flooding, compounded by the subsequent drought. This means
we shall have fewer beef cattle in the future. I am told that between 10 000 and 20 000 cattle
will be replaced by sheep over the next few years. Stock numbers are unlikely to increase for
another year or two, but then the annual growth rate of about 2 percent should be achieved
again. This will bring us back to the average stock growth numbers for the whole country.
I know the adequacy of stock-killing facilities is a contentious issue that could be
accentuated by a substantial shift from cattle to sheep, and the rising transport costs that are
in prospect. One possible solution to the industrial discord that has plagued freezing works,
and aggravated already severe farming problems, is to combine the best principles of

member for Roskill-who is promising us so much-was Minister of Labour, over $50

The cause of the recent industrial dispute was clearly an attempt by some sectors of the

discretion to suspend workers who cannot be kept in work which they normally perform
because of strike activity. That is an important provision in our legislation. It is a provision
that gives some sort of control over rolling strikes that some union sectors want to hold. The
Labour Party supports that sector of unions, and has said so publicly.
The Government stood firm. The Prime Minister made it clear that there would be no
financial support for Kawerau unless Government policy was followed in broad terms. He

constructive settlement that one person has described as the dawn of a new era for the
Tasman company and its workers. The important point is that it has solved not only the
dispute in question, but also went a long way towards solving many of the basic problems at
Kawerau. The member for Roskill gave the House half the truth about the agreement
reached. I shall tell the House and the country the whole truth.
The agreement comprised a number of clauses. It provides: "Each union will confer
with the other unions before notifying the company of any industrial action which could
result in suspension of other workers. The union in dispute must notify the company at least
1 week before planned industrial action. The company will then meet all other unions to
review the dispute in the hope of preventing a stoppage of work, or, if this is not possible,


## p. 159 (#167) ############################################

19 May
159
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
minimising any possible suspensions. To this end available work will be shared to equalise
the impact of suspensions as far as practicable. This could require a transfer of workers from
their normal tasks to other work performed by members of their own union. The company
will endeavour to find useful work to defer suspension of workers as long as possible. The
company, for its part, will give a week's notice of any suspensions resulting from industrial
action, but not to members of the union taking industrial action."
That is a good formula for resolving disputes and preventing them from reaching the
type of confrontation situation we have had. In fact, the settlement reached will work. The
final provision in the settlement, which the member for Roskill conveniently forgot, is that if
a union takes industrial action without taking all reasonable steps to comply with the agreed
procedures, then the company is relieved of having to give notice before suspending other
workers under the agreement. The type of agreement reached in Kawerau has been made
possible only by the suspension provisions in the National Government's legislation. Those
provisions have enabled the negotiation of a firm and fair agreement to materialise.
Clearly, in the future, in a place such as Kawerau, early discussions will assist in the

agreement by negotiation, and made a strike inevitable. Every responsible employer
organisation was appalled by the passage of the regulations. In March the unions and the
employers went into conciliation, certain that a deadlock, which the Government had
engineered, would result.
I draw the Government's attention to the Industrial Relations Act, which is printed in
the 1973 edition of New Zealand Statutes. I wonder whether the Government knows that this
Act exists. Section 84, which covers deadlocks in conciliation, states: "If a dispute of interest
is not settled and is not withdrawn in the course of an inquiry before a conciliation council
the conciliator shall refer the dispute to the Commission for settlement." That section says
nothing about sending it to the Prime Minister's Department. However, the Prime Minister
and his department decided they would have a go at settling the dispute, and the first thing
they did was insist that the freezing companies disclose their profits. I am no great friend of
freezing companies, but I am a friend of the law and believe that it should be followed by
everybody, including the Government.
The freezing companies were still in conciliation when the request for information on
their profits was made, and, for the benefit of the Government, I quote from section 77(11):
"No person shall be bound at any inquiry before the council to give evidence with regard to
trade secrets, profits, losses, receipts, or outgoings in his business, or in respect of his
financial position, or to produce the books kept by him in connection with his business."
That is the law, yet the first action taken by the Prime Minister's Department was to insist
that those books be produced. Rumour hath it that when the Government was reminded of
section 77(11) of the Industrial Relations Act the Minister of Finance said he might order a
tax audit. President Nixon used that tactic on his political opponents with intimidating effect.
That is not the way industrial law should be carried out, and, if the rumour is correct, it is
outrageous. I say that as someone who has severe criticism for the freezing companies, but I
believe they are entitled to the protection of the law if they have to follow it.
I turn to what happened next. On 16 March the Government stopped talking to the
employers and decided to talk only to the unions. The Government decided—I understand
that it was the Prime Minister who decided, and that the Minister of Labour had very little to
do with it-to thrash out a union settlement on its own. I draw attention to another section of
the Industrial Relations Act that the Government should have read. Section 146 reads:
"Obstruction of conciliation council, Commission, or Court-Every person who prints or
publishes anything calculated to obstruct or in any way interfere with or prejudicially affect
any matter before a conciliation council, the Commission, or the Industrial Court is liable on
conviction by the Industrial Court to a fine not exceeding $200." Is the Government going to
send the Prime Minister to the Industrial Court? The parties were still in conciliation. Then
one of the parties was taken out of conciliation and the other party, with the Prime Minister,
made a half-baked agreement. That was the settlement that gave $3.5 million. It did not
cover everything, but only a minute part of the total settlement.
Freezing industry awards and settlements in the freezing industry go back to the 1930s,
when the chains were introduced. This half-baked agreement takes no notice of traditional
relativities, bonuses, piecework payments, and the like. The freezing industry's complete
payment system has been thrown into chaos. We will hear more about this—not just until the
election, but for the next 10 years. Members opposite were elected on a law and order
policy, to give leadership.

Rural Intermediate Credit Amendment Bill
TUESDAY, 23 MAY 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
RURAL INTERMEDIATE CREDIT AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): I move, That the Rural Intermediate Credit Amendment Bill be introduced.
The original Act was passed in 1927. This short Bill is required to remove an anomaly that
now exists between interest rates that can be charged to borrowers, mainly sharemilkers, by
rural intermediate credit associations and the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation of
New Zealand, and the opportunity is being taken to give effect to some minor administrative
changes.
Subclause (1) of clause 2 of the Bill provides that the maximum rate of interest to be
charged by associations when on lending will be fixed from time to time by the Rural Bank.
The removal of this anomaly will permit the rural intermediate credit associations to charge
the same rate to their borrowers as is charged to those who borrow direct from the Rural
Bank. Subclause (2) of clause 2 is a validating subclause because some loans made by
associations since the 1977 Budget have been at interest rates of up to 7 percent, although
the actual rate charged may be as low as 6 percent. The aforesaid rate of 7 percent exceeds
the allowable limit of 7 percent, which is now amended by the preceding subclause (1), and
subclause (2) is necessary to regularise the position. Clause 3 transfers into the principal Act
provisions relating to the terms and conditions on which these loans may be granted, which
are at present contained in the Finance Act 1932-33 (No. 2). This action will allow the
Finance Act 1932-33 (No. 2) to be repealed later.
Clause 4 is a procedural matter that extends the time for the regulations to be laid
before the House from 14 days to the now common 28 days. Although 50 associations were
established under the original Act, only 4 now exist: Hamilton, Hauraki, Matamata, and
Morrinsville. The rural intermediate credit associations deal almost exclusively with the
lending to dairy farmers' sharemilkers, and the terms and conditions of the loan, including
the interest rate, have traditionally been granted on the same basis as those of the Rural
Bank. The associations are funded directly by the Rural Bank, which allows for a 1 percent
margin to cover managerial expenses. The current Rural Bank lending rate to sharemilkers
for the initial purchase of stock and plant is 7 percent, rebated to 6 percent for the first 3
years, and the repayment term is normally 5 years. The existing legislation restricts the
associations to a maximum interest rate of 7 percent, and the Bill removes this anomaly.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): The Bill appears to validate the
National Government's policy of increasing interest rates.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Could we have a discussion on whether the Bill should or should
not be introduced, not a discussion about interest rates, or the Government's policy on
interest rates.
Hon. W. W. Freer: A point of order, Mr Speaker. With due respect, I draw attention to
the fact that the purpose of the Bill is to vary the interest rates charged to farmers, especially
sharemilkers. I think, therefore, it is necessary for the Minister and the Government to
explain why such a Bill is necessary at a time when we have been given an indication that
interest rates might be moving in the other direction.
Mr SPEAKER: It is pertinent to ask questions of the Minister about why the Bill should
be introduced, but that does not open up the whole subject of interest rates, and the
Government's policy on interest rates, at this stage. Such a discussion on interest rates as
they relate to the Rural Intermediate Credit Amendment Bill would, I think, be appropriate
in the second reading. I know this has been a very difficult and vexed question in the House
for many years. However, I think more time than was contemplated by the Standing Orders
is being spent on the introduction of Bills. I earnestly ask honourable members to address
themselves to the question before the House-whether the Bill should or should not be
introduced.

Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance

down for the Rural Bank.

opportunity, therefore, to express its views at a formative stage of the negotiations. Our
special concern was that this would create a precedent for the future, especially in relation to
treaties of greater concern to New Zealand, such as a comprehensive test-ban treaty. In the
light of possible changes expressed by member States at the session, the Government
proposes to keep the question of signature under review.
Mr Prebble: Is one of the reasons the New Zealand Government has refused to sign the
environmental modification convention, supported by the Committee on Disarmament, the
fact that nuclear warships are allowed into New Zealand ports, and the convention would
prevent their entry?
Rt. Hon. B. É. TALBOYS: The answer is no.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister indicate the parts of the convention with which the
Government disagrees? As he has said that the convention does not go far enough or does
not encompass some areas, does the Government not consider it wise to sign for the sake of
those areas it does encompass, with which the Government agrees?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The convention seeks to prohibit environmental
modification techniques that are widespread—that is, that affect several hundreds of square
kilometres; long lasting a period of months or a season; or severe-involving serious or
significant disruption or harm to human life. The examples cited are earthquakes, ecological
disturbances, and changes in weather patterns, climatic patterns, and ocean currents. The
convention does not cover those that are not widespread, those that are not long lasting, and


## p. 181 (#189) ############################################

Questions-Oral
those that are not severe. This has been one of the objections.

adopted are capable of verification, will the Minister now state that the Government is not
prepared to make a stand on any resolutions passed by the United Nations unless it believes

Employment of Women
7. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the Minister of
Labour: In view of the statement in the National Party's 1975 election manifesto that "To
encourage women who wish to enter, return to, or to remain in employment, National will
encourage employers to establish flexible working patterns, such as glide time, etc.", will he
please detail what constructive action the Government has so far taken to alleviate the
unemployment of women in the provincial areas, secondary urban areas, and small towns?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Job creation measures recently introduced
by the Government are aimed at assisting unemployed persons of all ages to find suitable
employment. The first job, additional job, and skill promotion programmes as well as the
farm employment scheme provide wage subsidies to participating private sector employers.
The temporary employment programme provides additional temporary employment in the
public sector. There is no differentiation between these sectors in determining eligibility to
participate in any of these programmes. As at the end of April these job creation
programmes provided employment for 3129 females. Special training programmes are also
under way in a number of areas to help upgrade the vocational skills of women and men
finding difficulty in obtaining employment.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: In view of the Minister's statement in the
Evening Post of 20 May that he would expect to see a jump in unemployment figures as the
22 satellite job centres encouraged people to register, can the Minister detail what moves are
being made to encourage married women who are not eligible for unemployment benefits to
register?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I regret that the member did not see fit to read the whole extract,
which went on to say that just as we were getting more registrations in the satellite offices,
equally we were getting, pro rata, a greater number of job vacancies being given to us by
employers. This has been borne out in the Auckland area and the two satellite offices in
Henderson and Takapuna. On that score the quotation was only half correct. What the
member sought in the original question is precisely what is happening.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: Would the Minister detail concrete examples of
job sharing that have been encouraged by this Government?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Specific job sharing would be all-embracing. At present, in the
Public Service we have one pilot scheme in operation. It will be remembered that the Public
Service sector led in the matter of glide time. We are now looking at the possibility of
providing permanent part-time employment to cover married women willing to work less
than 30 hours a week. At present, they cannot register and obtain unemployment benefit. As
with glide time, the private sector may well follow the example of the Public Service sector.

Energy-Geothermal Exploration Expenditure
11. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: To what extent has the
$7.5 million budgeted in a full year for a programme to develop geothermal exploration been
expended, and with what result?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The $7.5 million to which the honourable
member refers is the budget estimate of the cost of the accelerated geothermal exploration
and support programme in a full year. In the last financial year the Ministry of Works and
Development was allocated $4 million and spent $3.75 million. Main items of expenditure
were: two holes at Broadlands, $940,000; one hole at Ngawha, $520,000; two holes at
Kawerau, $720,000; one hole at Rotokaua, $340,000; Broadlands condenser and cooling
tower experiments, $160,000; and establishment, expansion, and upgrading of drilling
equipment, $1,000,000. In 1977-78 the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research
spent approximately $878,200 of the allocated $915,000. This covered scientific work in
conjunction with the accelerated programme for activities at Ngawha, Kawerau, Atiamuri,
and the Ruahine Springs.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Is this exploration programme for geothermal energy likely to be
proven to the extent that further development can be planned to take place shortly?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: My recollection is that the rate of development in exploration was of
four holes to six holes per annum prior to this acceleration. The plan is for 14 holes to 16
holes per year. It will take some little time to achieve this higher level of activity. There is
every reason to believe that there is considerable future potential in geothermal energy, and
it is important that this programme be sustained.

Energy-Wind Research Programmes
21. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of MARILYN WARING (Raglan), to the
Minister of Energy: What wind energy programmes in research and development are now
under way or in prospect?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The New Zealand Energy Research and
Development Committee is sponsoring a programme to evaluate New Zealand's wind
energy resources. An analysis of the meteorological data on wind has been completed and
detailed investigations of wind characteristics at selected sites in the South Island are nearing
completion. Further detailed work, to be funded by the N. Z. E. R. D. C. and the electricity
division of the Ministry of Energy, will be carried out at a limited number of potentially
favourable North Island sites. The Meteorological Service has started a resource assessment
programme in areas of the country which have not yet been covered. The service is
participating in an international energy agency co-operative research programme studying
the uncertainty of wind forecasts. Finally, the departments of mechanical engineering at the
Universities of Auckland and Canterbury are investigating wind flow around structures and
have small wind-powered electricity generators in operation for research purposes. The
estimated expenditure on wind energy research for 1977-78 is $84,000.

Railways Road Services Passenger Statistics
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) to the Minister of Railways: What has been the
average number of passengers on all NZR Road Services Buses during the last 3 months for
which statistics are available on the Whangarei-Auckland, Rotorua-Auckland, and New
Plymouth-Wellington services, and what has been the profit or loss on each of these routes?
Hon. A. MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Railways) replied: The average number of
passengers carried on the services requested for a recent 13-week period was as follows:
Whangarei-Auckland, average per service 25; Auckland-Rotorua, average per service 29;
and Wellington-New Plymouth, average per service 31. As the Railways Department is
operating in a competitive situation it is not desirable for details of the trading results of
individual services to be made public. However, I can indicate that the Whangarei-Auckland
and Auckland-Rotorua services operate profitably but that, despite the higher average
loading, the Wellington-New Plymouth services make a small loss. This is because of the
very high ratio of short- to long-distance passengers carried on this route.

2. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) to the Minister of Forests: What decision has he

Railways Freight Services, Christchurch-Wellington
3. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Railways: Can he give (a) the
approximate time taken to freight goods by rail to Picton from Christchurch and on to
Wellington, (b) the approximate time that it took for the Coastal Ranger to freight goods
from Lyttelton to Wellington, and (c) examples of typical total charges for each alternative
method of transporting freight north for a given commodity, as the charges stood at the time
the Coastal Ranger was withdrawn?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Transport) replied: (a) In normal
circumstances wagons loaded in Christchurch arrive in Picton within 24 hours and in
Wellington within 36 hours. Generally, goods loaded on, say, Tuesday are available for
delivery on Thursday. (b) The average voyage time of the Coastal Ranger between Lyttelton
and Wellington was 12 hours. This does not take into account the loading and unloading of
freight. (c) It is extremely difficult to compare the rates charged by New Zealand Railways


## p. 188 (#196) ############################################

188
23 May
Questions-Oral
with those which applied on the Coastal Ranger for transporting freight north. In particular,
comparison is difficult because of basic differences in methods of acceptance, loading,
carriage, and costing for freight. For instance, the Railways accept consignments of any size
and arrange consolidation of the goods for transport, whereas on the Coastal Ranger service,
freight was carried in sea freighter loads only, and these were stowed by the shipper. The
total charge for a loaded sea freighter carried on the Coastal Ranger did not vary with the
type of freight, while Railways' charges vary from commodity to commodity. It is also
difficult to draw any direct comparison because the rates charged by New Zealand Railways
and on the Coastal Ranger covered different services. For example, the Coastal Ranger
freight charges were for transport only and did not include the cost of consolidation or
stowage. Railways' charges, on the other hand, include consolidation, handling, stowage,
and insurance. Furthermore, on the Coastal Ranger service different freight rates per cubic
metre were offered depending on the size of sea freighter or combination of sizes used by the
shipper. It is against this background that the different rates charged on each service must be
viewed. It is stressed that the following figures cannot be used as a basis for direct
comparison between the services.

Coastal Shipping Services
4. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Transport: Can he list each of
the coastal shipping services around the New Zealand coast that have (a) been withdrawn,
and (b) commenced since 1 December 1975?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Transport) replied: The following
coastal shipping services around the New Zealand coast have been withdrawn since 1
December 1975: (1) The Rangitira passenger-freight service, was withdrawn in September
1976; (2) the Coastal Ranger freight-only service, instituted as a replacment for the Rangitira
service, was withdrawn in January 1978; (3) the Union Steam Ship Co's coal service between
Westport, Greymouth, and Wellington ceased in August 1977. This service is now provided
by other transport modes; (4) Timaru was omitted from the scheduled ports of call on the
Auckland-South Island Coastal Trader service in October 1976. The following coastal
shipping services around the New Zealand coast have commenced since 1 December 1975:
(1) a freight-only service provided by the Union Steam Ship Co. was commenced in January
1978. This service incorporated coastal services into the existing trans-Tasman schedules.
Wellington-Nelson and Wellington-Lyttelton-Dunedin links are also provided by this
service; (2) the conversion of the Cook Strait rail ferry Aratika from a freight-only service to
a freight-passenger vessel has increased the passenger capacity of the Cook Strait ferry
service.

WEST COAST RAIL SERVICES-NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr SPEAKER: I have received a letter dated 23 May from the member for Christchurch
Central, seeking a motion to adjourn the House. The letter reads: "In terms of Standing
Order 89, I wish to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a particular case of recent
occurrence which requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government and
which involves the administrative and ministerial responsibility of the Government, namely
the proposed intending cuts on rail services between Christchurch and Greymouth which, in
effect, would cut by 40 percent the services being offered prospective rail passengers. This is
a matter of urgent public concern as manifested by the urgent public meeting held in
Greymouth on Sunday, 21 May, very shortly after the cuts were announced, attended by 300
people, and reported in yesterday's Press, 22 May 1978. There is widespread concern that the
proposed cuts in the services will isolate the West Coast and diminish progress in the
development of areas of the South Island. Yet, the resolution adopted unanimously by the
meeting, refers to 'assurances that the present railcars can be refurbished and improved to
allow for the retention of the number of services at present provided'. This matter affects the
whole future of the South Island's transport system. It is essential that a discussion be held
today because Budget details are being finalised and, if the House is to persuade the
Government to vary the Minister of Railways' already stated decision to suspend these
services, then the Minister of Finance should know of this as soon as possible. Yours
sincerely, Bruce Barclay."
The letter was received by me within the time specified in the Standing Order. It is not
for me to consider the importance of the issue; it is simply for me to decide whether the
request falls within the requirements of the Standing Order and is therefore sufficiently
urgent to justify the House setting aside its ordinary business in order to discuss the matter.
It is not, therefore, a question of its importance but of its urgency—that is, does it need to be
debated today rather than, say, tomorrow or the day after? That is how I view urgency.
Although the meeting held in Greymouth on Sunday was reported to have been urgent the
fact is that according to the Press—and the member has kindly given me a copy dated 22 May
the conversion of railcars and the changed timetables were notified to the public by the
Minister of Railways in September 1976. It was announced in April of this year that the
changes affecting the West Coast would be introduced in August.
The request to adjourn the House meets at least some of the requirements of the
Standing Order. First, it does involve the administrative or ministerial responsibility of the
Government; and, secondly, it is a particular case and not couched entirely in general terms
although there is a general reference to the South Island. Although the meeting referred to
was recent- that is, it was on Sunday-the events discussed were not recent, because they
were first announced in September 1976, and further reference was made to them in April of
this year. Although they doubtless could require the attention of the House and the
Government the need for urgency does not exist, because changes will not come into force
until August of this year. If urgency is claimed in order to give the Government an
opportunity to consider a change in its expenditure proposals for the Budget then I believe
that the opportunity is available very shortly for members during the formal procedures of
the House in the Address in Reply debate. I do not believe that the request falls into either
of the categories of urgency or of being of recent occurrence, so I must regretfully decline to
accept the proposed motion.

Planning Perspectives 1978-1983, issued by the Planning Council. On page 11, in chapter 2,
under the heading "New Zealand 1978-Where Are We?" it is stated: "Before laying plans,
it is important to know where we are now. The choices open to us for our future

for too long; negative economic growth and falling real income per head; unemployment

I want to say a few words on energy, which is one of the major problems facing New
Zealand and is critical to the country's future well-being. The cost of importing energy into
New Zealand during the current year is estimated at $550 million, compared with $96 million
in 1972-73—a five-fold increase, or $1 in every $6 of our export receipts. That is a very high
price, and should be of major concern to every New Zealander. It is certainly a problem that
people expect the Government to be grappling with positively. We should be doing
something about it today, and urgently, because in the next few years the cost is likely to
increase further, and we could be spending as much as $1 in every $4 of our export receipts
on energy. Under the present Administration there have been two Ministers of Energy
Resources, neither of whom has shown the sense of urgency so badly needed.
It is now 5 years since the energy crisis hit the world. New Zealand was hit very hard. In
its latest report to the Government, the International Energy Agency stated that it is not
satisfied with the effort New Zealand is making to solve its energy problem. The
Government does not propose to reduce the country's dependence on the imports of oil. On
page 1 of its report the agency states that the Government's target is to restrain oil imports at
current levels, which are about 4 000 000 tonnes a year, and to maintain that level until 1990.
At present we are paying $550 million for imported energy, and the prospects are that that
amount will double, or even quadruple, in the years ahead. What does that mean to the
economy of New Zealand? Can we afford to pay $1,000 million in a few years for importing
energy? Can we pay $1,500 million? According to the International Energy Agency that is a
possibility if the Government's present policies are continued. Is this good enough?
Again, I wish to quote from the Planning Council's report on energy-and I hope the
Government takes note. The report states: "New Zealand's vulnerability to external
influences is well illustrated by the impact of rapidly rising oil prices. By 1975 oil imports
were equivalent in value to about 21 percent of our export receipts. Even though volumes
have since been reduced the proportion was still 15.4 percent in the 1977 June year. This

Hon. G. F. GAIR: I should like to discuss with the House two or three important
specifics in the energy policy. The first is the Government's oil programme for on-shore
exploration. There has been much misunderstanding about why the Government has
become involved. Essentially there are two reasons. The first is that the likelihood of a find

on-shore is not great. In fact, it might be rather slim, and for other than gas it might be very
slim indeed. The second is that there has not been a ready wish on the part of the
multinationals to meet the Government in the matter of taxation regimes, and the
Government, as a responsible Government, could not wait for ever and a day to resolve
what threatened to become an academic argument on tax matters.
It was absolutely essential that the Government establish and know the nature of the
energy resources available to New Zealand before it decides on the long-term parameters for
energy policy formation. We must know the true nature of our coal resources. Therefore we
have embarked upon a coal-proving programme that will cost about $40 million and take
from 12 to 15 years. We must know the true nature of our geothermal prospects, the subject
of a question asked in the House earlier today. We have greatly accelerated our geothermal
exploration programme. It is essential that we know the nature of our gas and oil resources,
and an exploration programme has been designed to prove them on shore. We have a joint
programme with the Sea Hunt Group for off-shore exploration in the Great South Basin. We
have completed the drilling of five holes. There was an inability to reach agreement on
certain tax matters before the drilling of the sixth hole, and the Government exercised an
option available to it under the terms of the contract to drill sole risk on holes 6 and 7, which
are close to shore and in comparatively shallow water off the south-east coast of Otago. In
the event of there being a commercial discovery, either could be developed with the present
state of technology.
Criticism of our programme has come from only four quarters, as far as I know. One is
an overseas geophysicist, who was relieved of his position and has since returned abroad with
a self-acknowledged health problem, and another is a former DSIR geophysicist who had,
before he spoke, left for Iran, where he had arranged a job. Incidentally, these two persons
were criticising the Government's programme for different reasons. The overseas
geophysicist said we should not be involved in Taranaki but should be doing more seismic
work on the West Coast, while the former DSIR employee made exactly the opposite
criticism, his contention being that we should concern ourselves with Taranaki alone. To my
best knowledge, the only other area of criticism has come from the Geological Society. I
remind the society's spokesman that some of its leading members are among the
Government's closest advisers on its energy programme. The last quarter from which I have
heard criticism is the Labour Party itself—a little Sir Echo when given the chance to criticise
the Government's exploration programme.
If the Labour Party wishes to side with the multinationals on New Zealand's oil-tax
arrangements, that is its business. The National Government will continue resolutely with its
policy of doing those things that must be done in the energy field, and in such a way that the
best interests of New Zealand will be served. The Labour Party's approach has been to
knock what is being done by the Government. I invite members opposite to compare their
record with that of the National Government. When speaking earlier in this debate, the
Prime Minister drew the battle lines in the economic area between the things the Labour
Party stood for and what we stood for. I invite the people to draw up similar battle lines in
the matter of energy-in policy formation, paralysis on the part of the Labour Government,
compared with action by the National Government. The Government has shown a
willingness to reach out and consult the people and the Planning Council and in energy
matters where long-term decisions must be made.
During the term of the Labour Government three different Ministers and three separate
departments dealt with energy administration, and at times they were in conflict with one
another. In contrast, the National Government has grasped the nettle of administrative
reorganisation, has brought the three energy portfolios together in one strong central
ministry, and, in future, will give a lead in energy planning matters by ensuring that
electricity plans are not carried out regardless of the impact on other energy forms.
Electricity, coal, and geothermal planning, together with plans for all other energy forms,
will be developed together. In this way, the people will get the best value from the country's
energy resources. With the consultation process through Goals and Guidelines, we have the
best possible chance of ensuring that conservation programmes and efforts made by the
leadership of the present Government will be most successful.
I invite members to turn, not to a National Party document, but to the independent
authority of the International Energy Agency and see there confirmation of our progress in a
range of very important areas: a comprehensive energy pricing policy, reinforcement of
some energy conservation incentives, mandatory building codes in the residential sector, an

I regret to have to say this-are able supported by newspapers that have no interest in the
whole truth, but rather a desire to publicise a small portion of the facts. A classic example of
poor reporting of that kind is a recent newspaper article that did its best to destroy the hard
work put into the community house by normal, healthy, everyday housewives. What did the
newspapers call these normal, healthy, everyday housewives who are working so hard to
make a good community? This group, which has been responsible for making a great success
out of its community house, including the establishment of Plunket facilities, family
planning, play evenings, macrame, and many other activities, was described by the
newspapers as neurotic. This claim is so irresponsible as to be laughable. I can conclude only
that the reporter was suffering from a neurosis of his own. The men and women who are
working at the Massey community house are too busy to have time to be neurotic.
I suggest that, before a newspaper reporter or an ivory tower university intellectual
decides to make his reputation out of the area, he should contact the Pam Bells, the Eddie
Eyres, the Chris Duncans, and the Janette Shepherds of this world-who are probably too
busy being constructive to find the time to speak to a university lecturer who works a 6-hour
week.
The area, like all growing areas, has its difficulties. Not so long ago, Takapuna,
Birkenhead, and St Heliers were at the same stage that Massey is at today. All one asks is
some degree of good will from the intellectuals and the press to ensure that Massey follows in
the footsteps of these other areas. Of course there are difficulties. But by August-
September, for example, everyone in Massey will have a telephone, and there will be lines to
spare. About $1.5 million is being spent on new primary schools in that portion of my
electorate. The new shops at Royal Heights have made a great difference, and the Auckland
Regional Authority bus service that travels through the Bahari Drive subdivision is also a
great improvement for the Ranui area. The Colwill Road community is making great
progress by its own hard work in the establishment of a committee to raise funds for a
proposed community school in the area. Steps are also under way for a kindergarten to be
established.
These are the actions of a group that is leading by example. I was interested to see that
Glen Innes is now to receive a community house, and this is obviously a credit to the people
of the Massey community house, who have shown by their example that making a former
State house available to a public-spirited group can make a tremendous difference to the
outlook of a community. The Minister of Housing, the Minister of Social Welfare, and the
Minister of Recreation and Sport have played an extremely important role in helping these
people make a success of their area.

well in the future. He and I disagree in our political philosophies, but we are both trying to
achieve the same end result: the well-being of the community. I look forward to being joined
in Parliament next year by National members for Te Atatu and Waitakere.

Opposition members criticised the export policy, and the member for Christchurch
Central suggested ways in which it might be improved. One has only to look at page 13 of the
National Planning Council's report to know what has been done under this Government and
what happened under the Labour Government. Opposition members have said that import
volumes are too high and should be cut down. I suggest that anyone who hears that sort of
statement should look at page 13 of the National Planning Council's report, where they will
see what happened to import volumes from 1972 to 1975. They will see also what happened
to export volumes from 1972 to 1975. Import volumes shot right up and were totally
excessive under the last Labour Government. Export volumes went down, and there is a
wide gap rather like a wide open mouth in the middle of the 1974 year when one looks at
import and export volumes under the last Labour Government. However, for 1976, 1977,
and 1978 the import volumes are less than export volumes, and in fact those two lines have
crossed so that now we are exporting more by volume than we are importing by volume.
The natural corollary to that is that, if we are importing less by volume, we are paying
less for imported goods; not only are we paying less because overseas prices have gone up,
but also, if we are importing less, we are paying less on a higher overseas price rate. That is
one of the miracles to which I am sure Mr George Chapman was referring—although it is not
a phrase that I particularly like using, because there are no such things as miracles in this life;
it is just what one works for. The Government has been working to that end. It has been
difficult; no one suggests it is easy, but the Government has been working towards that end,
and that is one of the reasons why it will be voted in again in 1978. People realise we have to
export to survive, and we have to import less; otherwise we will have what happened under
the Labour Government. We can always increase import volumes-provided we want an
overseas deficit of about $1,200 million; and that is in 1975 terms. That is what the Labour
Opposition suggests it would do. Opposition members say they would cut down on imports,
and then they say, "However, we would also reduce unemployment." Well, the two just do
not go together. If you cut down on imports, you inevitably have a difficult economic
situation in the country.

I need not remind members of the very serious situation facing young people and people
generally who require employment in Otago. What has caused this downturn? It is true that
the overseas returns for primary products are not what we would like, and the situation could
worsen. No one knows that better than the five of us who returned recently from a number
of EEC capitals, where we tried to support our case for better access for lamb and dairy
products. The Deputy Prime Minister is due to go overseas shortly to visit the nine EEC
capitals, and every member in the Parliamentary Labour Party wishes him the very best in
his efforts for New Zealand; but that is only part of the problem. At a time when
manufacturing needed encouragement under the regional development scheme, the
Government wielded the scalpal: freight subsidies were slashed, and, if the Government
survives the election, freight subsidies will be a thing of the past. It is all very well for the
Minister to say that such crutches should not be provided for industry. He would not say that
if he lived in the South Island. These subsidies are needed and must be restored.
During the recent visit to EEC capitals I had an opportunity to talk to officers of the
Industrial Development Authority in Dublin. Figures I requested have just been received,
and I want to quote them to the House. From 1970 until 1977 the Industrial Development
Authority created about 137 000 new jobs in Ireland, which has a population similar to New
Zealand's. In 2 years the Labour Government created thousands of jobs in this country. I
do not deny that Ireland has a bigger unemployment problem than New Zealand, but its
level of unemployment would have been higher had these jobs not been found. If it can be
done there, it can be done here.
Our transport system is one of the major hindrances to regional development. Railway
services have been run down, and I refute the claim made last week by the member for
Marlborough that the Labour Government gave the kiss of death to the railways. Services
have been run down under this Administration. Railcars have been scrapped, and the
Wellington to Lyttelton ferry service has been torpedoed. The new road tax has added to the
problem, and businesses in the South Island will probably move closer to their major
market. I have made the point several times that about 80 percent of goods manufactured in
Dunedin is sold in the North Island, yet 80 percent of goods manufactured in Auckland is
sold in the greater Auckland area. Surely this indicates that some effort must be made to
ensure that manufacturers in the South Island receive some assistance in getting their goods
to their major North Island markets. The Government has moved away from freight
subsidies, and has said that they are not needed. However, it has been proved that subsidies
are needed. Legislative provision has been made for the setting up of a small business
agency, but to my knowledge no provision has been made for an office in Dunedin. Such an
agency should work closely with the Government's regional development programme, and
an office should be opened in Otago.

The debate has inevitably widened to encompass issues on which the parties are at
variance. I want to turn briefly to the subject of health, because no other subject so well
illustrates the gulf between the National Party and the Labour Party. It is a difference
between shadow on the one hand and substance on the other; promises on the one hand, and
performance on the other. I understand that the member for New Lynn is the Opposition
spokesman on health, so I listened with much interest to his speech last week. I was not
surprised that he shied away from the subject and said not one word about a matter of such
vital public importance. By saying nothing, he drew an appropriate veil of silence over the
years 1972 to 1975. I analysed the reasons for his silence. In 1972 the infamous white paper
on health was produced. Members opposite had a vision, and still have, of socialised
medicine and salaried doctors working for a New Zealand health authority, to whom all GPs
would be indentured civil servants. A vision was conjured up of a health authority that would
be the apex of a new bureaucracy to which everyone involved in the delivery of health care

would be beholden. That, I remind the House and the country, was primarily the work of the
present Deputy Leader of the Opposition-who is still here-and also the work of a Dr
Bassett, who, I believe, is trying to return here. The white paper was the blueprint for a
socialist future for the health services, in which the hospital boards would be destroyed and
the important principle of local representation and involvement would be expunged. The
Labour Party would obliterate the voluntary organisations by compelling their integration
into the State sector. That is the background.
The principle of the National Government's approach over the past 2 years has been
simple, direct, and purposeful. Its aim has been to take primary medical care out into the
community and to concentrate on the means by which that care is delivered-mobility,
flexibility, and diversity. It is appropriate to say that the old formulas will not work in a
community that increasingly displays considerable demographic, cultural, ethnic, and
economic differences from region to region. The Government has had to weigh up the
immediate and long-term consequences of the impact of health, education, and social
welfare votes in Government expenditure. In 1937 the Health, Education, and Social
Welfare votes constituted 25.4 percent of total Government expenditure; by 1947 it had risen
to 32.8 percent; by 1957, 37 percent; by 1967, 40.1 percent; and last year it was 41.8 percent.
The Government has had to turn its attention to making better use of existing resources. In
coming to that conclusion the Government has been supported by Sir Frank Holmes,
Chairman of the Planning Council.
It is important to remember that human problems cannot be solved by throwing money
at them. Therefore, the National Government has concentrated on collaborating with the
voluntary organisations that have grown within the fabric of our society to meet particular
needs the Plunket Society, meals on wheels, the New Zealand Red Cross, the Multiple
Sclerosis Society, and the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped. A Labour
Government would consign those voluntary organisations to oblivion.
Hon. M. Rata: Nonsense.
Mr WELLINGTON: The member says, "Nonsense", but the principle and philosophy
of the white paper led me to no other conclusion. The Government contends that the
voluntary organisations warrant encouragement and support. There are three key reasons
for that: first, they are the key to better utilisation of our existing resources; secondly, the
voluntary organisations involve thousands of New Zealanders who give their own time and
effort; and, thirdly, and most importantly, the volunteers in the health system provide the
personal and human element in the delivery of health care. The Government's aim in
collaborating with the voluntary organisations has been to put primary health care on wheels
and to bring it within reach of the people, especially those in the outer and multi-cultural
suburbs of the cities and in the remote rural areas. The Government is concerned to
orientate the health service towards a front line role by giving it a new immediacy and
relevance, and by encouraging emphasis on family care.
During the last few weeks I have listened to the member for Mangere's criticism of the
Minister of Health and myself for what the member calls secret deals affecting south
Auckland. I shall give members opposite a list of the problems that existed in south
Auckland after the Labour Government was let loose there. The situation at the end of 1975
can best be summed up as follows: first, the provision of hospital beds was below the national
average; secondly, the doctor-population ratio was below the national average; thirdly, the
infant mortality rate was double that of other areas in greater Auckland; and, fourthly, the
admission rate to the pediatric wards at Auckland Hospital was more than the expected rate.
The logical conclusion that the District Medical Officer of Health rightly arrived at was,
"Some better system needed to be evolved." The Minister of Health has spent his energies
evolving a better system for the south Auckland region, which has one-third of a million New
Zealanders. The member for Mangere, like his leader, has visions and makes great and
wonderous noises about the welfare of the people, but when the Labour Government was in
power it did not act—it did nothing. In the final analysis, that is why the Labour Party has
enjoyed the confidence of the people for only 6 of the last 30 years.
What was the secret move that the member for Mangere so vehemently opposed?
Perhaps it was the Government's agreement with the Plunket Society last November. It was
a simple matter, and well publicised. The New Zealand Herald, to name but one paper, gave
the agreement plenty of coverage. The agreement between the Government and the Plunket
Society is quite simple. The Plunket Society is receiving a $1 million subsidy and in return
will be responsible for the health surveillance of infants and pre-school children in the

Those areas are represented by Labour members, but have benefited little or not at all
from their representation. Was the member for Mangere protesting at the establishing of the
new health centre at Wiri, which is within comfortable reach of the people of south
Auckland, especially those in the low socio-economic range? It is an area of rapid growth
and similar to the areas I have already mentioned-Mangere, Otara, and Otahuhu. Is this
the secret deal the member opposes? Is he also opposed, and is the Labour Party opposed, to
the Auckland Hospital Board's policy of establishing community-based hospitals in East
Tamaki and Papakura; the adoption of smaller low-rise buildings by the board in preference
to centralised high-rise institutions; the encouragement given to hospital boards to further
develop their community-based services such as home help, especially for the elderly, and
district nursing and meals on wheels necessary to maintain people in their own homes and
provide them with the necessary support and back-up services? I ask members to compare
those concrete achievements with the Labour Party's proposal following its recent
conference to hold a conference on health matters. That idea should be compared with the
remit sponsored by the member for New Lynn, the Labour Party's spokesman on health,
who would socialise the New Zealand health service.
The National Government has a blueprint not only for the south Auckland region but
also for the delivery of health care to the nation. I do not think it is dramatic. It is not
revolutionary, and it is not over-expansionary in fiscal terms. It certainly is not socialist, but
it is practical and flexible and, because of that, it works. It is down to earth; it is based on
skilled people, both professional and voluntary, supporting the needy in accordance with
local needs and requirements. Above all, it is based on consultation with local people at
board level, voluntary organisation level, and district medical office level.
There is a myth abroad, or there was, that the Labour Party has or had a monopoly on
social conscience, which I would define as a positive response to genuine human need. That
myth has been shattered by the Labour Government's record of inactivity between 1972 and
1975, and by the positive steps taken by the National Government in the last 21 years. Let me
elaborate. The revenue from the alcohol and tobacco levy, which was $27 million this year,
has been channelled into nursing schemes, physiotherapy and occupational therapy,
expansion of meals on wheels, home help, and those personal services that mean so much to
so many people. There is also the extension of the practice nurse subsidy scheme into urban
areas such as those some members opposite represent. These distinctions and contrasts
moved me to refer earlier to the difference between shadow and substance- the difference
between promise and performance.
Labour members opposite talk now about secret deals to disguise the paucity of their
performance, and their ideological bankruptcy. Two things disturb me about Labour
members. One is that they are wedded to and imbued with the philosophy born of
nineteenth century industrial Europe, which has no relevance to New Zealand in the 1970s.
It is summed up in the capital gains tax. The New Zealand Herald, reporting the Labour

expected to exceed $83 million, an increase of $32 million, or 63 percent in 3 years. That is a
great record. No wonder the Labour Party is a bit jealous. Police strength has gone from
4150 to 4786, an increase of 636 in 3 years. To free policemen from office duties, a further

There was a problem with pay and conditions. Last year adjustments were made under
the exceptional circumstances provision. An increase of 9.9 percent was granted, plus the
half-yearly survey, which brought the increase to almost 20 percent. It became obvious that
country policemen should be provided with motorcars rather than having to use their own.
In many cases the wife of a constable out in the district had no motorcar. We thought that
was wrong, and we now have a policy of providing vehicles. By next year every country
policeman in New Zealand will be provided with a motorcar or other four-wheeled vehicle,
complete with radio equipment. This year we have approved the purchase of a further 271
motor vehicles, and this year the police have more motor vehicles than ever before.
We saw a great deal of procrastination by the former Labour Government over the
Police College at Porirua. That Government agreed with the construction of the college in
principle; it agreed again in principle, and agreed yet again in principle, but made no
financial provision whatsoever for it. Anyone can agree with anything if one has no intention
of making any financial provision for it. The National Government not only agreed with the
policy, but it made the necessary financial provision. When the college is completed it will be
possibly the most modern police college in the world. Stage 1, comprising classrooms and
amenities blocks, is now well under way, and the contract for Stage 2 -the residential block
to house 256 students-has been let. We are now calling tenders for the construction of a
swimming pool and gymnasium.
We have upgraded the whole of the police communications system. The Wellington
communications centre is as modern as one would find anywhere in the world, and it is
gratifying to know that the police themselves designed the whole system. It will be followed
by new communications centres at Auckland, Rotorua, and Palmerston North.
We have formed a diplomatic protection squad in Wellington. We have increased the
staff at international airports, and have done so without waiting for trouble to come. We are
being notified of problems at international airports throughout the world, and we are
preparing for any that might arise. We hope they never come, but if they do we are prepared
for them here.
We have provided for a narcotics liaison officer based at Bangkok. When I was there
last year, and while I was travelling throughout South-east Asia, I had top-level discussions
with all their narcotics people. It became obvious to me that New Zealand should play its
part in trying to counter the narcotics problem in that part of the world. I made a
recommendation, and the Government agreed that we should post a man to Bangkok to
work alongside people of other nations who are doing all they can to counter the drug
problem.
We have appointed 9 additional community liaison officers and 18 additional youth aid
officers. We have formed crime control squads in Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch.
We have formed a Police terrorist intelligence unit-an anti-terrorist squad. We have
increased allowances paid to policemen at one-man outstations to $9.45 a week, and we have
approved special allowances for members of the armed offenders squad, who are on call 24
hours a day. The financial allocation for crime prevention in 1976-77 was $1,500. This year,
1978-79, the allocation is $73,100, as a follow-up to that splendid Lions Club project "Speak
up".

QUESTIONS-ORAL
Ngati Whatua Elders—Meeting with Ministers
1. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central), on behalf of Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) to
the Minister of Lands: Did any Government official assist with the arrangements for the
meeting of Ngati Whatua elders with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Maori Affairs, and
himself at the Auckland City Council chambers recently, and who met the cost for the hire of
the meeting place?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The use of the Auckland City Council
chambers was arranged by the Commissioner of Crown Lands, Auckland, after discussion
with, and at the request of, the Ngati Whatua elders of Tamaki, who had already indicated
their wish to speak with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Maori Affairs, and myself on the
land use proposals contained in the Bastion Point planning report. No charge was made for
the use of the council chambers for this meeting.
Labour Department Safety Regulations
2. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Labour: What changes have been
made, or are planned, to cover safety matters that come within the jurisdiction of the
Department of Labour, as promised in the manifesto?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): In its manifesto, the Government stated
that safe and suitable working conditions should be insisted on, and enforced if necessary,
and that the status of the department and a separate safety-in-industry division would be
looked into. A number of changes have been made and others are planned in order to
implement this policy. For example, the Agricultural Workers Act was completely revised in
1977 when a number of safety, health, and welfare provisions were incorporated in the Act.
A complete review of the Factories Act 1946 and the safety provisions of the Shops and
Offices Act 1955 was undertaken during the past 2 years. It is proposed that changes will be
incorporated in a new Act covering all workers employed in factory and commercial
premises, and possibly, as a result of a meeting this morning, industry as well. Other safety
legislation is currently under review. In addition, the Government has had the safety
activities of the department under review for some time in association with a State Services
exercise, which takes into account the occupational safety responsibilities of Labour and
other Government departments, together with the Accident Compensation Commission.
Export Incentives
3. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is it still the
Government's intention to change present export incentives by giving preference to new
"high priority status" goods?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): It is the
Government's intention to revise the present programme of export incentives, but not in the
manner suggested by the honourable member. The benefits available to "high priority
status" holders are in addition to the export incentives available to manufacturers in general.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Could the Minister give the House some indication of where the
major import replacement industries stand regarding high priority status?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It is difficult to deal with that question briefly,
because there are seven areas of incentive for high priority status which are mainly additional
to export incentives. They involve exemption from price control, for example; adjustment of
the maximum profit ceiling, which has nothing to do with export incentives; special
assistance with import licences; additional assistance with finance through the Development
Finance Corporation; some preferential treatment with export suspensory loans; special

Pacific Training Awards
4. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: To what extent are
countries in the Pacific taking advantage of third countries' training awards under the New
Zealand bilateral aid programme by sending students to educational institutions in the South
Pacific?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The number of those taking
advantage of the training awards has increased. In 1976, there were 153 recipients; in 1977,
244; and, so far this year, 299 persons have taken up, or have been nominated for, the
awards. The 10 countries involved have taken up fully their quota of 1978 awards funded
from the training vote. In addition, many have opted to increase the number of their awards
by charging them to 1978-79 forward-aid programmes, and to project funds when training is
project-related.
Mr W. R. Austin: Could the Minister indicate the names of the 10 countries involved?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: They are the countries of the area, and I can tell the
honourable gentleman that students on third country training awards are studying
agriculture, medicine, engineering, and forestry in Papua New Guinea and also Fiji. They
are studying surveying in Honiara Technical Institute, and trade courses both there and in
Fiji.
-
Hon. W. W. Freer: On behalf of my colleague from Awarua, may I ask the Minister if
he would answer the member's question: which are the 10 countries?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: They are the countries of the South Pacific.

Government Life Insurance Office Interest Rates
7. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister in Charge of the Government Life
Insurance Office: Has the Government Life Insurance Office followed the example of the
Guardian Royal Exchange Assurance Company, which, on the passing of the Moneylenders
Amendment Act, increased interest rates on policyholder loans to 12 percent?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Government Life Insurance Office):
The answer is, no. The Government Life Insurance Office rate of interest is 11 percent, not
12 percent. However, the Government Life Insurance Office increased the rate of interest
charged on loans on the security of policies from 9 percent to 11 percent with effect from 1
January 1978. That was done by Order in Council in accordance with the Government Life
Insurance Act 1953. The commissioner is aware that some private life insurance offices
charge 11 percent, and some charge a higher rate.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Can the Minister confirm that at the time of the change of
Government the rate charged to policyholders was 7.5 percent, and that he has increased the
rate on at least two occasions since the National Government was elected to office?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: If reduced interest rates were given to certain policyholders, that
would in turn reduce the bonuses payable to the remainder-about 90 percent-who do not
borrow on their policies. It would mean also that the Government Life Insurance Office
would be paying bonuses at a rate lower than that paid by its competitors.
Mr Comber: Is it not a fact that, if the Government Life Insurance Office did not follow
the lead of other competitors in this field, it would lose business in the long term and that
would reflect finally on the viability and the profitability of the office?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can confirm that.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Can the Minister confirm also that in making loans available the
Government Life Insurance Office and other insurance companies are lending only their
own money to policyholders?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: That is true, but there is no reason why special privileges should
be given to a few, and thus have the bonuses paid to the remainder of the policyholders
reduced to a rate lower than that paid by the office's competitors.

Mortality Rate-Pre-school Children
9. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: In view of the fact that he is quoted
in the New Zealand Herald of 10 May as saying that he was "very concerned" at the high rate
of pre-school age mortality in New Zealand and that the "Government should do something
about it", could he indicate what will be done about this matter this year?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I was referring to the fact that approximately 40
percent of children who die between the ages of 1 and 5 years do so as a result of accidents,
such as poisonings, drownings, and motor vehicle mishaps. If it were not for the high level of
accidental death, New Zealand's position in the world would be very much improved. The
answer lies in inculcating a greater sense of responsibility among those who have direct care
of children. This can be done through health education and preventive health measures, and
the provision of additional health workers. These personnel would not only undertake
therapeutic medicine, but would be able to spend time educating parents and guardians in
ways of preventing accidents and on recognising early symptoms of disease so that
appropriate treatment could be sought.
Mr Hunt: Will the Minister confirm the view of Mr Foster, the chief health statistician in
New Zealand, who said in the same article that "the adequacy of the supervision accorded to
to the young, rather than the provision of additional pediatric services, should be our first
concern", and that that is the concern of the Department of Health and the Minister of
Health?
Hon. T. F. GILL: If the member had listened to my reply to the original question he
would have known that the point I made was that we need education of parents in the
supervision of their children. That is the most desirable way of reducing the mortality rate of
children between the ages of 1 and 5 in New Zealand.
Mr Hunt: Then, what provision does the Minister intend to make during the course of
this year to change the situation? Whereas New Zealand had the lowest infant mortality rate
in the world, between 1912 and 1950, apart from the year 1943, it now has a much poorer
record.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Questions must be brief and without a speech.
Hon. T. F. GILL: There is not time to enumerate them all during the questions period.
However, a number of measures taken are: the provision of additional district nurses,
practice nurses, public health nurses, and health assistants; and a doubling of the money we
are to spend on the education vote in the Department of Health. As I have indicated, a
number of measures have been taken to help in that direction. I emphasise that if mortality
through accidents to those aged between 1 and 5 years in New Zealand equalled the average
rate of the 10 best countries in the world, we would lie sixth for the rate of infant mortality.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister indicate how a doubling or an increase that he referred to in
the Education vote will help with the problem of pre-school mortality rates, when usually,
children do not start school until they are 5 years old?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I did not say the Department of Education vote was to be increased.

Hon. T. F. GILL: I spoke of the education vote in the Department of Health. The

to those people who have the responsibility of caring for children.

area.
Mr Lange: How many unemployed did' the Department of Labour fail to place in

Whales Stranding
12. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Fisheries: Following the recent stranding
of whales at Waiau Pa, has a policy for co-ordination been established in the event of future
strandings, and, if so, whose responsibility is it to undertake that co-ordination?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The Minister of Fisheries replies: "The
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries is currently preparing a paper on whale strandings. It
will contain information on first-aid procedures, humane killing, biological sampling, and
the reasons why certain samples are taken, disposal of carcasses, and the chain of
responsibilities within various Government departments involved. It is also compiling a list
of persons or organisations that may be contacted, so that people finding a stranding will be
able to obtain information quickly on the measures that are being, or need to be, taken to
deal with the stranding situation.”
Mr Malcolm: Is the Minister aware of a statement made in Epicentre News, an Auckland
publication, claiming that, as a result of discussions among memers of the organisations
concerned it is proposed in the case of future strandings that the police should be the first
point of contact, and they should inform and co-ordinate other organisations? If so, is the
statement in any way contradictory to what the Minister has just said?
Hon. D. MacIntyre: The statement has been brought to my attention. However, it is
considered that the position will not be fully satisfactory until the Marine Mammals
Protection Bill has been passed. The question of authority to carry out mercy killings of
stranded whales is at present in some doubt. The Minister is to introduce the Bill shortly, and
it will go to a select committee, so that interested parties may give evidence.
Dr Shearer: Will the Minister confirm that potential wastage of the carcasses was
minimal due to prompt action taken by a Waikato processer of fallen stock?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Yes, that is my understanding of the matter. In fact, as Minister
of Agriculture, I was harassed by certain members who were trying to contact the Minister of
Fisheries so that the whales could be uplifted and used.

Kawerau Settlement Agreement
16. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Labour: Is it correct that, under the

association of unions, which must meet before any union gives 7 days' notice of strike, and

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Yes, it is correct that under the terms of the
Kawerau settlement each union represented at Tasman Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd has
undertaken to confer with other site unions before notifying the company of any industrial
action that could result in the suspension of other workers. In addition, the union in dispute
with the company, after consulting other unions, is required to give one week's notice of
intended industrial action. If these procedures are not followed by the unions, then the
company is relieved of the necessity to give notice of suspension to any other workers.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Minister confirm that, notwithstanding the terms of the
Industrial Relations Act, the company has agreed that should it become necessary to
suspend employees as a result of industrial action the company will give each employee one
calendar week's notice of suspension after his available work has expired?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The latter part of the question is correct, but I fail to see what
relevance it has to the Industrial Relations Act. There is no breach, difference, or departure
from the Industrial Relations Act. It is correct that, once unions have consulted each other,
they give 7 days' notice of a strike. When the available work, without crossing demarcation
lines, runs out, there is 7 days' notice before suspension takes place.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Notwithstanding that the suspension clause is not mandatory
