Wheat Plantings
17. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Trade and
Industry: In the light of the "real" manifesto pledge that “National will implement a policy
aimed at making N.Z. self-sufficient in wheat", why does the report of the Agricultural
Review Committee 1978 show a drop in plantings from 103 700 hectares in 1975-76 to only
88 900 in 1977-78, and why did the Christchurch Press of 16 May 1978 state that “N.Z. will
have to import wheat this year to meet requirements"?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The estimate of 88
900 ha was made before all sowings had been completed for the 1977-78 season. An estimate
made by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries at the conclusion of sowings was 94 300
ha. This was up on the sowings of 93 700 ha for the previous season, 1976-77, which gave
New Zealand self-sufficiency in wheat. I can claim reasonably, therefore, that if we do not
achieve self-sufficiency this season it will be because of wet conditions in much of 1977 and
the drought during the past summer.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Does that mean that the election manifesto's promise of self-
sufficiency in wheat is a policy dependent only on the weather?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: My judgment would be, as the member for
Waikato, that a great deal of the farming industry's success is dependent on the weather. In
this particular wheat season we have had both drought and very wet weather. The fact is that
with a lesser tonnage last year than in the previous year we attained self-sufficiency, and it
was expected that with slightly larger sowings we could certainly attain self-sufficiency this
year. In the last year for which the Labour Government was responsible we had to export 14
000 tonnes at a loss of $12 a tonne to the wheat producers.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Does the Minister propose in his next election manifesto to put in a
clause in relation to agricultural policy, "subject to weather conditions"?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The answer is no. I submit that, in the first year for
which we were responsible, with greater planting we obtained self-sufficiency, and would
have done so this year had it not been for the drought and wet weather.

Regional Development-Clothing Industry
1. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the Minister of
Regional Development: Can he indicate how many clothing industry concerns that received
regional development assistance in the period 1 January 1973 to 1 December 1975 have (i)
closed down since 1 December 1975, or (ii) moved from a location qualifying for regional
development assistance, in each case indicating the location of the concern and whether the
concern closed down or moved location?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: Twenty-seven clothing
manufacturers received regional development assistance in the period 1 January 1973 to 1
December 1975. Since 1 December 1975, three of these manufacturers located at Ruawai
(Northland), Stratford (Taranaki), and Whakatane (Bay of Plenty) respectively have closed
down. A further company which received regional development assistance for a clothing
factory at Foxton closed this factory and moved its operations to Levin. The main
contributing factors in these closures were the downturn in the local market and limits
imposed by Australia on our clothing exports.
(24/5/78)
Road User Limit-Officials Committee
2. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Transport: What conclusions did the
officials committee, set up to consider the implications of the relaxation of the 150 km road
transport limit, come to in each of the following three areas: (a) fuel usage, (b) safety
aspects, and (c) environmental impact?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Transport) replied: (a) The officials
committee concluded that if road/rail competition was completely relaxed there would be an
increase of 7.5 percent in fuel used in the cartage of long-distance goods traffic. However,
any additional fuel used due to the 40 mile rail restriction being raised to 150 kilometres
would be outweighed by the economic benefits to the country accruing from such a
relaxation. (b) The officials committee considered the impact on road safety of fully relaxing
the limits on road/rail competition is a minimum, and using as a basis the 1969 figures, which
give the truck injury rate at 1 accident per million vehicle miles, it was estimated that total
injury accidents could increase by 0.29 percent if the limit was totally relaxed. As a positive
measure to forestall any increase in accidents attributable to increased road haulage the
Ministry of Transport has just published Professional Drivers Guide to Traffic Law and will
shortly be releasing a Professional Drivers Handbook. (c) It is possible that where rail
terminals are presently situated in city centres and thus generate truck movements in heavily
congested areas, a switch to road haulage may reduce noise pollution in these areas. The
officials committee was aware that increased usage of trucks on the open road might increase
noise and exhaust emissions, but was satisified that adequate regulations are in existence for
enforcement personnel to exercise effective control.

Industrial Mediators

support for the strikers and the union leaders. "Congratulations on your attitude and stand

coming from inside the town, not from the Labour Party conference.

Select Committee Membership
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): I move, That the member for Rangitikei, Mr Bruce
Beetham, be appointed as an additional member to the Statutes Revision and Library
Committees of the House. This year the House is in an unusual situation. For many years we
have had a two-party system, with no problems in catering for the wishes of members and
their allocation to committees and in debates. This year, we have not one but three members
who are outside the usual two parties represented in this House, and therefore several issues
must be resolved. The Opposition, in so far as it has any say in these matters, has
endeavoured to be co-operative, as I think most people will have realised. Last week's
Address in Reply debate showed that there can be some resolution to that part of the debate
although, frankly, we had hoped that the matter would have been resolved a little
differently. It was good to see that it was possible to make room for the Social Credit Party
Leader, as was worked out last Thursday. Other matters still have to be resolved, such as
debates on notices of motion and on the Supplementary Order Paper.
A most vexed question, that does not usually reach the eyes and ears of the public, is the
allocation of members to select committees. All members appreciate the importance of
select committee work, and, naturally, any new member is anxious to take his or her place
on those committees. It is unfortunate that we have got this far into the session without a
satisfactory resolution. The Opposition has chosen to move that the new member for
Rangitikei be appointed to one major committee, the Statutes Revision Committee, that
would meet regularly, and to the lesser Library Committee. If the House agrees to our
motion, the Statutes Revision Committee will still have a Government majority of one, in
addition to the casting vote of the chairman. Therefore, we see no reason why our suggestion
should not be accepted. The Library Committee, largely, is a non-party committee. In 1968,
the last year when this situation applied, Government and Opposition members on the
Library Committee were equal—a useful precedent for the House to follow. If a matter of
contention on party lines arose, the chairman would have his casting vote. It is interesting to
note that this applied not only to the Library Committee, but also to the House Committee
and the External Affairs Committee, as it was then called, on which the Government was
dependent on the casting vote of the chairman, if necessary.
Hon. David Thomson: Nonsense.

year. If the other two independent members wish to be on committees, I am sure
arrangements could be made to appoint them in addition to the existing membership. These
days, for a number of reasons, Parliament has fallen to rather low esteem in the eyes of the
public. We are called upon to be responsible and reasonable in conducting the business of
the House. The member for Rangitikei was elected democratically by the people of his
constituency. He will be here at least until the next election, and therefore has a right to play
a full part in the affairs of this House. We do not want to play games. Provision is made in
the Standing Orders for members to be nominated to committees, and I contend that the
Opposition is offering the Government a very helpful way out, within the terms of the

Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): From the outset I want to emphasise that the Government
supports the wish of the member for Rangitikei to be appointed to a select committee of the
House, particularly to the Statutes Revision Committee. As chairman of that committee, I
shall welcome him to it. I am sure he will find, if and when he gets the opportunity, the work
done by the committee to be very fruitful indeed. It works largely on a non-partisan basis.
However, I suggest that the appointment of any member-and this includes the member for
Rangitikei-to a select committee must be done, first, in accordance with the Standing
Orders, and, secondly, in accordance with past precedents established by the House,
recommendations of Standing Orders committees, and the like. These include a very clear
understanding that there must be a Government majority on select committees in the case
of the Statutes Revision Committee, a Government majority of two.
The recommendation that there should be a Government majority of two was made by a
Standing Orders Committee that reported in 1972-and the member for New Lynn and the
member for Henderson were members of the committee. The precedents also include a
proposition that the member for Rangitikei, like his predecessor in this House in the 1960s,
Mr Cracknell, must be regarded as a member of the Opposition. Therefore, if he is to
replace anybody on a select committee then inevitably he must replace an Opposition
member. It is implicit in the motion just moved by the Senior Opposition Whip that, if it was
passed, the member for Rangitikei would, for the purposes of his appointment to a select
committee, be regarded as a Government member, and that proposition is simply not
correct, as was made clear in a ruling given by you, Mr Speaker, last week on the question of
the order in which members should be called upon to speak in a debate.
When the question whether a member of a third party should be regarded as a
Government or Opposition member was raised during the 3 years that Mr Cracknell was in
the House, the late Mr Kirk said, and I quote from Hansard, Volume 364, at page 3809, in
1969, "The practice has been to alternate the call as though the member for Hobson"-Mr
Cracknell "were an Opposition member, although he is not a member of the majority
Opposition party." If one reads the remainder of Mr Kirk's speech it is clear that he was
citing that practice with approval. However, regardless of his approval, the ruling given on
that occasion by Mr Speaker Jack was that the member for Hobson should be treated as a
member of the Opposition, though not of the major Opposition party. He specifically said,
"He is not of the Government, and therefore he is opposed to the Government." That
adequately summarises the matter. I am quite sure the member for Rangitikei himself would
not want it to be said of him that he was a member of the Government. To quote Mr Speaker
Jack, he is opposed to the Government and must be regarded as a member of the Opposition
though not of the Opposition party. Earlier this afternoon in another debate the member for
Rangitikei, quite rightly, sought the call-unsuccessfully as it turned out—at a time when an
Opposition member was due to speak.
Mr Hunt: What has that to do with the debate?
Mr McLAY: There is authority for the proposition that the Government must have a
majority on all select committees.
Mr Hunt: But it has a majority on the Statutes Revision Committee.
Mr McLAY: It must have a majority of two members on the Statutes Revision

recommendation of the 1972 committee, of which the member for New Lynn was a member.
Some time ago, outside this House, the Leader of the Opposition suggested that the
Government should give away one of its seats on a select committee to the member for
Rangitikei and that the committee should be run on the basis of the chairman's casting vote.
That proposition was repeated this afternoon in a slightly different form by the Senior
Government Whip. I can honestly say that I have not heard a more naive statement or such a
lack of appreciation of parliamentary procedure.
I think we would all accept Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice as the authority on
parliamentary procedure. There we find that the chairman's casting vote is intended to be
used for breaking a deadlock and not for the purpose of the day-to-day running of a select
committee. It is quite ludicrous to suggest that on every occasion when the Government and
Opposition divide on an issue in a select committee the chairman should have to exercise his
casting vote. On only one occasion in my time as a chairman of a select committee over the
last 2 years have I had to use my casting vote, and that was on a liquor Bill when members of
the House had a free vote according to their consciences, and it was therefore appropriate
for the chairman to exercise a vote in order to break a deadlock.
The member for Wanganui, the Senior Opposition Whip, has referred to the
composition of select committees from 1967 to 1969, but to a very large degree the
composition of committees then is largely irrelevant to the discussion we are having today,
because since then we have had a new set of Standing Orders, and we have had a report from
a committee on which both the member for New Lynn and the member for Henderson were
members, and that committee recommended that there should be six members of the
Government and four members of the Opposition on the Statutes Revision Committee. It
would not be proper for me to refer to a proposed motion that appears on the Order Paper.
However, everyone knows that a solution has been proposed by the Government, and one
that is eminently suitable. It is that the member for Rangitikei should become a member of
the Statutes Revision Committee in place of another member of the Labour Opposition. If
members of the Labour Opposition wish to argue against that proposition they must first

that.

Rangitikei to accept the viewpoint that he was a member of the Government. I am quite

Revision Committee, and we would welcome him on that committee, he must be appointed
as an Opposition member in place of one who is now sitting there as a member of the

difficult to have a full complement of members attending at select committees, particularly

Party that the member for Rangitikei should be appointed to the Statutes Revision

Freezing Workers Settlement
Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua): I move, That this House notes the firm and decisive action
taken by the Government on the freezing workers settlement to protect New Zealand's overseas
meat exports and to keep this vital industry working, and calls on the Labour Opposition to
come off the fence and declare its position on the basis of the settlement. During the debate the
Opposition might commit itself to statements about the economy, and not just find words or
$700 to give to the workers at Kawerau to prolong their strike.
The industrial action was taken during one of New Zealand's worst droughts. Forty
areas have been declared drought and disaster areas. The industry being discussed accounted
for half the man-days lost last year. It is New Zealand's most important industry. Initially my
electorate and I wanted blood over this issue. I do not think anyone has had sympathy for the
industry during the last 2 or 3 years. The worst story that I have heard occurred last week.
On Monday stock were brought from Rotorua to Hawke's Bay and were sent back because
of a stoppage. The stock arrived home on the Friday night at midnight. Farmers have been
putting up with things like that for the last few years. There is no doubt that the dispute was
beyond any individual's wants or needs; it was a national problem. If the Government had
wanted to make itself unpopular it could not have chosen a better issue, because New
Zealanders have no sympathy for the freezing industry. The Government must look at the
positive side and the justice of an issue, and not act emotionally. It must look at each
individual case within the issue and decide which way and how it should move. For that
reason I have great pleasure in defending what has happened in spite of my earlier doubts
about the settlement.
The industry produces annual export earnings of about $900 million. It is New Zealand's
largest industry. The workers who went on strike, helped over the last year by the
companies, process about 1 000 000 tonnes of meat in a seasonal industry that has no job
security. The annual turnover in the industry is more than $1 billion. About $248 million is
paid in wages to 27 000 workers. The statistics are important so that people will realise the
importance of the issue and why the Government had to act so decisively in solving the
problem, at least in the short term. The dispute would have made the Tasman dispute look
like a Sunday school picnic if the Government had allowed its emotions to overrule its
reason. With 40 drought areas declared the farming industry was not in a position to sustain
the stoppage that could have occurred. Earlier today members heard that the Socialist Unity
Party was prepared to bring down the Government at any price. In a newspaper dated 5
April 1978 the member for Wanganui was reported as stating at the freezing works
conference that a dangerous precedent had been set and that it should never have happened.
He also said that the claim was justified.
What would have happened if the industrial action had developed? A national stoppage
would have occurred, lasting until now. From the settlement to 6 May, 6 297 038 sheep and
334 000 cattle have been processed. The value of that produce is about $100 million. If the
industry had stopped completely the cost would have been far greater, because, apart from
the sheep that had died, farms would have had a feed supply crisis. So the Government
stepped in and acted, and, apart from the loss that would have occurred, it saved the farmers
$21 million, all of which would have been passed on. With Government help, the freezing

## p. 275 (#283) ############################################

24 May
275
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
a generation of New Zealanders has grown up unaware of hard times. It is untutored and ill
prepared to face the harsh realities of economic adversity. Since the second world war we
have gone through a period of rising expectation and continuing improvement in the
standard of living. The fulfilment of those expectations was regarded as the norm, and many
New Zealanders, including some today, claimed them as of right.
I believe that premise is false, and I believe also that all who encourage that premise
without due qualification are wrong. What those people ignore is that our society has
become increasingly consumer and leisure orientated. Certainly the most tragic and
destructive development has been the growing illusion that the work ethic is no longer basic.
That is what causes the unease and disturbance throughout the length and breadth of the
country. There is a growing sector of society that has no strong, basic belief in the work
ethic. It is the combination of those false attitudes and faults, linked with a slackening
overseas demand for our exports, and further frustrated by a lack of any real growth in the
New Zealand economy, that is at the very heart of the present problem.
What the country desperately needs is the realisation that a nation must sometime learn
how and when to say no: no to an overpermissive undisciplined society; no to the demands
for rights without an equal degree of responsibility; no to Government department empire
building for the sake of empire building; no to those who deliberately seek to exploit our
social and social welfare systems; no to the extreme elements within the trade union
movement; and last, but by no means least, we must learn to say no to both extravagant
profit margins and extravagant wage demands above an acceptable level of inflation. Order
is a prerequisite of a stable society, and when a nation lacks the fortitude to say no there is no
balance to the quality of discretion. Good order can survive in that society, but often it is
irretrievably undermined. To learn when and how to say no is, I believe, basic truth No. 1.
Let us look at No. 2—a re-examination of efficiency and wastefulness pertaining to our
resources. This country's greatest inefficiency and most wasteful practice occur not with
fossil fuels, but with fossil people, hamstrung by fossilised ideas. Our greatest inefficiency is
not so much the utilisation of our capital, but its underutilisation. Our greatest wastage is the
enshrined slavish rigidity which preserves the 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. work day and the 40-hour
working week. It continues to survive in this country like some ghoulish prehistoric monster
threatening, if abused, to engulf us all. The problem of unemployment could be substantially
attacked overnight. What is required is that a useful percentage of our manufacturing
industries at present engaged in the export of goods should move from a single-shift to a
double-shift work day. If such an exercise were properly planned, with one-fifth of our
export industry so motivated, we could immediately create up to 50 000 new job
opportunities.
What are we afraid of? Are we afraid of work, of profits, of full employment, of
productivity, or of substantially increased exports? Do we want prosperity? Surely most of
those things would follow automatically if such a system were pursued. The benefits to the
work force would be full employment, many more new job opportunities, greater scope for
promotion, regular work, regular wages, and, with national superannuation, an even earlier
retirement. Industry's reward would follow if millions of dollars worth of machinery, plant,
equipment, buildings, investments, and stock, now lying idle for 16 hours a day, became
mobile and productive.
In a sentence, I believe that this country's greatest folly is self-imposed idleness, and I
see no valid reason why fully grown active working men cannot emulate the teenage nurses
who are at present toiling through the night in the hospitals of Awarua and every other
electorate. Surely we can mobilise the work force in safe employment. That is a great deal
more than the police in this country have, with no guarantee of security. What the potline
worker at the Tiwai smelter accepts as his conditions of employment should not be beyond
the ability of a great many more people. That is basic truth No. 2-the deployment of
resources. We have one of the best educated work forces in the world. There is no question
of its ability; all that is required is the will to make it work, plus a taxation system of
encouragement.
I come now to the third fundamental truth in the Speech from the Throne; and I am

a great speech, and the three basic truths contained therein deserve the attention of the
House and the country. The question is, can we, as a nation, live within our income over the
longer term? My response is that that should not even be a question; surely it has to be an
answer. The plain fact of the matter is that since 1969 our greatest essay into self-delusion

interests of New Zealand. Too often, such monopolies kill initiative and stifle imagination.

November sold out in 3 weeks. The retailers were told that no more would be available until
March. Sound, up-to-date marketing methods would not have allowed that to happen. I am
sure that our manufacturers, using their own expertise and marketing organisation, are not
doing that sort of thing.

I believe that the charges have been grossly overstated, and are based on inadequate
facts. Comments on incidents have been misunderstood or half understood, seized on
gleefully by the media, and subjected to mindless repetition until they have become part of
our folklore. I propose to invite a close re-examination of each of the charges.
The first is the constant claim that the Government has bypassed Parliament and
enacted too many regulations. No regulation can be made unless the House passes a statute
expressly delegating power to the Executive, and every regulation must be within the
objectives and intentions of the parent Act. With few exceptions, all of the regulations of the
past 2 years have been passed under laws enacted by the former Labour Government or
allowed to remain in force by the last Labour Government.
Mr Lange: What about the rock lobster regulations?
Mr BRILL: The rock lobster regulations were passed under an enactment that was
allowed to remain in force by the last Labour Government.
More than 25 years ago, in 1962, a previous National Government passed a law
requiring that all regulations be tabled in the House. At the same time it was decreed that
every regulation was subject to review by the Statutes Revision Committee if the committee
was convened for that purpose by its chairman or by any five members of the House. Under
that provision two sets of regulations have been reviewed during the past year. Regulations
are also subject to restraint by the courts. They can be declared invalid if they are not within
the intention of the parent Act or if their meaning is uncertain. The Leader of the
Opposition claimed that the number of regulations passed last year was a record. As usual,
he was wrong.
Mr Prebble: No, he wasn't.
Mr BRILL: He was wrong and, as usual, the member for Auckland Central is wrong.
Numbers fluctuate from year to year, but the record of 358 was actually reached 36 years
ago.
Mr Lange: Your record was 377 last year.
Mr BRILL: It was 337 last year, and 36 years ago it was 358. The main reason for the
increased number last year was merely the adjustment of myriad fees to take account of
inflation-a prime example of an efficient Government reviewing and overhauling
regulations as conditions change. It is perhaps notable that the United Kingdom
Government regularly passes 2000 or more regulations each year-about seven times the
New Zealand average yet it puts fewer Bills through the Westminster Parliament than we
pass in New Zealand. Clearly, we have a great deal to learn about the business of bypassing
Parliament by using regulations.
A second major charge is that too many laws are passed by Parliament itself. This could
be avoided by making more regulations or by giving the Executive wider and more
discretionary powers. By confining laws to as narrow an area as possible, we make it
inevitable that further laws and amendments will be required when new situations arise that
were not contemplated when the principal Act was drafted.
In any event, the passage of a statute does not necessarily add to the sum total of our
laws. Some of the most heated debates relate to a Bill that proposes the repeal or
modification of a law introduced by a previous Government. Many statutes codify the
common law or simplify an existing complexity, often on the recommendation of a law
reform committee or other informed body. Virtually every transaction is now governed by
some law, whether it be statute, regulation, common law, customary law, or perhaps an
ancient imperial statute predating Magna Carta. Most statutes passed through the House
merely update or vary such existing laws. A small number do create new requirements or
prohibitions, and they are a small proportion of the total number of laws that go through the
House. These additional ones usually arise by public demand, probably reflecting the New
Zealand syndrome of crying, at the slightest provocation, "There ought to be a law."
Thirdly, it is claimed that the Government has rushed legislation through the House.
This can only be considered in the light of specific examples. The example inevitably cited is
that of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act of 1977. In fact, that Bill was on
the Order Paper for 4 months, which is a longer period than for any other law enacted by this
Government.
Mr Lange: What about the Town and Country Planning Act?

to keep on talking as long as they wish, the only requirement being that the House keeps
sitting until the talking is over and the vote is finally taken.
Members know in advance how they propose to vote, and the endless speeches are
merely for public consumption-and highly tedious after the first four or five 20-minute
speeches. Again, we have the double standard. When the Labour Government was in power
it kept the House sitting for two full days and nights continuously, and still failed to
introduce its superannuation scheme in a single sitting. This Government has never faced
such determined opposition, nor has it gone to such extremes.
More double standards arise from the question of extending broadcasting hours—a
matter that was raised again in this debate by the Opposition. Not once during the 3-year
term of the Labour Government did it allow broadcasting to extend beyond 10.30 p.m. when
considering contentious Bills, whether conscience matters or otherwise, yet members
opposite are harshly critical of the present Government, which has allowed an extension of
broadcasting more than once.
Perhaps the most fundamental charge laid against the National Government is that it
has allowed bureaucracy to run riot. I have already demonstrated that one cannot draw any
such conclusion from merely counting regulations, the important factor being the degree of
power that is moved into the public sector.
By ignoring Labour's words and looking at its actions, one sees the very clear contrast in
the attitude of the respective parties to the centralisation of power in the Public Service.
Such bureaucracy lies close to the socialist heart, and was demonstrated by the spectacular
rise in Government spending from 29 percent of the GNP in 1972 to 42 percent in 1975. The
Goverment's share of New Zealand's wealth increased by more than one-third in only 3
years.

Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
Perhaps more significant is the increase in the number of people on the public sector pay
roll. In the last year of the Labour Government, to October 1975, the number of public
servants increased by 12 918. In the last 12 months of this Government, to October 1977, the
increase was held to 267. In fact, if one excludes Government corporations the number of
public servants actually decreased by 866.
If we had increased bureaucracy by the same percentage as the Labour Government, an
additional 14 127 public servants would have been employed during last year. That would
have accounted for nearly two-thirds of those who are now registered as unemployed, and
would have reduced the unemployment figure to one lower than that during the term of the
Labour Government.
This demonstrates the amount of taxpayers' money the Labour Government was
prepared to spend to improve the employment statistics for election year. More importantly,
it completely explodes the pious utterings of the Leader of the Opposition about the Labour
Party being opposed to burgeoning bureaucracy.
The final charge I will deal with is that the present Parliament is given to excessive
personality arguments. It is first necessary to clear away light-hearted comments that are
given and received in good humour, and without which discussions in this Chamber would be
the poorer. It is also necessary to distinguish those instances in which previous political
actions or speeches of a member may have direct relevance to the attitude he displays to the
debate before the House.
What is to be avoided is direct or indirect reference to the private or business affairs of a
member, or his personal characteristics, which have nothing whatever to do with the
business before the House. In my time in the House I have heard only one serious charge
and countercharge of this nature. They occurred in the year before last, in what has become
known as "the Moyle affair". I think one could say they have been adequately analysed and
condemned by the news media. That incident may have had a cathartic effect, and may have
served as a salient reminder to members of the dangers of allowing debates to become too
heated. Whatever the reason, I believe the record long sitting of 1977 was noteworthy for the
relative absence of attacks based on personal characteristics or private lives.
Certainly, no New Zealand parliamentarian has used the mace to do battle, as it has
been used in London, or has become involved in fisticuffs, as has occurred more than once in
Canberra. I have recently had the opportunity to observe the proceedings of the Parliaments
of some nine countries, and I thought that the general standard of behaviour of all compared
unfavourably with that in New Zealand's Parliament.
Over the past 2 years various members have been subjected to attacks in the news
media. At least one member was charged with a criminal offence, but these matters have
never been raised in the course of debate, no matter how strongly feelings may have been
running.
There is one exception to the generally good behaviour of the New Zealand Parliament
regarding personality arguments. I refer to the Opposition's obsession with the personality
and character of the Prime Minister. I invite regular listeners to take careful note of any
Opposition speech-

TV2 Reception in Western Hills, Hutt Valley
2. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) to the Minister of Broadcasting: When will the new

Statistics, has now reported to me, and I will put the results to Cabinet for a decision. New
Zealand statistical methods have been the same with successive Governments, and our
registration scheme is the same as that in operation in other countries, such as Australia and
the United Kingdom."
Mr Prebble: Can the Minister give an assurance that, until the recommendations of the

Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, I will not give such an assurance so long as it is
recognised as the Minister of Labour's reply states-that our registration of unemployed is
the same as that in operation in other countries, such as Australia and the United Kingdom.
That is as far as it is necessary to go.

Maui Field Platforms
7. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Energy: Is it correct that the
second development phase of the Maui field platforms will be built overseas, and, if so, what

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): Following an evaluation of the possibility of
constructing a concrete tower locally, which was undertaken by the Ministry of Works and
Development on behalf of the Government, a decision was taken to use a steel structure for
the second Maui platform. This decision was made after taking fully into account all aspects
of the costs and the benefits of alternative proposals. The steel structure will be constructed
overseas, possibly in Japan. I hope that a significant New Zealand content will be possible
through the manufacture in New Zealand of some of the platform modules that will house
production equipment. Design studies for the tower are not yet completed, and therefore
only a broad assessment of the cost of the second phase can be made at this time. On the

the margin of advantage was greatly in favour of a steel structure that could be delivered by

Government generally that the maximum reasonable New Zealand content should be
achieved, but it would be improper for us to oblige the company to make decisions which are
clearly not in the company's interests.

Federated Farmers-Ballot on Unionism
9. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Labour: When will
he hold a ballot on Federated Farmers of New Zealand Inc. as to whether it would like to
remain a compulsory union?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Labour replies that he is
not empowered to conduct such a ballot as Federated Farmers of New Zealand Inc. is not a
union under the Industrial Relations Act, and, as the honourable member knows,
membership of Federated Farmers is not compulsory.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Could the Minister explain the difference between a compulsory levy
to Federated Farmers and fees paid to a union?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That is irrelevant to the question of compulsory membership
of a union. The member has asked for an explanation. There are compulsory levies upon all
farm products in the various classes to support such organisations as the Dairy Research
Institute, the Meat Research Institute, and the Wool Research Institute, but that does not
make the members working in those institutes compulsory members of Federated Farmers.
The compulsory element of unionism is quite clear, that in a particular occupation, according
to the award that affects it or covers it-and there is virtually no escape-the member of that
union, whether he likes it or not, has to pay the levy. That is certainly not the practice with
Federated Farmers.
Mr Latter: Would it be correct to say that the difference is that levies to Federated
Farmers are for work for the nation whereas the levy by a union goes to a political party?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Not all levies made on union members go to political parties,
but, as members well know, many unions have resolved to send money to the Labour Party.
The levy that is paid by farmers for Federated Farmers' work is for an industry, and that is
equally so in regard to research work. The levy is on all farmers, whether or not they are
members of Federated Farmers.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Can the Minister explain the difference between a farmer who
exercises his choice not to join Federated Farmers and a worker who refrains from joining an
industrial union on the grounds of conscience by applying the appropriate procedure?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The farmer who is not a member of Federated Farmers, to
whom the member has referred, is very much freer than a tradesman who tries to escape
from the clutches of compulsory unionism.
Bay of Islands Historic and Maritime Park
10. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) to the Minister of Lands: Can he inform the House

park complex, and it is now appropriate that the Bay of Islands Maritime and Historic Park

Rural Bank Refinancing
12. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking
and Finance Corporation: What progress is being made by the Rural Bank in the refinancing
of farm loans when short-term mortgages have fallen due?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): A total of 1201 loans for $22.22 million has been approved for refinance
purposes by the Rural Bank to 31 March in the financial year just ended. Many of these
loans were to refinance debts incurred through development which farmers were not in a
position to meet from their cash flows. Others had substantial amounts of on demand and
short-term debts raised from a variety of sources on conditions which could not be met if
development was to proceed in an orderly manner.
Property-owning Policy
13. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) to the Minister of Lands: Can he outline how the
Government has fulfilled its pledge in the “real” manifesto that “A National Government
will ensure that all New Zealanders have the opportunity to own property, whether this be a
home or a farm"?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I thank the member for asking the question,
but regret that in the short time allotted for an oral answer I cannot do justice to the
question. Briefly, the Government has increased the opportunity for all New Zealanders to
own property through the stabilisation of house, section, and farm prices, which has
improved the relativity between wage levels and property values. The limit on first home
mortgages from the Housing Corporation has been substantially increased, and additional
funds have been provided to the Rural Bank for the purchase of a first farm. This, coupled
with the 85 percent special settlement loans, enabled the Government to assist 1154 young
farmers on to their own farms through the Rural Bank in the 1977-78 year. In addition, 55
young farmers have been settled through the Government's farm settlement scheme
administered by the Department of Lands and Survey. These results compare favourably
with those of the last Labour Government, which will be remembered for increasing the cost
of sections by about 140 percent, houses by about 90 percent, and farms by about 100
percent.
Hon. M. Rata: Notwithstanding all the reasons the Minister has advanced about making
it possible for people to own their own homes, how does he explain the lower level of home
ownership and the difficulties in obtaining finance?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The reduced demand at present results, in many instances, from
the demand having been met. Many people who are experiencing difficulty raising finance
are those trying to refinance mortgages raised during the term of the Labour Government.
Mr Talbot: The Minister said that 1154 young farmers had settled on their own farms
with the assistance of the Rural Bank. How does that figure compare with assistance given
by the Rural Bank during the term of the Labour Government?
Mr SPEAKER: That is extending the scope of the original question and the answer
already given.

South Korea-Protectionism
14. Mr LUXTON (Piako) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Is he aware that the South
Korean Government is establishing an organisation similar to Japan's Livestock
Improvement Promotion Corporation, and, if so, has he embarked on any action that will
persuade the Koreans to avoid protectionism similar to that adopted by Japan and enable the
Koreans to see the advantages of comparative production efficiency?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): I am aware that the
Government of the Republic of Korea established a Livestock Industry Development
Corporation on 1 April 1978. The New Zealand Government has made particular efforts in
its trade relations with the Republic of Korea to ensure that a policy of protectionism in
livestock products is avoided, and to show the advantages of comparative production
efficiency. In particular, the Government is raising regularly with the Korean authorities the
need for an improved beef importing regime. It is expected that a delegation from the New
Zealand meat industry will visit the Republic of Korea shortly for technical and marketing
discussions.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Minister give the House an assurance that any aid given to
South Korea by New Zealand will not be used to purchase breeding stock from the United
States in preference to breeding stock from New Zealand, as has already occurred?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What action is the Minister taking to ensure it does not happen
again?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I am having discussions with the Government of the
Republic of Korea.
Chatham Islands Air Fares
15. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Internal Affairs: Why was the air fare to
the Chatham Islands recently increased, did he approve of the increase, and how much was
it?
Mr COMBER (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to Minister of Internal Affairs): The
Minister replies: "The air fare to the Chatham Islands has not yet been increased. The
Government has asked Safe Air Ltd to apply to the Air Services Licensing Authority for
approval of increases that will do no more than meet half the cost of a recent increase in
charter rates and other charges. The increases being sought are $20 for an adult single fare
and $10 for children."
Mr Kirk: How does the Government reconcile this fare increase with its public
statements of support for the Chatham Islands?
Mr COMBER: The Government is committed to providing a sealed runway at Karewa
Point, which is a move the Labour Government could have made had it had the best interests
of the Chatham Islands at heart. A subsidy is paid towards the cost of providing this vital air
link, and amounted to $169,000 in the 1977-78 year.
Miss Dewe: Could the Minister tell the House what proportion of the increase is to cover
the Chatham Islands County Council charges and what proportion is to cover Air New
Zealand charter rate?
Mr COMBER: I am advised that, included in the payments already referred to there
would be a payment to Air New Zealand of $100 a flight to cover ticketing, aircraft loading,
and freight acceptance. A payment is also made to the local county council for similar
services on the island, and for operating a bus that is supplied by the Crown. This payment
has been increased recently to $6 for an adult passenger and $3 for children.
Mr Prebble: Can the Minister say whether any representations against such savage
increases were made to him by the member for Lyttelton?
Miss Dewe: Yes.
Mr COMBER: I cannot answer that question directly, but I have no reason to doubt the
observation from the member for Lyttelton that she made representations directly to the
Minister.

Aid to South Pacific
17. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: In view of New
Zealand's decision not to contribute to the Asian Development Bank's aid programme, can
he say by how much New Zealand will increase its bilateral aid grants to the South Pacific, as
indicated by the Prime Minister in Vienna, and when this increase will take place?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The member appears to have
been misled by inaccurate reports of the Prime Minister's statement at the annual meeting of
the Asian Development Bank in Vienna.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Another occasion?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: It is true. If the member wants the answer I am prepared to
give it to him, but if he does not want it let him say so. The Prime Minister did not say that
New Zealand had decided not to contribute to the Asian Development Bank's aid
programme. Indeed, New Zealand this year will be contributing to the first replenishment of
the Asian Development Fund and the Asian Development Bank technical assistance special
fund, which are both ongoing commitments.
The Prime Minister also announced at the Vienna meeting that New Zealand would
contribute to the second general capital increase of the Asian Development Bank, which will
involve New Zealand in a pledge of $3.7 million over 4 years. The Prime Minister did,
however, say at the Vienna meeting that it would not be possible for New Zealand to commit
itself to the second replenishment of the Asian Development Fund, which is about to be
opened for subscription by aid donors. He said that, within the limits of funds available for
official development assistance in 1978-79, the Government had decided that it could not
accommodate both the contribution to the bank's capital increase and the second Asian
Development Fund replenishment without making substantial inroads into the existing
multilateral and bilateral commitments within the aid programme.

by how much it is proposed to increase aid to the Pacific?

presented. This year the Government is making a $1 million contribution to the annual
contribution of the first replenishment of the Asian Development Fund, a contribution of
$75,000 to the technical assistance special fund, and $920,000 to the second general capital
increase. It could not make a further contribution of $3 million to the third replenishment.
New Zealand is not contributing to that fund.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the fact that the Government is not prepared to accept the
responsibility for the $3 million request, can it be assumed that that amount will be added to
aid available to the Pacific or any other area?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The honourable member's curiosity will be well and truly
satisfied when he learns the amount of the aid vote.

Unemployment-Comparison with Australia
19. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Statistics: On what statistical
base is his assertion in Fact for April 1978 that "New Zealand's unemployment is
substantially less than Australia's"?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): It is based on the registers of
unemployment in both countries. At the end of April 1978 the number of registered
unemployed in New Zealand was 21 502, which was 1.8 percent of the estimated labour
force, and 0.7 percent of the total population. In Australia registered unemployed were
402 534 people, or 6.3 percent of the total labour force. Those figures are derived from the
Commonwealth employment service register. Using the registered-unemployed figures for
both countries we can see a far higher level of unemployment in Australia.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Is the Minister aware that if we use the same basis for registered
unemployed as Australia, New Zealand's unemployment is marginally worse when
considering its smaller population?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: That is a totally unproven assertion.
Mr Friedlander: Can the Minister advise the House if he has received any independent
comment that refers to unemployment in New Zealand-for example, from the OECD?
Mr SPEAKER: That question is beyond the scope of the original question, which asked
about the statistical base. It was a very simple question, and a very simple answer was given.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Minister confirm that, if his assertion is based on statistics,
they are not necessarily comparative?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I have received advice from the Government Statistician
that the systems are broadly similar in both countries. The system was used during the time
the member was a Minister so he should be aware that the statistical registers are broadly
similar, if not strictly comparable. The Australians use two systems, which both show similar
results.
Maoris and Islanders—Special Loans
20. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Maori Affairs: What loans are
available to people of Maori and Island extraction in addition to the loans normally available
to non-Maori or Island New Zealanders?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): Housing loans under the Maori
Housing Act 1935, and amendments, are available to people of both Maori and Pacific
Islands origin on terms similar to those of the Housing Corporation. In addition, loans for
farming purposes, under Part XXIV and section 460 of the Maori Affairs Act 1953 are
available to persons of Maori descent only as an alternative source of finance to that
provided by the Rural Bank and the Marginal Lands Board. Another avenue of loan finance
is provided by the Maori Trustee under the Maori Trustee Act 1953. Such loans are available
for a wide range of purposes on a three-fifths margin lending from the Maori Trustee's
common fund, and on a smaller security from the Maori Trustee's general purposes fund.
Mr Prebble: Can I take it from the Minister's reply that Government loans for Maoris
and non-Maoris are similar, whether loans from the Maori Trustee are the Maoris' own

Bastion Point-Use of Armed Services
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the Minister of
Defence: Is the Army being used in what the Government has described as "a simple case of
trespass" at Bastion Point, and can he give Parliament an assurance that the armed forces
are not being used and will not be used?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Defence): I will not give the House any
such assurance. The armed forces are involved today in an operation that has as its objective
the clearance of Bastion Point. Their role is strictly one of providing logistic support and
equipment assistance to the Police and the Department of Lands and Survey. They are not
involved in the process of law enforcement, arrest, or eviction of people. They are making it
possible for the police to carry out their duties.

Postage Costs

Westport Coal
2. Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast) to the Minister of Energy: Is he in a position to
report on the progress of the using of Westport coal in making activated carbon in Japan,
and, if so, presuming the experiments are successful, could he indicate the prospects of a
coal-processing plant being established in Buller?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The semi-commercial scale plant in Japan
has proved that high-quality activated carbon can be made from Buller coal. Development
effort is currently directed at extending the range of products and markets. In December last
year I agreed to the export of a further 10 000 tonnes of Buller coal for the plant. A
requirement of this was that a detailed feasibility study into the establishment of an activated
carbon plant on the West Coast would begin in April 1978. As I pointed out at the time the
feasibility study, which is now under way, is a further necessary step towards setting up this
plant. The first phase of the study is due to be completed in six months' time.

BUSH WORKERS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr MALCOLM (Eden): I am directed by the Labour Committee to present the report
of the committee on the Bush Workers Amendment Bill. The committee recommends that
the Bill be not allowed to proceed. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The Bush Workers Amendment Bill was primarily concerned with the powers of
inspectors, the appointments and duties of safety supervisors, and other sundry matters to do
with the safety of workers in bush undertakings. The safety of bush workers is of concern
because the bush is a dangerous work location. On average, about 12 men a year die in the
bush in New Zealand. Seven submissions were made to the committee and all were critical of
substantial portions of the Bill. The argument was that the nature of bush undertakings is
such that many legislative proposals that may work in a more static factory-type setting are
just not practical in the bush.
Further, it was argued that training and safety in bush work cannot be separated from
general job training in production and productivity. To make a legislative distinction in this
area would be false, while to make legislative intrusion into the whole area of training
programmes would be quite impractical. Additionally, modern bush undertakings involve a
diverse range of skills, and involvement with a wide range of equipment. Safety training is
always inextricably linked with practical training and field experience.
The committee heard, with some interest, that steps are being taken by members of the
logging industry to encourage the development of a group training scheme, leading to the
certification of correctly graded loggers. Safety will be totally integrated with all aspects of
job training. It was argued that this sort of co-operative approach was succeeding and that
the intrusion of inappropriate legislation might possibly be counter-productive. It would be
wrong to interpret the committee's decision not to proceed as an indication of lack of
concern about bush safety, or unwillingness on the part of the committee to consider
legislation in this field. Rather it was felt that the Bill in this form may not be helpful. The
committee's decision not to proceed is not an expression of lack of concern; it is an
expression of concern by the committee about the safety of bush workers, and an attempt to
be helpful. As a result, the committee has made a unanimous decision to recommend to the
House that the Bill should not proceed.
Mr CHRISTIE (Napier): Opposition members concur with the recommendation that
the Bill should not be allowed to proceed. Whilst the committee agreed that the Bill would
be reported back to the House this afternoon, I understand from the Opposition Whips that
the Senior Government Whip told them that no Bills would be reported back to the House
this afternoon. One wonders who is in control, and if the Opposition knows more about what
is going on in the House than the Senior Government Whip does.
The Bill is the result of the Government's mania last year for bringing in Bills. It
brought this Bill in without consulting the people it concerns. Four people attended the
committee's hearing, and gave evidence on behalf of five organisations. Those were totally
opposed to the Bill. They were not opposed to safety in the industry but to the provisions of
the Bill. The committee was told of a group training scheme operated by the Kaingaroa


## p. 305 (#313) ############################################

25 May
305
Bush Workers Amendment Bill
Logging Company in conjunction with New Zealand Forest Products Ltd and the New
Zealand Forest Service, and that any Bill dealing with safety in forests should be introduced
after experience had been gained from the group training scheme and the good and the bad
had been taken out. We all agreed, and I, as one who has come from the trade union, could
not stress it strongly enough that safety in any operation is paramount. Here the
Government brought in a Bill that did not have the support of people who had to work under
its provisions.
Evidence was given by Mr Colin McKenzie, who said he was the logging manager for
New Zealand Forest Products Ltd. I was impressed by his evidence. He was quite a young
man, and totally au fait with his job. Evidence was also given by Mr McKee, who is the
General Manager of the Kaingaroa Logging Company, which is probably one of the biggest
logging companies in New Zealand, along with New Zealand Forest Products. Both gave
expert advice to the committee. They were adamant that they were opposed to the powers
for safety supervisors contained in the Bill, because a safety supervisor, according to the Bill,
had to be a member of the gang.
Mr McKenzie gave a breakdown of what was happening at Forest Products Ltd, and I
wish to read some excerpts from the evidence he gave. He said, "In charge of each bush
undertaking is a foreman chosen for his maturity, ability to accept responsibility, and
knowledge of the job skills required. Rarely would he have less than 10 years' practical
experience on appointment." That was the type of man that Forest Products Ltd had in
charge of the logging operations, and in charge of the gang; but the Bill wanted to bring in a
safety supervisor to do exactly the same job that the foreman was now doing.
Mr McKenzie said, "Each foreman is also responsible for the on-going training of the
men under him. This training again emphasises the correct skills to undertake the job in
hand. The safe way is the correct way, and the correct way is an efficient way. Each foreman
is responsible to a supervisor. Supervisors have responsibility over three to six bush
undertakings." What he meant by "undertakings" was bush gangs. "Supervisors generally
come from the ranks of foremen, and, as such, are totally familiar with the skills that are
required to do the job correctly. Supervisors are responsible to a superintendent. In our
industry it is generally true that the superintendent has received extensive on-the-job
training, rising through the ranks to his position. Superintendents are responsible to their
manager." That is the type of man that Forest Products had in charge of logging operations.
Mr McKenzie also said, "New Zealand Forest Products Ltd has operated a formal
training scheme for bush employees for the last 4 years." Then he said, "It is a tragic statistic
of our industry that over the last 5 years an average of 12 men per year have died whilst
employed in a bush undertaking. As mentioned above, Kinleith operations represent one-
quarter of the logging activity in New Zealand." Forest Products Ltd stated that in their
operations safety is paramount. In the last 5 years, although Mr McKenzie said that on
average 12 men have died each year in the forestry industry, at Forest Products Ltd only two
men have died in the same period. That illustrates the type of training being given and the
safety precautions taken by Forest Products Ltd and the Kaingaroa Logging Company. The
Bill was hasty, and was unnecessary.
In 1973, the number of accidents resulting in lost time was 69. By 1976 that had been
reduced to 12, and in 1977 there were 13. Mr McKenzie said, "It is our goal that all our bush
workers may pursue an active and safe career in our operations until retirement. We see
nothing positive in the appointment of safety supervisors, under the terms of this Act, which
would help us to achieve this goal." Then he said, "Charitably, we view this proposed
legislation as a means of bringing the industry together, formally, to consider its collective
role in the safety aspects of bush undertakings. We urge that the members of the Labour
select committee listen to the voices of the industry, and observe the steps already being
taken." Then he said that he felt the Bill was premature and should not go ahead at this
stage. For that reason the committee decided that the Bill should not be allowed to proceed.
The information given by Mr McKenzie and Mr McKee was invaluable, and should be read
by everyone involved in bush undertakings.
Mr MALCOLM (Eden): Yesterday, when I told the member for Napier that the report
would be coming into the House today, I thought I had given him adequate notice. It has
since been pointed out to me that I failed to make the correct approach through the Whips.
As chairman of the committee, I accept responsibility for that, and I apologise.

consultation; but what is more significant is that, having looked carefully at the legislation

ADDDRESS IN REPLY-WANT OF CONFIDENCE
Interrupted debate on the question, That a respectful address be presented to His
Excellency the Governor-General in reply to His Excellency's speech; and the amendment
proposed thereto.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): I am sure, Mr Speaker, that the legal
profession was honoured that on that day of great personal significance to you, when you
took office, you allocated some of your precious time to give an indication of your feeling
towards lawyers. I have thought for a long time that you and the Speaker's chair were meant
for each other. I firmly believe that when the time comes to assess your stature alongside
your distinguished predecessors you will rank among the best. I should also like to add in
passing that you appear very much at home in the appurtenances as well as the duties of your
new office, and that the wig is a distinct improvement.
The other day I read the following words: "Men felt as if a scorpion lay under every
stone." These were the words of Erasmus describing the atmosphere in the 16th century at
the height of Thomas Cromwell's power, when England was going through a period of great
social and religious upheaval which, however historically inevitable, was a very ugly time in
which to live. Extremism and intolerance were the order of the day. A feeling of insecurity
hung over the land. People branded, victimised, and ostracised others of opposing points of
view. Fortunately, our own society is still free from the worst of such excesses, but such
situations do exist in a lot of countries today, and one gets the uneasy feeling that the
incidence is spreading.
Political life, even in the most stable Western countries, appears to be slowly but
perceptively becoming more extreme and more intolerant. As we in New Zealand watched
the worst of the campus and ghetto violence in the United States in the 1960s, or more
recently the political terrorism in Western Europe and the growing extremism in Britain, I
think most of us believed, and probably still do believe, that we are too much on the
periphery, too much outside the mainstream, too basically tolerant, and too free of the social
and economic contrasts that give rise to such strife to get too deeply caught up ourselves in a
political climate that produces such excesses. We do not have to look far to see real danger
signs in our own midst, and politicians may well ask themselves whether they are not making
the situation worse. Extremist terms such as "fascist” and “racist" nowadays roll easily off
many tongues.
The bitterly divisive abortion issue seems to have brought some surprisingly intense
bigotry to the surface, and many pressure groups appear to think more and more in terms of
their own as opposed to national-interests. From time to time we see evidence of what
looks like a subtle and apparently deep-rooted assault on the institutions on which our
society's stability depends. Certain pressure groups in our midst jump at any opportunity or
any cause in which they see the chance of showing the State as being repressive, the classic
example being Andersen and the Socialist Unity Party, who more than anyone else are
responsible for the fact that the Bastion Point problem went on as long as it did and came so

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Already in this Address in Reply debate we have been
accused, directly or by implication, of, among other things, using our position as a
Government to break the law and hold it in contempt, of running the country on the lines of

of threatening personal freedoms, and of falling down in our constitutional duties. These
charges should not be dismissed as just a bit more political invective. They are too serious for
that. Either they are true, or they are not. If they could be substantiated it would indeed be a
critical indictment on the Government. If they cannot be substantiated the Opposition
stands condemned for deliberately inflaming the fires of extremism and intolerance in this

Many of the Opposition charges of the Government's flaunting the law have been too
conveniently generalised to rebut. They have been fine for whipping up anti-Government
feeling on campuses, at stop-work meetings, or at tame Labour Party conferences. However,
as they could mean anything or nothing they have not been worth too much attention. Some
Labour Party speakers, especially in this debate, have also made specific charges. Let us
look at some of these. First, the NAC - Air New Zealand merger. Much has been made of
this by several speakers in this debate. The Opposition well knows that there is nothing in
the Memorandum or Articles of Association of Air New Zealand, nor in the NAC
Empowering Act, to prevent such a merger. There was nothing in any way illegal about such
a merger, yet the Labour speakers keep citing it as if it was illegal, presumably on the basis
that if they create the impression of a bit of smoke people will always assume that where
there is smoke there is fire. Of course, they do not remind the public that they have every
right, and many opportunities, to debate the pros and cons of the merger in this House.
The member for Auckland Central alleged that the Government had ignored or broken
the law in no fewer than three ways in bringing the parties involved in the recent freezing
works dispute to a settlement. First, he alleged that the Government had no right, under the
Industrial Relations Act 1973, to insist that the freezing companies provide details of their
profits. I have news for him. The truth of the matter is that the Prime Minister has never
required the companies to disclose their profits. The industry is already required under the
Stabilisation of Prices Regulations to provide that information to the Minister of Agriculture
as the price-fixing authority.
Mr Prebble: On a confidential basis.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: On a confidential basis, and let me assure the member that
that confidentiality has been observed. Interestingly enough, Mr Hinchcliffe, the acting
Chairman of the Freezing Companies Association, offered of his own volition to give that
information on a confidential basis to the Prime Minister. Next, the member for Auckland
Central asserted that the Government had no right to interfere in the dispute while the

In a regrettable lapse, the member for Southern Maori also threw facts to the wind in
another set of wild accusations that simply disintegrate when looked at more closely. Playing
on the theme of Ministers failing in their constitutional duties, she condemned two of my
colleagues for failure to publish reports. First, she named the Minister of Health for not
publishing the report on women and health. In fact, it was completed only recently, and is
now at the printers awaiting delivery. Yet last week the member accused the Minister of
failing in his duty to publish it. Secondly, she criticised the Minister of Social Welfare for not
publishing the report of the New Zealand Social Services Council. In fact, it is now being
studied by the Ministers of Health and of Maori Affairs, and may have to be returned to the
Social Services Council for further work. But perhaps the most condemnable thing that the
lady member has said was her reference to the Government using the domestic purposes
benefit report selectively. That, to me, implies that certain aspects of the reports were
published, and others were not. Of course, the full report was published. That again is the
type of thing that we have had to put up with, designed to deceive the country.
Another category of Opposition accusations, alleges or implies that the Government
has eroded personal liberty. Typical of this was the reference earlier in the debate to the New
Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Act, darkly described as having touched
our basic freedoms more than any other legislation. Nothing specific, notice, just innuendo,
and that is presumably enough. What the New Zealand Security Intelligence Amendment
Act did do was to put on a proper legal basis practices to protect our national security, which
until now would have had to be done without legal authority. Norman Kirk would have
understood the need for that Act, even if those who uphold his memory do not. Two old
favourites of the Labour Opposition in creating the impression that the Government has
contempt for the law have been the Prime Minister's Bill of Rights case and my own action in
staying the Ford Motor Co. prosecutions. The Bill of Rights case in fact involved a debatable
judgment on a technical interpretation of a 300-year-old statute. The legality of the Ford
Motor Co. prosecution stays was, of course, beyond debate.
Mr Prebble: Rubbish!
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Has the member not read the Summary Proceedings Act? If
he reads section 77 of that Act, he will learn something. The legality was beyond debate. The
decisions to stay had to be sustainable on grounds of public interest, but could not take into
account any speculation that the prosecutors might be using the law for political ends. If the
member likes to study the reaction of the New Zealand Law Society at the time it will
enlighten him. In a transparent effort to clothe its accusations with authority, the Labour
Party often quote left-wing academics and the objectivity of left-wing academics is
somewhat suspect. Unfortunately, it is also able from time to time to glean the odd helpful
point from the comments of a handful of woolly-minded people without a political axe to
grind, who, frankly, should know better. It quotes, for example, an uncharacteristic lapse by
a Supreme Court judge, who made a wholly unexpected and unsubstantiated statement
when he referred to the tendency in this country for Ministers of the Crown to place
themselves above the law. Frankly, it would have been better unsaid, because it was never
substantiated, but it is quoted in this debate as if it was evidence in itself.
Labour Party members also quote from a former Supreme Court judge and
Ombudsman, who have recently spoken out on that perennial subject so dear to the hearts of
academic purists, amateur constitutional dabblers, and anti-establishment groups of all
shapes and sizes-namely, the growing power of the Executive at the expense of Parliament.

Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
Virtually every criticism I have read on this subject appears to originate from a basic
misunderstanding of our constitution. None of those criticism ever cites an authority for
saying that Parliament should control the Executive. They all assume that Parliament's role
is declining, when, in fact, it is increasing. They all ignore the fact that all the Executive's
powers are given by Parliament and can be taken away by Parliament at any time.
Admittedly, the Labour Party has had more to say about Executive power than the National
Party in the last two decades. That is probably because it has been in Opposition for most of
that time. It is great to rant on about Executive power when one is in Opposition. There are
always receptive ears, and no one need remember that in those few years that Labour was
the Government it did nothing whatsoever to curtail the power of the Executive.
The member for New Lynn, who is not here today, is a meticulous student of the
constitution, and he has never been able to answer the challenge about what concrete
measures the Labour Party took when it was in office to curtail the power of the Executive.
As the party that wants to centralise political and economic power, how could the Labour
Government have done anything? It would be a contradiction in terms for it to turn round
and do anything to block the growing power of the Executive. I think I have stated enough
examples to show how much credence can be placed on Labour members' attacks in the
constitutional area, to which they have given so much time and effort in the debate. I
challenge any Labour speaker to cite me one example when the Government has, since it
came to power, taken any action knowing it would break a law. [Interruption.] The member
for Napier would not know constitutional law from a tally sheet on the wharf.
Members of the Labour Party have fanned the flames of intolerance and extremism in
this country for political ends, and in doing so they are playing a very dangerous game. The
member for Auckland Central came to the crux of the matter the other night when he asked
why, if the Government of the day is seen to break the law and hold it in contempt,
individuals and organisations should not take the same attitude. A fair enough question, and
it was right to ask. But if the Government of the day is seen as a lawbreaker because of
charges that cannot be sustained by the Opposition, then it is the Opposition and not the
Government that is responsible for the consequences, in the same way that someone who
makes false charges of racism is as guilty of stirring race feeling as any avowed racist. I put it
to those members of the Labour Opposition who go in for this sort of thing that it is not in
their interests to contribute to the climate of extremism and intolerance in this country,
because sooner or later they will find themselves up against the same forces they are now
helping to unleash, whether they realise it or not.
There is another reason why they should leave the theme of constitutional and legal
impropriety alone, and that is that their own record reveals some very interesting episodes―
such as when they lifted, without the authority of Parliament, the legal duty of 20-year-olds
to register for compulsory military training; and when they incurred expenditure of $238
million without the authority of Parliament-examples that were referred to very effectively
by the member for Hastings when he spoke last week. Our democratic institutions are
vulnerable to attack, and anyone seeking to undermine them in this day and age will find
receptive ears, and a variety of means to reach those ears with ease. It is easy to put our legal
system under pressure. Anyone of moderate ingenuity can find a way to make many laws
look silly. Anyone of moderate intelligence can find a way to use the law for his or her own
ends. Ways can always be found to make the most moderate and most reasonable
Government appear oppressive. These things can be done with ease.
If all this places some strain on our institutions perhaps it is not necessarily a bad thing—
the institutions should not be so brittle that they cannot stand up to some stress. But there
have to be limits. If extremism and intolerance are allowed to get out of hand no democratic
institution in this country can thrive, whether it is Parliament or some football club in a
suburb. Exactly when this point is reached may not be too obvious. Perhaps we will find out
only with the wisdom of hindsight. I do not believe we have reached that stage in New
Zealand yet, but there are far more signs of stress than there were, say, two decades ago.
The stage has already been reached when both the Government and the Opposition must be
mindful of the example they set, because we are strategically placed to aggravate a situation
that has already begun to be a cause for concern.

preceded me in this debate. To do so would be unduly burdensome and lengthy. Although I
appreciate that reply and riposte are the essence of debate, what so often passes for that in
the House consists of verbal vilification and rhetorical mayhem, and that brings the House
into disrepute. It is something I have tried to avoid during my term here, and I am certainly

May I take the opportunity of complimenting you, Mr Speaker, on your preferment,
however unwelcome the translation was made to appear. I am sure you will fill the office
with distinction and dignity. May I add further that its authority is accepted without question
in the House, and perhaps I may be bold enough to suggest that when exercised in debate it
