suffering listeners.
What I want to try to do today is to speak about a problem with which we are all too
familiar, and one that becomes more and more pressing every year—that is, the continuing
access of our primary products to Europe, and especially to the United Kingdom. I have
written something about this problem and I do not want to repeat here what I stated there,
but I do want to develop the same kind of theme along somewhat different lines. I begin,
however, by making a point I tried to make then-that our case, as expressed to and through
Europe ever since it became necessary to express it, has been essentially based on appeals to
the nobler instincts of mankind. We have solicited sympathy; we have hinted at compassion;
we have sought a fair go, suggesting that we deserve a better deal. Of course, all those are
admirable sentiments, but I do not believe it is necessary for me to tell an audience of 86
professional politicians that they do not pull in the votes.
The reality is more banal than that, and it was expressed in perhaps the starkest form in
which I have ever encountered it in a training manual published by the Republican Party of
America. I quote from that manual: "Greed is the only consistent human characteristic.
Nobody does something for nothing in the final sense. The payback may not always be
physical or monetary-it can be spiritual, ethical, or biological-but somehow if you are
going to get someone to vote for you, you have to offer him something in return”—a
philosophy, I add, by which ex-Presidents lived and politically died. However, there have
been two recent departures from what might be called "the world owes us a living
approach", but before going on to mention them I want to say that any appeal of this nature,
which is essentially an appeal to charity, is not only a poor argument in principle but also one
that is bound to fail on the facts, or at any rate the facts as perceived by those to whom we
address the argument. Because of this, when we say the world owes us a living the world
does not believe it.
We have a reputation overseas-or, to use a more trendy word, an image—and it is one
that others very much admire; and I believe it is one that has been deserved. It is the image
of a wealthy, privileged-perhaps overprivileged-country, and one that is quite
inconsistent with any pleas of poverty; but I must go on to say it is one that few would
willingly decry or certainly want to decry. If any one of us in this Parliament were to go to
Europe and there publicly knock New Zealand in that way the rest of us would very soon be
at his throat, screaming "foul", "disloyal", "traitor", or, even worse than all of those,
"playing politics". Lofty sentiments, it happens, pay small dividends, and I suggest that we
have to arouse or appeal to some baser but more practical instincts.
I believe we do not need to go fully to the lengths of the Republican Party that I set out,
but, I want to return to the two incidents that came to my notice when I was overseas and
which aroused my admiration; I thought they were much more positive in their aspect and, I
suggest, in their likely consequences than other gestures that have been made. The first was
a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture, I think to the Commonwealth Association in
Britain. I have quoted that, saying that he addressed his audience in a vivid manner by telling
them that it had required him to sell five lambs to buy the spectacle frame that he held out to
show them. I now stand corrected by him, because he tells me that the figure was eight,
which makes the case even stronger: to buy the pair of spectacle frames that he has caused
him to sell eight lambs. That is a vivid, telling demonstration of our predicament and plight. I

Earlier this year I had the honour to represent New Zealand at the United Nations
Commission on the Status of Women, which met in New York. This was perhaps the most
interesting, yet perhaps the most frustrating, experience of my life. The commission's task is
to lay down a policy for the implementation of, and to give priorities to, programmes to
eliminate discrimination against women. My report on the legal condition of women in New
Zealand was much envied by most of the delegates. Most of the delegates came from
developing countries, and have problems of which people in New Zealand have little
understanding. The illiteracy, ill health and high mortality rate, and the lack of job
opportunities for women in developing countries were frightening in their totality.
The average New Zealand citizen does not realise how fortunate he is, and certainly the
women of New Zealand must be made to realise how wide are their opportunities and how
great is their protection under the law when compared with their sisters overseas. The
knowledge that every second woman in the world is leading an underprivileged life, during
which she is not likely to be compensated in any shape or form for the work she does in her
community and towards the productivity of her country, is sad indeed.
One of the subjects on the commission's agenda was the programme for the 1980 world
conference in Teheran. It was the commission's desire that the agenda for this conference be
action oriented and based on three main themes: education, health, and employment-
avoiding political issues. The political manipulation and motivation of the east European
delegates were frightening. It seemed to me that they really had no great desire to see the
commission functioning in a practical manner, promoting policies and programmes that
would have a benefit at ground level among the developing nations. In my opinion, they
wanted to stifle the work of the commission.
The problem is that the commission is not master of its own destiny. It can only make
recommendations to the Economic and Social Council, which, at its political or economic
whim, may change the stress and the thrust of any programmes the commission places before
it. To be effective the commission must be master of its own programme, and I wonder
whether it would be possible to redefine its terms of reference or for it to decide its own
agenda, and for this to be accepted by the Economic and Social Council without further
debate. Unless some positive action is taken to raise the living conditions of 50 percent of the
developing countries' population we shall face considerable problems.

brief illustration. The value of a 1965 housing loan of $10,000 would have been equivalent to
the purchase price of four large motor vehicles. By the time the loan was repaid in 1985 the

the money lent on mortgage would have been grossly devalued.
Some way must be found to promote the interest in thrift and savings that the member
for Lyttelton so strongly advocated. Members must promote a policy to achieve that, and the
only way is by ensuring that savings are not eroded by the effluxion of time. No one but a
fool would lend money at the present long-term interest rates, because in 20 years its value
will have been reduced from that of four motorcars to less than one. To retain their equity,
people must pay back what they borrow.
Surely members see the advantage of the indexation of all debt money. If we are
prepared to adopt this approach it is feasible to reduce interest rates drastically. In its very
limited and token acceptance of the principle, by the introduction of single Government
bonds and indexed bonds, the Government has presumed, and probably with justification,
that an adequate interest rate is 2 percent. One can realise the effect this would have on the
economy, and how attractive it would be for people who have so long advocated low interest
rates within the context of the policies of the Social Credit League. It would be feasible to
reduce interest rates to 2, 3, or 4 percent and at the same time preserve the equity of loan
money. That would have the advantage of facing the realities of the present economy instead
of pretending that, in our approach to accountancy, taxation, wages, and prices, money will
remain the same and inflation will somehow disappear. We would face reality, and say

I want also to discuss problems in my electorate, which are constantly a matter of
concern to me. A problem among the Polynesian people, both of Maori and Island origin,
has recently blown up because of some restrictions in the immigration policy concerning
family reunification. This problem arises because Government departments are
administered solely in the context of the European cultural tradition. We have repeatedly
paid tribute in the House to the fact that we are a multicultural country. When it comes to
adoption procedures, however, there is very little definition of legal responsibilities,
although there are considerable departmental administrative procedures. Without
exception, the administrators seem to favour the European style, under which an adopted
person is lost from the mother and family, and moves into the family of adoption, becoming
a member of that family as though legally born into it, and being cut off from the natural
family.
We are becoming increasingly aware of the psychological difficulties experienced by
adopted children. The Polynesian tradition, however, is not to cut children off from the
family they have left; they are in the fortunate position of having two families. Their
obligation to the family they have left becomes somewhat diminished, but they acquire full
rights, obligations, and privileges as a member of the new family. Dissociation from the
child's previous family is not forced on it, so a feeling of rejection does not grow up in the
child, and the adoption does not have the hazards, psychologically and developmentally,
that it has under the European tradition. One would have thought that everyone would
realise the immense psychological advantages of this to the child, and the social advantages
to the community. Many arguments about wanted and unwanted children are solved by this
approach to adoption.
With this vastly superior tradition of adoption still flourishing in our community, it is
disappointing that Government departments insist on the worst type of adoption procedures
being applied here. Recently, when I had cause to take this matter up with the immigration

And now to look further afield. I believe our pioneering forebears would turn in their
graves if they could see the disintegration of the inheritance they so proudly handed down to
this generation. They took a pride in their skills, their resourcefulness, their ability to
improvise, and to make do with what they had to beat the job in hand. Work was a challenge
to them; it was a team effort by Indians and chiefs to achieve results. They would be aghast
to see how our industries today are split by a kind of class warfare more pronounced than
anything that existed in their day.
Employers struggle merely to keep the wheels turning in the face of industrial sabotage
practised by strategically chosen unions owing loyalty to the Communist Party, and plotting
disruption and intimidation in industry. I am not referring to the many responsible workers,
but to the more militant unions, of which there are only about eight or nine in the
extraordinary army of more than 300. However, their attitude of apathy, self-interest, and
irresponsibility has infected some areas of our work force so that we find groups of workers
greedily concerned with getting a bigger share of the cake for themselves, and to hell with
their employers, their workmates in other unions, and the welfare of the economy.
Time and again we see our hard-won export contracts thrown away because unions are
more interested in getting their demands than in filling export orders and getting them away.
The recent 7 weeks dispute at Kawerau was a typical instance of one of our biggest export
industries being nearly brought to its knees. Delegates at the Labour Party conference took
around the bucket to collect funds to help those people. We are falling victims to what has
been called the "English disease" with its slowly destructive symptoms of apathy and
selfishness, and the attitude that life is a big lolly scramble; you get all the goodies you can
for nothing, and grab as much as you can without regard for anybody else. That is what the
Labour Party is promising in its election bribes. I do not blame New Zealanders for this
malaise, because I believe the pioneering instincts of getting stuck in and getting things done
are still alive in this country. However, I do blame those professional stirrers who have
infiltrated our trade unions, who know all the tricks of industrial espionage, and who have no
more loyalty to this country or to the members of the unions they lead than any double-
dealing traitor who would sell out his mates or his country for political pragmatism.
At long last, however, we are seeing a return to sanity. We saw it at Kawerau when the
workers got fed up with the strike and went back to work on reasonable terms. We saw it in
Auckland when the communist union boss, Andersen, threatened strike action when the
submarine Pintaldo came in, and then could not get it off the ground. There is now some
room for optimism. We have seen the communists booted out of the principal freezing works
union, and there are some grounds for optimism that, with more united and disciplined
behaviour, that troubled industry could settle down.
The people of New Zealand now realise that the Government's industrial relations
policies are starting to take effect. Do not think I am advocating that either side, employers
or unions, should have the whip hand. I believe that the future lies not in confrontation but
in industrial co-operation. I have mentioned the industrial battlefield of the meat industry,
yet in Petone, in my electorate, we have a freezing works which, by comparison, is a model
of industrial harmony. I refer to the Gear Meat Company, where the management is
working successfully on a policy of consultation with the union on production problems, and
where union spoilers are finding their fellow workers would rather take their problems to
management than go out on strike.
If our pioneering grandparents would have turned in disgust from fruitless
confrontation, I believe they would have been proud of the good sense and resolution with
which people have faced up to the economic problems which have pinched this country for
the last 3 years. They have tightened their belts and accepted lower living standards, to
enable the Government they elected to accomplish its promise of getting our economy
straight. That is what is being achieved today. Those policies can be seen to be working in
terms of our present capacity to produce. Our external deficit is now less than half as high as
it was when Labour left office in 1975. Inflation has begun to move downwards, with the best

I want to take this opportunity to set the record straight. When Professor Kawharu
came to see me in 1977 he said, "There is no inherent or delegated right to speak for the
Ngati Whatua held by either the Orakei Marae Trust Board or by the Orakei Maori
Committee, or by any ad hoc or other group at present squatting at Bastion Point. The Ngati
Whatua of Orakei dissociate themselves totally from these groups in this matter." Later, a
letter to the Minister of Maori Affairs dated 1 August 1977 and signed by 13 senior elders of
the Ngati Whatua, said: "We wish to state emphatically that we give no support whatever to
various widely publicised proposals, claims, and allegations made on our behalf. While we
recognise the democratic right of individuals to express personal opinions, we deny anyone
the right to speak for the Ngati Whatua of Orakei on any subject without our collective
consent and the authority of the Kaumatua. We base this claim on custom and genealogy
tied to title to land."
Throughout all the dealings on this problem the Government has dealt with those who
in their own right are able to speak on behalf of the people of the Ngati Whatua. The
Government will not speak with protesters who elevate themselves to a position of
prominence, or, I might add, who are elevated to that position by the news media, which
must examine their own record during the Bastion Point dispute. From the outset the
Government has dealt with the Ngati Whatua elders, who have been ready and willing to
negotiate with the Government. On 14 January 1977—and the member for Northern Maori
knows this, because he made representations to me-the Ngati Whatua elders, through
Professor Kawharu, put forward proposals that differed considerably from the
Government's original plans for Bastion Point. The Government examined the proposals
and recognised that there were differences to be considered. Accordingly, on 18 February
1977, I convened a public meeting at the Auckland Building Centre to which all interested
parties were invited. Various Maori factions attended, as did environmental groups, the
Auckland City Council, the Auckland Regional Authority, and the member for Northern
Maori.
At that meeting the Government indicated its willingness to consider the elders'
proposals. Most significantly, I said I was willing to start from scratch to review the land use
proposals. The public was invited to make submissions to a joint Lands and Survey,
Auckland Regional Authority, and Auckland City Council planning team under a four-man
steering committee. Its members were: Mr George McMillan, Commissioner of Crown
Lands Auckland; Professor Hugh Kawharu, representing the Ngati Whatua elders; Dr
Lindo Ferguson of the Auckland City Council; and Mr Jim Holdaway of the Auckland
Regional Authority.
On 7 July 1977 the Crown lodged an application in the Supreme Court for an injunction
against the protest leaders to desist from illegally occupying the land at Bastion Point. The
application was made on the recommendation of the Solicitor-General, and the decision to
serve an injunction was made after close consultation with the departments affected. The
application for an injunction gave all parties an opportunity to state their cases in the
Supreme Court; that is why the action was taken.
On 16 November the steering committee released its land use proposals, which
suggested that the largest area, about 12 ha, including the houses in which members of the
tribe are still living together, be vested in a trust board. That land is valued at $2 million, and
it is proposed that it be vested in the Ngati Whatua Housing Trust, and that the trust should
pay about $250,000, which represents an equivalent exchange of land originally taken under
the Public Works Act. Frequent meetings have been held with the people who are involved
and who have a responsibility for the Maori people at Tamaki. At the most recent meeting
the elders made it clear that they accepted the recommendation put forward in the planning


## p. 327 (#335) ############################################

25 May
327
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
report. The proposals included a greater area for open space, a greater area to go to the
proposed trust board, a smaller area for new Crown development for town houses,
empowering legislation to give effect to the whole transaction, and the payment by the trust
board of $257,000.
On 11 April the Crown's injunction was heard by the Supreme Court. Mr Justice
Speight issued his judgment on 20 April. It held that the land at Bastion Point was Crown
land, and was being occupied without right, title, or licence by the defendants. The historical
events associated with the transfer of ownership of land were not in question today. At stake
were the law, the protection of the law, the judgment of the courts, and the security of
tenure of the land we all occupy. Mr Justice Speight also said that absolutely no grounds had
been produced to persuade the court that the plaintiff-the Crown-is barred from his relief
on equitable grounds, and that an injunction would issue in the terms sought. His judgment
is an exceptional document and with Mr Justice Speight's permission copies are being
printed. I shall see that every member receives a copy. Mr Justice Speight's judgment also
said: "The substituted scheme of 1978, approved by the Maori elders and adopted by
Cabinet, is a handsome remedy of long felt wrongs, whether real or imagined. The public in
general will applaud that much of this vacant land will be public reserve accessible to all." I
believe that Mr Justice Speight's words describe the position accurately, that "this scheme
worked out by four wise men and acceptable to the majority of the tribal elders and the
Government, appears, if I may say so, to bring peace with honour."

balance of payments indicates that over the past 3 years import volumes have no longer
increased at about 18 percent; there is no longer a marginal increase in volume. If members

payments. Added to that, there has been an increase in export volume in the last 2 years of

another 2.5 percent decrease. Yet Opposition members say that the Government has done
little or nothing about the balance of trade situation. If they cared to read the latest statistics,
they would see that there has been a dramatic move towards a balance, and the latest figures
show an even greater improvement.

A most intelligent and positive response would be to examine the significant ways in
which the resources of New Zealand can be most effectively used-indeed, more effectively
used than they are now. It is for this reason that much of what has been said about industrial
relations has relevance. The high cost to the nation of continuing stoppages and disruptions
represents a wastage of resources at a time when that wastage can be ill afforded.
In this debate a number of matters have been established as being very clear and beyond
dispute. For instance, no one with good sense is against strong and responsible unionism. No
one with good sense agrees with the misuse of the union movement in the interests of
subversive ideologies imported from Moscow and Peking. As to the motivation of those
people I quote from the master, Lenin. These are his words on trade union movements: “It
is necessary to resort to all sorts of devices, manoeuvres and illegal methods, to evasion and
subterfuge, in order to penetrate into the trade unions, to remain in them and carry on
communist work in them at all costs." This is the gospel of the Andersens and the Willy
Wilsons of this world, and I am certain that no one in the House would endorse that gospel.
These words of Lenin explain not merely the motivation of such people, but also the
tactics that have been employed in recent industrial disputes in this country: the tactics of
stand-over and intimidation. We are all united-members of Parliament and responsible
members of the trade union movement— in deploring and resolving to fight this kind of
subversion. No one of good sense can attribute the fact of inflation exclusively to union wage
demands. As much responsible for inflation in today's world are the price-fixing and other
practices of international corporations and cartels, and the actions of governments that
embark on inflationary expenditure without regard to the wider consequences.
No one of good sense can fail to see the political power of unions and of the huge
corporations as a fact to which modern governments must accommodate themselves. It is a
fact that is producing new tension and new conflict in the world. It is a modern phenomenon,
and where it may lead the Western World is doubtful. To the pessimist, it means a
continuing destructive power struggle between those major elements, the end result of which
may be authoritarian government of some kind, be it of the right or of the left. Those are the
very real fears of all intelligent people throughout the Western World, and the literature and
the political commentary of the day is full of this kind of dire prophecy and commentary.
However, we live in a small and relatively favoured country, and it should be possible
for us, at least, to moderate that conflict, and to ensure the survival of parliamentary
traditions of government in this country. It should be possible, but it is by no means certain.
And so the importance of managing industrial dispute and conflict is not to be found purely
in economic considerations, basic though they may be. That dispute and conflict also has
political connotations and ramifications of a most serious nature. So responsible government
today has two major concerns: first, to maintain the economic and social well-being of its
people; secondly, and very closely allied to it, the responsibility to maintain the stability of
the political system known as parliamentary democracy. These two responsibilities are
interrelated and inseparable. They cannot be considered as though they involved separate
and distinct issues.
For these reasons, I have been disappointed, to say the least, if not alarmed, to hear, in
the course of the debate, members denying the need to examine carefully the practices and
procedures of the House, to ensure that the time of members and all who work within its
orbit is constructively used—and in my view it is not, altogether—and to ensure also that this
institution's continued relevance and authority are maintained through this era of quite
radical economic, social, and political change, and to ensure perhaps its very survival as a
democratic institution. Those who have lightly dismissed the suggestion that reform should
be examined—and the suggestion was made early and indeed at all stages of the debate by a
variety of speakers-people who are saying there is no necessity for this, no necessity to
examine the methods and procedures of this establishment-need to think again.
It is plainly a reverse of the truth, and I want to throw this at the gentleman who made
the suggestion—he knows who he is. To suggest, as one speaker did this afternoon, that
those who are propounding the necessity for reform of this establishment are in some way
subversive is the ultimate in nonsense, and the ultimate in infantile reaction to quite
responsible suggestions. It is plainly the reverse of the truth. Indeed, the subversives in this
institution are those who are so preoccupied with the maintenance of the status quo and their
own position in it that they do not even choose to examine the facts of life about them. I
throw that accusation back at the gentleman who made it. Subversion indeed!

He referred to the undermining of public confidence. If he consulted the people he

I propose now to look at one or two other established practices we ought to be
examining to ensure better resource utilisation, which to me is the key necessity in the
present economic circumstances. I shall mention two or three specific instances of what seem
to me to be wastage of resources. Taxation can be, and is at present, an inducement to
resource wastage. Inflation taxation can operate not merely as a disincentive to work, but as
an incentive to migration. It can also be a direct incentive to the wastage of resources. As a
simple illustration, I understand that farmers receive a 60 percent tax rebate on the purchase
of new tractors, and that their accountants advise them to get rid of their present tractors and
to buy new ones for tax purposes. The results of this are two-fold. The dealers' yards at
present are full of perfectly good and useful secondhand tractors, but, worse than that, while
only 3000 tractors are likely to be sold in New Zealand this year, and while 2000 of these are
likely to be sold by two major dealers, 26 different brands of tractors are available for sale.
The result is the necessity for 26 separate servicing arrangements and 26 separate
arrangements for the supply of spare parts. The country cannot stand much of that sort of
wastage, which I would call nonsense. We are offering tax incentives to farmers so that they,
and the country, may perpetuate a totally wasteful and insupportable situation. Our
economy demands an end to the wasteful use of all resources. I have always believed, and
always shall believe, that that is the first practical priority in dealing with our economy.
As a further example of the wastage of resources, about 300 high country farms in the
South Island are currently the subject of study by about 50 scientists of various kinds. That is
the equivalent of one scientist to every six farms. The scientists work for various agencies,
including the DSIR, the Ministry of Works and Development, and the New Zealand Forest
Service. Their work inevitably overlaps, which to me plainly indicates a lack of effective
integration and use of scarce resources.
I have previously referred in the House to the fragmentation of planning, especially land
use planning, at various levels. In the same vein I should like to refer to the problem of
young farmers who are struggling to develop and enhance the productivity of their marginal
farms. I know of such young farmers who complain bitterly that they have gained nothing
whatsoever from the stock incentive scheme. They simply cannot take advantage of it,
because of existing restrictions. They operate on a hand-to-mouth basis. The stock incentive

Mr SCHULTZ: I ask the member for Onehunga whether that Bill would be
reintroduced if a Labour Government was returned.
Mr Hunt: Of course we shall bring in a similar measure.
Mr SCHULTZ: Will the new Bill have a means test in it, or will it have a clause classing
superannuation as unearned income and therefore attracting double taxation, as it did
during the time of an earlier Labour Government? We should like to have a clear answer
from the Labour Party on that. We are very interested to hear that a Labour Government
would bring in a superannuation Bill of its own, because we have experienced one disaster
and the people will not want a second one from Labour's superannuation policy. It was the
National Party's policy to wind it up and sell the assets that had been acquired.
It is well known that under the Labour Party's policy no one would have received any
benefit for 5 years. People would have had to live to the year 2020 to receive the maximum
benefit. None of us, including the member for Wigram who is trying to interject, would have
benefited from it, and the member from Wigram knows that very well. I am trying to deal
with misstatements and quotations made by Opposition members who try to put across the
wrong story to the public.
A number of Labour members have said that greater emphasis should be placed on the
processing of raw materials. In 1975, under the Labour Government, 1 800 000 square
metres of carpet wool were processed here. In 2 years that figure increased to 3 000 000
square metres. That shows a very rapid increase in domestic processing for the export
market. The same applies to the sawn timber industry, which is now processing increased
quantities of that natural resource. That figure has increased from 2 000 000 cubic metres to 2
670 000 cubic metres. The amount of meat processed has increased from 1500 tonnes to
2400. In 2 years the amount of fish processed has increased from 13 000 tonnes to 27 000
tonnes. In other words, it has almost doubled.
Mr MacDonell: What about the clothing industry?
Mr SCHULTZ: If the member cannot keep warm, that is his business. I have here a
newspaper cutting of one of the most outlandish policy statements I have ever seen printed.
Recently the Labour Party stated that it would put a quota on every home for power use;
every home would need a ration card depending on the number of people living in it. Some
departmental officer would have to go along and decide how many in the family would
qualify for a certain allocation. What sort of bureaucracy would that be if a Labour
Government put a quota on the electricity used by every home? That is not the sort of
democracy the people of this country would want.
Comment has been made about the expansion in our overseas trade. The criticism of
NAFTA has been quite unjustified; members opposite know that the agreement is working
extremely well. We only need to consider the results. In 1974 total trade between the two
countries amounted to $624 million. Today that total trade is equal to $1.1 billion. That is the
figure for the past 12 months, and it is moving in New Zealand's favour. It is almost down to
a 1 to 1.2 ratio. Trade with the United Kingdom stands at $1.18 billion, and is only just above
the trade figures with Australia. Because of reduced costs across the Tasman, I am sure there
will be a further rapid increase in trade with Australia.
I want to make one other comment, and that is on the industrial scene, which has been
covered very well by many of my colleagues and particularly the Minister of Labour. The
Government has dealt with many problems, and has dealt with those problems as they
arise-whether they be economic, trade, social, or industrial. Last year 328 disputes were
settled by the mediation service of the Department of Labour, which was established by the
present Minister of Labour. Very few people give him any credit for what he has done.
It is noticeable that the Labour Party keeps quiet when there is an industrial stoppage.
Whose side is it on? Does it want to see New Zealand make industrial progress, or does it
want to back the people causing those disruptions? I wonder what the Labour Party's
attitude to Kawerau was. The member for New Lynn is smiling. No doubt he put his hand in
his pocket and said he supported the strike, and that it was good to have a strike, because it
might help to put the Government out of office. Bill Andersen held a rally in Auckland and a
few people attended— amongst them the member for New Lynn. They both spoke to that
meeting, which was designed to create rolling strikes and to try to get the National
Government out of office. Most unions are responsible, and the Government commends
those unions for their co-operation. However, some unions are not, and it is nothing short of
criminal to let livestock die, as has been permitted on many occasions. Every time that
happens the Opposition is strangely silent. One might ask where is the Labour Party's loyalty

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Perhaps at this stage, as is customary on a
Friday morning, I could outline the business for next week. It is not yet clear when the
Address in Reply debate will finish, because we have a private member's Bill to discuss later
this morning and I do not know how much time that will take. However, we expect the
Address in Reply debate to finish on either Tuesday or Wednesday. On Wednesday
afternoon we will consider private members' Bills and private members' notices of motion.
After the Address in Reply debate finishes we will consider legislation. As I indicated
earlier, I propose to move the second reading of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and
Abortion Amendment Bill, at present in second place on the Order Paper, to No. 1 position
and see how far we can proceed with that.
I will present the Budget on Thursday night, and my present intention is to have the first
Imprest Supply Bill introduced and passed next Friday, as is customary.

Electric Power Consumption-Labour Party's Policy
2. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) to the Minister of Energy: Has he seen the Labour Party's
policy on electric power consumption, as outlined in the New Zealand Herald of 21 March,
which would ration initial supplies at certain price levels to families according to family size;
and, if so, has he considered what difficulties there would be in implementation by power
supply authorities?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I have seen the Labour Party's policy on electric
power consumption as outlined in the newspaper article of 21 March, and as released by the
Leader of the Opposition on 26 February. The difficulties involved in its implementation by
power supply authorities, with family size as a factor to be taken into account in the billing
process, would be very great indeed. Frequent checking on the number of persons in each
household would involve a major increase in administrative work load, and an undesirable
intrusion into the private affairs of consumers. However, the Government is investigating
the potential advantages and disadvantages of inverted energy tariffs and will be holding
discussions with electricity and gas distributing authorities.
Mr Falloon: Would the implementation of such a policy create higher costs for power
consumers than would otherwise be the case?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: That would certainly be the case, and if the cost was not properly
charged against any individual consumer then it would have to be born by other consumers.
The administrative complications that would be created by the proposal would add
considerably to the overheads of the supply authorities.
Hon. F. M. Colman: The Minister would be aware of the policy that has been in
operation in California since 1971, and that it has been so successful that it is likely to be
adopted as policy throughout the United States. If that is the case, then surely what is good
for the United States is good enough for New Zealand.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I would have hoped that the spokesman on energy matters in the
Labour Party would have done his homework more carefully before he proposed this as a
firm policy, because experience in California shows that the policy does not contain several
important features included in the Labour Party's proposals. I shall refer to two particularly.
The first is that no attempt is made to intrude into the private affairs of families to find out
how many people are there, and, second, it applies to other energy forms. If the Labour
Party's proposal were to be adopted then even to attempt to be fair, it would have to apply to
all energy forms.

other group for the purposes of political advantage. The general election this year will be
fought on the strength of what is presented by the parties to the electorate. It will be for the
public to decide what is or is not an issue."

14. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Labour: To what extent does he receive
complaints about the slowness of service from the Accident Compensation Commission, and
what is the average time for settlement after claim, bearing in mind the need to obtain
medical services?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Labour replies: "I
receive an average of one letter a week alleging slowness in handling compensation claims by
either the commission or the State Insurance Office. This is in contrast to the 2500 claims
that enter the system every week. I observe that in his last annual report the Ombudsman
found that only six allegations of delay against the commission were justified. The
commission informs me that the average time between lodging a claim, with its necessary
supporting certificates, and the date of the first payment is 12 days. The comparable period
for all workers compensation boards in the United States is 33 days."
Mr Malcolm: Has the Minister any figures on complaints or the length of time it takes to
process delays broken down into geographic areas?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, but that information might be available upon notice.

Account, and shall be credited to the Consolidated Revenue Account. I am not

Hon. F. M. Colman: The Minister has said that the levy is being used for research,

should have read $28 million. The total of $32.5 million is correct. The main areas of
Government expenditure are exploration. In 1977-78 the Government spent $1.75 million on
coal; about $12 million on offshore petroleum; $8 million on onshore petroleum, which
includes the purchase of the rig that has yet to be used; $3.8 million on geothermal by the
Ministry of Works and Development; and $900,000 million for the DSIR geothermal support

liability that could be between $400 million and $500 million, but some of this capital cost
overrun could be disqualified pursuant to the precise terms of the contract. In other words,

deal of work is going into future development, some of which will benefit the South Island.

Electricity Supply Authorities-Small Hydro Scheme
20. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Energy: How many electricity supply
authorities have taken advantage of the Government's small hydro scheme provisions
announced last year, and what are the results?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): Ten supply authorities have received assistance
under the Government's small hydro scheme proposal, with one supply authority having two
small schemes approved. Construction loans amounting to $41.9 million have been made for
four schemes with a capacity of 57.7 MW. Investigation and design grants amounting to
$568,000 have been made for seven schemes with a capacity of 81 MW.
Mr Latter: The Marlborough Electric Power Board has had one supplementary grant. Is
there anything to prevent it applying for another grant on another scheme before it has
finished the first one?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: No, provided the second scheme complies with the criteria and, in
the judgment of the committee, is considered to be correctly placed in the order of priority
that is accorded these schemes.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Does the Minister know that late in 1975 the Labour Minister of
Electricity initiated discussions between the power supply authorities and the Government
on proceeding with the development of small hydro schemes?
Mr SPEAKER: That is only barely related to the question, but the Minister may
comment briefly.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: There were a number of discussions between the Labour Minister of
Electricity and the supply authorities, and none of the problems was resolved. It was not
until the new Government came into office that they were resolved.
Mr T. J. Young: Have any of the power supply authorities that seek to take advantage
of this scheme had their schemes rejected?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I have a list of the authorities that have received support and have
been declined. Only one has been declined so far. Some proposals are still under discussion,
and I cannot say how they will be finally judged.
State House Applications
21. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), on behalf of Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda), to the
Minister of Housing: How many applications to be placed on a State house waiting list has
the Housing Corporation received in each of the last 3 financial years, and, in each financial
year, how many applications were turned down on the grounds that the applicant's income
or assets were too high?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The number of applications received
during each of the last three financial years was as follows: year ended 31 March 1976,
14 255; year ended 31 March 1977, 12 949; and year ended 31 March 1978, 11 599. Income is
not a factor taken into account when an applicant's eligibility is determined, but when
assessing the priority of each applicant a maximum of up to 20 points out of 100 may be
awarded. Separate figures are not kept when an applicant's assets are found to be too high,
but the corporation advises that there would be comparatively few declines a year in this
category.

Mortgage Interest Rates
24. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), on behalf of Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the
Minister of Finance: What were the average mortgage interest rates of all mortgages
registered in the month of May in each of the years 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978, and can he
confirm that the average interest rates prevailing in the calendar year 1977 and those
prevailing to the date of 1978 are the highest ever recorded since records were first kept in
1913?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The question stated "to date in
1978", according to the copy I have, and not "to the date of 1978". I have only some of the
information the honourable member has requested, because data on mortgage registrations
are not available subsequent to October 1977. The figures available are: May 1975, 8.28
percent; May 1976, 9.24 percent; and May 1977, 10.45 percent. The average rate of interest
on mortgages registered in the first 10 months of 1977 was 10.29 percent, and it is expected
that that downward trend will continue. Records are in fact available prior to 1913, but it is
correct that this figure of the nominal mortgage interest rates has not been exceeded in any
year since that time. However, when these average rates are compared with the rates of
inflation prevailing at the time it can readily be seen that interest rates have been lower in
relation to the rate of inflation in the last 2 years than in the majority of years between 1913
and 1976.
Mr Rogers: When the Minister mentioned that he believes interest rates will fall, can he
give a figure of what he expects, or does he believe he can get it back to the 8.2 percent
average of when he took over power in this country?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The member has to understand that, when the rate of
inflation went up over 15 percent in the last year of the Labour Government, that inevitably
pulled interest rates up. As the rate of inflation comes down, as it is doing now, interest rates
come down in sympathy with it. Where they pass a particular figure is for the future, but the
rate of inflation is now coming down and the process will continue. The last quarter was at an
annual rate of 8.2 percent, and that, combined with fairly easy credit conditions at present, is
having a downward influence on interest rates, which will certainly continue through the
remainder of this year. Beyond that, much will depend on the state of the economy generally
as the economy moves up.

Taxation Rebates
25. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: Why is the young family rebate paid out on a weekly basis and the single
income family rebate on an annual return basis?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of Inland Revenue Department): As was
stated in the 1977 Budget introducing the single income family rebate, it simply cannot be
incorporated into the PAYE tables because of the number of additional tax codes required
to cover the variety of family circumstances. Although the PAYE tax tables provide for the
young family rebate, the member will be interested to know that a recent survey showed that
over 60 percent of those entitled to this rebate elected to claim it as an end-of-the-year
assessment rather than altering their tax codes.

the paper's value will last well beyond the present discussions in New York. The member will
no doubt agree that the negotiations referred to in the paper will still be current for years
ahead and the information in it will remain relevant.

when considering its policy about the attitudes it will take at the United Nations conference?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The Government has given consideration to a number of
suggestions made, has taken those into account, and determined its attitude as a result of
that consideration.
QUESTIONS-WRITTEN
Accident and Emergency Facilities
1. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Health: What accident and
emergency facilities are available to cities about the size of Upper Hutt, and would he detail
these services in each of the cities?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Accident and emergency facilities are based
at a general hospital because of the need for back-up facilities such as resuscitation and
intensive care units, X-ray and laboratory departments, blood bank facilities, and fully
staffed and equipped operating theatres. The situation in areas of a similar size to Upper
Hutt varies extensively throughout New Zealand mainly for historical and geographical
reasons. For communities such as Timaru, Gisborne, Nelson, Taranaki, and Wanganui there
are base hospital facilities that serve the total population for the hospital board district.
However, there are other cities that form part of a larger metropolitan area which do not
have accident and emergency services of their own but have access to such services in an
adjacent city in the same hospital board district. Porirua, Henderson, South Auckland,
Birkenhead, and East Coast Bays are examples of such areas.

Secondary School Rolls Increase
6. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: Can he give an indication
from the March 1978 returns of State secondary school rolls throughout the country of areas
where there has been a marked increase over previous years in the number of pupils in the
fifth and higher forms?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Provisional figures from the 1
March 1978 returns show that there has been an increase from 1977 to 1978 in the fifth, sixth,
and seventh form rolls of State secondary schools of 5920 pupils. This represents an increase
of 6.2 percent. Education board districts with the greatest percentage increases are:
Auckland, 8.4 percent (2306); Taranaki, 8.4 percent (279); Canterbury, 6.4 percent (797);
South Auckland, 6.3 percent (1044).

Questions-Written
Roadway Replacements-Recycling
7. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and Development: Have
any estimates been made of the recovery costs that would be invoked in the "recycling" of
road pavements on sections of highways that are no longer in use, and can he indicate how
many kilometres of road fall into the latter category?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: Where a section of
highway is being replaced on a new alignment it is normal practice to reuse the old pavement
materials if this is more economic than the use of all new material. Each work is individually
costed and therefore no single recovery cost can be determined. About 40 km of State
highway pavement is replaced each year in a manner that would allow such a recycling of
materials.
(26/5/78)
Wellington Airport-Use of DC8s
8. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services:
How much longer will Air New Zealand's three DC8 aircraft be able to continue service
from Wellington airport, what are the present ages of these three aircraft, and what is the
service life expectancy of each of them?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services) replied: There is no practical limitation on the continued operation of DC8s into
Wellington Airport. Indeed, Air New Zealand has assured me that its remaining three DC8
aircraft will provide entirely adequate trans-Tasman services into Wellington. One of the
three aircraft is 12½ years old and the other two are just over 9 years old. Provided the
Douglas aircraft are well maintained and serviced there is no limitation on their service life.

LABOUR DEPARTMENT AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Labour
Department Amendment Bill. This Bill is not lengthy, but it aims at the adoption of a more
constructive approach to some of the problems caused in the workplace. It will be readily
seen that it imposes added duties and gives some initiatives to the Department of Labour in
the amalgamation of unions, in training, in research, and in increasing the number and
involvement of conciliators and mediators.
I am sure that everyone is heartily fed-up with the conflict among different sections of
our community, whether workers, employers, or just spectators, when dealing with
industrial relations. I remember the member for Hamilton West saying recently that getting
back to causes rather than trying to deal with symptoms is long overdue. I believe that
everything we do in this House dealing with industrial relations should be deliberately
designed to bring unity, between both the parties in the House and those in industry, and to
build responsibility in the community.
The accusations that have been hurled across the floor of this House in recent weeks-
and in recent years have done nothing to assist the Department of Labour in its work. They
do not help the Minister, or the economy, and they do nothing for the image of this
institution. There is no doubt that the problem is a complex one. For too long we have
neglected the need to arm the Department of Labour with the capacity to do what it can. We
could be forgiven for believing that the economic problems have been administered on a
day-to-day basis, with a lot of propaganda, but with no planning or programming.
It is time we came to grips with the problem. The way to deal with it is through the
Department of Labour, which is trusted by all the parties involved, and has a worthy history.
We have to face the fact that unemployment is running at an unprecedented level. A
conservative estimate of man-days lost is more than 1 000 000 in 3 months.
Something is wrong when not only militant unions but also Public Service typists are
involved in industrial stoppages. We must attempt to correct matters quickly, and I believe
the department can quickly become effective in four areas if we arm it with the necessary
money, and with power to take initiatives. The first is amalgamation, which would be


## p. 364 (#372) ############################################

364
26 May
Labour Department Amendment Bill
welcomed by many unions. Amalgamation would increase their support of research into
industrial problems, would improve their communication with the membership, would help
them to become aware of the problems of the other side, and would assist in the
establishment of industrial democracy and shared decision making and good will in the front
line of industry. Such constructive, not destructive, initiatives can only mean stronger
unions, better-informed unions, and unions better able to play their part. I believe we can be
rid of the penalties and tighten up the rules so that self-discipline within the unions—such as
they have attempted at Kawerau-will have a self-disciplining effect on the wildcat minority.
It is better for the organisations to deal with their own problems because it is less
disruptive, and better for everyone in the long term. Penalty after penalty will not solve the
wildcat strikes. Strong amalgamated unions properly staffed and properly resourced will
have the support of the membership, and will have the resources to deal with wildcat
strikes-which have been a problem for a long time. Research, which I mention only briefly,
is generally a compilation of statistics. We want the kind of research that homes in more
directly on techniques used for settling industrial disputes, and provides the kind of back-up
information that could be used successfully in the front line of industry, bringing the
management's front-line foreman and the union's delegate together, when a problem occurs.
The law, to which we have all been party, is complicated, when settling personal
grievances. It is protracted, causes friction, and, to my mind, needs a complete overhaul, in a
practical atmosphere. Grievances are just that-they can multiply into major disputes
unnecessarily, because of delay and outdated techniques for dealing with them. I believe we
should find more money to assist the department to carry out research into such problems.
Other members will talk about the educational and training aspects of the Bill. There is no
doubt that, in industry throughout the world, the foreman and shop steward must be trained
in their duties, each to have an understanding of the other's responsibilities to the people
they represent.
In this country we have a great opportunity-for our people are not necessarily
aggressive because of status-for each to gain an understanding of the other's responsibilities
and limits, and to learn the methods of getting grievances back quickly to management or to
the union leadership. In my opinion that will do a great deal to bring a more constructive
atmosphere to the workplace than at present exists. Such problems have affected our key
industries for many years. There has to be more understanding of the problems of others, if
they are to be solved. I want to speak briefly about increasing the number of conciliators and
mediators. I hope the Government takes up the suggestions in this private member's Bill,
which provides a constructive approach to a massive task. Our work force is spread over
1000 miles and throughout many different companies, concentrated in areas vital to our
economy.
The department must begin to train people in the workplace to be mediators, and
eventually leaders, as their career develops. I believe they would do a tremendous job of
marrying together the opinions of union representatives and the impartiality of the
Department of Labour when there is conflict. No one pretends it will be easy. However, we
must make the attempt, and soon. It must be remembered that any loss-whether it be
through unemployment, avoidable stoppage, or failure to expend money constructively to
build a unified work force-costs many millions more than the initial outlay to establish
harmony. I have always deplored the inability of the House to find a bipartisan approach to
this important resource.
I can see us disagreeing about detail-we will always do that, whatever the subject. But
why can the House not face up to the reality of finding a way to combine capital and labour,
of talking about productivity in a sensible manner, rather than using it, as we so often do, to
bash one another around the ears?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Perhaps I should start with the
honourable member's last point first, about why we cannot, in the House, find a bipartisan
approach to the matter. I would have thought the reason would be more obvious to him than
to anyone else, because he is the president of a party that is the trade union party—not a
bipartisan party, not the party of the employer and the workers, but the party of the
Federation of Labour. As long as the Labour Party is not a bipartisan party, it will not be
possible to get a bipartisan approach to industrial relations in the House.
On the other hand, the National Party is more than just a bipartisan party. It covers the
whole spectrum of New Zealand society. Something like 175 000 members cannot all be
wealthy capitalists; there are not so many in the country. Workers, trade unionists, trade
union officials, farmers, retired people, and professional men and women are members of


## p. 365 (#373) ############################################

26 May
365
Labour Department Amendment Bill
the National Party. If the Labour Party ever becomes a broad-spectrum party and gets rid of
its trade union links, then we could have a bipartisan approach to industrial relations in the
House- but not until. The Bill is a form of window dressing to enable the Labour Party to
continue the debate on industrial relations that started in the House a day or two ago.
Most employers have always had excellent relations with their workers. Something that
perhaps escapes the notice of the public, from time to time, is that industrial strife is limited
to a small number of industries and unions. Inside that group, it is significant that the same
names appear constantly in different industries and in different unions. I say no more than
that. The member who introduced the Bill was Minister of Labour for a short time a year or
two ago. I wonder that he did not introduce this as a Government Bill when he was the
Minister. He had the opportunity. Why did he not have these thoughts then? Perhaps he did
not want to do a window-dressing job when he was Minister of Labour. He was too busy
trying to keep his own friends from the industrial havoc that they were creating, even while
there was a Labour Government.
The Mangere Bridge job has now stopped, or is about to stop, and the whole work force
is about to be discharged. We inherited that dispute from him. It has not been solved, and it
was not solved by him as Minister of Labour. There were disputes at Kawerau that he could
not solve when he was Minister, and more recently the Labour Party conference expressed
support for the strikers at Kawerau. That is the Labour Party in action, and not just window
dressing.
Looking at the details of the Bill, it proposes to amend the duties of the department in
the following manner: "To take such steps as are necessary to assist and encourage the
amalgamation of unions". Of course, the department does that now, to the extent that it is
invited to. Does he want the department to do it compulsorily, because it is the policy of the
present Minister to encourage the amalgamation of unions -just as it is, I believe, the policy
of the Federation of Labour? There is no difference between the two, and no need for a
statutory requirement of any kind on the department. That is plain window dressing.
The Bill goes on: "To undertake concerted research into techniques for settling
industrial disputes". In other days the member claimed to have all the answers, and, indeed,
he was rather on that tack this morning. We do not need research; he knows how to settle
industrial disputes. He knows how to settle them all right—no penalties, and give way every
time; that is the end product of his research. Of course, you can settle any dispute by that
means, but it is a little more difficult to settle fairly, as he found out when he was Minister of
Labour. He did not have an outstanding success in that portfolio. He used to say in the
House, "I like to stand aloof from these things", which is another way of saying, "I have not
got an answer."
The next provision is: "To establish centres for employer-employee education and
training". I hoped he would explain a little more of what that meant. What does he want the
Department of Labour to do? We need a little more detail on exactly what that is all about-
employer-employee training in what? What kind of establishment is intended? Does he
mean some kind of college? What is wrong with the polytechnics? Is that what he has in
mind? It is all very peculiar, and I suggest again it is simply window dressing.
The last provision is: "To ensure that industrial conciliation and mediation services are
developed to their fullest extent". That is vague: there is a nice sound about it, but it signifies
very little. What does "their fullest extent" mean? We have got the services, they are
developing, they are doing a good job. I suggest that the whole of the Bill is window
dressing. It adds nothing to the law to say that these are the duties of the department, and it
could create some difficulties. The member talks of assisting and encouraging the
amalgamation of unions, but the department does that now. We do not need anything in the
Act to enable it to do more. If the Bill took positive steps, that would be the point at which
some of the unions might bridle and not be entirely happy about the proposal.
The Labour Party has to do something better than put forward a Bill such as this. If the
party is serious in its concern for bipartisanship it should be getting in behind the
Government in tackling the militants, instead of criticising it and giving them support
through the party conference. The Labour Party should be coming in behind the
Government and saying, "We are on the side of the Government. These are wreckers and
we are opposed to them" I do not believe I have ever heard a Labour spokesman or leader
say that about a dispute when a National Government has been in office. They have never
said they are opposed to the militants, and that they back the Government. Has the member
for Roskill any recollection of that happening? I might be corrected, but I do not think he
can recall a single occasion—and it is obvious that he cannot-when the Labour Opposition

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I welcome the Bill brought forward by the member
for Roskill, the Labour Party spokesman on industrial relations and the alternative Minister
of Labour. He is the man New Zealanders now recognise as the best Minister of Labour the
country has had since World War II. I regret that the Prime Minister made the speech he did,
and I regret that in the House he refused to accept a genuine offer made by the Labour Party
of a bipartisan approach to industrial relations.
Members on this side recognise that the 1 000 000 working days lost in 3 months
represents the worst record of any Government, except for that in power during the time of
the 1951 strike. We on this side also recognise that it is twice as bad as the record of any
Labour Government during the 20 years when Labour was in office. We know something
about industrial relations, and we are prepared to share our knowledge with Government
members. We recognise that when 1 000 000 working days are lost in a period of 3 months we
have not only poor industrial relations, but we have a crisis. We also recognise that the Prime
Minister's words and actions are not helping, and we are trying to help.
I should like to take up one or two of the remarks made by the Prime Minister. I
understood him to say that 90 percent of disputes in New Zealand are caused by militants,
such as members of the Socialist Unity Party. I shall remind him of some recent disputes. In
the past 3 months we have had strikes by typists, journalists, bank officers, film
projectionists, film cameramen, school teachers, kindergarten school teachers, clerical
workers, social workers, probation officers, and librarians. Is the Prime Minister's
Government now employing militant Socialist Unity Party people in the probation service,
in the kindergartens, and as librarians?
For goodness sake, that is
ridiculous answer to the major crisis facing New Zealand.
We should not look for scapegoats, but for causes. For that reason, I believe the Bill brought
forward by the member for Roskill is a constructive and helpful measure, because it goes to
the causes of industrial disputes. As 1 000 000 working days have been lost in 3 months, it is a
good time to consider the Bill. Now we have a loadout ban, and the Prime Minister has told
us of another dispute he thinks is going to occur tomorrow. We now have what can be
regarded as lull in bad industrial relations. Normally, with a loadout ban and a strike about
to break out, we would consider industrial relations as being at crisis point. This year that
represents a lull between the great industrial storms we have had, and it is a good time to try
to determine the basic causes of strikes and seek ways of solving them.
Let us look at the operative clauses of the Bill. The first paragraph proposed to be
inserted is: "To take such steps as are necessary to assist and encourage the amalgamation of
unions". I draw the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that we have 338 unions in New
Zealand. In contrast, West Germany has only 16 unions—and we know which of the two
countries has the best industrial relations. The recent dispute at Kawerau began as a result of
fewer than a dozen men in one union having a dispute with the management. That led to a
stoppage involving more than 10 unions, thousands of men, and millions of dollars. If only
one union had been involved it would have been easier to solve the strike, because when the
management began to negotiate it had to talk to a number of unions.
I also bring to the Prime Minister's attention the fact that it is not just the Federation of
Labour that is in favour of amalgamation. The National Party's thick manifesto-the one

Andersen, President of the Auckland Trades Council, said the meeting was a resounding
success." Fortunately, his campaign was spurned and destroyed by the moderates in the
trade union movement, and I pay tribute to those moderates who are trying to get away from
this socialist blight that has damaged our industrial scene for so many decades.
I now come back to the Bill, and point out that the new paragraph (g) states, "To take
such steps as are necessary to assist and encourage the amalgamation of unions". The
Industrial Relations Act has detailed provisions giving that statutory authority. Three
parties—and not only the Labour Department in a dictatorial, centralised, bureauratic way,
as the Labour spokesman would have it, but the trade union movement through its central
organisation the Federation of Labour, and the employers' representatives through their
central organisation the Employers Federation, and the Labour Department—are already
working together to encourage amalgamation of unions. Therefore, that part of the Bill is
unnecessary.
Paragraph (h) states, "To undertake concerted research into techniques for settling
industrial disputes". I have already referred to work done in the universities with the backing
of this Government. Already, the Labour Department has a research and planning division,
with a special industrial relations section, so that provision in this Bill is unnecessary.
Paragraph (i) states, "To establish centres for employer-employee education and
training". I have already referred to the Industrial Relations Foundation and to the
Industrial Relations Centre. There is also, of course, the Vocational Training Council,
properly constituted under statute, and encouraged, developed, and expanded by the
National Government over the years, and, I am glad to say, given some support by the last
Labour Government. Therefore, this provision is unnecessary.

Mr SPEAKER: I do not think we need to go any further into this matter. It is clear that,
if a member makes a statement in the House, it must be accepted. There are occasions when
there is conflict about this. Two members may be present at the same meeting and have
different recollections of what happened. In those circumstances we do our best with it. I
think all members are aware that they have attended meetings with people they do not
normally like to associate with, or whose ideas they do not hold with. Association with
another person does not really imply anything at all, except that two people are at the same
meeting or place at the same time. It is out of order to say or to insinuate that a member has
been dominated by, manipulated by, instructed by, or directed by somebody outside
Parliament, or some outside organisation. It is not out of order to say that a party or a
member-Government or Opposition member-has been advised by or influenced by
somebody. There is a fine dividing line between "influence", and "direction" or
"instruction".
We must leave it to the good sense of honourable members to take the spirit of what
rulings have been given. The spirit is based probably on two facts. If we are to have proper
debate in the House, there must be freedom of speech and there must also be relevance. In
those circumstances it is not relevant to refer to honourable members as having been
dominated, manipulated, instructed, or directed by somebody. If members think it is
relevant to say that a member has been advised by or influenced by somebody, I suppose
that is all right; it depends on the circumstances. Obviously, I was not here when the earlier
points of order were raised, but some references were made to it. I am not aware of how the
Deputy Speaker ruled. My ruling is that it is not in order to imply that a member has been
dominated, directed, instructed, or manipulated by people or organisations outside the
House. It is in order to say that he has been influenced or advised. It is not in order to make a
suggestion by way of innuendo or implication-by what I call a back-door debating device-
to get around this practice of saying, "influenced" as opposed to "domination". I hope that
makes it clear to the honourable member.

lost-more than double the number of days lost under any Labour Administration. The
purpose of the Bill is to strengthen the Department of Labour and to direct it as to how it
should carry out its functions. The Bill states: "Section 9 of the principal Act is hereby
amended by adding the following subsections: (g) To take such steps as are necessary to
assist and encourage the amalgamation of unions. (h) To undertake concerted research into
techniques for settling industrial disputes. (i) To establish centres for employer-employee
education and training. (j) To ensure that industrial conciliation and mediation services are
developed to their fullest extent." What objection can Government members have to any of
those four cardinal provisions being added to the Act? That is the case the Opposition is
making, and it shows that the Government is completely out of touch with what is happening
today. It does not understand industrial relations, and prefers to take a heavy-handed
approach, which never works.
I refer Government members to the proposed new subsection (h). It is interesting to
consider why some sections of industry have good records in industrial relations, and others
have a deplorable record, to say the least. In an article in the latest issue of the Labour and
Employment Gazette Mr Noel Woods, a former Secretary of Labour whose opinions are
highly respected, points out the vast differences that occur in some of the very sensitive
industries in New Zealand. He quotes Turkington, who records on page 43 of Industrial
Conflict the variations in the numbers of stoppages in freezing works over a 7-year period.
Four works averaged only 0.29 stoppages a year while three other works averaged more than
seven stoppages a year. Such figures do not necessarily relate to managerial competence, but
exemplify the need for management to find specific rather than generalised reasons for
differences in performance. Is that not what the proposed new subsection (h) is all about?
Why should we not try to find out why some freezing works in New Zealand have a good
record with only 0.3 percent stoppages in a year, while others have a record of 7 percent,
which is a ratio of 1:20.
I turn now to training, and ask what the Government has done. The training programme
has remained relatively underdeveloped, in spite of technological changes in the past few
years and the new meat hygiene regulations which have placed increased demands on
workers and management. A much more vigorous approach to training is needed. One of
the major recommendations made by the Meat Industry Training Advisory Board was for a
Government subsidised special training incentive for supervisors in the meat industry. The
third Labour Government approved a maximum of $40,000 a year for the industry to
implement this scheme, which was a positive step towards grappling with the problems the
industry is facing. But what has happened since the National Government has been in charge
of that provision? In the year ended 31 March 1977, a pitiful grant of $16,800 was made for
21 trainees-less than half the amount made available under the Labour Government.

DEBATES-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BILLS
Mr SPEAKER: Perhaps I can take the time of the House for a few minutes to make
some observations about the introduction of private members' Bills. The time of Parliament
is valuable, and it is important that members should have the opportunity to discuss matters
that are of particular interest to them. For that reason the House has the private members'
public Bill procedure. It seems to me that, by and large, those Bills can be divided into two
categories: those relating purely to a party philosophy-the so-called party political; and I
am not using the words in any other sense-and those that most members would agree have
some merit and deserve further consideration.
Many Bills involve an appropriation and would therefore be ruled out of order at some
stage unless the Government adopted them. It seems to me that private members' Bills
containing the germ of an idea that the House might like to consider further should be
entitled to further consideration. In those circumstances, the best procedure would be a brief
introductory debate so that members could study the Bill, with it then being brought back
and taken through the normal procedures of reference to a select committee, or of a second
reading debate, as though it were a Government Bill being considered in greater depth. The
party political Bill will be ruled out at some stage because it involves an appropriation.
I suggest that it would be appropriate for the Whips to get together and discuss whether
a debate of the nature we have just had should take place on the introduction or the second
reading. Members are wasting the valuable time of the House if they have, in effect, two
second reading debates. I am sure it is not beyond the wit of the Whips to come to a sensible
arrangement about the introduction and further debate of private members' Bills.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: There was an agreement on the Bill.
Mr SPEAKER: That is not debatable. I hope the Whips will make some progress on that
and inform me in due course.
