Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): First, I should like to join all those who
have congratulated His Excellency, Sir Keith Holyoake, on his first opening of Parliament. I
regret the Labour Party's embargo on official functions attended by the Governor-General,
but I have been delighted to notice that the Maori members have been able to overcome that
embargo and to meet His Excellency. I should like to congratulate you, Mr Speaker, on your
appointment to the Chair. With your long experience—and you have pointed out that you
once read jurisprudence-in Parliament and in the Army, to say nothing of your association
with Federated Farmers, I am sure you will add lustre to the seat. I join with others who have
congratulated the member for Rangitikei on his maiden speech, and I should like to
congratulate the member for Henderson on a very interesting speech on the problems of the
sheepmeats agreement as he saw them when he was overseas recently. I thought that the
mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply handled the subject of exports very well.
I was not surprised that the Leader of the Opposition decided to rubbish this year's
export drive. The drive is being taken up by farmers, foresters, and horticulturists, who hope
to increase their exports shortly to $100 million. Manufacturers, assisted by the
Government, hope to open up new markets for new products as well as for old products. The
Opposition seems to shut its eyes to exports—why, I do not know. Using 1971 as a base—I
am speaking of volume-and using a base figure of 1000, we find that in 1972 exports went
up by 4.8 percent, in 1973 by 2.5 percent, but in 1974 they declined by 11.3 percent, and in
1975 by 2.5 percent. The year before that the Labour Government tried the interesting
experiment of revaluing our currency, which meant that a New Zealand lamb was more
expensive to buy in Honolulu than a freshly killed Californian lamb. The currency was
revalued so that there would be a flood of imports-the Labour Government was not
interested in exports. In 1976, exports increased by 17.8 percent, and in 1977 by 11.8
percent.
Why does the Labour Party rubbish our export efforts? Obviously the exporters are
taking advantage of the Government's incentives. There have been some outstanding
achievements, and there are many more to come. People with ideas are building things in
New Zealand and finding that they can export them for the benefit of the country. The
horticultural industry in particular is bursting with ideas and enthusiasm for exports.
Recently I set up a horticultural export promotion committee so that horticulturists could
share their problems and help one another for their own benefit and for the benefit of the
country.
The Labour Party has unveiled some of its policies, including its policy on industrial
relations. It will repeal all the strong legislation of the past 2 years. Does that include Section
128 of the Industrial Relations Act? Would some Opposition speaker tell us whether his
party would repeal this section, which allows a company to suspend men when there is no
longer work for them, or whether it will force a company to go on paying those men when
they can no longer produce? Will there be a resurgence of the threat of rolling strikes
organised by the Socialist Unity Party? Members opposite are very quiet on that. Will they
do away with the Arbitration Court set up by the National Government, with a consequent
return to the chaos we had before? They have said they will repeal all the restrictive
measures in the Industrial Relations Act. Will they tear up the agreement with the freezing
workers on the 3-day killing? I wonder if they will then continue to support stopwork
meetings around the country.
The member for Christchurch Central, a successful farmer, said, “Taxation and the
escalating paper value of land means many people view a farm in terms of capital gains.

One of the most serious threats to the New Zealand economy is the growing agricultural
protectionism throughout the world. New Zealand, with 75 percent of its overseas funds
earned by the primary producer, has to resist agricultural protectionism. Some countries are
striving for self-sufficiency in agricultural products. The EEC, the United States, Japan, and
Australia, all have barriers against the free flow of our agricultural products. New Zealand is
open so long as the product meets our hygiene requirements. It is interesting to note that
when the American Secretary for Agriculture, Mr Butz, was in this country a few years ago,
he complained to me that we had a tariff against their beef. We removed it, and America
now has no complaint. I have not heard of any American beef coming into New Zealand, but
if that country met our standards its beef could be imported.
The OECD countries, of which New Zealand is one, have a very strong industrial policy
aimed at removing restrictions on manufactured goods so that they can flow freely. Last
year, at the OECD financial conference, the Prime Minister succeeded in getting the word
"agricultural" tacked on, so that the agreement now reads, “industrial and agricultural
goods". This year, when we were discussing grains-mostly stock food-with the EEC, we
managed, with the help of Canada and Australia, to get the conference to accept, after the
word "grains", the words "and dairy and livestock products". It is a long haul from the
inclusion of words in a communique to their acceptance as common practice. We must keep

Talks will begin at the end of the year on what will happen after 1980. Ireland has
already proposed that after 1982 we should have no quota for butter into the Common
Market. On 1 January 1978, Britain, Denmark, and Ireland became full members of the
community; the commission has therefore stated that they must have a sheepmeat
agreement. It is interesting to note that when I talked to Ministers overseas in November the
Netherlands and Germany were not very interested, France said it was prepared to accept
the status quo, Denmark asked why we did not send more lamb, because it had a market for
it, and Italy was more interested in the entry of Greece, Spain, and Portugal, so that it could
have a market for its wines, olive oil, and oranges.
Greece is of great concern to us, because of our specialised and very valuable market for
lamb, which would come into a quota if Greece goes into the Common Market. Ireland has
its own arrangement, breaking the EEC rules, and last year it sent something like 5000
tonnes of lamb to France. British farmers are keen to equate with the Irish, because they
would like to get the same price.
As a result of the effect upon production if the price is doubled, we have spoken to the
British Ministers and shown the effect of what quotas would do. I was very interested to hear
the member for Henderson talking about this. There would be no expansion for growth, and
it is not just the lambmeat trade that would be affected; the effect would flow on into wool
and by-products, and would be catastrophic for New Zealand.
At present we have one trump card, the GATT binding, which means we have no quota

## p. 391 (#399) ############################################

30 May
391
Select Committee Membership
Washington the position is reversed: instead of party politics that mark the committee
procedures of Britain there is there less adherence to the party machine, as is common in
Washington and in American politics, and the senators and congressmen respond to the
merits of a case as each one assesses it.
I now come back to New Zealand. When I first came into this House, over 30 years ago,
voting in committees was rare. Unhappily, it is becoming more common, but it is still the
exception rather than the rule. My experience is that there still is some degree of voting
across party lines in committees, even on non-conscience issues. To me, there seems to be a
number of reasons for that, the main one being the attitude of mind that members bring to
committee work. In the main, I think that persists, with one or two notable exceptions. This
motion is a bad omen for its continuance. I believe that the province of a committee is
practice, not principle. For instance, an Opposition member, an Independent member, or
even a Government member might find the policy expressed in a Government measure
totally unacceptable, and would resist its passage relentlessly in the House or in the
Committee of the Whole during what we know here as the Committee stage. But, in the
select committee to which a Bill has been referred, he may—and I think he should—
reconcile himself to the fact that the Government majority will ultimately prevail, and that
the Bill will be enacted. His responsibility, behind the closed doors of a committee's
deliberations, should be to make the best of a bad bargain, and co-operate to produce
legislation that will work in practice, however offensive in principle it may be. In other
words, to make it as little harmful as possible.
I should like to make these two points in relation to the operation and functioning of the
Statutes Revision Committee. First, in examining witnesses it is perfectly legitimate for a
member to illustrate a party point he could use in debate in the House, and secondly, it
would be quite wrong to hold it against a member in open House if he voted for a clause, or
an amendment to a clause, in the committee. It is not inconsistent with the true role of the
committee for him to vote against it in the House. If the Government's undoubtedly narrow
view of this role is accepted, no great harm is done, because if the Government is defeated in
the committee, and its pride wounded, or its self-esteem dented, it is a simple matter for the
point to be recommitted when the full membership is there to establish its majority.
Finally, I should like to see the scope of the committee work extended along the lines
already followed by the Public Expenditure Committee. The Statutes Revision Committee is
essentially concerned with a review of matters referred to it by the House, and there is no
reason why the Education Committee, the Social Services Committee, and other committees
should not initiate inquiries. Indeed they could well have a number of statutory commissions
of inquiry-
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Would the honourable member please come back to a discussion
of the motion before the House, which is the appointment of the member for Rangitikei to
the Statutes Revision Committee in place of an Opposition member. We should not get into
a discussion on the role of select committees.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: In coming back to the matter before us I express my regret that
select committees are not put to greater work than they are, and that the robust common
sense of members of Parliament, when they forget party politics and apply themselves to a
job, is not as appreciated by the community as it ought to be. It is too much to hope that the

as the necessity of preserving its majority on all committees. Doing my best to combine

4. Mr BELL (Gisborne) to the Minister for the Environment: Can he confirm that the

Horticultural Products-Prospects on European Market
10. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Agriculture: What are the
market prospects for horticultural products on this year's European market, and how do
these compare with last year's sales?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The market prospects for horticultural
products on the European market this season are good, although the prices and qualities of
some of our major horticultural commodities are not expected to give as high a return as last
season. A brief resume of the main products is as follows: for apples and pears, the board
reports that quantities are considerably increased compared to 1977 exports, but market
prices are not as high; for kiwi fruit, in spite of increased quantities being sent to Europe this
season, the demand seems unsatisfied and prices are higher than last year; for ornamentals,
the value of cut flowers and bulb exports to Europe is similar to last year, with Europe
remaining New Zealand's main market.
Mineral Resources Advisory Board
11. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: In view of the fact that a
mineral resources advisory board was promised in the National Party manifesto's mining
policy, can he explain why it has not yet been set up 2 years after the election?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The establishment of the new Ministry of
Energy makes provision for the reorganisation of departmental and official activity in
planning, research, and administration of minerals, and particularly energy resources. The
Act that created the new Ministry of Energy has already put in place the legislative action
necessary to provide for the appointment of advisory committees. The document Goals and
Guidelines-An Energy Strategy For New Zealand, published recently, refers to the
proposed establishment of an energy advisory council and possible alternative forms of
composition for such a council. The Government wishes to have the advantage of comments
from the public, and especially the various sectors of the energy industry, before it finalises
its plans on this aspect of the new administration for energy that it is setting up. It should also
be noted that, for the first time, the Ministry of Energy Act 1977 gives a department of State
specific responsibilities in relation to minerals.
Hon. F. M. Colman: As the Minister's predecessor intimated in the House in October
1976 that he was carrying out an investigation to establish such a committee, why has it taken
so long to come to a decision on this matter?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The honourable member, as a former Minister of an energy
portfolio, will appreciate that a great deal of change for the better has been effected in the
last 2 years, and it may not be possible to achieve all our objectives immediately.

Squid Exports to Japan
13. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Fisheries: What is the current
quota held by New Zealand for the export to Japan of squid caught by New Zealand owned
and operated fishing boats.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The Minister of Fisheries replies:
"There is no specific quota restriction on New Zealand's export of squid to Japan. However,
Japan does set an annual global quota on the amount of squid allowed into that country from
all sources."
Hon. W. W. Freer: What incentives are being given by the Government to New Zealand
operators to catch and export squid to Japan?
Mr SPEAKER: That question is beyond the scope of the original one, which asks the
current quota held by New Zealand for the export to Japan of squid caught by New Zealand
owned and operated fishing boats. I cannot see that the honourable member's question is
relevant.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What action is being taken by the Government to ensure that there
is a quota, and that such a quota will be profitable for New Zealand fishermen?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Japan's annual squid import quota applies to some 81 countries,
of which New Zealand is one. There is no fixed quota on the amount of squid New Zealand
sends to Japan. Although some squid has been sent from New Zealand without problems,
the Japanese apply a 10 percent tariff, which is a matter for discussion between the two
Governments at present.
Mr Courtney: What quantity has been sent from New Zealand to Japan?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Between July 1976 and June 1977, 255.7 tonnes of squid, worth
$140,144, was exported from New Zealand. Of that amount, 211.6 tonnes, worth $98,700,
went to Japan.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What is the advantage in New Zealand operating within this global
quota when squid sent by New Zealand fishermen is sold at a price that is 20 percent lower
than that sent to Japan by Japanese fishermen?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I have already said that the Japanese apply a 10 percent levy on
squid caught and exported to Japan by other than Japanese fishermen. That matter is being
negotiated at present between the Japanese Government and the New Zealand
Government. As I am not the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of Trade and Industry, or
the Minister of Overseas Trade, I have no knowledge of whether the 20 percent mentioned
by the honourable member is correct.

Japanese Proposals "Fish for Beef"
17. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Prime Minister: In view of the statement on
Morning Report on Wednesday, 24 May, that the proposals put to him in Melbourne by
Mr Suzuki were in each case an advance on the offers made in Wellington some weeks
previously, could he give details of the exact offer made by Mr Suzuki in Melbourne for the
importation of New Zealand dairy products, beef, and squid, and also explain how they
differ in each case from the offer made by Mr Suzuki in February this year?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The detail that I give was not all given to
me in Melbourne. Some of it has come subsequently in messages from Tokyo. As to beef,
the action taken in March to hold the basic price for this year at the same level as last year
has resulted in a reduction in the retail price of 4.1 percent as against the same period last
year, while the consumer price index showed a general price increase of 4.8 percent; the
relative difference in the case of beef being the combination of the two. Various specific
changes in the beef distribution system will increase the amount sold through price-
controlled outlets and make provision of l.i.p.c. loans to retailers to allow the joint purchase
of beef with the goal of selling at 10 percent below the market price.
Financial assistance will be provided to retailers to establish joint processing facilities,
and the establishment of new meat centres will be promoted. A new distribution centre for
cut meats will be established this year. We are told that these measures will be continued and
may be expanded next year. An annual quota, as distinct from the present position, is under
serious discussion in the ministry, and if an annual quota is not finally acceptable, annual
forecasts are likely to be given. That is just as good for the New Zealand meat trade, or it is
about as good.
As to dairy products, the Japanese have now firmed up their proposal to buy a
substantial quantity of milk powder and milk fat from New Zealand, whereas previously this
was merely a suggestion. The amount involved may well increase as further responses come
from countries that have been approached. It has become clear that the Japanese envisage a
continuing programme, not only a one-off operation. As far as squid is concerned, the new
suggestion Mr Suzuki made in Melbourne was that Japan should reduce the duty by half.
Japanese joint-venture squid will enter Japan free of duty. It has, of course, been announced
in New Zealand since then that a royalty of 5 percent would be payable to New Zealand on
any squid caught in our 200-mile zone.
Mr Suzuki was also optimistic about our chances of having our pinus radiata timber
accepted in Japan, although the scientific data sent by New Zealand is still being evaluated.
We have subsequently been told that if it is acceptable the duty of 10 percent will no longer
apply. He made it clear to me that on his return from New Zealand he had worked hard to
get some movement on all of these things, and his efforts have had some success. There are,
of course, a number of areas where clarification is necessary. We are still in a negotiating
situation with Japan, and we are instructing our embassy there to continue its discussions in
order to carry the process forward.

Immigration—Work Permit Scheme
18. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: What changes have
been made to the work permit scheme covering Fiji, Western Samoa, and Tonga?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): When the Government took office there
were separate work permit schemes for the citizens of Tonga and Fiji. Arrangements had
been made to extend the work permit scheme to citizens of Western Samoa. Then the
Government revised and amalgamated all these schemes into a single work permit scheme
following my visit to the South Pacific in November 1976. The work permit scheme allows
workers from all three countries to come to New Zealand for up to 6 months, with provision
for extensions to 11 months. Employers may nominate particular workers, and the
employers' guarantee of accommodation may include accommodation provided by a friend
or relative of the worker. The work permit scheme was also extended in April 1977 to
provide employment opportunities in New Zealand for 12 workers from Tuvalu on a trial
basis. Following the successful operation of the trial scheme it has been agreed that further
provision be made for the entry of up to 20 workers from Tuvalu.
Mr Elworthy: Have those changes been accepted and considered satisfactory by the
authorities involved in those countries?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes. Basically the changes were made as a result of representations
either by the Governments of the countries concerned or by the employers or local societies
representing the people primarily in Auckland. They wanted the same sort of arrangements
for different reasons, and we reached agreement on the arrangements made.

Housing Corporation Policy-Previous Ownership
7. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: What are the criteria and
procedures used by the Housing Corporation to ascertain whether (a) applicants for
residential loans, and (b) applicants for rental housing, have or have not had an interest in

and (b) have been turned down in each of the last 3 financial years because applicants could
not meet these criteria?

requires applicants to complete questions to this effect in the statutory declarations

applicants under either (a) or (b) which have been declined because of property ownership.

Christchurch South Flood Victims-Government Assistance
8. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Works and Development: What steps have he
and his department taken to provide assistance for the victims of chronic flooding in south
Christchurch?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The Ministry of
Works and Development is not directly involved in flood relief for this area, as this is the
responsibility of the Christchurch Drainage Board. However, it is understood that the board
is implementing a programme of work to alleviate the flooding, and target dates for various
works have been set. The board has given considerable publicity to the proposed works,
known as the Woolston Cut, and has advised householders in the affected area of details of
the work involved and the expected timetable. The board also proposes to carry out hillside
drainage work in the Bowenvale area to assist with the problem of flooding from the
Heathcote River, and a contract is about to be let for work on the Wilderness drain.
(30/5/78)
Special Workers and Staff Ceilings-Government Departments
9. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of State Services: (a) How many
special workers were employed in each department, including the Railways Department and

SECONDARY TEACHING-NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received a letter from the
member for Wanganui, addressed to me as Speaker of the House of Representatives, and
dated 30 May 1978. The letter reads: "In view of the widespread unrest among members of
the secondary teaching profession, resulting in stopwork meetings being currently held
throughout the country, I give you notice of my intention to move the adjournment of the
House under Standing Order 89. This is for the purpose of discussing the refusal of the
Minister of Education to allow negotiations to recommence with the Education Service
Committee. The teachers' salary claim was lodged with this committee in June 1977, and the
Post-Primary Teachers Association considers they have not had an opportunity to discuss the
subsequent rejection of the claim or present a revised statement. The teachers have been
told that their only recourse is to the Government Service Tribunal, which is not a
negotiating body. I enclose evidence of these matters.
"I submit to you that this application falls within the requirements of Standing Orders
89 and 90 for the following reasons: (1) It is a matter of urgent public importance. Constant
reports appear in the news media of the serious conditions in secondary schools. Unless
something is done to alleviate these conditions, from the point of view of both teachers and
pupils, the loss of secondary teachers will be even greater than at present. (2) It is clearly a
matter requiring immediate attention by the House and the Government. Teachers are


## p. 408 (#416) ############################################

408
30 May
Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
holding stopwork meetings in different parts of the country this week, and some have
already been held. Their mood is militant, and unless urgent action is taken the children of
New Zealand will suffer from further cuts in their schooling. (3) The matter clearly involves
the administrative responsibility of the Government. Yours faithfully, C. R. Marshall,
M.P."
As is mentioned in the letter, it had various enclosures. I have studied the request very
carefully, and I must agree with the member for Wanganui that the House and the
Government should have the opportunity to discuss it, that it does involve the administrative
responsibility of the Government, and that it is of urgent public importance. However, the
House has the opportunity to discuss the matter in the Address in Reply debate, although
that in itself is not a reason for accepting or declining such a request. I do not believe that this
is a particular case, as required by the Standing Orders; it is a continuing situation, and
indeed the honourable member suggested that in various references in his letter to me—
"Constant reports appear in the news media of the serious conditions in secondary schools",
and others I could quote.
The report of 13 April, which the member was good enough to give me in the material
supporting his letter, refers to the 1-day strikes as having occurred 7 weeks before that date
because of lack of progress in negotiations at that time. So it is not a particular case; it is a
continuing situation, and not just one event, as I said before. It is similar to one or two other
matters that have been referred to on earlier occasions—and I think of unemployment and
inflation. In addition, it is not a matter of recent occurrence. The Post-Primary Teachers
Association meeting was held on 8 and 9 May, according to the newspaper reports the
honourable member gave me. It is also stated in one of the reports that the apparent
stalemate that exists between the PPTA and the Minister was referred to at that meeting on 8
and 9 May; so I do not consider that it can be considered to be a matter of recent occurrence.
I therefore find that the application to adjourn the House to discuss this matter is not one
really contemplated by the Standing Orders, and I must reject it.

Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): First, I congratulate you, Mr
Speaker, on your appointment to the high office of Speaker of the House. I might add that a
little of the glory of your appointment reflects on me, inasmuch as we shared a bench in the

offer them, but I do wish you a very long and successful term in your high office. I also offer
my congratulations to the mover and the seconder- the member for Palmerston North and
the member for Invercargill. They are two very hardworking members, who give outstanding
service to their electorates. I have no doubt that they will both be returned with substantially
increased majorities at the next election.
While I am handing out compliments, I should like to say also what a fine Minister of
Labour we have. He is an extremely hardworking Minister, and enjoys the respect of New
Zealanders generally. However, I assure the House and the country that his difficult task has
not been made easier by those members of the Opposition who have stood on platforms with
members of the Socialist Unity Party in support of work stoppages. The fact that the
Minister makes firm and fair decisions can be seen in the decision of the harbour board
employees to return to work. He threatened to refer their case to the Arbitration Court, and
they could not return to work quickly enough.
During the debate I was particularly interested in the attack by the member for Wigram,
the Labour Party's spokesman on social welfare, on the Cabinet committee on family affairs.
Why should he attack a committee whose efforts have been acknowledged from one end of
the country to the other?—that is, with the exception of Opposition members who,
apparently, have been so busy trying to score political points here, there, and everywhere,
that they have not noticed what the committee has been doing. The committee was
established to strengthen the family unit. It is all very well for the member for Wigram to talk
about the strain put on families today. The family unit is under pressure and strain, but that
has not developed in the past 2 years only. We shall not find a way out of our present social
problems until all of us-the Opposition included-have the courage to look honestly at
ourselves and call dishonour and injustice by their right names, and until all of us, whether

Mr Courtney: Rubbish!
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The last Labour Government, by its shortsightedness, did untold

Hon. Michael Connelly: The price of houses is still going up.
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I am happy to talk about that. The price of a new house is not

percent for the last quarter. The price of building sections in the South Island went up by 136
percent under the Labour Government, because of its deliberate inflationary policies. That
really hurt the young people, and put home ownership completely out of their reach. In
1972, the average price of a section was $3,800. After 3 short years of a Labour Government
that same section cost $9,100. In 1972, under the National Government, a section owner
could build a good house for $13,000, a house in which a couple could raise a family and be
comfortable for the rest of their married life. Under the Labour Government, that same
house cost not $13,000 but $25,000-an increase of 87 percent; yet members opposite have
the cheek to say that the National Government has been attacking the South Island.
The Labour Government completely ignored the welfare of the South Island. The

did the Labour Government do about taxation during its 3 years in office? In November,
every working man and woman will remember that a Labour Government increased taxation
by 73 percent. No wonder the Leader of the Opposition bows his head in shame. During his
administration, inflation got out of hand, taxation went up by 73 percent, and the cost of
building a new house rose from $13,000 to $25,000.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Goodbye.
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, goodbye. The Leader of the Opposition has a tough
candidate against him this time, and Tasman will become a National seat, beyond a doubt.
In its disastrous 3 years in office, the last Labour Government turned the 1972 trade

to the manufacturers and exporters in the South Island, and to the country as a whole. The
president of the Labour Party, the member for Roskill, laughs because costs went up. He
laughs because the cost of housing went out of reach of young married couples. He laughs
because his Government did away with coastal shipping from the South. It is clear that the
Labour Government, not this Government, savagely attacked the people in the South
Island. Labour members know that the people in the South Island have no regard for their
tactics, and the lavish promises they are now making do them no credit.

Address in Reply-Want of Confidence
I challenge the Leader of the Opposition to say what a Labour Government would do
about national superannuation. We have been told by him, and by other Labour members,
that the scheme is extravagant, and that we cannot afford it. That silly comment was even
repeated last night on "Checkpoint". Of course we can afford it, as long as there is a
National Government in office; but I should like Labour Party members to say what a
Labour Government would do with it. We have heard all sorts of stories. Even the Labour
Party candidate for the West Coast said that a Labour Government would reintroduce the
New Zealand superannuation scheme-the scheme that discriminated against women,
against the sick, and against those who cannot fend for themselves. The leader of the
Opposition or one of his colleagues should tell us where they stand on this issue. They
remind me of the person who said, "These are my views, the views of an honest politician,
but if they don't suit you I will change them." Now is the time for members opposite to be
positive and to say what they would do about national superannuation.
In addition to the tremendous tax rates under the last Labour Government, employees
and employers both had to pay a 4 percent payroll tax to support a superannuation scheme
that would not start operating until 2023. Is it any wonder that New Zealanders opted for the
very fine national superannuation scheme? I confirm that from 31 August this year national
superannuation will increase to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage for a
married couple, and that the single rate will be 60 percent of the married rate.
Dr Shearer: How much will that work out at?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: There will be a substantial increase from 31 August. It is too
early to give the exact figure, but the figure I have here will not be far out. Married couples
will receive an increase of about $13 a week, which will bring their income to $90.14, while
single people will receive an increase of $7 a week, bringing their income to a total of $52.94
a week. It is only fair to tell the House that my slogan last year-which was based on fact-
was: "No one will be worse off because of the introduction of national superannuation.” I
now want to amend that slightly to: "Everybody is better off because of the introduction of
national superannuation."
I now want to deal with the domestic purposes benefit, for which, also, the Government
has introduced new policies since taking office. I am very pleased to say that the results of
these policy changes are now becoming evident. Before looking at some of the
developments, I should like briefly to reiterate the two-fold responsibility that the
Government has in framing policies that affect solo families. The policies must first aim to
prevent any aggravation of the disadvantages and difficulties inherent in the solo-parent
family situation by providing adequate financial assistance where it is required, and by
providing any other services or facilities, such as counselling and child care, where these are
seen to promote the well-being of the family unit. At the same time, the Government has a
duty to ensure that its policies do not of themselves contribute to the increase in solo-parent
units.
It was in the light of this dual responsibility that the revised policy for the payment of
benefits to solo parents with dependent children was developed, based on the
recommendation of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee. Statistics now
available show that there has been a reduction in the rate of increase in the number of
domestic purposes benefits granted in the 12 months to 31 March 1978 compared with the
previous 12 months. For the 12 months to 31 March last year, there was an increase of 23.3
percent in the applications, but the latest figures taken to 31 March of this year show that the
increase is down to 10 percent. This decline in applications, the result of new provisions that
provide for early counselling and other assistance, confirms beyond doubt that the benefit
adjustments were in the interests of the people concerned.
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda): We have just been entertained by one of the National
Party's big guns, or, to be more correct, a pop gun. He tried to tell us that the beneficiaries,
the solo parents, and the single-income families are better off. No Government in the last 45
years has hit and hurt those people more than the present Administration. It is easy to stand
up and boast in the Chamber, but the Minister should wait until he goes out and faces those
people in a few months' time, when he might hear some of the things that we heard recently
in Palmerston North. He did make one statement of substance. He said that today the family
is under pressure and strain, but he might have finished the sentence and said, "more so than
at any time since the 1930s".
He had the temerity to spend a good deal of time berating the last Labour
Government's housing policy. I put this question to him, and to his bright colleagues on the
other side of the House: where would New Zealand families be today without the 100 000

I should like now to refer to a couple of issues that affect Dunedin and Otago. The

The second point I want to mention is education. Many people in Dunedin are

that some of the State schools are badly in need of upgrading to meet the standards already
set by the school I have mentioned.
Queen's High School, in my electorate, has an excellent staff with good morale, but its
pupils are disadvantaged. The school was built for 350 pupils, but it now caters for more than
600 pupils, and it lacks essential requirements-offices for heads of departments, staff room
space, and senior studies rooms. In addition, the library is inadequate, the laboratories need
upgrading, there are no toilet facilities for male teachers or pupils attending from the
adjacent King's High School, and there is no gymnasium. I trust that these problems will be
remedied this year, and I hope that my faith is well placed.
For reasons such as those I have outlined, the people have expressed opposition to a
private school with superior facilities receiving day-to-day running costs from the
Government when State schools do not have the essential requirements. The people feel that
State schools should be upgraded before schools with superior facilities are integrated,
otherwise pupils in the State schools will be placed at a serious disadvantage.
Another matter of serious concern to the people of Dunedin and Otago is the
procrastination about the Otago Polytechnic. I regard this as the first priority in education. I
am sure my feelings are shared by thousands of people in Dunedin and Otago. To trace the
history of the polytechnic would take more time than I have available. In April, the Minister
of Education visited the splintered polytechnic to see for himself the difficulties that staff and
students work under and the condition of the buildings, which can only be described as
antiquities. The people were perhaps overoptimistic that they would at least receive a
favourable decision. The Minister's visit was followed by a visit by departmental officers,
who spent several days at the polytechnic. This apparent interest and action left the
polytechnic council with the distinct impression that they could expect a decision at the end
of the month.
Hon. L. W. Gandar: They had no right to expect that. They were not given that
impression.
Hon. W. A. FRASER: That is the impression that was left by the Minister.
Hon. L. W. Gandar: No, I did not leave that impression.
Hon. W. A. FRASER: Instead of approval to proceed, the council has gain received a
request for further information. The polytechnic is the poor relation of the tertiary education

I should like to speak about something that concerns me, but obviously not many
members of the Labour Party-and that is the future-the future for people of my
generation, and the future for more than half of the population, those under 35. Let us talk
about 1980 and beyond, boys, and not go back to the 1930s.
I was privileged to be a member of a deputation to Europe to discuss the sheepmeats
regime. I returned, one of five members of a very happy delegation, perhaps a little more
pessimistic than the others. Again, perhaps that is a consequence of age. Perhaps I am
pessimistic because I might still be here when any transitional arrangements that the others
will enjoy have run out. In the foreseeable future there appear to be no alternative markets
able to absorb the quantity of New Zealand lamb that is currently consumed in the United
Kingdom. It is only through exporting to the United Kingdom that a viable sheep-farming
industry can be maintained in New Zealand. So what can we do? I heard some very
creditable and worth-while suggestions from the member for Henderson last week in his
speech on the same topic. I thank him for those. Our Deputy Prime Minister leaves tonight,
again to state New Zealand's case, and I am sure that the best wishes of the House go with
him. Further ministerial and parliamentary visits to Europe will undoubtedly be undertaken,
and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' scheme of inviting opinion leaders and politicians from
Europe to come to New Zealand to see for themselves will undoubtedly be continued.
I have read that the Meat Producers Board is increasing by 50 percent this year its
advertising and publicity in Britain for promotion of lamb. That is well timed. The
consumers' interest in election year in Britain is to the forefront, and, with British elections
only months away, it is obviously an avenue to be exploited. In addition, the consumer in
Ireland is paying a higher price for his domestic lamb because of exports to France, and
Ireland, too, may be interested in our case. The Danes, now taking our lamb and sheepmeat,
also have an active consumer lobby. Next year the first direct elections to the European
Parliament will be held. A consumer lobby has emerged at last in Brussels, and in the
February debate on the common agriculture policy in the European Parliament in Strasburg,
the voice of the commissioner's spokesman on consumer affairs was heard to intervene in the
agriculture debate for the first time, promoting a 2 percent rather than a 4 percent increase in
the common agricultural policy. The European consumer lobby will play an increasing
political role with time; time that will assist our case. In time we might also see the expansion
of the community to include Spain, Portugal, and Greece.
British politicians I spoke with feel that the common agriculture policy will not be able
to cope with such divergent economies, and the Community may well be forced to return to a
national pricing policy. I sat in the House of Commons one evening to listen to the debate on
the 2 percent rise in the common agriculture policy. I was both relieved and apalled to realise
that the standard of debate is no better or worse than ours. During the debate, one of the
Conservative shadow spokesmen on agriculture said that British farmers would have to learn
that they could no longer go on producing increasing volumes and expect higher prices and
the sale of all products. It was, of course, a political statement directed at consumers, and
referred largely to those engaged in the dairy industry.
Having returned, my feeling is that there is an analogy there for New Zealand that I am
concerned we should all understand. Europe, in its hard-headed moments of decision, is
saying it does not owe us a living; that we can no longer go on producing increased volumes
for European markets and expect our prices. Despite the protestations of Phil Holloway and
Joe Walding, we are diversifying. We are expanding markets in Asia and the Middle East,
and our diplomatic posts are exploring all avenues for further market opportunities. Our
future now lies in the willingness of the producers to work hard, and the New Zealand
public's understanding of its dependence on that for its life style, and on the enterprise and
initiative of our exporters—and the occasional stroke of luck, I guess, will not go astray.
On my return I read that Export Year had been launched whilst I had been away. I
read, also, comments by such as Jim Gemmell, President of the New Zealand Manufacturers
Federation, who said at a public meeting in Wellington: "It is unfortunate that too many of
us feel that the world owes us a living, that such benefits are ours by right. It is high time that
myth was dispelled." He went on: "It is no use blaming the European Community for our
misfortunes, or to complain about practices that make it more difficult to sell on world
markets. We must face the fact that the cause is our inability to increase productivity and
expand our overseas markets." He added: "We will not achieve our objectives by increased
Government role in the economy."

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I support the call made earlier in the debate by the
member for New Lynn for the updating of parliamentary procedures and the restoration of
greater sovereignty to Parliament, as opposed to Cabinet. On its own, however, I am not
sure that the mere updating of parliamentary procedures will be enough. If any move is to be
successful, all members need to have a genuine desire to stop and have a hard look at the
way we are attempting to run the country. The House needs to have a year out for new
legislation and new regulations, during which time members should concentrate on cleaning
out the mass of red tape and useless bureaucracy that is now driving the people mad. We
need to return to an open and efficient society in which people have a chance of controlling
their lives and that is certainly not possible in New Zealand today.
If we were to adopt the year-out principle I have suggested, it would involve accepting
the following course: the setting up of various select committees on all main subjects to have
a complete look at legislation and regulations still in existence, with a view to getting rid of
anything that is unnecessary. It is legislation that builds up the bureaucracy and demands
more and more public servants to service that legislation. The select committees should be
supported by groups of full-time officials drawn from departments and private enterprise.
The important criterion is that they should all have practical experience of actually working
in the community. The committees would be charged with asking themselves the following
questions: What would happen if this law or this regulation did not exist? What does it cost
to service? What does it contribute to the happiness or progress of the community? Anything
that did not measure up should be killed stone dead, and buried.
The House continues to pass laws and regulations; departments adopt new policies
without regard to how they relate to one another, or to their impact on individuals. I wish to
deal with one or two examples. First, I will take the example of a widow or a solo parent with
two dependent children, living in a State house, and consider the impact of various
Government policies or laws controlled by separate departments, and how they influence the
position of such people. Let us look at the impact of taxation, abatement policies, and State
house rent policies, and see how widows and solo parents who want to work are affected by
interrelated policies. The simple fact is that people in this position-widows and solo parents
with two children—are actually being penalised for going to work. It pays them to stay at
home. The more they earn, the worse off they become. The widow or the solo parent with
two children, who works 1 day a week and earns $21, has a net income of $78 after paying tax
and the rent for a State house. If, however, that person elects to continue to work, and earns
$100 a week, the net income drops by $4.37 a week to $73.63, after the payment of tax and
rent. In other words, for the privilege of going out to work a substantial drop in net income is
suffered. If that person tries even harder, and earns $124 a week, there is a further penalty in
that the net income is $70.45 after the payment of tax and rent-a reduction of $7.55 a week.
That does not take into account the cost of transport or child care. It is absolutely crazy that
widows and solo parents who dare to work are being penalised by the Government for doing
So.
When will this stop? Shortly after his appointment, the Minister of Social Welfare said:
"We are also examining all proposed legislation to ensure that any effect of it on the family is
understood and that it will be positive rather than negative." On another occasion he said:
"We are reviewing all existing legislation to examine the extent to which the present law and
policy aids or hinders good strong family life."
We have been waiting for some action. What happened to that proposed review? Did
the Minister have a change of mind? I think he did, because later on he started on another
tack, and said: "My efforts have been directed at cheats, the people who have in effect been
stealing from the State and stealing from you." In an article in the Sunday News headed: "It
is going to end-bludgers bleeding you" the Minister of Social Welfare is reported as saying:
"The social security rip-off is going to end. How is it that some people can live like parasites
off the State?" The Minister talks of cheats and of parasites, but in my opinion the biggest
rip-off is being carried out by the Government, which takes $1.25 for every $1 over $100 that
a widow or solo parent earns.

Talking about rip-offs, I want to refer to one or two being carried out in the community.
A dairy proprietor in my electorate, who purchased his Otara dairy 6 years ago, paid
approximately $18,000 in goodwill in addition to stock and plant at valuation. However,
when the lease was up for review 5 years later, the landlord demanded a further $10,000
before he would sign the new lease. What does the Government, especially the Minister of
Trade and Industry, intend to do about such rip-offs? That dairy proprietor and his wife had
worked hard and for long hours to build up their business. He refuses to pay the $10,000, and
the landlord refuses to sign the new lease. The proprietor has either to pay the $10,000 and
then sell the business and hope to get back his $18,000 goodwill, or continue the lease on a
monthly basis. He was told by the landlord that if he wanted to get out the landlord's
brother-in-law would be quite happy to run the business. No doubt he would have run it for 3
months and then sold it at a substantial price. The Government should introduce legislation
to stop that sort of thing.

CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I said on the introduction of the Bill, it is before the House at the specific
request of the Abortion Supervisory Committee. I think all of us would agree that the
supervisory committee has been charged with a difficult task. Broadly, it must ensure the
effective operation of a new statute and new procedures, which have met with a mixed
response within and outside the medical profession. The supervisory committee has had to
break entirely new ground, and, though I need hardly add that it has been given all possible
administrative assistance, as an independent body it has necessarily had to tread a rather
lonely path. After grappling for some months with the practical problems thrown up by the
legislation, the supervisory committee has turned to the 86 voting members of Parliament for
help in the shape of two amendments to the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act
and one to the Crimes Amendment Act. Parliament unanimously appointed the committee
and made it accountable to Parliament. The personnel of the committee-two women and
one man, two of whom are doctors and one of whom is a judicial officer-were appointed by
Parliament.
The committee has now reported back to us with amendments, which, in its considered
opinion, are essential to make the Act work as intended. In my view, therefore, any member
who feels disposed to vote against the Bill should weigh matters very carefully before doing
so. Of course, I do not question a member's right to vote against the clauses, or any one of
them, if in all conscience he feels he must, but I do urge a restrained and cautious attitude. I
believe that the supervisory committee's efforts deserve our appreciation and support, and
that we should try to facilitate the committee's task. For these broad reasons I will be voting
for the Bill as recommended by the committee.
I turn now to a consideration of what the Bill proposes. I should mention that the short
title is "an Act to give effect to recommendations made by the Abortion Supervisory
Committee for the amendment of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977
and the Crimes Amendment Act 1977." Clauses 1 and 2 are machinery clauses, and clause 3
sets out a new procedure to be followed when a woman seeks an abortion. Section 32 of the
principal Act will be replaced by new provisions designed to bring the role of the operating
surgeon into much greater prominence. Accordingly, if the woman's own doctor proposes
not to perform the abortion himself, he will refer his patient to a practitioner who may be
willing to perform the operation. If the woman's own doctor is willing to perform the
operation, the next step depends on whether he is a certifying consultant. If he is a certifying
consultant, the woman is then referred on to one other certifying consultant. If he is not, the
woman is referred, as required by the Act, to two certifying consultants. Subsection (3) of
the new section 32 goes on to deal with the role of the operating surgeon to whom a woman is
referred. It provides that if the surgeon is a certifying consultant he must refer her to one
other certifying consultant. If he is not a certifying consultant, then the reference must be to
two certifying consultants.
The differences between this procedure and the existing procedure are basically
differences of emphasis rather than substance, except on the point I mentioned in the first
reading debate. This is that under the new section 32(2) the woman's own doctor will have to
consider that she may have grounds for any abortion before referring her on. Again, this has
been inserted at the request of the supervisory committee in the interests of good medical
practice. Clause 3 also contains the second amendment requested by the supervisory
committee. This is that a certifying consultant should be given an explicit right to see the
patient before determining her case. Apparently there is confusion among doctors over


## p. 435 (#443) ############################################

30 May
435
Contraception, Sterilisation and Abortion Amendment Bill
whether they have this right at present. I am sure they do have it, but that is not really the
point. The supervisory committee considers it is desirable to have the matter spelt out
explicitly in the statute, and I believe there can be no objection to that course. Clause 4
makes consequential amendments to section 33 of the Act. Clause 5 makes it clear that when
an abortion is duly authorised it may be performed by any medical practitioner and does not
have to be performed by the operating surgeon within the meaning of section 32. This is put
in to cover the situation in hospitals, where at times it may be convenient and, indeed,
necessary for someone other than the surgeon who has participated in the consideration of
the case to perform the operation.
This brings us to clauses 6 and 7, which contain the one substantive provision in the Bill.
Clause 7 is substantive because it concerns the primary test for abortion under the Crimes
Act-namely, that the continuance of the pregnancy would result in serious danger to the
life or physical or mental health of the woman or girl, and that the danger cannot be averted
by any other means. It is this last phrase that clause 7 proposes to delete on the
recommendation of the supervisory committee. The reasons are so well known that it is
hardly necessary to traverse them. Suffice it to say that there are divergent legal opinions on
what the phrase actually means. In this situation, many doctors are clearly unhappy about
the gloss placed on the previous law, with a consequent prejudicial effect on the smooth
operation of the new procedures. The supervisory committee therefore urges that the
problem be resolved by deleting the words in question. After due consideration I have come
to the conclusion that this would be a reasonable course to adopt. If the Solicitor-General is
correct in saying that the words add virtually nothing to the earlier law, and merely make
explicit what was already implicit, then they are redundant and can be deleted without loss.
If, on the other hand, the words do materially restrict and tighten the earlier law, as some
believe, then it is an open question whether that result was intended by the majority of
members who voted for them.
It must be remembered that the words in question did not appear on the formulation
adopted by the royal commission, after such long study. They were inserted by means of an
amendment moved by the member for Porirua. I think that even in the course of a lengthy
and emotionally-charged debate most members would have hesitated to alter the royal
commission's considered recommendations on this crucial matter-which, after all, concerns
the principal ground for a lawful abortion-if they thought they were making a really
substantial change to a recommendation of the royal commission. I believe that most of us
who voted for the amendment regarded its purpose as clarifying the royal commission's
formulation rather than changing it. I do not believe its deletion, as recommended by the
supervisory committee, will lead to abortion on request, which is what some people fear.
I should add a word about the suggestion that the amendment could be softened by the
addition of some such wording as "reasonable" or "reasonable and practical" to qualify the
word "means". Legally speaking, I believe the effect of this would be minimal, and, in any
event, it is absolutely patent that it would not have the effect desired by the supervisory
committee. In other words, many in the medical profession would be likely to regard it as no
more than unacceptable tinkering with the problem they see. I propose, therefore, to vote
for clause 7, and I urge my parliamentary colleagues to support me and the supervisory
committee in its onerous task.
In conclusion, I point out that there is nothing in the Bill that requires Parliament to
abandon any decisions of principle taken last year. The Bill is squarely within the spirit and
framework of the existing Act. Rightly, in my view, the supervisory committee has not felt it
proper to ask Parliament to reconsider questions of policy and principle such as abortion on
the ground of fetal abnormality. the committee has limited itself to seeking the minimum
changes necessary to remove impediments to the day-to-day operation of the Act. The Bill is
therefore a moderate and restrained measure, and I believe it deserves our support. I
commend the Bill to the House.

Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Before calling the next speaker, I should like to point out that

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): May I start by setting out three points for the
record, and by way of background to my observations in the debate. First, an issue like
abortion, which arouses deep emotional responses from substantial sections of the
community, and which brings the law to bear so strongly on what is not just a medical or
legal matter, but also a moral and social issue involving subjective judgments and highly
personalised values and standards, is not an issue that can be wished away because it is
embarrassing or inconvenient or divisive. The history of this question in other countries
serves to confirm that the issue of abortion stays centre stage in politics until eventually the
law of the land and the will of the majority find common ground and move forward along the
same path.
Secondly, this issue has been painfully divisive in the House and throughout the ranks of
the two major political parties and one of the two minor parties, and every politician in the
House or aspiring to enter the House at the election in November knows there are many
other issues that should more properly be set out as the political battleground for the voters'
choice in November. It would be far better for politicians, for politics, and for the people
who must judge them and decide with their ballots in November, if we could somehow
succeed in defusing the abortion issue. Desirable as this outcome may be, it cannot be
achieved if the extreme position on either side of the abortion issue insists that its will, and its
will alone, must prevail. The defusing can be achieved only if both sides are prepared to
move a little towards the middle ground. This brings me to my third point, a point that is
appropriately prefaced by two quite well known quotations bearing on the realities of
politics. Chancellor Bismarck described politics as the art of the possible. Benjamin Franklin
gave Bismarck's truism a further dimension of realism when he said—and I paraphrase to
relate it to the here and now-"No Parliament can long travel at a faster gait than, or in a
different direction from, the thinking of the people it represents."
My personal wish, my preferred recommendation, would be that the abortion
legislation passed by the House in December last should be repealed. But is is not possible,
within the ambit of this amendment Bill, to prosecute this line of argument, nor do I believe


## p. 438 (#446) ############################################

30 May
Contraception, Sterilisation and Abortion Amendment Bill
that, with the present comparatively entrenched positions taken by so many members, this
would be a successful case to press. On the other side of the issue we have the picture of a
substantial proportion of the populace—in my judgment a sizeable majority—most unhappy
with the present law on abortion and the two key Bills that were its vehicle, passed in
December by 40-26 and 39-28 majorities respectively. Quite apart from the more than
300 000 repeal petitioners, the several adverse public opinion polls and the tenor of some
resolutions from the conferences of the three political parties represented by members of the
House, the recent comments of the chairman of the Abortion Supervisory Committee and
the continuing reluctance of many members of the medical profession to co-operate should
be cause for our concern.
I would make the point also that the medical profession's criticisms since the law was
passed are not new. The same criticisms were publicly expressed before the House saw fit to
change the law. There is good reason, therefore, for both sides of the House, on this issue, to
seek earnestly, and if necessary courageously, for ways to repair and improve what has been
done so that it comes more closely to the middle ground, so that the tensions this law has
aroused may be eased a little, so that the medical profession might be able, in all conscience,
to co-operate more willingly, and the women of the country seeking abortions might be
helped rather than harassed. The question now arises: Is there this middle ground, and, if so,
what is it? I believe there is, but the three amendments now before us do not reach that
middle ground— and nor do they meet the minimum requirements of either the Medical
Association of New Zealand or the General Practitioners Society.
As I mentioned in my comments on the introduction of the Bill, the two machinery
matters are largely cosmetic. Without any change in the law, it is possible now, under the
rules of the supervisory committee and the ethical code of the medical profession, for a
certifying consultant to insist on seeing the patient if he wants to, and for the operating
doctor to involve himself in the decision taking. According to the Solicitor-General, even the
third provision, the removal of the so-called Wall amendment and those objectionable words
"and that the danger cannot be averted by any other means", is also cosmetic, although I,
for one, propose to support the removal of that provision. The Bill before us does not meet
the very real objections of the majority of the medical profession. It is hoped by the
supervisory committee that it will be an adequate gesture to appease some of the obstetrical
and gynaecological specialists. That can be no more than a hope, and, even if it is successful,
it would move the abortion business into a virtual closed shop for obstetricians and
gynaecologists-a medically and socially retrograde step.
What is needed to reach the middle ground and approach the essential minimum
modifications to meet the publicly expressed wishes of a majority of doctors are the
provisions I have set out in two Supplementary Order Papers, which contain five changes,
one substantial and four of lesser moment, which, individually and collectively, are within
the relatively narrow parameters of the terms of this amendment Bill. Would members
please note that there are contained in the Supplementary Order Papers released earlier
today.
The changes I shall invite the House to consider and support in the committee stage are:
first, the removal of the so-called conscience clause, which the Minister of Health has said
publicly should not disqualify a doctor from volunteering his services, and which the
supervisory committee has already decided was a matter which it could not enforce or apply
as it had no inquisitorial powers, but which has served to prevent many good, conscientious,
and suitable doctors from applying, for they choose to read the law literally as Parliament
passed it—and can they be criticised for that? Let us, therefore, remove the offensive section
30(5).
Secondly, at present, under section 30(4)(a), at least one-half of the total number of
appointees shall be practising obstetricians and gynaecologists. The provision is not working
in many parts of New Zealand, and the supervisory committee cannot apply it or enforce it.
In fact, the committee is left exposed to the threat of actions against it for failing to perform a
statutory provision required of it. Better, surely, that the law and common sense converge.
Let us preface this requirement of the committee by adding the words "to the extent that it is
practicable."
The third proposed amendment, which would do so much to make the legislation
acceptable to the medical profession, is to reverse the present situation under which all
doctors are legally unacceptable as certifying consultants unless selected by the committee
and certified as acceptable, and change it to one in which all experienced doctors are legally
acceptable as certifying consultants unless declared by the committee to be unacceptable.

This could be achieved with the Supplementary Order Paper provision "for the purposes of
this Act and subject to the provisions of this section, any registered medical practitioner of
not less than 5 years' practice, shall be entitled, at his own request, to be appointed to the list
of certifying consultants." This suggested provision is consistent with the second alternative
proposed by the royal commission, and is not far removed from the position taken last year
by the NZMA Council, and amended earlier this year by a vote to move the full distance to
repeal. This would be additional to the provisions of section 30(2), which would continue,
and leave with the committee the question of appointments when the practitioner had less
than 5 years' practice.
The second Supplementary Order Paper I circulated today would prohibit a doctor from
acting, whether as a certifying consultant or an operating surgeon, when, for example, both
he and a certifying consultant with whom he is in partnership are involved in the same case.
This adds a protection to the original Act. The fifth proposal in my amending Supplementary
Order Paper is an appropriate supplement to one of the previous points, namely, that clause
30(6) should be amended so that appointments of certifying consultants should continue
until revoked by the supervisory committee, or the certifying consultant resigns by notice to
the supervisory committee. The present law is made to appear absurd for there is no
provision for a certifying consultant to resign. To meet this situation, he must ask the
supervisory committee to revoke its appointment of him—a matter, I am told, of
unnecessary embarrassment in at least one case already.
One further proposed amendment, in a Supplementary Order Paper in the name of the
Minister of Education, calls for the repeal of the so-called Arthur section, and the
reinstatement of foetal abnormality as a ground for abortion, which I would also commend
to the House for support at the appropriate time. Given these modifications to the Bill now
before us I believe Parliament can produce legislation that will work, which will be
acceptable to all but those at the extreme ends of the argument, which would give the issue
time to cool and people time to think in a less emotional environment, and give people and
politicians the chance to direct their attention to other more appropriate political
battlegrounds in this election year. To fail to grasp this chance will just as certainly leave the
abortion issue unresolved and running hot, mauling political parties, and scarring
parliamentarians in the process, until such time as we in this House awaken to the immutable
fact that the thrust of the law and the will of the majority will find a way of meeting in the
end.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I find myself supporting the first part of the Bill for basically the
same reasons given by the Minister of Justice when introducing the legislation, that the
provisions are machinery ones for administration purposes and requested by those whom we

The second part is rather a different matter. It is not a question just of administrative
procedure, but also of deciding when the child should be killed, and on what grounds.
Unfortunately, one thing affecting the abortion discussion is the use of the word "abortion",
which tends to promote the idea that it is just something happening to a woman, from which
she will certainly recover and which has no great physical consequence, no matter what the
severity of the psychological consequences may be. What tends to be overlooked by the
constant reference to the woman is the fact that, although physical damage to the woman
may be minor, there is in every case complete destruction of a child. If the long title of the
legislation was "an Act to control the destruction of certain unwanted children”, it would
approximate more accurately to the matter before the House than any reference to abortion,
which tends to gloss over certain features in a way that those of us who have been watching
the films about the bestialities associated with the Hitler regime in Germany realise is
possible. Even the most disgusting human behaviour can be described in a way that can be
acceptable. In that case, the term used was the "final solution of the Jewish problem”. I
suggest that accidentally, and not by design, this constant reference to the word "abortion",
to what happens to the woman, rather than to what is happening to the child, has had a
lulling effect in the same way as the use of that terminology apparently had a lulling effect on
so many good and conscientious Germans.
I draw your attention to the sort of being that is destroyed by abortion-and I shall not
quote any partisan opinion. I do not think it would be possible to give a more dispassionate
authority than Gray's Anatomy, which has been in existence for 100-odd years. Its
description of what the child is like at the 8- to 12-week stage is quite significant and can be
accepted by the House as totally unprejudiced on any side of the argument. It says that at


## p. 440 (#448) ############################################

440
30 May
Contraception, Sterilisation and Abortion Amendment Bill
about the seventh or eighth week, which is about the earliest time an abortion would be
carried out—and I am quoting from the middle of the whole discussion on the growth of a
child—"the flexure of the head is gradually reduced and the neck is somewhat lengthened.
The upper lip is developed and the nostrils are directed forward. The palate is not
completely developed. The eyelids are present in the shape of folds above and below the
eye." It goes on to state that in the third lunar month-that is, before 12 weeks-"The head
is extended and lengthened, the eyelids meet and fuse and remain closed until 6 months. The
limbs are well developed and nails appear on the digit. The crown rump length is 55 mm". In
a system we are more familiar with, that means that the child is about 3 in. long. So that we
are not talking about an amorphous mass of jelly, but about a child with, according to this
book, well developed limbs, and even fingernails; and the nervous system is intact.
I ask members to think of a medical situation with which they must all be fairly familiar.
It is well known that there are restrictions on the use of medications in the first trimester, or
the first 3 months, of pregnancy, which do not apply with nearly the same severity later. In
fact, there is considerable latitude in the use of drugs given to a pregnant woman after 12
weeks. The reason is that at 12 weeks all the organs are so completely formed that a major
foetal abnormality as a result of the toxic effects of medicines is unlikely. It is fairly common
knowledge that the distinction is made at the point of 12 weeks. Therefore, what we are
talking about is the destruction of a child whose organs and development are so far advanced
that ordinary poisoning from the effects of therapeutically used drugs is no longer a great
hazard. Let members have no doubt whatsoever that that is what it is all about.
Recently New Zealanders have been devastated by witnessing on television scenes of
the destruction of human beings in a series depicting the Third Reich. However, they have
congratulated themselves that that sort of thing could not happen again, and certainly could
not happen here. I ask them to think again, because what is being destroyed in every
abortion is what the anatomy book describes as limbs which are well developed—and the
rest of the body has developed along with those limbs. It is clear that the public generally is
unaware that limbs are torn from trunks by the suction methods used in abortion factories,
and that those limbs are of a child whose central nervous system is well enough developed for
joints to form and be sensitive to the action taken. Therefore this child has its central
nervous system attacked while it is being torn apart, piece by piece. I am not being
emotional. Those are the hard, cold facts, exactly as we have seen them on the television
screen recently. The only difference is that the scenes were shown in a different context and
depicted the killings of older people some years ago.
The House is being asked to consider machinery to control a procedure as destructive
and disturbing as I have described, and therefore all members should be concerned to ensure
that the administrative machinery is satisfactory. I agree with the Minister that the House
should take the necessary action. However, when members consider the conditions under
which the destruction of a child should take place we owe a duty not just to ourselves, but to
the whole of our society, and to the whole of the future of our society. If we do so, it is
inevitable that we should view the laws governing abortion with the greatest possible
concern. I understand that the supervisory committee is concerned that the terms and
conditions laid down in an amendment I moved before the Act was passed might be unduly
tight. I make no apologies for moving the amendment. I know what is happening in the
abortion factories. I know exactly what is happening to those children, and I make no
apology for moving that amendment.
However, I realise that I am speaking in the House of Parliament where other members
do not see the destruction of a child in quite the same way, and that I live in a society where
many people do not view the matter with the same concern. Indeed, many members of my
own profession do not view the destruction of these children with the same concern that I do.
In order to accommodate the differing attitudes of other people, I think we should still
preserve an attitude which shows that the destruction of this child is not to be equated with
giving a pill or any other simple remedy-perhaps counselling, supportive psychological
services, or what you like. If they are not to be treated on the basis of equality with the
destruction of a child, then, in considering the problems facing a pregnant woman, we must
preserve the principles enshrined in the amendment that stood in my name. For this reason I
propose to introduce a Supplementary Order Paper which amends my amendment to take
into account the differing opinions and to approach what a former speaker has called for, the
middle road. When one considers what is happening in these abortion clinics-the
destruction of these children-it is hard to find a middle position.
I myself am quite unable to adopt a middle, dispassionate, view because I know what is

This legislation will surely go down in history as the most amended, patched-up,

Unfortunately, the people who do want to safeguard the sanctity of life are the same
people who oppose contraception, and this creates a problem for society, including people of
the same religious belief. Sanctity of life is one of the noblest of concepts. "Thou shalt not
kill" is one of the Ten Commandments. It is one of the things that distinguishes humans from
animals. Animals kill because of the need of food to survive. Human beings have killed for
greed, conquest, and bigotry—much of this has been in the glorification of war and in the
name of God. We are debating a compromise between those who believe that a woman has

any abortion at all—that no human being may decide. We are debating a compromise; it

semantic slogan that has been invoked by one of the extreme parties to this issue about all
who disagree with its viewpoint.
I am of the view that a woman should have the right to make a choice herself in
consultation with her doctor. I am concerned for the woman, her existing children, and her
family. I do not exclude entirely her right of decision on a matter that concerns her most of
all, and finally only her. Life is sacred, and safeguarding the sanctity of life means ensuring
that a life is lived, not just endured. The quality of life throughout childhood in our society is
behind my amendment and behind the views I have held and expressed in the House for

to whether a safe legal abortion should be permitted is surely not ours, but that of the parent
who goes through the experience of bearing a child, sometimes in very difficult
circumstances, and of rearing the mentally subnormal child who might be born.
Having addressed myself, because of what the previous speaker said, to that point, I
