since the hospital board was asked to carry out the survey. The original question was not
about geriatric wards, but about geriatric hospitals. The patients are sometimes placed in
geriatric wards because of the proximity of their parents for visiting purposes. That is often
more important than a child not being in a geriatric ward. While the geriatric ward is
sometimes acceptable, the geriatric hospital atmosphere is unacceptable, and it is hoped to
ease that problem.
Mr Beetham: Is the Minister aware that in the geriatric ward, as against the geriatric
hospital, the patients feel soul-destroyed?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, I am aware of that. The family often feels that, more than the
child. It also goes the other way; some of the geriatric patients look upon themselves as being
elderly, but not incurably ill. They are depressed when they see these patients in the ward.

facilities in the time during which growth occurred in the district.
Mr Hunt: Is it not a fact that the main reason for the delay-which the Minister has
pointed out was because of expansion in the population and the need for a new intermediate
school-was the step, taken by the member for Waitemata, to prevent the school being
built?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I believe that every member has a right and an obligation to
question any development in his area. I took that into account. I do not admit that the action
taken by the member for Waitemata caused the delay. The member raised a legitimate
question, and the matter has been settled.

Immigration-Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement
9. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: What measures have
been taken to upgrade the trans-Tasman travel arrangement?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I recently reviewed the trans-Tasman
travel arrangement in discussion with the Australian Minister of Immigration and Ethnic
Affairs, the Hon. M. Mackellar, during his visit to New Zealand. We agreed that the
arrangement benefits both countries and that, on the information available, there is no
evidence of a need to change present arrangements for trans-Tasman travel. The two
Governments, nevertheless, agreed to carry out a joint exercise to assess whether the
arrangements are being abused in any way by criminals, illegal immigrants, or visitors
intending to overstay. We will also be considering measures to help identify persons entering
New Zealand from any source who have criminal backgrounds, who are travelling on false or
stolen passports, or who have connections with terrorist organisations.
Hon. F. M. Colman: The Minister said that the department would carry out checks
against undesirable people falsely identifying themselves. Does this mean that the average
New Zealand trans-Tasman passenger would need to carry some form of identification?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I do not remember saying that, and I cannot find it in my answer. I
said: "We will also be considering measures to help identify persons entering New Zealand
from any source who have criminal backgrounds, who are travelling on false or stolen
passports, or who have connections with terrorist organisations." I know the honourable
member supported the proposition that travellers should carry passports or some form of
identification when travelling between New Zealand and Australia. Both the present
Australian and New Zealand Governments reject any such concept, and it will not happen.

Government Life Insurance Office Interest Rates
12. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister in Charge of the Government Life
Insurance Office: Is the increase in Government Life Insurance Office interest rates, from
approximately 7.5 percent in 1975 to 11 percent at present, in line with Government policy,
and, if not, what does he propose to do about it?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Government Life Insurance Office): It
is in line with the provisions of section 27 of the Government Life Insurance Act, the same
Act and the same provisions that operated under the former Labour Government.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Would the Minister answer the other part of my question. Is this
interest rate in line with Government policy?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: It is in line with the Act, and the insurance office has an
obligation to the 90 percent of policy holders who have life policies but do not raise loans on
them, and who are entitled to a fair return on the premiums paid.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Will the Minister confirm that the decision to increase the interest
rates from 7 percent to 11 percent is one made by Cabinet, and not under the Act?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The increase is approved by the Governor-General in Council.
Yes, the interest rate has been raised to 11 percent, but I would emphasise that this is lower
than the interest rate charged by most life insurance offices. Also, no legal fees are payable
and the loans may be repaid without notice. I do not want to use the House to advertise the
Government Life Insurance Office, but its loans, generally, are cheaper.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: The Minister said that the interest rate was approved by Order in
Council. Was the Minister present at the Executive Council meeting when the decision was
made, and when the Governor-General's signature was obtained?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, undoubtedly I was present when the decision was made.
However, I would point out that 11 percent is below the rate generally charged by life
insurance offices on loans on policies.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! the Minister made that point before.
Drought Relief Programme
13. Mr BELL (Gisborne) to the Minister of Agriculture: Can he advise the advances
made to date under the drought relief programme, and forecasts of future total advances?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE Minister of Agriculture: Expenditure to 31 March 1978 recorded
by my ministry for drought relief totalled $21,817. In addition, the Rural Banking and
Finance Corporation advanced $710,000 for climatic relief loans in the year ended 31 March
1978, and has advanced a further $160,000 in such loans from 1 April to 2 May this year. At
this stage it is not possible to give a definite indication of likely expenditure on drought relief
during the 1978-79 financial year; as expenditure is substantially dependent on climatic
conditions during winter and early spring. Provision is being made in my ministry's 1978-79
estimates of expenditure for relief expenditure of up to $3 million.
Mr Bell: Is consideration being given to providing subsidy payments for hay, silage
purchases, and grazing costs under this programme?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Some drought relief committees have made that proposal, and
the suggestion is being looked at.

North-western Motorway-Resealing
17. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Works and Development: Which
company undertook the resealing of the north-western motorway earlier this year, and is the
National Roads Board satisfied with the standard of work, which has received much criticism
In the local area?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): This resealing work was
undertaken by Winstone Civil Construction Ltd, and the standards achieved on the
particular work have been a cause for concern. The contract involved an overlay of bitumen-
bound basecourse to add to the strength of the existing motorway pavement. Unlike similar
work carried out very successfully by the same company on the Bombay Hills section of State
Highway 1, the end result on the north-western motorway has been a rather rough surface,
requiring further treatment.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: When will this further treatment take place?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: It is intended that the existing surface should be allowed to settle.
Tenders will then be called for the remedial work, to carry out the required improvements
early in the spring.

Immigration-Private Overseas Students
19. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: What changes have
been made to the provisions allowing private overseas students to study in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): No recent changes have been made to the
provisions allowing private overseas students to study in New Zealand. The primary aim in
permitting persons from other countries to study in New Zealand is now accepted as being to
train them to a stage where they can be of value in the development programmes of their
own countries. For this reason, students from developing nations have preference; and,
within this broad context, first preference is given to students from the South Pacific region,
and second preference to those from South-east Asia. Opportunities for students from areas
beyond these regions are to be given to those coming from countries with which New
Zealand has close political and trade links. It has also been agreed that a secondary aim of
New Zealand student policy is to provide opportunities for cultural exchanges between the
people of New Zealand and people in other countries.
Mr Elworthy: Have any changes been made to the rights and privileges of these students
while they are in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I think the member is referring to students marrying for the purpose
of becoming permanent residents. The bar against their doing so has now been removed.
Students are considered on the same basis as everyone else.
Wages-Average Take-home Pay
20. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Finance: What previous year is
comparable to this year's current purchasing power of take-home pay (effective allowing for
tax) for the average male wage earner with two children, including child benefit?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The latest information for weekly
average male earnings is contained in the October 1977 half-yearly survey by the
Department of Labour, which shows the average weekly wage as $135.81. Adjusted for the
consumer price index, taxes, including the young family rebate, and the family benefit for
two children, the purchasing power of that gross wage for the married man with two children
was $121.55 in December 1977 terms. This level of after-tax real earnings is about
equivalent to that which prevailed throughout 1976.
Mr Beetham: Is the Minister satisfied that he should not go further back in time, in fact
to the early 1960s, to find a more comparable year?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The number asked which previous year is comparable to
this year's current purchasing power of take-home pay. I said that the previous year is
comparable. He asked why I should not take another year. I say, why should I? I have
already told him that the previous year is the comparable one?

Pricing Complaints
5. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: How many
complaints concerning the repricing of goods in stock at new prices have been brought to the
attention of his department in the last 12 months; (a) how many of these complaints were
found to be justified, and (b) in those cases where the complaint was found to be justified,
what action was taken?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: During the
last 12 months 128 complaints about the repricing of goods were brought to the attention of
my department. Of these it was found that 47 were justified. The action taken on these was:
in 28 cases, where a purchase had been made by the complainant, a refund was given and the
remaining stock was correctly repriced; in 19 cases, where the complainant had made no
purchase, the stock was correctly repriced. The traders were warned of their obligations
under the pricing legislation, and in three cases prosecutions were taken.

Regional Development
7. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department:
(1) (a) How many companies received first-year depreciation allowances on plant and
machinery under the regional development programme, as it existed prior to the 1977
Budget, in each of the financial years to March 1974, 1975, 1976, and 1977; (b) what were the
totals of assistance of this type granted in each of those same financial years; and (c) what
were the totals of assistance of this type granted in each of the regional development priority
regions respectively in each of these years, and what were the number of companies assisted
and the levels of assistance granted in each case; (2) (a) what reasons can he give for the
decision in the 1977 Budget to scrap the previous, regionally differentiated, first-year
depreciation allowances on plant and machinery, and replace them with a standard
allowance at a lower rate; and (b) can he give the number of companies which have (i)
applied, and (ii) received assistance under the new standard allowance scheme in each
regional development priority region since the July 1977 Budget; and (c) in each case where
a company was assisted, can he indicate the level of assistance granted?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department)
replied: The statistical information requested is not readily available. Regarding question
2 (a), I assume the member is referring to the 1976 Budget, in which it was announced that
the first-year depreciation allowance on plant and machinery would be reduced to a standard
rate of 25 percent. The Minister of Finance in his Budget speech made the following
statement: "The Government considers that the present broad range of first-year
depreciation allowances on plant and machinery should be replaced by a more selective
system of incentives designed to emphasise both export production and regional
development, and to encourage industries to plan their development in a co-ordinated
fashion." To this extent, a system of incentive allowances applying to new plant and
machinery was subsequently introduced to supplement the standard first-year depreciation
allowance. These supplementary allowances were: a regional investment allowance of up to
20 percent; and export incentive allowance of 20 percent; an industry development
allowance of up to 40 percent; farm and fishing investment allowances of 40 percent.

461
Discussion of Motions-Press Censorship
DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Press Censorship
Mr MALCOLM (Eden): I move, That this House notes the integrity of the Franklin
Times which has had the courage to publish an article that raises frightening questions on
censorship of information in the New Zealand press, and intimidation and standover tactics by
the Northern Journalists Union, and this House specifically notes the claim that the New
Zealand Herald has censored news to which the public of New Zealand was entitled, in
flagrant contradiction of all the principles of a free press in New Zealand; and, finally, that this
House, along with many New Zealanders, asks with horror "for how long has this sort of thing
been going on?"
There is a right of free speech in this House, which I intend to exercise today in the hope
that facts, which up to now have been suppressed by our so-called free press in New
Zealand, will become public. On Tuesday, 16 May, the Franklin Times newspaper ran an
article that was disturbing. This is the story it told. During the closing stages of the Kawerau
dispute some individuals who worked for two south Auckland newspapers decided, under
the terms of the Commerce Amendment Act, to seek an Arbitration Court direction to the
Kawerau unions to return to work and to settle their dispute while continuing to work. Those
individuals planned that action because they believed the newsprint shortage would threaten
their jobs. It is my personal judgment that it would have been unhelpful for them to have
exercised their rights at that time, but whatever my judgment may be, it was their judgment
to proceed with the action, and they were within their rights to do so.
At midday on 10 May a detailed press release was made concerning the proposed court
action and the reasons behind it. I suggest that this was important news. A major dispute, in
which there was a great deal of public interest, was about to be influenced by controversial
action by a group of individuals who were prepared to take on some of the most powerful
union groups in the country. Auckland private radio stations ran the story, the Auckland
Star ran it as a small item, TV1 mentioned it, but the New Zealand Herald published
nothing. The New Zealand Herald, as a user of newsprint, has an interest in this matter. On
11 May the staff of the south Auckland papers concerned were required to meet with officers
of the Northern Journalists Union-namely, Mr Tully of the Auckland Star, president; Mr
McLeod of the New Zealand Herald, vice-president; and Mr Harry Kelliher, a professional
union secretary. At that meeting, office holders of the Northern Journalists Union, who
were opposed to the court action being taken, threatened the staff members that if they did
not do as the union wanted they might never get jobs as journalists again. When asked at the
meeting why the press release of 10 May had not appeared in the New Zealand Herald, the
vice-president of the union, Mr McLeod, who works for the New Zealand Herald, stated
that the release had been censored by the management of the New Zealand Herald and the
union.
What I have told you so far is simply a precis of the front page article of the Franklin
Times of 16 May, which the New Zealand Herald did not run. If the original story about the
intervention by a group of individuals into the Kawerau dispute, which the New Zealand
Herald had not published, was not news, surely a front page article in the Franklin Times
accusing union members of standover tactics, the denial of human rights and freedoms, and
claiming censorship by the press, was news. However, on the morning of 17 May the New
Zealand Herald published nothing. On the afternoon of 17 May I decided to tweak the tail of
the lion, and gave notice of my intention to move the motion that we are now debating. That
notice of motion simply drew the attention of the House to the article in the Franklin Times,
and asked the question "For how long has this sort of thing been going on."
On the morning of 18 May the New Zealand Herald finally responded, after a fashion.
In a short article it stated that I had made allegations against it in the House. That is not true.
I simply drew the attention of the House to the Franklin Times article. Secondly, it claimed
that it learnt of the possible Kawerau court case from an Auckland Star item. But in fact Mr
McLeod, who works for the New Zealand Herald, and who is vice-president of the union,
had already stated that he had had the material, and had discussed it with the New Zealand
Herald management, and that the decision had been to censor it. Thirdly, the New Zealand
Herald gave as its published reason for not releasing the news the fact that papers had not yet
been filed in court. But that is ridiculous. The pages of the New Zealand Herald positively
drip with stories of pending court action when papers have not been filed. In any event, the
New Zealand Herald knew the papers were not to be filed until the Friday, because the press
release which Mr McLeod had, and which he claimed was censored by the New Zealand
Herald, made it clear that the papers were not to be filed until the Friday.


## p. 462 (#470) ############################################

462
31 May
Discussion of Motions-Press Censorship
At this stage my hackles started to rise, because what had simply begun as a claim by the
Franklin Times, about which I had no knowledge or proof, was beginning to develop a
decidedly fishy odour. On the evening of 18 May I made a brief statement to the New
Zealand Herald. In that statement I pointed out first, that it was not I who had made the
allegations, but the Franklin Times; secondly, as the issue involved the supply of newsprint
the New Zealand Herald had a self-interest; and, thirdly, that the reason for non-publication
given by the New Zealand Herald was self-evidently not normal New Zealand Herald policy.
On the morning of 19 May an item was run on Radio New Zealand news attributed to Mr
Hardingham, the New Zealand Herald editor, stating: "His paper will not print further
statements from Mr Malcolm on this issue, but he says it is not a question of censorship, but
rather that the paper regards the issue as sub judice. Mr Hardingham said the New Zealand
Herald is taking the issue to the Press Council for a ruling, because Mr Malcolm won't." To
which I say, rubbish.
The Press Council is not a judicial body, and discussing matters before it is not sub
judice, as Mr Hardingham, who is a member of the Press Council, well knows. Mr
Hardingham is quite wrong in saying I will not take the matter to the Press Council. I have
never said that. On 31 May the New Zealand Herald then claimed it had taken the matter to
the Press Council only because I had been invited to and had not. Once again, rubbish. The
facts are that I have not been invited to do so by the New Zealand Herald. The facts are that
on 23 May Mr Hardingham wrote to me, made no suggestion that I take the matter to the
Press Council, but threatened that he would unless I withdrew my notice of motion-a
parliamentary matter, I point out.
At this point, I am tempted to believe what the Franklin Times has said, and it is a sorry
affair. To me, the evidence is clear. The Northern Journalists Union executives have used
standover tactics, and have bullied and threatened other journalists who have not been
prepared to toe the party line. Two little south Auckland newspapers have had the guts to
publish the facts and be damned, and no major daily has had the courage to take up the
cudgels on behalf of the individuals concerned. Where is the integrity of the press? A blank
accusation of censorship has been levelled at New Zealand's largest daily newspaper by
another newspaper. The New Zealand Herald has wriggled, has squirmed, has misquoted
me on several occasions, has failed to publish my statement, has failed to report on the
Franklin Times article, has given weak, patently false excuses for non-publication, and has
hidden behind the Press Council as a reason for non-publication.
The incident that started all this is not very important. What is important is that the
Northern Journalists Union and the New Zealand Herald are exposed for what they are—
manipulators of news. The man who was reputed to have said that the censorship had
occurred is, himself, both a union official and a New Zealand Herald employee, and the fact
is that nothing has appeared in the New Zealand Herald, other than that which I have
shamed the paper into publishing by using my right of free speech in the House. Everything I
say today can be confirmed. I have here signed statements from those involved. I have tape
recordings of the meetings in question. I speak out on this issue so as to encourage and
support those who stood up to the standover tactics of the Northern Journalists Union, and I
do it to encourage and support the thousands of other New Zealanders who suffer from
union bullying tactics, from censorship of the press, and who also believe that it is time to
stand up and be counted. I do not represent vested interests, I represent the thousands of
ordinary folk who know that what I am saying is true, even if it is seldom published.
A small group of people in south Auckland have had the courage to take a stand on the
issue, and I stand behind them. I will be interested to hear where the Opposition stands. Is it
prepared to argue in the debate for the rights of the freedom of the individual against union
bullying tactics, and a free press; or will the Opposition curry favour with its left-wing
Northern Journalists Union friends who have been responsible for this disgusting display of
undemocratic behaviour that has involved victimisation, threats, and censorship.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I am sorry that the member for Eden spoke in the House in the
way he did under the cover of absolute parliamentary privilege-a privilege that must be
maintained in a democratic society, but one that carries with it a responsibility for accuracy,
and requires a high degree of integrity and common sense. I have not approached any
member of the Northern Journalists Union before making the contribution I am about to
make, but I did ring the editor of the New Zealand Herald this morning, and he informed me
that the member for Eden has not once deigned to ring him, or any of his immediate editorial
assistants, about this matter. The editor said he would be happy to speak to anybody
personally, or on the telephone.


## p. 463 (#471) ############################################

31 May
463
Discussion of Motions-Press Censorship
The editor states, and I accept his word, that it is completely untrue to say that he
requested anyone, or accepted any requests from anyone, to censor any item of news. He
said no request had been made to him by the union to censor any news, and if it had, none
would have been censored. I heard the member for Eden in complete silence, and I hope he
will give me a similar courtesy. The editor of the New Zealand Herald went on to say that
only he has the responsibility for seeing what goes into the paper. When Mr Hardingham
signed his appointment papers he made it absolutely clear that if he was ordered by his
editorial board to change news he would no longer remain its editor. I accept his word
absolutely.
What does this trifling little storm in a teacup, raised by the member for Eden, come to?
It all comes down to the operations of one of his mates, a Mr Harder, of Strikefree. He was
not mentioned once by the member for Eden. On the evening of the day the member for
Eden gave notice of his motion, Mr Harder rang TV1 news and said that the Newspaper
Publishers Association had proposed an action against Kawerau in the courts. Mr Harder
quoted that as fact, but we now know that it was a lie, because when TV1 came out with that
item of news it was rung by the New Zealand Herald-I do not know whether by Mr
Hardingham or his assistant-and told that that was not the case. To its credit, TV1
apologised later in the evening. But did Mr Harder apologise? I would like to know why TV1
did not have the decency to ring and ask the New Zealand Herald if the story was true. It was
a lie by Mr Harder, and the member for Eden should have known that was the case.
Last Tuesday, 8 days ago, the same Franklin Times that the member for Eden referred
to published an item on its front page, which he conveniently forgot to read out. It quoted
the report of 16 May, of which we received copies, which stated that the meeting was told
that "the reason the New Zealand Herald did not publish any news of the staff action was
due to the release being censored by the union and the management". It goes on to say:
"This allegation was not referred to the editor of the New Zealand Herald for comment
before it was published. Had it been, the allegation of censorship would have been denied.
The Franklin Times apologises to the New Zealand Herald for this oversight." So we have
the Franklin Times apologising for something that the member for Eden now raises in the
House-a very trifling little matter. The activities of Mr Harder are distinctly dubious. The
lie he told to TV1 has been exposed as such.
As far as Truth is concerned, it did publish the letter that Mr Hardingham wrote to the

Building Industry
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St Kilda): I move, That this House views with grave concern the
continuing deterioration of both the commercial and housing sectors of the building industry
right throughout New Zealand resulting in regular liquidations and with consequent massive
loss of skilled manpower, a serious downturn in apprenticeship contracts and destroyed
confidence and calls on the Government to speedily let more contracts for urgently required
public buildings and for housing to at least save the remnants of a key industry.
The present critical state of the building industry can be laid squarely at the feet of the
present National Government. Almost daily we read about an already seriously depleted
building labour force running out of work, skilled staff being dismissed, an increasing
number of firms in the hands of creditors, and bankruptcies; added to which are the number
of smaller builders who have left the industry before being forced out, uneconomic tendering
because of lack of contracts, and apprentices being swapped around, if they are lucky, or
having their apprenticeships terminated.
Mr Lithgow: Who wrote that?
Hon. W. A. FRASER: I did. Are you satisfied? All this is a direct result of the National
Government's deliberate policy of singling out the building industry for the axe, both in
commercial construction and house building. Every time the National Party comes to power
we have a building crisis, and a Labour Government is then called upon to clean up the mess.
We see history repeating itself, and history will also repeat itself towards the end of
November. I can just see the builders lining up at the polling booths very early that day.
While urgently needed public buildings, not the least being for education, remain on the
drawing boards-perhaps even farther back-commercial builders are being sent to the wall,
with a consequent outflow of valuable skills. These losses will seriously impede the massive
rebuilding programme needed in the future.
The other half of the building industry-the home building sector-was promised by the
National Party in November 1975, or at least by the member for North Shore, "a dynamic
new housing policy". Remember that one, George? It was so dynamic that production of
housing units has been permitted to drop to about the lean 1972 level, about 10 000 fewer
houses than were built 2 years ago. Is it any wonder that New Zealand has about 3000 fewer
practising carpenters? While firms are going bankrupt, out-of-work apprentices face a grim
future. Some obtain temporary work with alternative builders, only to find that they must be
shifted again as contracts continue to run out. Others have been cut off completely and have
then found that they did not qualify for employment under the Government's local body
special work scheme. What does the Government expect these young chaps to do? They are
keen to acquire building skills and to help build a better nation, but they are shut out. What a
sad picture!
New apprenticeship contracts in carpentry reached a record 2600 under the former
Labour Government. By last year the total had fallen to 1480, and the latest figure available
indicates that only 947 new apprenticeship contracts have been entered into. For the benefit
of the lady member who followed me in a debate yesterday, this is the trend, not only with
carpentry apprentices, but also in furniture manufacturing, which is down by 48 percent,
bricklaying, in which there has been a massive decline, plumbing, glazing, and painting. One
could go on right through the building trades.
For every house not built there is an effect on the livelihood of more than 200 people,
most of them breadwinners. Multiply that by 10 000 fewer houses and we get some
appreciation of the colossal cut in production and man-hours. It is crucial that the housing
industry be boosted, both because of its importance as an employer and because of its social
importance. We are witnessing an almost complete lack of social conscience in the present
Administration. While the National Government looks upon housing as an economic tool,
or, if you like, an element of economics, the Labour Party regards it as an important social
need.
Under a Labour Government the building industry will no longer be singled out as the
economic scapegoat. The Labour Party's housing policy will put an end to the start-and-stop
policies that have been practised so regularly by National Administrations—and the present

was a slackening of New Zealand's export trade with Japan in 1974." Anyone else would
have called that drop a disaster, but the Government of the day preferred to call it a
slackening. What a euphemism!
The report shows that export receipts totalled $223 million, compared with $243 million
in 1973. A slackening suggests a slight decrease, but that was a large drop. In fact, it was a
disaster under the Labour Government of the day. As I said before, Labour capitulated, as it
always has done in negotiating exports with Japan. I shall now quote from page 31 of the
report of the Department of Trade and Industry for the year ended 31 March 1977: "New
Zealand's export trade with Japan again expanded during 1976❞—a year when the National
Government was in office "with exports totalling $392 million compared with $261 million
in 1975." In the calendar year to the end of 1976, under the National Government, there was
a large increase in exports to Japan of about 50 percent over the previous year. Under the
National Government we do not see the capitulation we saw under the Labour
Administration.

CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 30 May 1978.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): In its approach to abortion legislation
Parliament has always recognised two rights: the right of the mother and the right of the
unborn child. It is clear that most New Zealanders are opposed to abortion on demand. The
fact is that, whilst New Zealand's laws have always protected the unborn child they have also
recognised that there are situations in which circumstances justify and moral considerations
permit the termination of a pregnancy. That is my view as well. Some people say that rape
could be one of those situations, or the age of the mother. Another circumstance could be a
medical condition that creates a serious threat to the life of the mother, or an operation that
would affect the life of the foetus. The legislation passed last year provides for these
conditions, and added other grounds for abortion as well. Further, if a check reveals a
suspected foetal abnormality and if the mother's knowledge of it threatens a serious risk to
her health, even temporarily, an abortion could be justified in the early stage of the
pregnancy under the present Act. Abortion can also be justified in all circumstances where
the injury to the mother's health may be permanent. On good legal authority I understand
that to be the present law. Parliament has always considered that there is need for some sort
of social control in this area. Hence in last year's legislation provision was made for its
continuance by means of the supervisory committee.
The committee was established by Parliament. It has now stated that the legislation
requires amending to enable it to function effectively. The committee has put forward
specific proposals to amend the law, which are the amendments now before the House.


## p. 483 (#491) ############################################

31 May
483
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Amendment Bill
Some medical authorities have expressed a similar view, so it is obvious that the proposals
must receive the attention of Parliament. The legislation follows the recommendations of the
royal commission, so it must be given reasonable time and the necessary provisions to enable
it to work. I go along with the general intent of the supervisory committee's amendments,
but I believe that the proposal now advanced by the member for Porirua could satisfactorily
clarify one particular aspect of the law. I note that the superintendent-in-chief of the
Auckland Hospital has taken a somewhat similar view, stating that the addition of the word
"reasonable" to the present law would make the implementation of the Act easier. The
member for Porirua has suggested that his proposal be referred to the supervisory committee
for an opinion. If the supervisory committee will go along with the amendment, well and
good; otherwise I support the amending Bill introduced by the Minister.
Finally, the publicity that the public is continually being subjected to indicates that
opinion on this issue is polarised at the two extremes--that there are only irreconcilable
differences of opinion and no middle ground. However, opinion is not polarised, and there is
a middle ground that has not received much attention from the media and other quarters.
The fact is that the argument about terminating or not terminating the life of an unborn child
tends to be a negative one. It completely ignores the positive and legitimate approaches
associated with the control of the size of families and the prevention of unwanted
pregnancies. There is scope for a massive and urgent programme of parent education on
family planning and the avoidance of unwanted pregnancies. This approach should not
ignore the rights and the proper exercise of parents' moral responsibilities and the proper
exercise of moral responsibility generally. In this the parents have a major role to play, and
most accept it and inform their children of the facts of life. But there are cases where
responsibilities of this kind are neglected. This is an area where acceptable social
organisations could have a role to play greater than that being attempted at present. I am
certain that if the necessary emphasis was placed upon the matters I have mentioned there
would be fewer unwanted pregnancies and less controversy. The time for positive action in
this field is long overdue.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert): Few people in the country would view the passage of
this legislation or the principal Act with satisfaction. Last year the principal Bill was
introduced, and the Prime Minister made a decision, which he is authorised and competent
to do, that because the argument was protracted and difficult the legislation would be the last
issue to be decided by Parliament, and that time would be given to members because, to use
his own words, "they would be using their own time to put through the Bill". It did not work
out that way.
Hon. David Thomson: It did.
Hon. W. W. FREER: No, it did not. The Prime Minister changed the order of business,
and the Bill was not the last matter to be considered by the House. As a result there was
some confusion, not only among parliamentarians, but also in the community. We have a
situation with this amending legislation, as we did with the principal Bill, where we have
what is known as a conscience vote. I have been in the House for nearly 31 years, and I can
truthfully say that I have never been satisfied with the overall outcome of conscience votes.
The majority of them have not been on moral or religious issues. The majority for some
reason that a political historian could have a wonderful exercise on-have been on liquor. I
recall listening one evening to a member, who is no longer in our presence, move an
amendment to a clause then before the House. Because he did not have the guidance of a
Whip, he misunderstood the way in which the question was put and voted against his own
amendment. A little of that happened last year.
This is a House of Representatives, and every member is elected to serve the majority of
the people in his constituency. Yet we persist, for some reason yet to be explained to me, in
having a conscience vote on such things as the sale and distribution of alcohol, and now on
contraception, sterilisation, and abortion. It disturbs me to find how few members have
bothered to assess the support in their own electorates, among the people they represent, for
their views on this issue. I commend my colleague the member for Onehunga, who last year
took the initiative, quite properly, of sending a letter to all the people on his electoral roll
asking them to express to him, as their parliamentary representative, their views on the
proposed legislation.
Mr Lithgow: Good move.
Hon. W. W. FREER: It was not only a good move, but it was also a democratic move,
the act of a competent, responsible parliamentarian who got the views of his electorate.

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): In this matter we are trying to weigh the rights of the
individual to freedom against those of society to responsibility. They must be balanced. I
would be one of the first to argue that the rights and privacy of individuals should be given
the maximum possible protection in law, subject to the common weal. Some activities are
forbidden in public, some are frowned on by sections of society, but a woman may perform
them in the privacy of her home and the law has no right to interfere.
However, there are more fundamental rights than the right to privacy, and the law
recognises this in many instances. For example, a woman may not carry on a business in her
own home in contravention of local authority regulations; she may not rob, assault, or
poison a guest; she may not contract an assassin to deal with her husband, no matter how
much he deserves it; she may not batter one of her children; and she may not rig a booby trap
which might seriously endanger the life or health of an intruder-after all, the intruder might
be intent only on one of the lesser crimes, such as, theft, not murder. In this instance, the
effects of prolonged fear upon her mental health are virtually disregarded by the law. When
health and life are at stake, even the privacy of a woman's body may be invaded. She must be
vaccinated before she is allowed to travel, certain quarantine and treatment regulations must
be complied with if she proves to be a carrier of a serious infectious disease, and when she


## p. 489 (#497) ############################################

31 May
489
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Amendment Bill
goes to the ultimate and attempts to commit suicide, any bystander may interfere, and
rightly so.
The right to abortion or to legislate against abortion must be assessed in the light of
similar priorities and precedents. Central to this assertion is the biological fact that the
embryo or foetus is almost unquestionably a separate human life in genetic, biochemical,
immunological, physiological, and anatomical terms. Abortion may be aesthetically less
deplorable than infanticide and child bashing, but in ethical terms it is closely similar. We
hear the cry that the decision regarding the termination of pregnancy should lie with the
woman alone. That is a frightening and possibly foolish misconception, because it lays the
whole burden of reproduction and contraception upon women; it absolves men from
obligation, it subtracts the idea of total mutual care from the sexual relationship, and it
negates the whole concept of fatherhood.
The eminent anthropologist, Dr Margaret Mead, has pointed out that the Hippocratic
oath marks the civilised separation of killing and curing, because throughout the primitive
world the doctor and the sorcerer tended to be one and the same person. Dr Margaret Mead
has warned that society has attempted, and is always attempting, to make the physician a
killer. We need to remember that abortion is almost invariably fatal to the foetus.
What role then should society and its ultimate political institution, Parliament, play in
this whole matter? Society as a whole must have a right to concern itself with decisions that
place the present and future health of women and children at risk. Although maternal deaths
as the result of early legal abortions are minimal, immediate complications range from the
fairly trivial to the very serious. I understand from the research I have done that menstrual
disorders, frigidity, sterility, and tubal pregnancies are much more common in women who
have been aborted, and that premature births-frequent causes of infant mortality and
retardation—are significantly increased by cervical incompetence resulting from abortion. I
also understand that complications are much more likely to occur and to be more tragic in
their consequences when abortions are performed in healthy young women pregnant for the
first time.
I was interested to hear the remarks made last evening by the member for Porirua. It is
claimed by many that political representatives should not have the right to impose their
personal beliefs and morals upon dissenting constituents, but not all constituents subscribe to
the same standards of truthfulness, honesty, thrift, diligence, and kindness. There is no
public outcry when legislation is introduced to encourage responsible behaviour in those
areas. Surely then it can be argued that politicians have a right to ask that when the question
of setting aside nascent life is under consideration, the decision should not be one based on
selfish convenience.
Today people are ready enough to acknowledge that consumer demands are shaped by
advertising, but they are less willing to believe that social mores and human sexuality are
carefully orchestrated for exactly the same motives as commercial gain. Girls are conned into
entering sexual relationships as transient and meaningless as a game of cards, and they are
taught that instant sexual responsibility is contained in a packet of contraceptives which, like
hair spray and deodorant, dispenses happy freedom and confidence. Forget about the legal
registration of marriage, which is only as valuable as we like to make it, but remember to ask
ourselves what sort of relationships are being indulged in and what sort of society are we
building for our children when even a normal, healthy pregnancy is regarded as a liability at
best, and a tragedy at worst.
I can understand the bitterness of women who, because they have given way to a
generous impulse—an impulse almost demanded of them by the nature of modern society—
have been called stupid, ignorant, irresponsible, promiscuous, improvident, or any of those
other charming adjectives used altogether too often by members of the public and sometimes
also by their agents in the welfare State.
Nothing sickens me so much as to see a pregnant woman discarded by her partner and
pilloried by society because the circumstances surrounding her pregnancy are less than ideal.
But is abortion the best option for her, even when it is possible for all concerned to shut their
intellects to the presence of the child? Experience overseas is proving that it certainly is not a
healthy option for women. Stalworthy of the Oxford obstetrics and gynaecological team has
spoken of a conspiracy of silence surrounding the morbid sequels to legal abortion-the safe,
clean, sympathetic treatment we are being urged to permit. I hope that women may soon be
liberated from the sort of society that is increasingly offering them as rubbish bins for casual
men, and that is vacuuming them tidily out and setting them back into circulation, often for
the convenience of the next passerby.

MARILYN WARING (Raglan): Several days ago I made a press statement saying that I
would take no part in this debate, because I could not take part in a procedure in which I was
called upon to compromise my conscience and my anger to an untenable level. Recent
events have meant that I do not stand here compromising my conscience, but I can no longer
control my anger.
Dr Peter Willcox applied in good faith to become a certifying consultant. He took the
House at its word that the law was liberal, reasonable, and workable, and responded to the
pleas of the supervisory committee and to the Auckland Hospital Board knowing that, right
now in Auckland, there is no operating doctor, and at least 12 women that I know of in the
area who have a certificate issued by two certifying consultants and are awaiting an operating
doctor. They are entitled to a legal abortion, and there is no one to operate. Knowing that,
Dr Willcox applied 5 weeks ago, in good faith, to become a certifying consultant. He is a
highly qualified and highly respected medical practitioner. He has been the superintendent
in charge of the maternity hospital for 11 years, and he has done over 2000 maternity
deliveries. He is experienced in the early termination of pregnancy. The Auckland Hospital
Board thought highly enough of him to approach and appoint him to the position, but he has
been turned down by the supervisory committee.
We knew the system would not work, and today that has been confirmed in no uncertain
terms. Today it was reported that an Auckland Hospital Board member, Mrs Connie
Purdue, on hearing the news, said that Auckland doctors were like freezing workers on
strike, who left animals to suffer in the yards. She went on to say that they had no right to
refuse to perform abortions until they got a law they liked. She also commented that it was
no wonder Peter Willcox wanted to be a certifying consultant, because no worker would turn
up his nose at a $25 perk. Dr Willcox informed my colleague, the member for North Shore,
last weekend that he would be donating his $25 fee to an organisation caring for battered
babies and children.
Last week I and many other members of the House were the recipients of a telegram
from a Dr Jean Dominique Peyroux, a certifying consultant in Dunedin. I do not wish to
read the whole of that lengthy telegram, but among sentences in it are: "After repeal the
deluge and holocaust with annihilation of future generations of New Zealanders through
abortion on request", and "Disregard of basic human rights or even its total denial is the
root cause of slavery and abortion on request." "It is also an essential ingredient of a
disruption of world peace today and throughout history." I have not checked, but I imagine
that Dr Jean Dominique Peyroux was one of the 21 signatories of the SPUC petition who
were then appointed certifying consultants. If his views are compatible with the tenor of the
Act, then what is wrong with Dr Willcox's views?
Before I leave this debate again I have only one more comment to make. Women in
New Zealand have had abortions since the first settlers arrived. They have continued having
them regardless of what happened in the House in 1974, 1976, and 1977; and they will

I commend the supervisory committee for the vigour and tolerance with which it has
approached its invidious and difficult task. The conclusion it reached-that the Act was
unworkable-confirms the generally held view of the community.
There was overwhelming objection to the proposals in the original Bill for a panel
system, even though that was a recommendation of the royal commission. That system was
crucial to the whole structure that was put forward, and the efforts of many members when
the Bill was first introduced into the House were directed to voting that proposal out. They
succeeded in this, partly through the acknowledgment by the forces supporting the general
principle of the Bill that that was quite manifestly unacceptable, but only at the cost of

as a whole, and I believe that some members concluded that once that bridge had been
crossed the unworkability of the scheme became manifest and it did not greatly matter if
other amendments were later added as they were-that made the scheme doubly
unworkable. I think the attitude of many members was that if the measure was 100 percent
unworkable it did not matter if it was 200 percent unworkable. Unworkable or not—and
there is still some argument as to this; I am fairly firm in my view, but some entertain a
different one-there is no doubt at all that it is incomprehensible as it stands. Even the
proponents of the law as amended have been unable to agree on what it actually means.

community, particularly the medical profession, citing an opinion from the Solicitor-General
that the Bill made no real change in the law as it then existed. I have invited him to give me
an unequivocal answer to the question whether the summing-up in the Woolnough case
would have been approved by the Court of Appeal-if the law had been as it is now, and not
as it was when the Court of Appeal was asked to give its ruling on that point. I failed to get
an answer.
Others of those who supported the Bill have said, on the one hand, that it tightened the
law; but, again, others have said that it clearly widened it. None of those succeeded in
convincing the supervisory committee. It, of course, was bound to take the Act as
Parliament made it, and if it concludes that its task is hopeless-—and it has so concluded— it
must recommend the making of a change, which it has done. I admire its courage and its
optimism. I think the committee is unduly optimistic in believing a few amendments can
remedy the manifest and multiple defects in the Bill. In my judgment the whole scheme is
fundamentally at fault and beyond retrieval by any of the cosmetic tinkering that we are told
is largely the content of this Bill. The only answer is total repeal, as has been advocated.
That would bring us back to the common law, as developed through the Bourne decision.
It is ironic, perhaps-looking back not too many years—that the impetus for statutory
review of the law came from what were called the liberals, a group among whose ranks I am
honoured to count myself. I must say I was not unhappy with the way the law was working
and being applied, but as a lawyer I was concerned that this should be at odds with and do
violence to the plain words of the Crimes Act. Believing that the law should mean what it
says and say what it means, some of us began to talk about the desirability of harmonising
theory and practice and rewriting the law to give effect to what it was actually interpreted as
saying. At that time that was hotly opposed by groups that have now arrogated to themselves
the title of "pro-life", who were then content that the law should remain vague and
uncertain.

PUBLIC TRUST OFFICE AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): I move, That
this Bill be now read a second time. Section 39 of the Public Trust Office Act 1957 provides
that the Public Trustee may, with the approval of the Investment Board, advance to an
estate money from the common fund for three main purposes: first, to meet expenses
properly incurred by the Public Trustee; secondly, to meet payments due to beneficiaries, or
creditors; and, thirdly, to enable the Public Trustee to carry out any power or discretion that
is vested in him. The estate must have sufficient real or personal property to provide security
for the advance, and the amount advanced is a charge on that property. The Bill proposes to
extend that power to advance money with the approval of the Public Trust Investment Board
so that the Public Trustee can make advances for similar purposes and carry out any power
or discretion conferred on the Public Trustee by power of attorney where he is acting as
agent. The principal would, of course, be fully consulted before the advance was made.
It is anticipated that this power would be used principally in farming operations for the
provision of short-term seasonal finance. In fact, the Public Trustee can make advances of
this nature provided the necessary mortgage documents are prepared and registered to
protect the advance. The Bill provides for a simple form of statutory charge, and it will
simplify the procedures associated with advances of this nature.
Clauses 3 and 4 of the Bill increase the size of an estate where the Public Trustee can
elect to administer an estate and also to assist in an estate where an executor or an
administrator appointed has died without completing his administration. The relevant
figures increase the size of the estate for which such an election may be made from $7,500 to
$15,000 and from $10,000 to $20,000, the limits which apply if the estate proves to be larger
than at first anticipated. That is the total substance of the Bill.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I have looked at the Bill and feel we should
consider it carefully before agreeing to its passage through the House. I say to the Minister,
not in a party political sense, that I do not think he has explained the Bill sufficiently to
members. As I understand it, from the explanation the Minister has given and from my own
reading of the measure, it means that the Public Trustee will be able to lend to beneficiaries
money he is holding as the trustee of other estates and from other sources.
It is worth remembering that the office of the Public Trustee has been in existence for a
very long time now, and the reason Parliament has not given him the proposed right before is
that it was considered that it would lead to a dangerous confusion of the Public Trustee's
roles, in that he could, in effect, lend to himself. I had hoped that the Minister would
advance some reasons for introducing the Bill. Frankly, I do not think the Government has
put up a good enough case, or the type of case that we as a Parliament should demand from a
Minister before agreeing to pass such legislation. I have some misgivings about the Bill. It is
extremely important that we as parliamentarians realise that the office of Public Trustee was
created by Parliament.
Mr Hunt: That's right, in 1872.
Mr PREBBLE: I rely on the member for New Lynn and his advice that the position of
Public Trustee was created as far back as 1872. I do not remember learning that at school,
when being taught about the time of the Vogel Government. However, that is irrelevant. We
as a Parliament have given the Public Trustee certain rights and obligations, and in the Bill it
is proposed to extend those rights and obligations.
I point out that not everybody goes to the Public Trustee by choice. For example, every
year a number of people who are confined to mental institutions have their estates taken

The member for Auckland Central centred his objection on the fact that moneys from

particular estates or properties being administered by the Public Trust Office. The Bill

Investment Board, not of one individual worried about a shortfall in an estate he wants to

Another point is that the principal will be fully consulted before any advance is made.

Personal Explanation on Notice of Motion
and I had been invited by the Vietnamese Government to visit Vietnam. On our return from

Wellington Teachers College Library Grant
2. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: In view of the ever-
increasing price of books, and the fact that they are a vital tool in the training of teachers,
can he explain the reasons for the 58 percent cut in the Wellington Teachers College library
grant this year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): There has been no cut in the Wellington
Teachers College library grant this year. In each of the last 7 years special grants, in addition
to annual per capita grants for library purposes, have been paid to the teachers colleges to
enable them to bring their library book stocks up to an acceptable level. The grant paid last
year completed the programme for upgrading the library stocks at a total cost of nearly
$68,000 over the 7-year period. There was, consequently, no commitment on the part of the
Government to continue with the special grants in addition to the annual per capita grant of
$35.80 per student for teaching and library purposes. Wellington Teachers College will
receive $26,500 in the 1978-79 year from its annual per capita grant.
Mr Marshall: As the Minister has, in a sense, confirmed my question, can he indicate
whether or not all teachers colleges are receiving less for library grants this year than they did
last year?
Mr SPEAKER: I am sure the Minister could confirm or deny it, but not now, because it
is not related to the question. The question refers to Wellington Teachers College, and if the
honourable member wanted a general question he could have asked it.
Mr Hunt: The Minister mentioned the sum of $26,000 for the coming year for
Wellington Teachers College library. How does that compare with last year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The library grant last year was made up of two components-the
per capita one, and part of a setting-up grant. The $26,500 paid in this year represents a
substantial percentage increase on last year.
Mr Hunt: What is this substantial percentage?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I do not have the figure with me, but it was in line with the
general increase in incidental grants made throughout the Education vote for primary and
secondary schools, and teachers colleges, the total of which was about 26 percent.
Mr Marshall: Does the policy relate particularly to Wellington Teachers College, or
does it apply to all teachers colleges?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It applied to all teachers colleges as a setting-up grant.

Golf Balls-Imports
4. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: What is the
situation regarding the importation of golf balls from overseas, and how does it affect the
golf ball manufacturing industry in New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): There is token
provision for the importation of golf balls under basic import licences issued under successive
Governments, both Labour and National. Because of rising overseas prices and a policy of
holding the value of basic licences to 100 percent over the last three licensing periods, the
volume of imports of golf balls has been reduced by about 50 percent during the last 3 years.
Imports of golf balls amount to less than 5 percent of total sales in New Zealand.
Mrs Batchelor: No matter how small the amount imported, how does it affect the
manufacturing industry in New Zealand? Do the imports have any affect on redundancies in
New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The small percentage is really a token type of
licence, and if it has any effect at all it will be minimal. The downturn in the economy has had
some effect, but the main feature, I am informed, is the improvement in the type of ball
manufactured in New Zealand. Balls manufactured in the past were said to be successful for
one to two rounds, whereas the ball now produced is suitable for four to six rounds. The golf
balls themselves are lasting longer.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What is the value of the token licences at present issued?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: In 1975-76 it was $19,331 for 8418 dozen. In 1976-
77, the only completed import licensing year since then, it was $17,215, a reduction of more
than $2,000, and the quantity was 4538 dozen. This year it will be less again—about
$14,800 and it is expected the number of balls will be slightly fewer-under 4500. The final
figures for this year are not available.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Do I understand from the Minister's reply that someone on his side
has a handicap that can make a golf ball last four to six rounds?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am informed that, if people can last the course, the
modern golf ball made in New Zealand will last for four to six rounds, instead of one or two.
I am bound to say I am president of the New Zealand Football Association; I have not been
captain of the Remuera Golf Club.

are not required to say why a particular individual is hired, fired, promoted, demoted, or
otherwise. It is submitted that the Minister does not have administrative responsibility, and
that the test of that is that he could not direct the Broadcasting Corporation or a private
radio station, for which he is also responsible to the House, in general terms, to dismiss any
individual or to employ any individual. Therefore, he cannot be held responsible to the
House for staffing matters that are undertaken by those bodies. I suggest it would be a highly
undesirable precedent, because we could have a spate of questions about staff members that
could be reopened in the House by questions to the Minister, who has no say whatever in
these matters, and cannot have a say in terms of the two statutes that cover the position.

Zealand both to prospective migrants and to recent arrivals. The interdepartmental
committee supported a pilot course on public-counter attendance for basic grade public
servants, focussing on Polynesian cultures and on general problems of migrant settlement in
New Zealand. The committee has also commissioned the preparation of scripts for two films
for screening to migrants before they depart for New Zealand. The first film will show day-
to-day living here, and is intended to be suitable for migrants from all countries. The second
film will be designed specifically to help migrants from the South Pacific.

verified, but it is about the same as for 1976,

URGENT QUESTIONS
Abortions Operating Surgeons
MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Health: What plans has the Auckland
Hospital Board to provide an operating surgeon to perform the abortions for those women
holding the necessary legal documentation entitling them to abortion and whose plight has
now become desperate and urgent as a result of the decision of the supervisory committee to
decline Dr Willcox's application as a consultant and to operate on other than the seven or
eight cases he had personally interviewed prior to the committee's decision not to appoint
him as a certifying consultant?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The situation in Auckland does not result from a
decision of the supervisory committee. The medical superintendent-in-chief of the Auckland
Hospital Board advises that Dr Willcox has agreed to perform the seven or eight abortions
on the patients he has seen. I can only appeal to operating surgeons in Auckland to deal in a
normal manner with cases referred to them for abortions, and not to discriminate against
them because their cases have been considered by certifying consultants who have certified
that such abortions would be lawful. Operating surgeons owe this to the patients, and I
appeal to them again not to withhold their services. It would assist the board if Parliament
passed quickly the Bill now before the House to amend the Contraception, Sterilisation, and
Abortion Act.
Abortions-Certifying Consultants
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Health: Did the Minister hear the
reported comments on "Morning Report" today by the chairman of the New Zealand
Medical Association that he can see no reason why Dr Willcox cannot carry out operations
for abortion in spite of the fact that he has not been appointed a certifying consultant, and is
this the same advice that the Minister has received from his medical advisers?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): My answer to this question must necessarily be
brief. I issued a press statement on 20 April 1978, and copies of this are available in my
office. There is nothing in legislation which requires an operating surgeon at an abortion
hospital to be a certifying consultant. My medical advisers agree that an operating surgeon is
entitled to have before him all the medical advice and information available on his patient
and to interview and examine the patient before he makes the decision as to whether or not
he will operate. In the event that it has already been agreed by two certifying consultants that
the operation would be lawful, the operating surgeon can proceed in the knowledge that
what he is doing is within the law In the event that the case has not been certified as lawful
by two certifying consultants, the operating surgeon must ensure that such certificates are
issued before he operates. Since there is some doubt in the minds of some doctors as to the
legal position, the legislation currently before the House should be passed quickly to ensure
that the unsatisfactory situation that has developed in Auckland is cleared up quickly in the
interests of the patients.

seems to me there are two matters I have been asked to decide. I will hear argument about
them in a moment, but I hope not too much argument. I hope that the points are succinct,
brief, and to the point so that I can understand what the matter is. One of the points I must
decide is whether the House should suspend the Standing Orders, and the second is whether
a member can move an amendment that involves an appropriation.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Mr Speaker, I sought your
recall after being advised by the Chairman of Committees that he would feel obliged to rule
out any amendment from any member of the House that he considered involved an
appropriation, and that the appropriation message the House received from the Governor-
General last evening would cover only the issues contained in the measure introduced by the
Minister, but not any amendment moved in Committee by members on either side.
Members felt that the message from the Governor-General was on all fours with that
received from the Governor-General when the principal Act was enacted. Since this is a free
vote, members felt that you should rule on this. If the majority agrees with any amendment,
it should not be frustrated on the ground that the amendment proposed contains an
appropriation. Therefore, in the light of the Chairman's ruling, I sought your return so that
the House could resolve the matter simply by resolution. If I read Standing Order 439
correctly, it is competent for any member to move that the Standing Orders relating to the
Bill be suspended in order to allow any member to move an amendment containing an
appropriation. If it is in order to do so at this stage I should like so to move.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Leader of the Opposition raised
this matter. The question clearly is whether there should be a further instruction from the
House to the Committee. There has been a message relating to an appropriation, and, as the
Leader of the Opposition will recall, we had called for last year's message to find out
whether it was exactly the same, but it had not arrived. I find it quite unreal to suggest that
all honourable members, the body of Parliament, should decide upon a certain course that is
a departure from the terms of the supervisory committee's Bill, and then no appropriation be
available. An appropriation will have to be available if members decide on a course different
from the course stated in the Bill.
As the Minister in charge of the Bill, and that being the position that I believe must
apply, the question really is, do we need anything more than we have already, which is an
appropriation message authorising the Committee to proceed with the consideration of the
Bill-and consideration does not, as I understand it, deny us debate on any proposed
amendments. The question really comes back to this: do we need to do anything more than

we have already done to allow the Committee to deal with the Bill as printed, and any

Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I am grateful to the Minister for that assurance,
which we all find helpful. We have before us, and in large part are guided by, a message from
His Excellency the Governor-General, which is cast in the time-honoured form of asking the
House to make provision for so-and-so and so-and-so for a Bill. It has been couched in those
words for as long as I can remember, and certainly for as long as I have been in the House. In
times past, and not so long ago, the invariable practice was to have the message from His
Excellency delivered to the House before the Bill was introduced. We all remember the
familiar procedure, "I have a message from His Excellency the Governor-General",
whereupon all stood, and, on the message being received, the Bill was introduced. That was
the first and the last we heard from His Excellency.
It is not uncommon for the Government to submit amendments to its own Bills, and on
many occasions such amendments involve appropriations. We had then, and we have now,
authority from the Governor-General to make provision for a Bill-a Bill that the
Government itself amends in the course of the hearing. Never have I found it necessary for a
subsequent Governor-General's message to make provision for the amendments so
introduced by the Government to its own Bill, and carried by the House. That is the position
we have at present. We have a Government Bill, as we had a Government Bill last time,
coupled with an assurance from the Government spokesman who introduced the Bill that its
fate will be determined by individuals in the House acting as individuals and not as members
of parties. On both occasions we were invited to seek the aid of parliamentary counsel in
drafting such amendments as any of us as individuals felt appropriate to the Bill that had
been introduced and for which we had been authorised to have sufficient financial provision
made.
The more recent practice is for the message from His Excellency to come not necessarily
at the beginning, but more often at various differing stages of the Bill's passage through the
House, sometimes right at the end. In the case of last year's cognate legislation, which we are
seeking to amend, that was the time the message as such came and was introduced into the
House, though its eventuality was foreshadowed by a motion by the Minister seeking an
instruction from the House to the Committee.
My submission is that, on past practice, the necessity for that has been put aside, and we
feel ourselves free to amend Bills and alter them from the form for which the Governor-
General authorised us to make provision, and no one challenges the validity of them, even
though the direct instruction of the Governor-General's message has been stretched. That is
exactly the position in which we find ourselves today, and I suggest that the Committee is
perfectly entitled to consider and vote on amendments before it, notwithstanding that they
might involve appropriations; and on the face of the assurance given us by the Minister of
Justice, who is in charge of the Bill, that he will seek validating instructions from the
Governor-General, I see absolutely no obstacle to our proceeding to consider any
amendment, however much an appropriation might flow from it.
Mr SPEAKER: Before we go any further, I should like to clarify the position as I see it
so far, so that we do not waste a lot of time discussing old ground that we do not need to
traverse again. First, the Leader of the Opposition said that the House can suspend the

Standing Orders, and that any member can move to do so. That is not correct. Standing
Order 439 states that the Standing Orders may be suspended by the House, but no member
other than a Minister shall move that. So if it is agreed that the Standing Orders should be
suspended, it must be done on the motion of a Minister.
The other point I want to make before we go any further is that Standing Order 420
states: "Any message from the Governor-General recommending an appropriation of
revenue or money for the purposes of an amendment to be moved to a Bill shall be
announced before the amendment is moved." I understand that this happened in the debate
on the main Bill last year; on the introduction of the Governor-General's message, it was
made clear that any amendments that were carried by the majority of the Committee would
be covered by that appropriation. This appropriation does not do that. It is a simple
appropriation in the normal way, and I could not allow it to be stretched in the way I think
the Committee would like it to be stretched, because, if I did, that would negate the whole
procedure of the ruling out of amendments involving appropriations in other Bills, and we
cannot do that.
The position is that, if honourable members wish to proceed with expedition to the
further consideration of the Bill, possibly the way out of it would be for the Minister, if he
agrees, to move that an instruction be given from the House to the Committee to allow for
the Standing Orders to be suspended in such a way that the Committee can proceed with the
consideration of amendments that involve an appropriation, and that those amendments,
provided they are carried by the majority of the Committee, should be incorporated in the
Bill.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Mr Speaker, thank you for your ruling.
The Clerk has assisted me, and I have the appropriate words. I move, That it be an
instruction to the Committee of the Whole House on the Contraception, Sterilisation, and
Abortion Amendment Bill that it considers the proposed amendments to the Bill involving an
appropriation notwithstanding the provisions of the Standing Orders 324 and 420 relating to
appropriations.
Motion agreed to.
