Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
International Situation
International trade is much more important to New Zealand than
to most other countries in the world, and, as a result, the international
economic situation affects New Zealand more than it does most other
countries. A world recession developed in 1974, partly as a result of
the increase in oil prices at the end of 1973. This recession came at a
time when the Bretton Woods system of international financial
discipline had finally broken down, while efforts to replace it had
made no progress.
Most of the developed countries of the world have recovered from
the worst effects of the 1974 recession, although some have not yet
made the structural changes that are needed to adapt to higher
energy prices.
Rates of inflation have diminished. Indeed, in the industrial countries
they have halved since the peak of 1974, but they are not back by
any means to the levels of earlier years.
A new phenomenon of large trade surpluses in the hands of a small
number of countries, balanced by deficits elsewhere in the world, has
caused problems which so far have defied solution. The surplus of
the major oil-exporting countries, although less than in the years
immediately following the price increases, still amounted to 35 billion
US dollars in 1977 and will continue at a high level for many years
yet.
Japan, Germany, and Switzerland have also shown massive sur-
pluses as they have overcome the impact of increased energy prices,
while Britain is moving from a massive deficit to a surplus as North
Sea oil comes on stream. The total sum of these surpluses must result
in corresponding deficits spread among the other countries of the
world. Although it is true that the United States has run a very large
deficit in the past year, a good deal of it comes from the import
of additional quantities of oil, and is simply cancelled out by increased
surpluses in the oil-exporting countries.
This new issue in the international economic debate has preoccupied
the decision makers of the major world economies to the extent that
no progress has been made in the pursuit of a new form of inter-
national financial discipline, while the deteriorating positions of the
developing countries and the developed primary producers have been
given totally inadequate attention.
At international conferences around the world in the past year,
I have consistently made the point that today many countries are
reaching the position where they can no longer afford to borrow. It


## p. 522 (#530) ############################################

522
1 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
would take only a collapse and default in one of these countries to start
a chain reaction which could do incalculable damage to the economies
of even the strongest industrial powers.
In the most recent conferences which I have attended I have seen
little sign that the attention of the major industrial countries has been
diverted from a defence of their own internal policies to a wider con-
sideration of their world-wide obligations.
One result of this situation has been an intensification of agricultural
protectionism in some countries. The surplus countries have paid
lip-service to a relaxation of protectionism without making any posi-
tive move to put such a policy into practice. World trade is languish-
ing and, for a country as dependent on international trade as New
Zealand, that is bad news.
The New Zealand Government has argued with greater and greater
force for a better deal for the exports of the primary producing
countries. We have lobbied hard and long to keep open our trading
channels to the European Economic Community, our most important
single market. Senior ministers have travelled regularly around the
capitals of the Community to present New Zealand's case to ears
which are far from receptive.
1977 was a bad year for New Zealand in Europe, although we did
succeed in negotiating with the Community an increase of 10 percent
in the c.i.f. price for butter and cheese from 1 October 1977. The
question of a further increase in the price of butter to cover recent
cost increases will soon be under discussion with the Commission.
New Zealand's access to the Community for cheese under protocol
18 was terminated on 31 December last. Negotiations to restore our
cheese outlets in the Community are now continuing in the GATT
multilateral trade negotiations.
The proposal of a Community regime for sheepmeats represents a
far greater danger to the New Zealand economy than anything that
we have faced in the field of dairy products. Our lamb trade with
Britain is worth more than $320 million per annum, but, more than
that, it is vital to our whole sheep industry. The best analysis of the
proposals at present under consideration indicates that they would
inevitably lead to a rise in the price of lamb on the British market and
a decline in consumption which could effectively destroy the New
Zealand trade built up over generations. An increase of 30 percent
in the price of lamb to the British housewife would price it out of her
reach and, as we have emphasised at the highest level, there is no
alternative market for over 200 000 tonnes of this highly specialised
product.

Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
In March the Deputy Prime Minister was assured by Mr
Gundelach, the Agricultural Commissioner for the Community, that
it was not the intention to disadvantage New Zealand by such a
regime. Both Mr Callaghan, the British Prime Minister, and Mrs.
Thatcher, the Leader of the Opposition, have assured me that, follow-
ing my discussions with them, they understand the seriousness of the
threat to the New Zealand economy and will take action accordingly.
Our experience with Community regulations is far from reassuring.
The best intentions to safeguard New Zealand can be frustrated by
the inevitable operation of a regulation which has as its basic inten-
tion the protection of the domestic producer and self-sufficiency
within the Community in the particular product.
Our economic relations with Japan are going through a period
of difficulty. The Government has been disappointed that Japan has
failed to deal adequately with our requests for better access for
beef, dairy produce, and other products. These are issues which in
some cases go back many years. The position today, however, is
that Japan has one of the strongest economies in the world, with a
trade surplus in excess of $17 billion a year. While the Japanese
Government is stating in the various fora of the world that it intends
to reduce its massive surplus in part by accepting more imports,
it has until recently opposed any worth-while relaxation in the fields in
which New Zealand is vitally interested. Only a very small move in
relation to the Japanese economy would be necessary to accommodate
the New Zealand position and it would have the merit of providing
cheaper food and thus increased consumption by the Japanese people.
After 2 years of unrewarding discussion following my visit to
Japan in early 1976, the Government decided that we would not
discuss the question of Japanese access to our 200-mile economic zone,
which became effective from 1 April, until progress was made on
these long-standing issues. In the meantime, we have reserved a
proportion of our fishing rights for allocation to Japan and if no
progress is made in our discussions the fishing stocks will benefit from
the smaller catch that will be taken this year. My recent talks in
Melbourne with a representative of the Japanese Government gave
reason to hope that at last some movement is possible, and this approach
will be followed up.
Trade with Australia continues to be of crucial importance to
our manufacturing sector. For the first time, total two-way trade
in the 1976-77 June year exceeded $1,000 million.
The visit in March of the Deputy Prime Minister and the NAFTA

ministerial discussions in April reaffirmed that it was in each country's

We in turn are prepared to respond positively to reasonable offers.
The New Zealand Economy
Since the oil shock at the end of 1973 I have constantly expressed
the view that New Zealand's economic expansion during that year was
excessive and unwise. The Government of the day failed to move to
rectify the consequences of the massive increase in the price of oil
which came on top of that expansion. This was a major error in
economic management.
By early 1975, New Zealand's terms of trade had declined by 43
percent as against the peak in 1973. In plain language, a given volume
of exports would in 1975 buy only 57 percent of the volume of imports
that it could in 1973. That situation has continued up until the present
day. Since the end of 1975 we have been adjusting to this grave
decline in our terms of trade.
The present Government on taking office was faced with the fact that
business confidence was excessive having regard to our real economic
difficulties. It took nearly 2 years for that confidence to be blunted, and
realisation of the situation did not come until the third quarter of 1977.
At that time manufacturers realised that they had been producing in
excess of the ability of the economy to absorb their products. A stock
overhang had resulted and the downturn in production with consequent
laying-off of staff was much greater than it need have been had the
real situation been understood sooner.
Following my attendance at the annual meetings of the International
Monetary Fund and the World Bank in October last, I took the view
that there would be no upturn in the world economy which would have
an impact on the New Zealand economy, and accordingly I introduced
a major package of economic measures at the end of October. It
included, among other things, a special supplementary family benefit
payment of $25 per child, an across-the-board cut in personal income tax


## p. 525 (#533) ############################################

1 June
525
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
of 5 percent from 1 February, additional Government expenditure, and
a number of monetary measures. In December I announced a reduction
in company tax to improve company liquidity in respect of the holding
of excessive stocks stemming from the low level of demand. In February
I announced the release of the Wool Income Retention Account funds
and the termination of the import deposit scheme, as well as a number
of further security ratio changes to expand the availability of credit.
A major package of measures to assist the housing sector was
announced at about the same time. Taken together, all these measures
amount to some $770 million at an annual rate. This substantial and
timely stimulus helped to steady the economy during a crucial period.
The indications now are that a degree of stability has returned at a
lower but sustainable level of activity. The last few steps of the adjust-
ment process have been taken very quickly. We have moved more
rapidly in the last 6 or 7 months to adjust our spending to match our
incomes than in the whole of the previous 4 years. The adjustment
process has inevitably produced a sharp rise in unemployment. This has
been compounded by the rapid downturn in absenteeism and labour
turnover. Workers are sticking to their jobs and attending regularly and
output per man has risen. Paradoxically this makes it more difficult to
get unemployed members of the workforce back into employment. A
wide range of measures to deal with the increased unemployment has
been introduced and these will continue. Perhaps the most important
are those which will upgrade the skill of individual members of the
workforce and thus lead to more satisfying jobs in the future.
When the Government took office we had had 3 years of inflation
rising from 5.4 percent in 1972 to 10.1 percent in 1973, 12.5 percent in
1974, and 15.7 percent in 1975. Inflation was accelerating and feeding
on itself. It was necessary, in order to get the Government accounts into
reasonable balance and reduce the growing internal deficit, to remove
certain subsidies which were generally agreed to be totally unjustified.
The effect of these moves, combined with the continuing increase in the
price of oil fuel, meant that it was impossible to reduce the rate of
inflation rapidly. As these adjustments were absorbed and left behind
us, however, the Government's policy of easing pressure on the economy
began to be felt and finally we have seen in the first quarter of this year
a return to an annual rate of single-figure inflation.
There is no need for a further downturn in the economy and indeed
the decision that was taken as far back as last October to stimulate
economic activity has produced results which are now beginning to be
felt.
The improvement in our balance of payments position caused by
increased returns from our exports and a reduction in volume of our


## p. 526 (#534) ############################################

526
1 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
imports has brought us to the position where it is possible to move to
reduce the present rate of unemployment by stimulating the economy
still further. The overall effect of tonight's Budget will be a further
stimulation of the economy, a reduction in unemployment, some
impact on our balance of payments, which nevertheless will continue
to improve, and, because there is excess capacity in the economy, little
or no pressure on the rate of inflation.
Looking beyond our present circumstances, our future depends
on our ability to export. The New Zealand Planning Council in its
first published document suggests that New Zealand should be able
to maintain a real growth rate of about 3 percent per annum pro-
vided we have continued export growth. Growth in the agricultural
sector will be essential if we are to achieve that result. The suggestion
is that we should have an increase of at least 2 percent per annum
in livestock numbers over the next few years. This target has been
in mind during the formulation of the proposals which I shall
announce tonight.
Lessened internal demand gives an added incentive for manu-
facturers to look to overseas markets. There have been some
spectacular performances in the export field by New Zealand manu-
facturers in the last year or two, and this development is continuing.
Market research is essential, but it is also essential that potential
exporters have confidence that they will be backed by the Govern-
ment with adequate incentives and the provision of supporting
services. The high priority scheme which has recently come into opera-
tion is the most recent in a succession of initiatives designed to see
that efficient activities are given every encouragement to expand.
The Government does not have a closed mind in these matters.
We are prepared to consider new and innovative proposals which
will help our exporters gain a foothold in new markets around the
world. The Bahrain/New Zealand venture for a free port establish-
ment in Bahrain is a case in point. We have built on the mutual
attraction of the two Governments to set up a facility which gives
New Zealand a preferred position and a launching pad for an export
drive into one of the most exciting markets in the world.
The Government realises the necessity for providing facilities for
training our young people so that they can best take advantage of
the opportunities that will open out as our export trade in a wide
variety of new products develops. I shall later tonight announce
changes in training and retraining schemes that represent a further
step forward in this direction.

Wage Negotiations
After extensive discussions between the Government, the Federation
of Labour, and the Employers' Federation last year, the wage freeze
was lifted on 15 August 1977 and free collective wage bargaining
was reinstituted between employers and employees. On 17 April
last, a new Arbitration Court comprising three Judges and employee
and employer representatives came into being, with a responsibility
for looking after the functions previously exercised by the Industrial
Court and the Industrial Commission. The Arbitration Court gives
effect to the Government's policy of a greater degree of co-ordination
among the many separate wage-fixing bodies as their chairmen are
taken from among the Judges of the Court. For the first time the State
sector has been brought into this co-ordinated framework, as a Judge
of the Arbitration Court is the Chairman of the Public Sector
Tribunal. The local body sector is also establishing an integrated
career and wage-fixing structure through the Joint Council for Local
Authority Services created by statute last session.
The 1977 wage round, held under conditions of free wage bargain-
ing, has not been without its difficulties. The early part of the round
produced wage rate increases of between 6 and 9 percent, with
larger increases for skilled people, movements which were within the
range the Government considered acceptable. In this context, it is not
sufficient to merely look at the wage rates. It is also necessary to take
account of increases in other forms of remuneration such as travelling
allowances, productivity incentive payments, and the like. These
contribute as much to labour costs as do wage rates themselves,
and therefore have an impact on inflation.
As the round has progressed, and certainly in recent weeks, the
increases sought by some groups of workers have clearly been
excessive. I am concerned that such movements, where granted,
will serve to feed excessive relativity-based increases in the next
wage round. This can only threaten free wage bargaining, under the
present and projected economic conditions, and all parties-unions,
employers, and Government-must consider the implications seriously.
This is particularly important in view of the need for our exports to
remain internationally competitive.
Fiscal Policy
The Government deficit before borrowing will be higher in
1978-79 than it was in 1977-78. In part this is a result of the major
tax reform initiated in this Budget, which involves a substantial
revenue loss, and of the further measures to help exporters, particu-


## p. 528 (#536) ############################################

528
1 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
larly farmers. In part, however, it is also a continuation of the
Government's policy to sustain the economy. If the Government did
not maintain its deficit at the level planned for this year, total demand
would be very much lower, production would be lower, and many
more would be unemployed. In this sense the high deficit is simply
an extension of the policy initiated with the October measures last
year.
In one other important respect also, this Budget represents another
step along a road first signposted in October. When it became clear
that a larger Government deficit would be necessary in order to
maintain employment, the Government had two options: it could
increase Government expenditure by providing additional services
to the public, or it could reduce its revenue by cutting taxation. The
Government chose to cut taxation. This means that the benefits of
the increased deficit will flow largely to the private sector through
increased after-tax incomes. This should soon lead to higher sales,
increased production, and additional employment in the private sector.
It means a continuation of the constraints we have placed on Govern-
ment expenditure, except to the extent necessary to directly maintain
employment or assist the export sector. This second tax cut can be
expected to strongly reinforce the expansionary impact of the first
which came into effect on 1 February this year.
Monetary Policy
Householders, farmers, industry, and the Government depend on an
adequate flow of funds from savers to finance a major part of their
capital requirements. When the Government took office it found that
interest rate controls were severely impeding and distorting this flow
of savings. Deposit interest rates offered by the controlled institutions,
and the interest rates on Government securities, were totally inadequate
to compensate savers for the effect of inflation, and saving was being
discouraged to the detriment of economic stability. Furthermore, the
enforcement of unreasonable interest rates on financial institutions was
diverting funds to operators on the fringe of the normal financial
system. Borrowers were being forced to rely on less satisfactory credit
channels, and the losses investors suffered are now a matter of record.
During the past 2 years the Government has moved to remedy this
situation by progressively freeing interest rates from control and by
increasing the rates of interest paid on Government securities. Savers
now get a more realistic reward and greater security, speculation is
less rife, and borrowers have a greater incentive to use borrowed
money more productively than was the case previously.


## p. 529 (#537) ############################################

1 June
529
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
The competitive markets in interest-bearing securities which are
now developing will enable the Government to finance its borrowing
requirement in a less inflationary way than in the past and will also
provide the means for the Reserve Bank to exercise greater influence
over the growth of both private sector credit and the money supply.
Measures to ease monetary conditions and to increase the availability
of credit have played an important part in the steps taken over recent
months to counter an undue reduction in economic activity.
Reductions in Government security ratios have released $96 million
for housing, $17 million for farming, and $39 million for the finance
of industry. The Wool Income Retention Accounts refund and the
termination of the import deposit scheme released a further $50
million into the economy.
In addition to their direct effects, the above measures have signifi-
cantly increased the liquidity of the financial system by increasing the
reserve assets of the banks. At the same time the margin of free
reserves aimed at under the reserve asset ratios applied to the trading
banks has been increased from $75 million to $125 million, thus
encouraging the banks to use their improved liquidity position to
support activity and stockholding.
Over the course of the coming year prospects are for a considerable
increase in the general liquidity of the economy with substantial
deposit growth in the financial system. The availability of finance for
priority areas such as housing should therefore be adequate without
further ratio reductions. The Government expects that the financial
institutions will maintain a responsible attitude in their lending and
direct credit into the priority areas of housing and export production,
especially agriculture. To a greater extent than in the recent past these
sectors should be able to look to the financial system, rather than
Government agencies, for their credit requirements.
The stance of monetary policy over recent months has been designed
to assist the recovery of domestic economic activity. Looking to the
future the Government will be concerned to see that the growth in the
reserve base of the financial system does not result in an excessive
expansion of credit when demand lifts. In order to avoid this the
Government may need to take action to finance its deficit to a greater
extent than in the past through the sale of Government securities to
the private sector. In general monetary policy will be adjusted as
appropriate to protect the balance of payments and to assist a continu-
ing reduction in the rate of inflation.
To summarise: there are many signs that we are now well on the
way towards establishing the conditions necessary for a sustainable

530
1 June

improvement in production, exports, and income.
• The rate of inflation during the March quarter this year was 2
percent, which is the lowest quarterly figure we have recorded
since December 1972. This compounds to an annual rate of 8.2
percent, which clearly represents a marked improvement on our
previous performance, and brings our inflation rate much closer
to the inflation recorded by our major trading partners.
• The balance of payments deficit continued to improve in 1977-78
although at a much slower rate than in 1976-77. In 1975-76
the current account deficit represented over 9 percent of GNP;
by 1977-78 it had fallen to less than 6 percent of GNP.
A further improvement is predicted for 1978-79.
• There is evidence of a substantial improvement in productivity
throughout industry.
If we are to consolidate on these gains there are some things we must
be careful to avoid. We must never again allow domestic expenditure
to outstrip national production by as much as it did in 1974-75 and
1975-76. Wage and salary settlements must not exceed the limits
we can afford. Our internal costs must not be allowed to increase faster
than costs are increasing overseas. To repeat mistakes like these would
be to throw away the fruits of all the sacrifices we have made since
the change of Government.
It will not be enough simply to avoid past mistakes. In the highly
competitive world in which we presently live we cannot expect to win
new markets and increased incomes without constant change and
adaptation. There must be a greater willingness to take positive steps
to secure the sort of changes in our economic structure, our institutional
framework, and our attitudes that will be required to ensure our
continued prosperity.

Training
Training and retraining to meet present and future skill needs form a
vital element in the Government's strategy for restructuring the
economy. To a large extent individual industries are in the best position
to identify needs and draw up detailed programmes. Considerable
importance is therefore attached to the activities of the Industry
Training Boards. There is a need to put the financial arrangements of
these boards on a more secure footing which will provide for an
equitable sharing of contributions among all firms in an industry. The
Government has therefore accepted the principle of a system of levy
financing to enable each industry to elect to levy itself to meet the
administrative expenses of its Industry Training Board. In particular,
legislation will be introduced this year to provide for a levy facility
linked to factory registration for those industries which operate on a
factory basis. For its part, the Government will increase its contribution
to the training boards from $900,000 to $1.1 million in 1978-79.
Exports
1978 has been designated "Export Year". The Government has

Export Incentives
In the 1977 Budget the Government announced its conclusion that
an export incentive scheme based on net foreign exchange earnings
and applied to a firm's total exports rather than only to the increase
in its exports would have substantial advantages over the present
system.
The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research was commis-
sioned to investigate the various ways in which the Government's
objectives could be met. Substantial progress has now been made
towards the completion of this review.
The Government promised in last year's Budget that consultations
on the revision of export incentives would be held with interested
parties. These consultations have begun and it is expected that a final
decision will be made later this year. In the meantime the tax incen-
tive for increased exports to new markets is to be extended by one
year; it will now terminate on 31 March 1980. Legislation imple-
menting any new scheme will contain a provision to ensure that
exporters to new markets do not gain a dual advantage after that
date.

Technical Help to Exporters
The Government realises that much costly duplication of time and
effort is involved in manufacturers individually researching the par-
ticular technical requirements of foreign markets with respect to
regulations, standards, and other controls affecting their products.
So that this function can be carried out more efficiently through one
central inquiry point in New Zealand, the Government will finance
the establishment of a "Technical Help to Exporters" service, to be
administered by the Standards Association of New Zealand.
Farming
I have stated on several occasions that if our overseas earnings are
to increase at the rate required to provide a basis for sound economic
growth, agricultural production must play a key role. Farming is,
however, an uncertain business. The past year has been a difficult
one, with the widespread drought and flooding earlier in the season
causing serious problems in many districts. Prices on overseas markets
have been relatively static Processing costs and the costs of getting
the produce to markets have increased rapidly so that the price to the
farmer has fallen and with it his income. This has again caused many
farmers to doubt the wisdom of increasing production.
Farm investment recovered well in 1976 but has not continued to
rise this season. To get the export growth we need, it is essential
that farm investment be maintained. This can only happen if farmers
have confidence that expenditure will be justified by future returns.
Tonight I intend to deal both with the immediate situation and with
the longer-term problem.
Short-Term Situation
In March, relief provisions to alleviate the effects of the drought
were considerably expanded, at an estimated cost of $3.4 million for
1978-79. The subsidy for transport of stock feed and livestock and
the regrassing subsidy were increased, and a new subsidy was intro-

Because of the drought, farmers in most districts will have suffered

Supplementary Minimum Prices
Successive Governments have followed the policy of adapting the
level of assistance to agriculture to the changing economic circum-
stances of the sector. More recently, the Government has altered the
thrust of its agricultural policy towards production-related measures
and away from indiscriminate input subsidies, the sum total of which
had been increasing rapidly. In particular, the Livestock Incentive
Scheme introduced in 1976 directly rewards increases in the produc-
tive capacity of livestock farms. The response to this scheme to date
has already fully justified the switch in emphasis. As at 2 May 1978
almost 5000 authorisations involving nearly 3.7 million stock units
had been approved.
Nevertheless, a major factor inhibiting the achievement of the
agricultural sector's potential is a lack of confidence in its future
prospects and profitability. The Government believes that the most
appropriate remedy is action that will help to ensure an adequate
return on the increased production that the sector is beginning to
realise.

To this end, the Government has decided to establish and under-

intended to provide for farmers' reasonable requirements for living

Assistance to farmers will continue to be provided through selective
measures, reviewed as necessary. I shall now outline alterations to
these, together with a number of new proposals. Further details will

Dairy Beef Market Guarantee Scheme
The existing scheme, introduced in 1976, has been reasonably success-
ful. The number of calves registered was 142 000 in 1976 and 130 000
in 1977. It is intended to increase the market guarantee level from
$50 per head to $60 per head. In addition to the supplementary pay-
ment of the difference between the average market price and the guar-
anteed price of $60, a flat payment of $10 will be made on registration
of each calf. This scheme is estimated to cost $4.5 million this year.
Fertiliser and Lime Subsidies
The subsidies on the price, transport, and spreading of fertiliser
have been fixed at levels designed to ensure that the rate of fertiliser
application is kept at a level which allows for both adequate pasture
maintenance and development needs.
The Road User Charges Act has had a significant impact on the
costs of transporting farm commodities. As indirect compensation for
the effects of these charges, fertiliser and lime transport subsidies
will be increased to the maximum possible without creating anomalies
with the new railway freight rates to which I shall shortly refer. Ferti-
liser price subsidies are also increased substantially. The new rates of
subsidies applying from tonight are:
a price subsidy on fertiliser of $32.00 per tonne (previously $22.50
per tonne);
transport subsidies on fertiliser and lime as follows:
per kilometre up to 65 kilometres;
8c/tonne per
5c/tonne per kilometre for the next 185 kilometres;
3c/tonne per kilometre beyond 250 kilometres.
The price subsidy will continue to be paid on the existing basis. The
new level takes into account prospective cost movements.
The fertiliser spreading bounty was originally introduced in 1975
as a temporary measure. Some distortions in the present differentials
for methods of spreading have become apparent. The Government has
therefore decided to abolish the spreading bounties from tonight, with
the exception of the aerial spreading bounty, which will continue, but
at a reduced level of $2 per tonne, to assist in particular the hill country
farmer.


## p. 537 (#545) ############################################

1 June
537
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
At these new rates, subsidies on fertilisers and lime are estimated to
cost $90 million this financial year, an increase of $7 million over

Inspection Fees
In recent years there has been a rapid escalation in the costs of
processing and marketing our primary produce. This has been an
important factor contributing to the recent decline in farm incomes.
There are several reasons why these particular costs have increased
more rapidly than costs generally. The imposition of exacting hygiene
standards by our overseas customers is a major cause. The sharp
increase in freight rates since the oil crisis in 1973 is a second cause.
More recently, however, the deterioration in industrial relations in the
freezing industry has imposed yet another cost burden on the farmer.
The Government recognised that it would be unreasonable to expect
farmers to bear the full costs of the wage settlement negotiated by the
freezing industry unions last March. It was for this reason that the
Government agreed to meet part of the costs of that settlement.
Obviously, however, this could be no more than a temporary expedient
to allow time to consider ways in which to achieve a more lasting
solution.
The Government has now decided upon the following arrangements
to obtain a more satisfactory and longer term solution to this problem.
The agreement under which the Government is funding part of the
costs of the March freezing worker wage settlement will be extended
to 30 September 1978. From 1 October 1978 all Government inspec-
tion fees will be cancelled. Simultaneously, the Government contribu-
tion to freezing worker wage costs will terminate. Freezing companies
will be required either to absorb the additional wage costs or to recover
them by increasing killing charges. Any increase in killing charges to
farmers through this arrangement will be more than offset by the
benefit farmers will receive from the cancellation of Government
inspection fees.
The full list of fees affected is as follows:
meat inspection fees
dairy product grading fees
• farm dairy instruction levies
seed certification fees
seed testing fees
game inspection fees
⚫ livestock inspection fees (except for domestic pets)

Commercial Trials of New Horticultural Crops
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and the
Research Division of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries are
continually striving to produce improved strains of well-known horti-

land conditions. Some of the new crops at present under research have
a promising export potential. Not unnaturally, however, most growers
are reluctant to face the considerable risks involved in establishing an

In order to encourage the establishment of commercial-size trial

Energy
Last year I announced an energy policy package aimed at reducing
our reliance on imported oil and at accelerating the development of
indigenous energy resources. The measures that I shall be outlining
tonight build on last year's package and the energy pricing policy
adopted in 1976. Taken together, they establish a national energy
policy for New Zealand.
Transportation Fuels
The Government is currently discussing with its Maui partners the
feasibility of producing liquid petroleum gas (LPG), particularly for
use as an automotive fuel. More than 10 percent of the transport
sector's fuel requirements could be met by indigenous LPG.
The establishment of appropriate relativities among the prices of
motor spirits, diesel, and LPG is essential for the successful marketing
of automotive LPG. The Government's aim is to see this product
priced competitively with imported liquid fuels.
A preliminary assessment of proposals to use Maui gas to make
methanol for blending with motor spirits indicates that a 15 percent
blend may be feasible. The annual savings in overseas funds would be
more than $40 million.
The Government has therefore decided to proceed with further
market feasibility studies and large-scale trials in conjunction with
the oil industry. It is expected that a final decision whether to proceed
with this option could be made in about 12 months.
A Liquid Fuels Trust Account is to be established to finance the
development of new indigenous fuels and more efficient distribution.
This account will be funded by a levy of 0.1 cents a litre on motor
spirits and automotive diesel. There will be no initial impact on the
retail and wholesale prices of these products as a consequence of this
levy, which will in the first instance be debited to the pool accounts.

Transport
This Government has initiated several major changes in transport
policy, with the aim of promoting the most efficient use of New Zea-
land's transport resources.
Freight transport users now have a choice between road and rail
over distances up to 150 kilometres, and the new road user charges
will assist the process of arriving at a proper competitive balance
between the two modes. Future steps will include a restructured annual
licence fee, a review of the transport licensing system, and a decision
on the next stage of extending competition between road and rail.
Action to encourage economic traffic allocation has taken place in
the rail sector. This must be pursued further if the Railways are to
exploit fully their competitive strengths. Railway rates must keep pace
with costs and, to reduce the present unsustainable losses, rates will
be increased by 12.5 percent on 2 July. Details will be announced by
the Minister of Railways. Operations must continue to be adjusted in
response to demand. Revised financial objectives for the Railways are
currently being worked out.
Railways continue to play a vital role in the provision of inter-
island shipping services. Investigations into the replacement of the
oldest rail ferry, the Aramoana, are under way.
In the urban transport field, the Government's manifesto under-
takings have been honoured, first with the $50 million bus replace-
ment programme to assist the four main local authority operators and
secondly with the recently-announced urban bus incentive scheme.
Planning work for the constitution of effective urban transport authori-
ties in major centres is well advanced and the Government intends to
hold further consultations with local authorities before legislation is
introduced.

Taxation
There is a real need in this country to improve the rewards for
extra individual effort and initiative. Wage increases negotiated under
free collective bargaining play an important part, but so do the taxes
paid on that increased income. The present form and level of taxation
removes much of the incentive that wage increases can give.
Before outlining the changes I propose to make, it is worth setting
out how the Government's revenue from taxation has changed in
recent years. In 1960, nearly two-thirds of the tax revenue collected
was from taxes on incomes. The remaining third was largely from
expenditure-based taxes such as customs and excise duties, motor
spirits duty, and sales taxes.
The rapid acceleration in inflation rates from the early 1970s,
combined with a progressive personal tax scale, increased the propor-
tion of tax collected on incomes. By 1978, over three-quarters of
taxation came from income tax. These shifts in total tax between 1960
and 1978 are large. More dramatic is the very rapid rise in the burden
of tax on salary and wage earners. In 1970, about 30 percent of tax
revenue came from income tax on salary and wage earners. By 1978,
it was around 45 percent of total taxation. These figures contrast with
between 20 and 25 percent in the decades of the 1950s and 1960s.
The present personal tax scale has two basic problems. First, the
taxes paid on additional earnings, such as overtime, at relatively low
income levels are too high. In the low-to-middle income range of $85
to $155 per week, the tax paid on each additional dollar of income
rises from 29 to 46 percent. This is the high marginal tax rate problem.
Salary and wage earners see this as discouraging personal initiative
and efforts to improve their standard of living.
Secondly, the total tax paid by the vast bulk of full time wage and


## p. 554 (#562) ############################################

554
1 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
salary earners is far too high. On average it is about a quarter of
their income. This is the high average tax rate problem.
The changes in personal taxation I am announcing tonight will go
some distance towards meeting these criticisms and achieving the
following goals:
a taxation scale which does not discourage the earning of
additional income from overtime and promotion;
a reduction in the average tax burden of the vast bulk of income
earners;
a concentration of tax relief on the full-time wage earner;
an improvement in the living standards of the low and single
income family with children.
Personal Income Tax
From 1 October this year new rates of personal income tax will
apply. The main features of the new scale will be:
• All taxable income up to $4,500 (cr $87 per week) will be taxed
at 14 cents in the dollar.
Taxable income between $4,500 and $10,000 a year (or $192 a
week) will be taxed at a flat 38 cents in the dollar. This
compares with the present marginal rate of tax, which begins
at 32 percent and rises to 46 percent over that income range.
The rate of tax on taxable income in excess of $10,000 a year will
rise in two steps from 48 cents to a maximum of 60 cents in
the dollar on taxable income exceeding $22,000.
Full details of the new rates are set out in the appendices to the
budget statement.
This represents a major change in the structure of income tax rates.
The present finely graduated scale with 19 steps will be replaced by
one with only 5 steps applying to broad income ranges.
In addition to these rate changes, the present personal rebate will be
abolished. The effect of the rebate has been that no individual currently
pays tax on his or her first $816 of annual income. The taxpayers who
benefit most from this are part-time workers and those who, for one
reason or another, derive incomes for part of the year only. For
example, a single person earning $5,000 a year currently pays $986
tax or 20 percent, whereas a part-timer earning $2,000 a year pays only
$217 or 11 percent.


## p. 555 (#563) ############################################

1 June
555
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
Typically these low-income earners are supplementing another
primary source of household income, either a husband's income, a
social security benefit, or a student bursary, and there is no reason why
they should pay substantially lower rates of tax than low-income full-
time workers. The new structure will increase tax on those whose
taxable income is less than $3,000 a year or $57 a week. In terms of
the example I quoted the person earning $5,000 a year would pay
16.5 percent of his income in tax and the part-timer 14.2 percent-a
substantial narrowing of the gap.
Most young, single employees, and those under training, are expected
to be earning more than $57 a week by October next and will therefore
benefit under the new tax scale. National superannuitants with no
other income will not be significantly affected by tonight's measures.
In a family where one spouse earns a small amount of part-time
income, the family is likely to pay less tax in total than at present,
because the additional tax payable on the spouse's income will be more
than offset by the lower tax on the principal income.
About 1.4 million taxpayers with taxable incomes between $3,000
and $27,000 a year will receive tax cuts ranging up to $382 a year or
$7.80 a week on a PAYE basis.
The benefits of the new tax scale are aimed at the average wage
earner. He or she will benefit substantially from the change. The tax
payable on a wage of $150 a week will, from next October, be reduced
by $4.61 a week. The reductions come on top of the 5 percent tax cut
which took effect last February. With these two cuts, the person on a
wage of $150
of $150 per week will have had his overall tax reduced by nearly
16 percent. This is equivalent to a wage increase of about 9 percent.
Examples of the effect of the tax changes on individuals at various
income levels and in different family situations are set out in the
appendices.

Family Taxation
In the last two Budgets the Government has introduced substantial
tax relief for young families with low incomes or only one income.
For the current year ending 31 March 1979 the single-income family
rebate, at present $208 a year, will be increased to $260. It will continue
as an end-of-year rebate. The rebate will also be extended to include
families whose youngest child is under 12 years of age. At present the
age limit is 10 years. The amount of income which a spouse may earn
before the single-income family rebate begins to reduce will rise from
$1,040 to $1,144 per annum. In addition the rate at which this rebate.
and the spouse rebate reduce will be less abrupt. Instead of diminishing
by 30 cents per dollar of income in excess of the allowable limits, both
rebates will diminish by 25 cents per dollar.
These changes will cost an estimated $14 million in a full year.
Combined with the changes in income tax rates, they will give signifi-
cant relief to principal income earners in families with young children.
Rebate for School Children
To avoid the need for pre-school and school children to pay tax
on small amounts of income, a special tax rebate of $78 a year will
be allowed to this group. A school boy or girl will thus be able to
earn up to $549 a year without being liable for tax.
The effect of the taxation measures I have just announced will
reduce Government income tax revenue by some $320 million in a full
year, or about 7 percent. The change in basic tax rates will cost $300
million for a full year and about $150 million in 1978-79. The
remaining $20 million is the full-year cost of the other tax adjust-
ments I have already announced. It is certainly the largest single
tax cut yet introduced in New Zealand. The combined effect of
the tax cuts in February and October 1978 will reduce the Govern-
ment's tax revenues by $520 million in annual terms. This will also
give the economy a powerful stimulus in 1978 and 1979.
Even with the new scale the 38 percent marginal tax paid over
the average income range is still too high. Further tax relief is
desirable but the Government must realistically appraise the extent
to which it can be given in the present difficult economic circum-
stances. Without a further reduction in the Government's share of
total output, it would not be possible or fiscally responsible to enlarge
the tax cuts. A reduction of Government expenditure involves
difficult decisions, but this Government has a policy of reducing the
State's share of total domestic spending which it has every intention.
of pursuing.

Conclusion
When the Government took office the economy was running at
an unsustainable level of activity. We stated plainly that before
growth could be resumed inflation would need to be brought under
control and our overseas deficit reduced to a less dangerous level.
We acknowledged that the necessary readjustments to the economy
would not be easy or painless, and that the beneficial results would
not be felt for some time.
Now the rate of inflation and the overseas deficit have been cut
by about half. To do this it has been necessary to put severe curbs on
personal and Government expenditure. Government expenditure will
continue to be closely scrutinised, but confidence in the private sector
needs to be boosted. The October measures began this process and the
stimulus was continued in later packages in December and February.
The measures that I have announced tonight will assist the improve-
ment that has been set in motion. We have shown farmers that we
are committed to maintaining their livelihood just as the country's
future is dependent on their efforts. Through our tax measures we have
shown wage and salary earners that increased efforts will bring increased
rewards. Our energy policy will ensure that we continue to adapt to
the world of the late 1970s where energy is no longer cheap and plenti-
ful. At the same time the welfare state is being maintained and
improved.
This is a generous Budget, but no more generous than economic
realities require. The Government is determined that the sacrifices
that have been made since the change of Government will lead to
steady growth in the economy over the next few years, and that the
fruits of growth will be equitably distributed.
ENERGY RESOURCES LEVY AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I move, That the Energy Resources Levy
Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of the Bill, which contains only two clauses, is to
amend the Energy Resources Levy Act 1976 to enable coal mined underground to be exempt
from payment of the levy. Coal mined underground is more costly to produce than that from
opencast sources. A quick review of underground costs of operation in the State coal mines
has revealed that even including the Huntly district, traditionally the lowest-cost district,


## p. 561 (#569) ############################################

1 June
561
Energy Resources Levy Amendment Bill
costs now exceed the average selling price by approximately $4 a tonne. The elimination of
the levy of $2 a tonne on this coal will be of considerable benefit to all underground coal
mines.
The first clause is the short title. The second clause amends the definition of "coal
mine" to limit its application to an "opencast coal quarry". There is then a consequential
change to the definition of "coal" to make the Act apply only to coal produced from an
"opencast coal quarry"
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Second Reading
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
The Energy Resources Levy Act was enacted in 1976 and came into force on 1 January 1977.
It imposed levies of $2 a tonne on coal, $1.50 a tonne on South Island lignite, and 45c a
gigajoule on natural gas. Those levies were introduced as part of the Government's energy-
pricing policy. Features of that policy were: that energy conservation should be encouraged
by ensuring that the prices of indigenous energy resources reflected their value; that
adequate promotional margins should exist for indigenous fuels to encourage their use in
preference to imported petroleum products; and that local energy producers and distributors
should have adequate profit margins, not only to be able to stay in business, but also to
expand.
The energy resources levy was used to relate the value of indigenous fuels to that of
imported oil. Industrial natural gas prices were to reach a target of 85 percent of the cost of
imported fuel oil, and effective coal prices a target of 68 percent of the cost of imported fuel
oil. While natural gas is currently at about 75 percent of the cost of imported fuel oil,
effective coal prices to large industrial users are near the target level. My ministry has been
undertaking a review of the capital and handling costs penalty associated with using coal by
large industrial users, and it appears that a penalty of about $15 a tonne needs to be allowed.
It is therefore not desirable to raise coal prices at present, particularly while crude oil prices
are frozen.
While some might argue that the State Coal Mines can absorb losses on underground
coal mining through the profitable opencasts, this type of theory has two major faults: first, it
ignores the situation of the private underground coal miners who do not have recourse to
opencast mines-it is essential that these miners be kept in a profitable situation if we are to
continue to have a viable and balanced coal industry in New Zealand in the longer term;
secondly, it fails to recognise that the State Coal Mines will be increasing the proportion of
coal mined underground as the new mines at Huntly are brought into production. As
opencast coal output is consequentially reduced, the profitability of the State Coal Mines
operation will be further eroded, and will be at best only marginally profitable after the
payment of interest on loans. Accordingly, it has been decided that the appropriate course of
action is the elimination of the levy on underground coal.
This was the sort of circumstance contemplated when the energy-pricing policy was
introduced in 1976. The present Minister of Housing, then the Minister of Energy
Resources, said, "flexibility will be a keynote of the levy in maintaining the direction and
purpose of the energy policy". As an example, section 7 of the Act made provision for the
Governor-General to reduce or remit the levy if, in his opinion, that particular resource
would not be produced. In this case, it is fairer to make a blanket change than to run a rule
over each individual case. In a full year, the change will cost about $1.5 million in terms of
losses of revenue from the levy. The change is made ungrudgingly, as we cannot afford to put
the industry at risk. In general, I am satisfied that the energy pricing policy is working well. It
has to be looked at together with other aspects of the Government's energy policies,
particularly the 100 percent tax rate write-off scheme for energy conservation and energy
substitution by business. That has been expanded considerably in tonight's Budget. In
addition, certain types of capital expenditure will also qualify for the grants at the rate of 25
percent.
The Government has been carefully establishing energy policies during its term of
office. The purpose of these policies has been explained, so that the public understands what
we are doing and why we are doing it. Further, the Government has developed an energy
strategy for New Zealand, and this was published only a few days ago as Goals and
Guidelines. The public is now also getting the opportunity to contribute to the development


## p. 562 (#570) ############################################

562
1 June
Energy Resources Levy Amendment Bill
of rational energy policies. The Royal Commission on Nuclear Power Generation in New
Zealand released its report only a few days earlier. We have also had the benefit of advice
from the International Energy Agency, which has examined our situation in its international
context, for we are just as vulnerable financially to oil price escalations as many of the other
IEA members.
There is no doubt in the mind of the International Energy Agency that coal is going to
have to return to a more prominent place in the energy economies as a substitute for oil. In
New Zealand we are fortunate to have both coal and natural gas to substitute for oil in the
bulk-heating market. We must ensure that both are used wisely. The Bill ensures that the
place of underground coal in our energy scene is not forgotten, and I commend it to the
House.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): The Bill just introduced by the Minister shows that the
Government does not know where it is going with its energy policy. Only 2 years ago the
introduction of the energy levy was stated to be a central and important part of its energy
policy. At that time the Opposition pointed out the folly of levies being introduced on our
own indigenous energy resources. At a time when the Government was, or should have
been, promoting our own coal and natural gas, it placed a levy on those two premium
indigenous fuels so that, as it claimed, it could maintain some relativity with imported oil. In
fact, the policy was to maintain the cost of our own indigenous resources in comparison with
the cost of imported oil. Surely the policy should have been to give the maximum
encouragement to our own energy resources.
I am pleased that the Government has seen the folly of its ways and has removed the
levy on coal and natural gas. I am particularly pleased because it will help the underground
coal-mining industry in the South Island. The levy from coal and natural gas went straight
into the Consolidated Account; it was a revenue earner for the Government. It was not a
promotion for coal or for the natural gas industry. In fact, it was a direct cost, particularly to
electricity consumers, because the Mines Department, on paying the levy into the
Consolidated Account, added it to the cost of the coal being used to generate electricity and
thereby put up the cost of electricity to the consumer. The consumer price index was
increased in that way.
The energy resources levy was a penalty on New Zealand consumers, and instead of
encouraging industrial users who were burning oil to convert to coal it had the opposite
effect. Therefore, I am pleased that the Government has seen fit to remove this imposition,
on the coal industry in particular. It justifies the strong criticism by the Opposition when the
levy was introduced. As I have already stated, this shows that the Government does not
know where it is going with its energy policy. It is on again and off again. The Bill reveals for
what they really are the claims that the Minister of Energy has a dynamic energy policy.

Bill introduced and read a first time.
Second Reading
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Clause 3 amends the customs tariff to provide for the 3c a litre increase in the
rate of imported motor spirits duty as announced in tonight's Budget. The new duty will be
12.7c a litre. It is necessary to amend the present tariff, as well as the new tariff, which is
effective from 1 July this year. The clause applies only when duty is payable at the time of
importation, and provides the same rate as that applying to locally refined motor spirits.


## p. 567 (#575) ############################################

1 June
567
Customs Acts Amendment Bill
Clause 5 amends the Motor Spirits Duty Act 1961 and provides for the 3c a litre increase
on locally produced motor spirits. The full increase in duty will not be passed on to the
consumer, because 1c will be absorbed by the motor spirits pool accounts. These accounts
are designed to cushion the effect of increases such as oil prices, freight charges, and the like,
and are in surplus at present because of the erosion of crude oil prices and the decline in the
United States dollar against the New Zealand dollar. It is therefore possible to defer the full
effect of the duty increase, which means that the retail price of premium grade petrol will
increase from 29.6c a litre to 31.6c a litre, or approximately $1.44 a gallon.
Jet fuel and aviation kerosene remain free of duty, and there is no change in the rate of
duty on spirit used as aviation fuel. This is a comment on the rather generalised suggestion
from the Opposition that all transport would be affected. Nor is there any change in the
0.66c a litre imposed by local authorities under the Local Authorities (Petroleum Tax) Act
1970. The present system of rebates of motor spirit duty to certain users will continue. The
Minister of Transport will be introducing legislation on this subject later in the evening.
The estimated additional revenue on motor spirits during the remainder of the financial
year is as I pointed out in the first reading, but it is worth repeating-$51 million and $65
million for a full year. The additional revenue will be directed into the Consolidated
Account. There are a number of other reasons for the increase. It is an energy conservation
measure, which should reduce imports to the extent that $3 million will be saved in overseas
funds annually. It will further encourage the Maui LPG investment, which could in due
course supply about 10 percent of transport fuels in the New Zealand economy. In addition,
members will be aware that the International Energy Agency has recommended that the
price of motor spirit should be raised for conservation reasons. It is estimated that an
increase of 2c a litre in the retail price of petrol would directly increase the consumer price
index by 0.2 percent.

TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Transport
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill amends the Transport Act to give effect to the
Budget measure increasing the petrol tax by 3c a litre. It provides for the additional 3c a litre
to be channelled into the Consolidated Account.
It provides, further, for two categories of petrol consumers to receive a petrol tax refund
of the additional 2c a litre they will pay after the resulting petrol price increase. The two
categories of consumers that will be able to obtain full refunds are basically commercial


## p. 576 (#584) ############################################

576
Transport Amendment Bill
1 June
of
fishermen and the users of petrol-driven farm vehicles. The importance to the economy
the activities of these two groups, and, in particular, the difficult position of farmers,
warrants their being able to obtain a full refund, notwithstanding the energy policy
considerations behind the increased tax.
All other groups that are at present entitled to petrol tax refunds will still be entitled to
them, but will not have refunded to them the extra 2c a litre they will pay at the petrol pump.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I have only one question for the Minister. Why are
licensed vehicles discriminated against, and why are they not in the same exempt position as
commercial fishing vehicles and vehicles used on farms?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The Government has given the
exemptions to the people who have them at the present time-mainly those in the farming
and fishing industries. Others who receive an exemption at the present time will not be
catered for with the extra 2c.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Second Reading
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. So that members can understand more clearly what the Bill does, I shall
briefly comment on the way petrol tax is imposed and petrol tax refunds are made. Petrol tax
is imposed on petrol wholesalers, and the tax element is passed on by them in the price to
consumers. As the petrol tax comes into the hands of the Government it is channelled into
the National Roads Board Fund and the Consolidated Account.
At present, 4.7c of the tax per litre goes into the Consolidated Account, and the balance
of 5c goes into the National Roads Board Fund. Petrol tax refunds are available to a number
of categories of petrol consumers, and the refunds are paid out of the Consolidated Account
and the National Roads Board Fund, in most cases in the proportions in which they were
paid in. The amount of tax that goes in and out of each fund when the tax is paid and
refunded is set out in the Transport Act 1962. That is the reason for passing this measure,
after the one my colleagues put before the House a while ago.
As I said when introducing the Bill, two categories of petrol consumers will be able to
obtain a full refund. The rest will simply remain entitled to the level of refund they are used
to at the moment. I think that answers the question of the member for Timaru. The two
special categories, which are those of commercial fishermen and the users of farm vehicles,
have been given special consideration because of the Government's wish to encourage the
fishing industry and to alleviate the present difficult position of farmers.
Clause 3 increases the refunds available to those industries and provides for the
additional refund to come out of the Consolidated Account. Other points have been covered
on the previous Bill. Finally, I draw attention to clause 3(2) which provides that the
adjustments I have just described must not apply to petrol purchases before 2 June.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The Opposition clearly indicated its objection to
the imposition of the tax in an earlier measure and, as this Bill is consequential upon that
measure and makes provision for the disposition of those funds and preserves the
exemptions, there is no reason to debate the matter further.
Bill read a second time.

ALCOHOLIC LIQUOR ADVISORY COUNCIL AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Alcoholic Liquor
Advisory Council Amendment Bill be introduced. The proposals in the Bill make more
appropriate provision for the calculation and collection of the levy payable by the
manufacturers and importers of liquor to finance the activities of the Alcoholic Liquor
Advisory Council. Members will recall that when the council was established late in 1976 the
principal Act included transitional arrangements for the council to be financed from that
time until 1 April this year from the profits of the existing Hotel Investment Account. This
breathing space was to allow time for the council to become established and to determine its
financial requirements. Since the permanent levy provisions have come into force it has
become apparent that a number of amendments, largely of a machinery nature, are
desirable. In addition, the opportunity has been taken to make some changes to the
functions and powers of the council. This has been requested by the council itself.
Dealing first with these changes, the ambit of the council's authority in respect of liquor
advertising is increased considerably. At present the council is required to make its


## p. 579 (#587) ############################################

2 June
579
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill
recommendations on this-and they are only recommendations-to the Minister of Justice
only. The council is of the view that there may be occasions when it would be advantageous
for it to recommend a particular course directly to the Press Association, to the Broadcasting
Council, or to a similar body rather than to the Minister of the day. Clause 4 gives effect to
that suggestion, and enables the council to make recommendations about the advertising of
liquor to any person or body. Clause 5 empowers the council to make advances to any person
engaged in work in any field with which the council is concerned. At present the council may
only make grants, and it has found this unduly restrictive.
Turning to the levy provisions, clause 2 deals with the particular problem raised by
bottled cocktail concoctions such as Screwdriver-whatever that is. These drinks, while
usually spirit based, none the less attract customs duty per litre rather than per proof litre, as
is the case with spirits. When these drinks are of a strength below 40 percent proof spirit
there are at present problems in collecting the council levy that is payable. This is because
they are classified as spirit under the Act, which attracts its council levy on a proof litre basis
that is collected by Customs at the same time duty is paid per proof litre. Cocktails under 40
percent proof, however, pay duty on a liquid litre basis, and the council levy should
therefore be on a liquid litre basis rather than a proof litre basis. Clause 2 provides for this by.
classifying such drinks as fortified wine, which pays its levy on a liquid litre basis.
Hon. M. Rata: How much will it change the council's income by changing the rate on
which it is calculated?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It is purely machinery in the sense that it is required by the
way the law is written. Clause 2 inserts into the definition section of the principal Act three
technical provisions to clarify the basis on which the levy is calculated and to avoid the need
for duplication of returns. Clause 9 clarifies the position about surplus funds that the council
may accumulate. As a responsible body the council must be able to employ its resources as
best it thinks fit and, where appropriate, to accumulate surplus funds for spending in a
subsequent year. The clause makes it quite clear that this can be done while giving the
Minister of Justice a discretion, if he so wishes, to take all or some of such funds into account
before determining the amount to be raised by way of levy.
Other clauses provide for the incorporation of the council, recovery of my department's
administrative costs, enforcement provisions, and other minor matters. Clause 11, which is
included at the request of the Wine Institute, enables grape winemakers to pay their levy by
instalments. This is quite an important provision for the Wine Institute. At present grape
winemakers must pay the levy, together with their institute levy, in full early in the financial
year. I am told that this will cause hardship to some winemakers, and have agreed to
promote an amendment to the principal Act to alleviate this. However, if instalment
payment is to be allowed this financial year it is imperative that the Bill proceed as soon as
possible. I have therefore obtained the views of the council, the Wine Institute, and the
Liquor Industry Council on those provisions in the Bill of direct relevance to each of them.
They are all agreeable in principle, and I do not therefore propose to refer the Bill to a select
committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Minister said it was not intended to refer the
Bill to a committee on the score that parties likely to be interested, or at any rate directly
interested, have been consulted, and that, therefore, there is no need for further
examination by a committee. I find that justification neither satisfactory nor sufficient,
because it may well be that people who are not regarded as directly interested could have a
view to express on it, and we ought to adopt the principle of sending any Bill dealing with
liquor licensing, which is always a debatable subject, to a committee. In particular, two
clauses might arouse some expression of views by people who are not immediately involved
in the liquor trade.
First, in the new definition clause, clause 2, we find that "beer" requires to be redefined
consequent on the enactment of the Beer Duty Act 1977. The 1977 statutes are not readily
available in our lobbies, so I am not clear what the provisions of the 1977 Act are that call for
this redefinition. However, when one looks at the redefinition and the consequent definition
of "fortified wine", one finds they are expressed in different terms. "Beer" is found to be
"the product of the alcoholic fermentation of liquid that on analysis is found to contain more
than 1.7 percent of alcohol by volume", whereas the definition of "fortified wine" adopts a
different criterion, namely "not exceeding 40 percent of proof spirit".
Recollecting what I can of the difference between measurement by volume and proof
spirit, I believe that 1.7 percent of alcohol by volume would represent something in the


## p. 580 (#588) ############################################

580
2 June
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill
nature of just under 4 percent of proof spirit, and I imagine that is just about as weak a beer
as you can possibly get, and it ceases to be entitled to an appellation if it goes below that. I
remember during the war there was a product on the market labelled as "near beer", and it
was said that the man who gave it that name was a very poor judge of distance. It ought to be
explained to a committee, and someone may very well have views on that, why the criterion
for determining the quantity of alcohol in each of these two categories of liquid provided for
consumption should not be in the same way, either both by volume or both by reference to
proof spirit.
Another innocent little clause might arouse some attention. Clause 4 simply inserts in
section 8(1)(f) of the principal Act the words "such person or persons as the council thinks
fit". When one refers back to paragraph (f) one finds that it is among the powers of the
council to make recommendations to the Minister about the advertising of liquor, whether
generally or through any particular medium, and the need to regulate or in any way restrict
any such advertising; so the effect of this change will be that the advice that the council may
give is not confined to being received by the Minister, but may be directed to such person or
persons as the council thinks fit. It is a matter of public record that there has been some
debate recently about the freedom with which broadcasting stations may advertise liquor for
sale or generally promote its use.
Can the Minister tell me whether this clause is in any way associated with that
controversy? If it is-or even if it is not-to give the council the right to make ex cathedra
pronouncements and give advice to anybody at all about how liquor should be advertised
will, I am sure, attract some attention from the publishing world and the advertising world,
and they and any others who might feel that this is an undue widening of the powers of the
council, perhaps enabling it to exert undue influence on bodies, would want to have
something to say about it. On those two particular instances and the general principle that
licensing legislation ought always to go to a committee, I urge the Minister to reconsider the
announcement he made, and see whether the Bill could not go to the Statutes Revision
Committee.
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): I support the arguments of the member for Henderson in
pleading with the Minister that the Bill goes to a committee. The Alcoholic Liquor Advisory
Council comes out of the Sale of Liquor Act as a council that was created by the Government
for the purpose of advising the Government on the consequences of the consumption of
liquor, and I become concerned when I see a body such as this, which is purely an advisory
body, now being set up as an incorporated body in clause 3 of the Bill. This is not a wise
move, and this clause should be probed to find out what will be the consequences of an
advisory council, appointed by the Government for the very purpose of advising the
Government, now being set up as an incorporated body that can, among other things, hold
and dispose of real and personal property, which is a very wide definition.
I am not happy to see this sort of council being given these powers. Such funds as come
to that council for the purpose of its work should be given over to proper areas of research.
The powers to go into this sort of activity are far beyond what was envisaged when the
council was set up under the Act, following the report of a royal commission. I question the
Minister about the wisdom of that, and ask if it is not a reason for referring the Bill to a
committee.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The members who have spoken see far
more in the Bill than is in fact there. When the member for Henderson suggested that it
should go to a select committee for study, he rightly said that Bills to do with liquor licensing
ought to go to a select committee. The Bill is not to do with liquor licensing; it is to make
better provision for the work of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council, which was set up
nearly 2 years ago with full support from both sides of the House. That council has a primary
objective in section 7 of its Act to encourage and promote moderation in the use of liquor, to
discourage and reduce its misuse, and to minimise the personal, social, and economic evils
resulting from the misuse of liquor. I should have thought that everybody in the House
would fully support that objective.
The member for Henderson referred to clause 4, dealing with advertising. At present
the Act limits the recommendations that the council may make to the Minister, and then the
Minister obviously, if the objectives of the council are to be properly advanced, has to send
them on to people who could most wisely use the recommendations and most beneficially
receive the recommendations of the council. Surely it is much better to allow them to go to
them direct rather than have everything filtered through the Minister. The member asked

QUESTIONS-ORAL
Overstayers
1. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: What changes have been
made to measures to control overstaying, and how successful have these changes been?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): In order to locate overstayers as quickly as
possible, arrival and departure information was computerised in October 1976. In addition,
a number of extra field officers have been appointed to combat the problem of overstayers.
Since the computer system of recording overstayers was introduced the total number of
persons so recorded increased until 22 March 1978, when a total of 5814 overstayers was
recorded. The number has, however, been decreasing since then and, as at 17 May, 5165
overstayers were recorded on the computer. Persons convicted of a breach of the
Immigration Act can now appeal to the Minister of Immigration to have the mandatory
deportation order lifted. If the Minister is satisfied that because of exceptional humanitarian
circumstances it would be unduly harsh or unjust to deport the person, he may order that the
person not be deported.
Mr Elworthy: What has been the reaction of the Governments involved to these
changes in the system?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The Governments of the people involved invariably welcome the sort
of progress we are making. They are in the same position as most other Governments;
although they do not want to place an embargo on their people leaving their country, they do
not wish them to be a nuisance in other communities. They welcome anything we can do to
tighten up and regularise the situation.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: What proportion of the overstayers are
Polynesians?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I am unable to say. I gave that answer to the House recently.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Non-Polynesians are the biggest proportion.
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, I think a little under 50 percent are Polynesians, although that
would not be right, because many of the Fijian overstayers are not Polynesians but Indians.
The figures have been published and have been produced in the House. I would be quite
happy to produce them again if the member wishes me to do so.
Mr T. J. Young: In his original answer the Minister referred to the increased number of
officers dealing with the overstayer problem. Are those officers within the immigration
division, and what powers are vested in them for legal enforcement?¸
Hon. T. F. GILL: I did not say the number of officers had been increased. I said that
extra field officers had been appointed. These officers are within the immigration division.
