Education-Secondary Teacher Resignations
12. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Is he aware of a recent survey,
undertaken by the New Zealand Post-Primary Teachers Association, of secondary teachers
leaving the service in the second and third terms of 1977, and that in this survey it was
revealed that 43.9 percent of teachers resigning were moving to occupations from which they
were unlikely to return to teaching in New Zealand State secondary schools, and if so, what
steps is he taking to make teaching more attractive to secondary school teachers?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I am aware that the Post-Primary
Teachers Association has undertaken a recent survey of secondary teachers leaving the
service. I cannot comment on the adequacy of the survey. Figures available to me show that
there was a net gain of 271, or a percentage of 2.3, in the secondary service in 1977. That
suggests that teaching is not unattractive to secondary teachers.
Mr Hunt: As 184 schools of the approximately 250 secondary schools in New Zealand
made one return, and 85 schools made both returns, does the Minister not feel that provides
an adequate cross-section on which to give the opinion requested in the original question?
Mr SPEAKER: That is seeking an opinion, but the Minister may comment if he wishes.
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The 1977 teacher movement survey- which is the one I have
here that is broken down-is the latest one available, and shows that 17.5 percent of the
teachers who left the service did so because of retirement, death, or ill health. I do not know
what can be taken from that except to show categorically that the people concerned are not
likely to return to teaching. As far as I am aware the only teachers who left to take up other
occupations numbered 313—that is, 20 percent, not 40 percent. I repeat that the number of
teachers increased and there was a net gain of 271 in the year, or an increase of 2.3 percent.
Mr Wellington: In view of the fact that there was a net gain of 271 teachers, is the
Minister aware of the criteria or sampling techniques used by the PPTA in the survey?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: No, I am not aware of the sampling taken in the survey, but I can
assure the member that the figures I quote, of the survey carried out by the department, will
not be based on a sampling. They will show the actual position, as is obviously necessary.
The Auditor-General would have a word to say if that were not the case.
Mr Elliott: In regard to the last part of the question asked by the member for New Lynn,
can the Minister confirm that if secondary teachers removed their strike threats the Minister
could make some determination about salaries, and so make secondary teaching more
attractive?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I certainly think it would be quite inappropriate for any
settlement to be contemplated while teachers are engaged in stopwork meetings or in any
other industrial action.
Mr Hunt: As 184 schools contributed to this survey, is the Minister not concerned that
many of those leaving for overseas stated that the strain of teaching had contributed to their
decision to leave?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I simply reiterate that the honourable member cannot
substantiate his question in the way he puts it-that they are unlikely to return to teaching. I
shall give two other figures: 367 teachers gave their reason for leaving as "domestic
occupation". Most of them, though not all, would be women who wished to have families,
and no doubt at some time in the future might return to teaching. Others went on overseas
travel, and it is our experience that most of those who return to New Zealand do return to
teaching. A large number went into other teaching and education services, and I believe this
is quite appropriate because they are still within the purview of education. A small number,
8 percent, took on relief and part-time teaching, and that may have been partly because of
their wish. I do not believe that what is stated in the honourable member's question has been
substantiated.

Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I wish to refer in this debate to one of the major
disaster areas in New Zealand-transport. Its sad situation has continued over the past 2

bungling in the transport field than really seemed possible."
If this Minister and this Government had deliberately set out to wreck completely our
transport system they could not have done a better job. No matter what the mode of travel-
whether it is by road, by rail, by sea or by air-this Government has made a mess, and that is
something we just cannot afford, not only at this time, but at any time. The 1975 National
Party manifesto stated: "A prime aim"-and prime means first-"of a National
Government in the transport field would be to co-ordinate all transport services and
equipment to obtain full utilisation so that the best results for the consumer could be
obtained."
That policy has been blatantly and continually ignored. Every country must maintain an
efficient transport system, but the Government has demonstrated that it does not appreciate
the special needs of New Zealand with its two-island character. About 14 months ago the
South Island Promotion Association challenged the Minister about the handling of his
portfolio. In a moment of candid confession he said: "I think the main reason I have come in
for a fair bit of criticism is that I am the fellow who stops things. I am the one who took off
the Rangatira, cut the railcars, and closed branch railway lines. While I have been Minister
NAC has trimmed its provincial services." NAC has been so completely trimmed that it has
gone. The Shipping Corporation of New Zealand has stopped calling at Timaru.
The Minister went on to say: "I would agree that on the face of it this does not seem to
do much for the development of transport in the South Island. I make no apology for what
has been done so far." Not satisified with that, over the past 15 months the Minister has
withdrawn the Coastal Ranger-which was the replacement ship for the Rangatira-from
service, and has cut rail services even further. Over the past 2 years the Government's arch-
conservative policies have gone from bad to worse, particularly over the last 15 months.
The Government talks glibly about seeing transport as a total entity, but every mode of
transport has been subjected to interference and discouragement, which has had an adverse
effect on the South Island.
On 1 April 1978 NAC was taken over by Air New Zealand—a takeover that was not
backed up by a substantiated point of justification. A feasibility study, that was rushed
through with indecent haste, is alleged to contain evidence that $10 million a year would be
saved. I say "alleged", because it is incorrect. The document has been kept secret from the
public, but I have read it, and I have taken careful note of the expected saving. The contents
of the report do not square with statements made by the Prime Minister, the Minister of
Transport, the general manager of Air New Zealand, or anybody else. The report makes no
mention of a figure of $10 million. I call on the Minister once again to release the report and
publicly apologise.
The Opposition sees New Zealand as an entity-not a South Island and a North Island
with separate transport and regional development policies. We are one country and one
people, and there is no need for different policies, yet everything the Government has done
in the transport sector has adversely affected the South Island in particular. That belief is
highlighted by the announcement last night that rail charges will increase by a further 12.5
percent as from 2 July. Sir Ronald Scott was the guest speaker at the South Island Promotion
Association's conference, at which the Minister confessed his sins. He said that he was
surprised that when the Minister of Transport opened the conference he had made no
reference to any large increase in transport charges that was in the pipeline.
He went on to say that he did not know of any Christchurch manufacturers of consumer
goods who were not genuinely thinking about moving to the North Island. Apart from the
reduced freight costs to the local market such a move would make it easier for some
manufacturers to export goods. However, he warned that if manufacturers left the South
Island the island would suffer a serious economic setback. Over the last 15 months a number
of industries have moved from the South Island, and these will be itemised by following
speakers. The main reason for moving was that, because the Government does not believe in
regional development, they had become less competitive. Industry in the South Island has
been discouraged by the Government's policies, and is now unable to compete with industry
in the North Island.
Transport must be given encouragement. We can call it a subsidy, or whatever we like,
but if we are to achieve balanced economic development and growth South Island industries
must be able to compete with North Island industries. If they cannot compete, the present
imbalance—which is unhealthy and every member recognises, but which only one side is
prepared to act on-will continue. The Minister of Regional Development is looking very

Opposition, was responsible for the strike. He was also the Minister of State Services, so air
traffic controllers came under his portfolio of Health. He could not be found, because he was
away on holiday. The Prime Minister at that time did not know where he was to be found.
The former Labour Government in action was chaos and confusion. And so it went on for 3
years. The former Labour Government kept rail freight rates at the 1971 level for 4 years,
and destroyed coastal shipping. It was impossible for coastal shipping, running on current
costs, to compete with the Railways running on 1971 charges.
A ludricrous situation arose because the railways were chock-a-block with loaded
wagons that could not be unloaded. Freight was piling on to them. The railways were
grinding to a halt in 1975. It reached such a point that the Railways accepted freight from
Auckland to the South Island that it could not carry, and put it onto the coastal ships, and
the consignor paid the railways. The railways paid the coastal shipping companies coastal
shipping rates and absorbed the difference. What coastal shipping carried for the Railways
was carried at a loss to the Railways.
The member for Timaru knows that is correct. The former Labour Government
destroyed coastal shipping. The Rangatira was a passenger ship, not for passengers but for
the crew. It had about 200 crew members going back and forth from Lyttelton to Wellington
night after night. It had a triple crew, and the crew priced themselves out of their jobs. The
ship was carrying more crew than passengers.
If the member for Timaru knew anything about his area of the South Island he would
know that the cargo service operating at present is adequate for the goods being carried from
the North Island to the South Island, and to Australia. The Government now has a better
trans-Tasman service from the South Island. If the member for Timaru knew anything about
shipping he would know that is correct. The former Labour Government had a green paper
on transport. I do not know what happened to it. I think it was another brain child of the
member for Manukau. This green paper came out, lay around for a year or two, and then
quietly disappeared.
The one thing the Labour Government overlooked in its transport policy, as it did in its
economic policy-and this gets to the heart of it—was the massive increase in oil prices that
occurred at the end of 1973. It failed totally to cope with that in the economic sense. The
moment the price of oil went up fourfold and fivefold, all transport in every country,
including freight to our markets overseas, was thrown into chaos. The Labour Government
made no moves whatever to cope with that situation, and we had it on our plate when we
came into office. We have moved in a number of directions. We have moved specifically to
rationalise transport, to get the railways doing what they can do best—that is, long hauls and
bulk hauls—and to give road transport what it can do best, in the form of flexibility and short
hauls. And we have rationalised charges between the modes.
That is what we have done in just on 2 years. It was a very complex question of bringing
together the transport charges and making these changes. These are things the Labour
Government should have got into in its term of office, but the three Ministers would not talk
to each other; they were mutually antagonistic. It is no wonder they could not make any
progress, or obtain support from each other. These changes have now been made. The
Minister said, when introducing them, that obviously this is not the last word. It is a major
change, and it will require amendment as it settles down, but certainly it is a move along the

Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I thank the Senior Government
Whip for his motion, and the House for its acquiescence. When the Minister of Finance
replied to the Budget debate last year he claimed with his opening remarks that the
Government had implemented every stage of its short-term economic strategy.
Hon. Members: That's right.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: “That's right", say Government members. I do not need to
point out its result, because there is hardly a family that has not felt the pain of that so-called
economic strategy. If there was anyone still clinging to the belief that the Government, the
Prime Minister, had some kind of economic expertise, some special aptitude to govern,
surely he must have been sadly disillusioned by recent events. Of all the stop-go, flip-flop,
jelly Governments that the country has ever seen, this one must surely take the biscuit. If
there were prizes for political humbug, Government members would take first, second, and
third. Some of them, including the member for Waitemata, would probably get a highly
commended just for being there, because those strong words of 1976 and 1977 turned out to
be so much rubbish.
I remember the Prime Minister in March 1976, just over 3 months after the Government
was given a mandate to make the country the way New Zealand wanted it, coming out on the
subject of borrowing. According to the Evening Post of 16 March that year, he said, "I
promise you"-ringing words-"that you have seen the last for some considerable time of
Government policies of borrow and hope.” When he talked about some considerable time,
perhaps he meant some considerable time until next election year, because he has definitely
got into the policies right now. We have record borrowing at home, record borrowing
overseas, and a Budget deficit this time of $1,050 million. That will not be the end of the
story by a long chalk. The Minister of Finance was $300 million out last year; he was 80
percent wrong in his estimate. Lord knows how far he will be out this time. He has to be only
half as wrong and we will have a deficit of $1,500 million. When I predicted in March this
year a Budget deficit of more than $1,000 million, the Prime Minister immediately resorted
to his usual put-down tactics. We have seen them before, and no doubt we shall see them
again.
The Auckland Star of 30 March carried the following report: "The Prime Minister, Mr
Muldoon, described the estimate by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Rowling, that the
Government would have $1,000 million deficit before borrowing in this Budget as just a shot
in the dark. Asked if he thought it was a reasonable estimate, he replied, 'No'." That was the
Prime Minister and Minister of Finance. He said that the Leader of the Opposition did not
know what the figure would be. Asked for his own estimate of the likely deficit, the Prime
Minister said, "I haven't got one." I do not blame him for that. He has one in the Budget,
because he has to have one, but I suggest that it will not be very close at all to the final out-
turn at the end of the year. The Prime Minister's bluff and bluster have run their race. The
people are not fools, and they do not want to be treated like fools any longer.
Mr Comber: They aren't fools-they tossed you out in 1975.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: I would tell the member for Wellington Central that, if

## p. 625 (#633) ############################################

Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
with that in the days of the great depression of the 1930s, a country in which race is being
deliberately divided against race, and a country in which thousands of women are being
made, as a direct result of the Government's actions, to feel that they are almost second-class
citizens. This cannot continue, and, with a change of Government after the general election
this year, it will not continue.
I turn now to some specific elements of the Budget, and some of the real alternatives
that New Zealanders can look to. The big deal of the Budget was supposed to be tax reform.
One could have supposed that, with a Government that was committed-at least so it
claimed-to private enterprise, two major changes would have come through the Budget:
first, that we would see Government spending as a percentage of the total economic scene
considerably diminish, and, secondly, that we would see a major shift from income tax to
other forms of tax revenue. In the event, we got neither-and again many of the strong-
sounding National Party words of earlier days have been revealed a wind rather than
substance.
I am sure people will remember how the National Party proclaimed again and again
against the increasing share of the gross national product that was being taken up by
Government expenditure. They called it "creeping socialism". They rolled the phrase so
easily. If that was their view, and one presumes that is still their view today, one can also
presume that they will call the 1978 Budget "crawling nationalism", because the one thing
that this Budget proves is that an all-time record has been established for the percentage of
the gross national product taken up by Government expenditure-41.7 percent-and a great
deal of that had to be borrowed even to do that.
Then there is this question of the expectation of a shift of the burden of income tax.
Some shift! In the 1977 Budget, income tax accounted for 75.2 percent of the total tax
revenue of the Government. In the 1978 Budget, income tax accounts for 75.3 percent of the
total tax revenue of the Government. In dollar terms, the Minister of Finance expects to
collect 11 percent, or $385 million more, from the taxpayers than he did last year. He has
certainly been bitten by the reform bug. One cannot say otherwise. After all, this is the
Minister of Finance who, in just three successive Budgets, has lifted the income tax take
from the taxpaying public by 68 percent. That is quite a record.
Let us look closer at what the Budget has done in the income tax field. It has adopted a
plateau or a tier system of income tax. That is good. Then it has placed many thousands of
people in the lower income groups, particularly part-time workers, more particularly women
who are out trying to get a few bob together to help the family budget, in an infinitely worse
position. That is bad, and everyone recognises it as such. Then it has taken another age
group, 11-year-olds and 12-year-olds, into consideration for a dependant's concession. That
is good; I concede that. But it has left out of consideration every teenager in the country-
and any parent who is looking after a teenager will tell you something about what those
young people cost. They have been left out, and that is not bad, it is very bad.
The Budget has failed completely to accept the principle of need in the distribution of
concessions. That is disastrous. As I suggested earlier, those who have been particularly
mauled are the part-time workers, including women and students. It is very curious that, if a
high school student and a tertiary student work side by side, the high school student will get a
tax concession, but the student who is trying to make a few bob to help him or her through
university or the polytechnic will be taxed for doing it. That suggests how much thought has
gone into the matter. Thousands of people, all at the bottom end, are being scraped into the
tax net. If you want to look for relief you have to look at the people on higher incomes,
because that is where it happens. It all adds up to the fact that genuine tax reform in this
country is still awaited.
I shall release details of very genuine tax reform fairly soon, but I can mention some of
the things that will be included. First, a basic income completely free from tax; secondly, the
amount of tax-free income will increase with the number of dependants; thirdly, dependent
children, including teenagers, will qualify for the dependants rebate; fourthly, the plateau
system will be fundamental to the structure, but will be designed so as to improve
considerably the benefits to all, not to some, of those in the lower and middle income groups
in relation to the present Budget proposal. Since the member for Waitemata, who is trying to
interject, is obviously interested, I make the further observation that tax for those at the top
end of the scale will remain relatively unchanged. Fifthly, overtime will be taken at the
standard rate. In other words, a worker who gets out and makes that extra effort will not be
dragged into the higher tax bracket, as he is at present. Furthermore, because of the nature


## p. 626 (#634) ############################################

626
6 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
of our plateau structure, a great deal more encouragement will be given to workers to get on
with the job that needs to be done.
The sixth point is this: to protect the improvements we will have produced, the rates will
in future be indexed to wage rates. I have already said that the amount of the deficit of this
Budget is economically irresponsible. It is therefore obvious that when producing details of
the new rates we must not only take into account what has already been done in the Budget,
but also indicate clearly to the public the amount and the source of the Government revenue
to offset the proposals we are offering. Clearly this will include some deficit financing, and
will include some advantages from growth that will be infinitely better under a Labour
Government.
There will be some alternative revenue sources, which will be spelled out in a way that
will show the public that the package we propose is balanced, responsible, practicable, and
aimed directly not only at stimulating the New Zealand economy, but also at creating the
foundation that will give New Zealand industry confidence in which to build. It will create
job opportunities for our people, and provide further protection against those international
shock waves that too often have battered this country. Perhaps more importantly, it will
certainly create a greater sense of national identity than that which can prevail under a
National Government. If this country is to climb on its feet again, this will not be achieved by
bribes to sectional interests. It will be done because the work force, both labour and
management, will have been given the incentive and the weapons to do the job. It will be
done because the great potential of people and resources will be brought together in a plan
that can be understood by the people, and in which they can see a future for themselves and
their families.
I do not think there should be too much argument that a great deal of the potential lies
in the regions, yet in the Budget the regions are once again subject to what can only be
described as absolute neglect. In real terms the regional development vote is down by 6
percent. The underexpenditure last year made it the worst year on record since regional
development was introduced by the third Labour Government. We are dealing with people
and their jobs; people and their homes; people and their schools; people and their hospitals;
and people and their communities. We are talking about areas that produce with
unparalleled efficiency hage quantities of raw materials-for the information of the member
for Invercargill, who is trying to interject, but who does not seem to care very much-only to
see those raw materials carted off to the metropolitan areas, or worse still, and more often
the case, carted overseas to provide the raw materials for someone else's industry. We have
gone as far down that road as we can afford to go, even if the Government does not appear
to realise it. The farmers and the people in the support industries will get no great joy if they
are propped up in one direction, only to find that their lives and those of their families are
pulled out from underneath them in another.
The revitalisation of regional development is a must. The people in the regions must be
given the necessary authority, they must be given the political and financial support to
initiate and pursue local plans and development projects. It is quite clear that under existing
economic circumstances the resources will not be unlimited. However, the priorities that we
recognise are much higher than the Government rates them. Given those new priorities, and
by requiring the Government agencies to co-ordinate more closely with local bodies, much
more can be achieved with existing resources. As I said on a previous occasion, this is the
real springboard for the economic revival of New Zealand.
The basic type of incentive we will offer will be a variety of grants in aid related to the
establishment of industry, backed by low-interest loans. In other words, we expect that once
an industry gets through that establishment period it will stand on its own feet. We are not
there to support the inefficient or the ineffective. However, we do recognise that there is a
right of access to markets at equitable freight rates. We do recognise that a Government
must accept some of the responsibility for retraining, especially as this Government has
created an unemployment pool of considerable dimensions. We recognise that a
Government must play its part, together with the private sector, in the securing of access to
and promotion of both existing and potential markets. This is where the scheme will tie in
with industrial development generally and with overseas trade. In consultation with the
manufacturers and exporters we propose to produce a clear and simplified code of
incentives, ironing out anomalies, and filling in the gaps.
We will significantly expand the work of the Export-Import Corporation, which will be
a matter of principle, not of political convenience. How well I remember the bitter

prospects of getting inflation back to a single figure this year are good. It will require the co-
operation of the whole country, and in particular wage-led inflation is to be avoided.
Our balance of payments position has improved despite the terms of trade. The Leader

I shall now discuss some of the stumps raised by the proposed controls. The Leader of
the Opposition is preparing to set us back on the restrictive path of control. The matter is a
very real challenge and should be an election issue. Do the people want the controls the
Labour Party suggests, or do they want to free the economy so that we can live in the world?
Our only opportunity to live in the world is by freeing our system and by going out and
competing. The proposals the Leader of the Opposition has in mind are very close to those
of small controlled economies. I should not like New Zealand to end up like Albania. Is that
the way the Leader of the Opposition wants to go, with his rear vision mirrors? He claims he
is a man of vision. His proposals use rear vision mirrors. In monetary policy he is aiming to
go back to an out-of-date system.
During the Labour Government's term in office the National Party learned that
controlled rates distort savings. They undermine our financial institutions, and the Leader of
the Opposition knows that is true. He denied that the Government has any strategy. Its
strategy is clearly set out if fools can only see. Any fool can criticise, and most of them do. If
the Leader of the Opposition is prepared to give up his role of criticism and examine the
history of the last three Budgets he will find steady evolution in the Government's monetary
policy. I shall ask a very simple question. Who will pay for the controlled low-interest rates?
Will the lender or the taxpayer pay? Two people are involved, the lender and the borrower.
The Government's aim has been to set interest rates at a level at which people will lend and
save, and that is what has happened. The Government has freed the monetary system and
savings have increased. The financial institutions have become competitive.
The Government is now sure of better management of the monetary system. It is not
simple for the Leader of the Opposition or one man in the Reserve Bank, to control the
system; the whole of the financial system must take part in the management, under the broad
direction of the Reserve Bank. The Reserve Bank has representatives in whom both sides of
the House can have confidence. The board of the Reserve Bank wants a continuation of the
present monetary policies, because those policies are in the country's interests. The
Government's policy fits in with a very good Budget.
I shall now discuss five of the key parameters that the Leader of the Opposition
suggested added up to a "lolly scramble". I do not think New Zealanders like to be
compared to school children. The New Zealanders we deal with in our constituencies know
perfectly well-even if they do not understand every detail-that they have the most
effective leader and Minister of Finance the country has known. If the world stopped
tomorrow, history books would show that. I have already quoted the example of the 1967
devaluation. During this time I have worked closely with the Minister and with Treasury.
The Budget is finely honed and was drawn together with difficulty to try to meet the times we
face. New Zealand faces very difficult times, but times full of opportunity. The five key
parameters of taxation, the social programme, farming, exporting, and energy all show this.
The Government moved on tax reform because the opportunity was there to assist an upturn
in the economy.
Tax reform is the heart of the 1978 Budget. It enables the people to come to grips with
the problem of overtime earnings. It enables the Govenrment to reduce the burden on the
average taxpayer. It concentrates on the full-time taxpayer. The strategy is quite clear. The
Government's aim is to improve the living standard of the low-income and single-income
families with children. The policies follow those introduced in 1977. The Budget is very good
for the taxpayer. It has the biggest possible tax reduction that the economy can bear. It
comes at the right time, after the mini-Budgets introduced in October and November. It
should move the economy through the 1978 recovery period into a growth period in 1979.
The Budget places emphasis on the international economy. These tax adjustments are
sensible, from minor measures about fees for kindergartens and the building-in of the $52
expenses for the average man-which is very good for me, because I do not have to add it in
and I am grateful to the Inland Revenue Department for thinking of it-to the very major
changes totalling over $300 million in terms of the personal tax tables. Let us look at some of
the tax tables. I know it is sinful to bore people with figures, but I wish to mention some of
the changes. For a code S man on $4,000, at March 1976 his tax was $754 and at March 1979
it will be $637, or $117 less; on $8,000, at March 1976 his tax was $2,374 and at March 1979 it
will be $2,097, or $377 less; on $12,000, at March 1976 his tax was $4,317 and at March 1979
it will be $3,879, or $538 less. The aim is to help the low-income and middle-income people.

road"--and he mentioned a mutual friend-"reckons he has been hit for $12,000 by the
Government's failure to maintain decent industrial relations in the freezing works." That is
what the handout is all about; the Government has failed to allow the economy to work
properly.
The National Party said it would abolish controls. Let us look at its record. It said there
would be free wage bargaining. How free is it? One of its controls has been instant
suspension of innocent parties in industrial disputes. We have never had that sort of control
in our history, but this Government, which is so against controls, has introduced it. There
are provisions in the Commerce Act, the Human Rights Commission Act, and in the
Industrial Relations Act to punish workers when they are exercising the freedom they are
supposed to have under this Government to work or not to work while bargaining for
improvements in their conditions of employment.
The National Government, which is not supposed to be in favour of controls, has
invoked all those regulations. It has imposed all those penalties, and, just to make sure there
is no favouritism, it imposed them on civil servants also. It has said, "If we are to have
controls, let us have them right across the board."
Let us get rid of this nonsense about no controls; there are controls on those the
Government wants to smash. Unfortunately, as my farmer friend told me tonight, they have
smashed their own cobbers, because worsening industrial relations caused by controls have
affected farmers, and will continue to do so.
I do not know the details of the dispute about back pay, but it appears to me most
significant that workers have picked on loading-out as the point of impact. Once that stops
the people who want to load in, then, under the regulations, every person in the works can
be put off work. Will they be? Will we have a major confrontation between the freezing
workers and the Government, as we did at Kawerau, caused almost entirely by the
Government's determination to impose controls and penalties on the innocent as well as the
guilty in any industrial dispute?
If the Government does not like controls, let us get rid of that threat, and I guarantee
that disruption over killing stock will recede tremendously. Unease throughout the freezing
industry has its basis in that sort of threat. Any pretence of solving industrial disputes by
threatening the freezing industry with that sort of big stick will be unsuccessful. So will any
idea of splitting up unions by forcing those who are thrown out of work by Government
action on to the backs of parties to a justifiable dispute. If Government members think that
type of tactic will succeed they should explain to farmers that there will be continued
disruption in the freezing works, and tell them why they had to pay out $3 million—or nearer
$5 million by the end of the year-instead of aiming for good industrial relations.
It is a shame that history is not included in the instructions given to those working on the
Government's industrial relations policy. Right back in Anglo-Saxon times I think both King
Canute and Ethelred the Unready realised that one cannot buy people off in the hope of
reaching a lasting settlement. Instead of reaching a proper negotiated settlement and
ensuring good industrial relations in the future, the Government just buys people off.
I suggest that if the Minister and the Government want farmers' stock killed
expeditiously this year and next year they should stop buying off and start to concentrate on
sensible negotiations—or at least they should listen to the advice of members on this side of
the House. Better still, they could resign, and allow others who know something about
industrial relations to take over, thus ensuring some prospect of good industrial relations in
the freezing industry, if only for the sake of the farmers.
Let us look, too, at other steps taken by the Government, which it claims will help the
farming community. The big problems have been high interest rates, ever-increasing

NOTICE OF MOTION—ADMISSIBILITY
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I give notice that next sitting day I shall move, That
this House records with concern, the gross discourtesy of National Party members of
Parliament who last night, while the Leader of the Opposition was speaking, wandered
around the Chamber, with up to seven National members on their feet at one time, and
stood in the passageways, contrary to Standing Order 159, carrying on conversations, and
this House wonders whether the actions of the National members were just rudeness or was
it an organised tactic by the National Party caucus to disrupt the Leader of the Opposition's
speech, and this House calls upon the National Party caucus not to indulge in these childish
tactics, which lower the standing of Parliament.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Is the Senior
Opposition Whip entitled to stand in the corridor and talk to a member while another
honourable member is giving a notice of motion?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I have no difficulty in dealing with that point of order, which is
coming fairly close to being frivolous. It is a Standing Order of the House that honourable
members in the Chamber are to be seated, and that they are not to carry on conversations in
the aisles. If they are in the Chamber they should be seated, taking part in discussions or
listening to discussions in the Chamber, or carrying on their work in their own way.
However, it is an accepted convention that the leaders of parties-and that applies to all of
them now-and their Whips, if they have Whips, can move around the aisles and talk to their
members, either by way of exhortation or to pass on suggestions and instructions, as
apparently Whips do from time to time-so there is nothing I can take exception to in the
Senior Opposition Whip's being not seated at the time.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Obviously,
this motion has been cleared by someone, but it seems to me to be a considerable reflection
on whoever was in the chair at the time, and thus is probably out of order, because this
matter of dealing with people who walk around the Chamber and stand in the aisles is very
much in the hands of the Chair. Of his own volition, Mr Speaker normally takes care of such
a situation. I invite you to reflect on that aspect of this notice of motion.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Mr Speaker, as you were
absent at a public function last night and the Prime Minister was not aware of the
circumstances, I point out that the Junior Opposition Whip attempted to raise this as a point
of order, but it was ruled out on the grouhds that it should have been raised at the time the
persons objected to were on their feet. Therefore, there is no slight to anyone who was in the
chair at the time. It is simply observing the Standing Orders of the House to bring the matter
to the notice of the House.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Mr Speaker, in those circumstances, and
as both you and I were absent on a public occasion, surely there is no point, because if it did
not catch the eye of the Deputy Speaker it could not have been nearly as bad as this notice of
motion makes out, so the motion falls to the ground.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): Mr Speaker, under the Standing Orders, if a
member desires to bring conduct in the House to the attention of the Chair and the House,
there is only one way in which that can properly be done, and that is by notice of motion. I
feel strongly about this matter and believe that, if the tactic is continued, it will disrupt the
House. This is why I have brought what went on last night to the attention of the House; the
House should reflect upon it, and decide whether that is the sort of conduct we want in
Parliament.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Speaking to the point of order as the senior
Minister in the House when the occasion arose last night, there was a little emotion at the
time, and the member tried to raise a point of order after the Leader of the Opposition sat
down. The Deputy Speaker ruled that the time to raise it was when the members were on
their feet. I responded from the Government side by indicating that, if this sort of sniping

Unemployment Benefit
2. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Can he confirm the
statement made on "Sunday Supplement" on 28 May that an unemployed female


## p. 652 (#660) ############################################

652
7 June
Questions-Oral
breadwinner receives only $36.90 in benefit, while an unemployed male is entitled to $73.80,
plus dependent child allowance, and, if so, what action does he propose to take on this
obvious discrimination?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): As far as I am aware, the basis of
payment of unemployment benefit has remained unchanged since the inception of the Act,
and is the same today as when administered by the three previous Labour Governments. An
unemployed male breadwinner receives the married rate of benefit plus dependent child
allowance, whereas an unemployed female breadwinner will receive the maximum single
rate plus dependent child allowance. She would, of course, qualify for an additional benefit
if circumstances warranted it.

Hon. H. J. WALKER: This matter was considered by the 1971-72 Royal Commission on
Social Security, which decided that no action would be taken. If a male is unemployed he will
receive a married couple rate plus child allowance, but if a woman is unemployed the
question is, where is her husband? Is he living at home? If so, he could obtain a married
couple rate if he were genuinely unemployed. If he is living away from home, then there is
no reason why he should get it. If he is a student, he will obtain a bursary. There is no
discrimination against women.

Mr SPEAKER: That is seeking an opinion from the Minister.

the discrimination, which is clearly shown up, to continue?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The so-called discrimination was introduced by a former Labour
Government. However, it was considered by the 1971-72 Royal Commission on Social
Security, which decided there was no discrimination. I would be pleased to note any factual
information the Opposition can give to show me that there is discrimination. On the basis of
the Act as written, and other benefits available, I say there is no discrimination.

Domestic Purposes Benefit
6. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Have the modifications to the
domestic purposes benefit, recommended by the review committee for (a) reduced benefit in
the first 6 months, (b) increased counselling and advice services, and (c) early referral to
marriage guidance, been introduced?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Yes, those three recommendations
were implemented from 26 September 1977, and results to date show that the adjustments
have resulted in positive help being given to a substantially increased percentage of women
applying for the domestic purposes benefit.
Mr Brill: In view of the Minister's reply that results have been achieved since the
recommendations were introduced, can he advise whether there is any evidence of decreased
separations or decreased applications for domestic purposes benefits?

percent. Following the introduction of these measures, the rate for the last financial year was
reduced to 10 percent.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Are the needs of a genuine domestic purposes benefit
beneficiary to provide for her children and herself any greater at the expiration of 6 months
than earlier and, if not, why discriminate financially against such persons and their children?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: One of the provisions of the adjustment was that hardship would
not be permitted, particularly where children are concerned. If the emergency maintenance
allowance is insufficient, the woman can apply for an additional benefit. But the Social
Security Commission has discretion and will always ensure that there is no hardship.

Taneatua Food-Processing Factory
9. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Labour: Why was special
dispensation not given by the Secretary of Labour to allow the 15 women at the Taneatua
food-processing factory to work after 11 p.m.?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Saxpack Foods Ltd in Taneatua had applied
for approval to employ women 24 hours a day, 12 months a year, to process vegetables that
were subject to rapid deterioration. The company was informed that approval of its
application could not be granted as such approvals were limited to specific situations that did
not occur on a regular or continuing basis. The night work provisions in the Factories Act
accord with ILO Convention 89, which New Zealand has ratified. The Federation of Labour
supports that convention. To renounce it unilaterally would be a very serious step and is not
recommended by constitutional lawyers or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It is to be
reviewed in 1981, and New Zealand can move then.
Marilyn Waring: Will the Minister confirm that the Employers Federation supports the
renouncement of ILO Convention 89 and that the Netherlands has renounced it?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I can confirm the first part of the question, and, indeed, go
further and say that in Geneva last year New Zealand explored the possibility of being able
to reach agreement with the ILO to renounce it. I am not aware of the circumstances in
which the Netherlands renounced it or whether, in fact, that country has renounced it.

being perused and studied at head office. Other statistics for the districts were not available
within the brief compass of time between notice being given of the question and the answer
being given by the Development Finance Corporation.
Education-Maori Language
14. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Education: Apart from his personal
rapid progress with the Maori language, what developments have occurred in the teaching of
Maori language in our teachers colleges and in our schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The teaching of Maori has increased
considerably in the last 2 years. The appointment of 30 itinerant teachers of Maori in 1975
enabled support to be given to policies for the inclusion of Maori language and studies
integrated into the programmes of primary schools. Some 250 intermediate and primary
schools have programmes involving more than 46 000 pupils. The Budget allows for the
appointment of 10 additional itinerant teachers and for the provision of resource materials to
assist teachers. A programme in which the Maori language as well as English is used as the
medium of instruction was begun at Ruatoki School in 1977. In 1974, 96 secondary schools
taught Maori to 9000 pupils. In 1977, 153 secondary schools taught Maori to more than
13 000 pupils. All teachers colleges offer selected studies in the Maori language and 19 Maori
studies lecturers are involved in teaching those courses.
Mr Elliott: The figures given are very impressive. What further developments are
expected; and can the Minister give an assurance that the National Government's policy will
continue to promote the teaching of the Maori language?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I hope the answer will not infringe the Standing Order relating
to questions seeking elucidation of the policy of the Government on matters in such a way

Energy Production
21. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) to the Minister of Energy: What percentage of New
Zealand's total energy is produced from its own resources?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): In 1977, 55 percent of New Zealand's total
energy use was produced from indigenous resources. This represents continued progress to
greater self-sufficiency. As recently as 1973 only 40 percent of our total energy use was from
indigenous resources.
Mr Hunt: Do I take it that an improvement of from 40 percent to 55 percent in just 3
years occurred during the 3 years the third Labour Government was in power?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: There has been a steady improvement for two basic reasons. The first
is the development of Kapuni and the condensate from Kapuni as an input for the Marsden
Point refinery. The second is prices and the level of conservation that has been achieved.

the Government changed in November 1975 and that since then it has been a National
Government.
Abortion-Repeal Petition
22. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the member for New Plymouth: Can he, as chairman
of the Petitions Committee, confirm the published advice that the committee proposes to call
only written evidence in the case of the Repeal petition, and, if so, what were the grounds for
the decision and can he name any precedent for this action?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I want
you to make sure that this question is not in conflict with Standing Order 87(3)(a), which
states that questions shall not refer to proceedings in committee not open to the news media
that have not been reported to the House.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): I understand that the question arises as the subject of a press
release authorised by the committee itself. Would not the question be perfectly in order,
therefore? Further, the member for Avon has asked for the grounds for the decision and
whether the member can name any precedent. The naming of a precedent would not involve
any prohibition being broken. As for the grounds, the member for New Plymouth should
give the House and the country reasons for this most important matter not being open to the
press. I should have thought that the grounds he could have given might also be grounds
which might not necessarily have bounded the argument.
MARILYN WARING (Raglan): I refer you to two new statements. One is reported in
the Dominion of 1 June 1978, and the other in the Evening Post of 1 June 1978. They are
statements released by the member for New Plymouth, and in the Dominion report there are
further statements which are obviously not from the press statement but are in answer to
questions by members of the news media. I believe it is from these two press statements that
the question asked by the member for Avon has arisen.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I accept that Standing Order 368(b)
provides that a limitation on the publication of any proceedings of a select committee does
not apply to any press release or public statement made by a Minister or by the chairman of a
select committee or subcommittee with a view to informing the public of the nature of its
inquiry. It may well be that confirmation of what has been printed in the press is needed
from the member who is the chairman of the select committee, the member for New
Plymouth, but I should have thought that any question must be limited to the confirmation
of statements produced with the authority of that select committee, for no chairman of a


## p. 660 (#668) ############################################

660
7 June
Questions-Oral
select committee would be able to answer any question on matters other than those which he
had been authorised to release by the select committee. You would be putting the member
for New Plymouth in an impossible position if you asked him to do so.
Mr SPEAKER: I am glad this point has been raised. It was drawn to my attention quite
recently that there could be some breach of the Standing Orders in this question, and indeed
in the next question, which we will come to. In essence, the question asks three things:
confirmation of published advice given by the chairman of the Petitions Committee by way
of a press statement; information about the grounds for the decision made by him or by the
committee; and any precedent for the action.
It seems to me that the chairman can make a statement, and I imagine, quite properly,
made a statement to the press in terms of Standing Order 368(b), which has been referred to
by the Minister of Justice. I do not think it would be right for me to hold that a statement
made by the chairman of a select committee in these circumstances would constitute part of
the proceedings of the committee for the purposes of Standing Order 87.
I rule therefore, that a question can be addressed to a chairman of a select committee
regarding a statement he has made under Standing Order 368(b), notwithstanding that the
matter under consideration by the committee to which the statement relates is itself not open
to the news media. So the committee can decide that the chairman can make a statement
outlining the sort of procedures that the committee will follow, despite the fact that it is not
open to the news media.
It is not out of order to ask a question in elucidation of the statement he has made if
there is any ambiguity in the statement, but, having said that, it is explicit in Standing Order
87 that a question cannot refer to proceedings in the committee itself. Though a question
may ask for the elucidation of an ambiguity in such a statement as was made in this case, it
cannot ask for the committee's reasons for so directing because those reasons must of
necessity have been discussed in the committee and so constitute part of the proceedings in
the committee. I therefore rule that the first part of the question is in order.
The last two lines "and, if so, what were the grounds for the decision and can he name
any precedent for this action?" should be expunged from the Order Paper. The member
should resubmit the question bearing that in mind, and should not seek information about
what took place at the committee, which prompted the statement the chairman gave to the
news media. The question can ask only for elucidation of any statement he has made.

news media. Therefore, the chairman is being asked to answer questions he is not competent
to answer in terms of Standing Order 368(b), because he cannot answer questions on the
proceedings of a committee. The discussion that took place at the committee, which led to
the statement being made, is part of the proceedings of the committee. The statement made
by the chairman is not-it is a statement that the committee authorised him to make on its
behalf to the news media. I regret that question 23 must be deleted altogether.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): This is a matter of widespread concern,
and it was my intention to consult the Clerk to ensure that under Standing Order 368 a
committee had adequate power to authorise its chairman to make a public statement in
answer to any question put to the committee clerk. That would seem to be the appropriate
way of handling any matters that are of concern to any member of the House, or to any
person outside the House. Questions should be directed to the committee, which would

committee thought it right that such statements should be made.
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): In your ruling you might be able to confirm that it is open to

Mr SPEAKER: That is an interesting point, which I should like to think about. It may
anticipate an Order of the Day, in which case it would not be allowed.
The member for Grey Lynn asked how he or other members could find out what is in
the mind of a select committee that is not open to the news media. He could wait until the
committee reports to the House, in which case it is all open, or, alternatively, he could take
up the option mentioned by the Minister of Justice, which I think I suggested earlier. It is
over to the committee to authorise the chairman to make whatever statement the committee
feels should be made-whether by way of a press statement or by authorising him to answer

Farmers' Planning for Investment
105. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Agriculture:
Does he remember the promise in the National Party's glossy manifesto that its policies
would "enable farmers to confidently plan for investment", and, if so, could he outline what
measures he has taken to achieve this, and could he explain why they have failed?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I cannot explain why the measures
have failed, because they are a success story. I presume the reference is to the introductory
statement in the manifesto on agricultural policy, which states: "National will ensure that
farmers have sufficient confidence in the future of their industry to continue to invest in farm
development, in the knowledge that they will not be subject to the arbitrary interference of
the Government." Detailed policy objectives for agriculture were set out in section 31 of the
manifesto. Action has been taken on all of them, and the Government will take further
action and initiate new measures as these are needed. By way of example, the livestock
incentive scheme introduced in the 1976 Budget offered special inducements to farmers with
a potential to expand stock numbers. The magnitude of the response has shown the worth of
the scheme. The additional resources made available to the Rural Bank have been designed
to help farmers develop their properties and to promote efficiency and flexibility.

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The $7.5 million to which the honourable
member refers is the budget estimate of the cost of the accelerated geothermal exploration
and support programme in a full year. In the last financial year the Ministry of Works and
Development was allocated $4 million and spent $3.75 million. Main items of expenditure

(23/5/78)
Energy-Wind Research Programmes
153. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the
Minister of Energy: What wind energy programmes in research and development are now
under way or in prospect?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The New Zealand Energy Research and
Development Committee is sponsoring a programme to evaluate New Zealand's wind
energy resources. An analysis of the meteorological data on wind has been completed and
detailed investigations of wind characteristics at selected sites in the South Island are nearing
completion. Further detailed work, to be funded by the NZERDC and the Electricity
Division of the Ministry of Energy, will be carried out at a limited number of potentially
favourable North Island sites. The Meteorological Service has started a resource assessment
programme in areas of the country which have not yet been covered. The service is
participating in an International Energy Agency co-operative research programme studying
the uncertainty of wind forecasts. Finally, the Departments of Mechanical Engineering at
the Universities of Auckland and Canterbury are investigating wind flows around structures
and have small wind-powered electricity generators in operation for research purposes. The
estimated expenditure on wind energy research for 1977-78 is $84,000.

Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Government Life Insurance Office):
The answer is no. The Government Life Insurance Office rate of interest is 11 percent, not
12 percent. However, the Government Life Insurance Office increased the rate of interest
charged on loans on the security of policies from 9 percent to 11 percent with effect from 1
January 1978. That was done by Order in accordance with the Government Life Insurance
Act 1953. The commissioner is aware that some private life insurance offices charge 11
percent, and some charge a higher rate.

Mortgage Interest Rates
213. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), on behalf of Hon. W. A. FRASER (St Kilda) to the
Minister of Finance: What were the average mortgage interest rates of all mortgages
registered in the month of May in each of the years 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978, and can he
confirm that the average interest rates prevailing in the calendar year 1977 and those
prevailing to the date of 1978 are the highest ever recorded since records were first kept in
1913?
Rt Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The question stated "to date in 1978",
according to the copy I have, and not "to the date of 1978". I have only some of the
information the honourable member has requested, because data on mortgage registrations
are not available subsequent to October 1977. The figures available are: May 1975, 8.28
percent; May 1976, 9.24 percent; and May 1977, 10.45 percent. The average rate of interest
on mortgages registered in the first 10 months of 1977 was 10.29 percent, and it is expected
that that downward trend will continue. Records are in fact available prior to 1913, but it is
correct that this figure of the nominal mortgage interest rates, has not been exceeded in any
year since that time. However, when these average rates are compared with the rates of
inflation prevailing at the time, it can readily be seen that interest rates have been lower in
relation to the rate of inflation in the last 2 years than in the majority of years between 1913
and 1976.

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I propose to talk to the same questions and answers
as those referred to by the member for New Lynn. Opposition members have debated today
the problems in Auckland. We make no apologies for doing that, because history has shown
that the problems faced by Auckland today are the problems that the rest of New Zealand
will face tomorrow. I grew up in Auckland. I went to school there, and I took my first job in
Auckland. I still live within half of mile of Queen Street, and I know that Auckland today,
under the National Government, is not a happy city. As the questions and answers showed,
Auckland is suffering from 20 years of neglect by the National Government. The only
contribution it has made to Auckland that I can think of is the motorway system, which has
torn the heart out of my electorate. During the last election campaign, National Party
candidates exploited Auckland's problems, but the questions asked recently and the answers
given showed clearly that those problems have not been dealt with by the National
Government.
I draw the attention of Government members to an election pamphlet on which most of
them were elected. Of course, they may have forgotten about it, because I have not seen any
sign of it in the past 2 years, but it is entitled The Cities. During the campaign we were shown
a television cartoon-a nice, pretty little cartoon, showing the then Deputy Leader of the
Opposition, now the Deputy Prime Minister, as the spokesman on cities. However, I remind
the House that he has not spoken about our cities in the past 2 years. The cartoon contained
all sorts of nice promises, and we heard a fruity voice saying, "There was a time when New
Zealand cities were quiet and clean. The people said they were nice places to bring up
children. But the cities grew alarmingly. People poured in, not just from the country but
from other countries as well-60 000 in 2 years. No one could build enough houses, so the
price went up. No one could afford one. Soon there were not enough schools or hospitals,
and then one day there were not enough jobs either, and the people became angry and
violence broke out."
None of the promises made in the pamphlet on which Government members were
elected has been carried out. Let us consider some of the statements in it. First, there was the
suggestion that Auckland's problems were caused by too many immigrants. I point out that
in the past 2 years 40 000 people have left the country, but Auckland's population has
increased because of migration from the South Island. The statistics published by the
Government's own department show that the population of Southland decreased in the past
2 years, but that the population of Auckland increased by 26 000 in that period. Therefore,
because the National Government's policies have forced people to migrate from the South
Island to Auckland, Auckland's problems have continued.
Let us now consider other problems. First, I take hospitals. At the moment the
Auckland Hospital Board has a waiting list of 10 000. What does the Minister of Health say
about that problem, which has arisen under the National Government? He represents an
Auckland electorate, but he made the incredible statement that the sort of hospital service
needed to eliminate waiting lists would be hopelessly uneconomic. That is the National
Government's answer to those 10 000 people in Auckland who are awaiting admission to
hospitals.
I also draw attention to the fact that we are still waiting for a children's hospital in
Auckland. A survey on the health of Auckland's school children carried out by Professor
Lines showed that only one child in three was healthy, but in 1975 National Party candidates
told us in their pamphlet that Auckland would be a good place to bring up children. Let me
repeat what they said then: “On your way to work tomorrow, take a look around you. Ask
yourself how much longer must your family live in this kind of environment. Then remember
that we have a plan to make our cities nice places to bring up children again." That must be
the biggest secret for the last 2 years. Where is the Government plan to make Auckland a
better place in which to bring up children, when a professor tells us that only one child in
three is healthy? Apparently the member for Rangitikei thinks this is funny, but I tell him
that this is a major problem facing Auckland today, and I am angry about it. Through
deceptive advertising the Auckland people were persuaded that a National Government
would do something about these problems.
We remember that the Government intended doing something about law and order,
too. Well, in last night's Auckland Star we read the headline, "Vandal raid forces new school
shut after 2 weeks". The article states, “A $1 million Otara primary school-which opened
only 2 weeks ago-was closed today after an attack by vandals." Where is the Government's
promised policy on law and order?

APPROPRIATION BILL-FINANCIAL STATEMENT
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Mr FENTON (Hastings): We are faced with several possibilities but few probabilities
when comparing the Labour Government's 1975 Budget and the Opposition's 1978 ghost
budget with the Government's 1978 Budget, and we are reminded of the words of a
somewhat little-known poet, who said: "I feel most generous today, the taxpayers' money
I'll give away." That was said, of course, in 1978, as it was in 1972 by the Labour
Government. I suppose we can predict that in 1979 the Opposition will say: “On second
thoughts I think it best, to lock it in the old oak chest", which was what was said in 1952 after
a similar promise made in 1951. Be that as it may, one of the comparisons we should make,
when comparing the Government's Budget with the Opposition's budget, is to set out the
differences between the Labour Government's 1975 Budget and the Budget presented last
week by the present Government.
In 1975 inflation was running at 15.7 percent, having accelerated from 5.5 percent
during the Labour Government's 3 years in office. The internal deficit was $1,000 million,
and was projected to $1,300 million. The deficit predicted in the Government's Budget is
$1,000 million. In 1975 the Labour Government found it necessary to increase the tax on
stereos, cosmetics, ammunition, and many other items, in a last-ditch effort to repair an
ailing economy. The internal deficit in 1975 represented 9.2 percent of the gross national
product. Farm stock was not given a rebirth or a chance of living when their owners had
prospects of a better livelihood; but the owners were paid in a peculiar kind of way to kill
their stock. No farm incentives were offered, and there was no export drive of any
significance.
In the 1978 Budget, which the Opposition is criticising so severely, inflation is estimated
to be 8.2 percent, and the deficit will be $1,000 million. However, included in that deficit will
be $320 million which has been given away in tax concessions and other productivity
incentives. Farm incentives, which were totally lacking in 1975, now amount to $60 million
and will rise to $109 million. Allied to that is an export drive, which has more than small
potential because it is being undertaken positively and with determination, and has aroused
the enthusiasm and the excitement of people who, until now, had not thought of exporting
their products. The internal deficit now represents 6.4 percent of the gross national product,
compared with 9.2 percent in 1975. The $320 million that has been given away in tax
concessions is in addition to the 5 percent concession introduced earlier this year.
If people are interested in this kind of comparison they will not look for parallels, but
for the sharp contrasts which must lie within those figures. One thing I am certain of, and it is


## p. 678 (#686) ############################################

678
7 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
that, notwithstanding any platitudes that may be mounted by the Opposition, the people of
New Zealand are not fools-as the Leader of the Opposition has suggested. They will
understand that there is something meaningful and something significant for them in a
Budget that deliberately produces incentives to work. If only we would be rid, in some way
or other-preferably by persuasion-of the troublemakers who are spoiling our export drive
and causing large losses of earnings amongst the work force, the Budget would become even
more meaningful. Last night I spent some time on a brief discourse on the Opposition's
alternative budget-and a short time was all that was required. That astonishing document
warranted nothing more. In the words of a famous travelogue narrator, whose era was on a
par with the Labour Party's alternative Budget, "We all leave with reluctance an idyllic
paradise of political fiction and fantasy as the Labour Party's sun pulls slowly away from the
shore, and its ship sinks slowly in the west."
It is now time to focus attention once again on the benefits to be derived from the
realistic and practical Budget presented last week and to dismiss the fantasies and fiction of a
flagging philosopher of finance that were inflicted upon us yesterday. The press has dealt
quite adequately with Labour's misconceptions and contemporary presumptions. Illusion
has been dispelled quickly in the clean surgery of public analysis. Government members will
point to progress in spheres that require positive remedies and action-remedies that could
not have been applied had it not been for an effective approach to the economy, and action
that only a concerned and aware Government could have initiated in the national interest.
Among the first factors justifying support for our primary producers was the
comprehension of two alarming influences. The first of these was the trading world's
disinclination to encourage us to believe that our agricultural capabilities were outstanding
and merited continued patronage. The other was the debilitating effect of a prolonged
drought on production, which threw thousands of farmers into despair, almost apathy. This
knowledge prompted budgetary measures to sustain vital livestock percentages, and to
return farming to a condition of basic viability. To most critics who are prepared to condemn
these provisions as a panacea for agriculture, a telling reminder can be given; we have
insufficiently diverisified in alternative export adventures to enable us to reduce our concern
for the largest foreign exchange earner the country has known, and on whose continued
efforts we all depend for a reasonable standard of living. That is why $60 million rising to
$109 million has been reserved for farm support. I draw attention to pages 15 to 18 of the
Budget where the essential elements of those proposals are confirmed. Every move is
intended to assist producers in programmes arranged to benefit this country.
We have the stimulation of our most essential industry encompassing cash payments
worth $60 million in stock holdings of sheep, beef cattle, and dairy cattle; supplementary
minimum prices for benchmark grades achieved by Government underwriting; a dairy beef
market guarantee scheme worth $4.5 million; an increase in fertiliser and lime subsidies of $7
million, representing an outlay of $90 million; the cancellation of 11 varieties of agricultural
and horticultural inspection fees at an initial cost of $8 million and rising to $19 million; and a
broad range of incentives, projects, and other development subsidies to restore buoyancy
and confidence. That outlines the Budget that has been criticised so severely, although
innocuously, by an innocuous leader of an innocuous Opposition. If we turn to the pages I
have referred to, I am certain we shall see that the farm support programme is extremely
vital if the economy is to be sustained until it can reach out to the markets that, surely, will
be won back.
I was reminded only a day or two ago of a rather extraordinary series of contradictory
statements made by representatives of two different farming interests in Hawke's Bay. One
set out to say--which I believe-that the Budget would make a large difference to his
farming projects and to those of his contemporaries. He was contradicted by another who
said that the Budget would not bring back the swinging vote, and that in any case the
initiatives were insignificant. I would say to that farmer that no compulsion whatsoever is
imposed upon him to count his stock, nor is there any compulsion upon him to take
advantage of the large increase in the lime and fertiliser subsidy. In fact, if he wishes, he can
separate himself, and his altruism, entirely from the Budget; and I can find every possible
means of helping him do so. For some reason he thinks, as the Labour Party does, that the
Budget is designed to catch the swinging vote. It is not. It is designed to stop the body from
swinging, and at the moment the body is certainly that of the farming community—the
primary export producer, making the greatest progress and earning overseas exchange for
the country.

Other facets of the Budget have been criticised by the Labour Party. The Leader of the
Opposition failed to mention anything about the incentives given in the Budget for planting
new crops. In my area, where the land is rich, where agriculture flourishes normally, and
where there are canneries and other processing plants exporting the products, many people
with small holdings are now planting new experimental crops, and before planting they have
developed a good amount of their programme in plant propagation. They recognise and
acknowledge that the Budget will help them considerably. The measures that will help them
are allied to the export incentives, which will operate as soon as they start producing. A
considerable amount of export fruit will leave Hastings and Hawke's Bay. Until now we have
thought of these export fruits as purely exotic fruits, for which the Americans will pay high
prices. To me that is significant, and it is significant for Hawke's Bay and Hastings.
Another aspect of the Budget that has been criticised is house finance. I cannot begin to
appreciate how the Labour Party has the effrontery and the audacity to discuss housing,
because it is too delicate for the Labour Party to broach. Because of the Labour Party's
unrestrained policy of immigration, which thrust an impossible demand on slender
resources, the former Labour Government managed to increase the price of houses by 100
percent and the price of sections by about 200 percent―a phenomenal performance from a
party that prides itself on great records. That record will stand eternally to its credit,
although I suppose one should say to its debit. In discussing this matter one could say the
Labour Party has put its own clumsy finger on its own clumsy keyboard. It represents one of
Labour's greatest failures, but one which only exemplifies everything else it did in the 3 years
it was in office.
I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition could persuade his colleagues to tell
prospective home owners what advantages will be introduced by the Government to help
them purchase a home. Opposition members should drop the canard that the financial
system is not assisting home owners, when trustee savings bank managers have informed us
that the system is working, complete with the variable mortgage scheme, to which the
Leader of the Opposition has referred. The Government's variable mortgage scheme is
operating with the 3-year suspension on the early payments. It is a beginning, and a good
beginning. It would be advisable if the export incentives could be brought to the notice of
potential exporters by Opposition members. If, as they claim, they are doing their duty, they
would be well advised not to spend too much time in denegrating, and spend a little more
time in constructive thinking. They should not describe the export drive as a farce, but as
something they are delighted to assist.

In the 1975 Labour Budget-this yellow-covered document, bearing the name of the

for supplementaries in the 1975 Labour Budget was $50 million. In the event, it proved to be
$182 million, making a total provision for the year to March 1975 of $5,120 million, but the
actual expenditure was $5,397 million.

without authorisation. It was the next National Government that had to put that right, by

and equipment, from 20 percent to 30 percent of building costs. There have been suspensory
