The Budget presented by the Government at least recognises the problem, but, in true
Tory style, assumes that nothing can be done. Apart from election year largesse, there is
nothing in the Government's Budget to indicate that chronic social and economic problems
can be corrected. This typical election-year Budget will be followed by two bad years within
a downward spiralling 3-year cycle.
A statement in the Budget makes an interesting assertion: "The Bretton Woods system
of international financial discipline has finally broken down." I should like to know what the
Minister of Finance means by that statement. His Budget recognises the problem of
international finance, but offers no remedy. I have said already that it is an immoral system,
because it forces the poor to sell to the United States-the world's wealthiest nation. The
poor must have a surplus in their balance of payments with the United States to obtain
reserve currency to trade with each other. The United States alone prints new money to pay
for trade purposes. The source of international trading money is United States deficits or
capital purchases of other countries' assets. The contradiction is that the system will not
work without United States deficits, and without those deficits feeding money into the
world's money markets in a most unfair way. The total is now $300 billion, and in the first
quarter of this year an additional $11 billion was pumped in.
If this amount of money had not been pumped in by way of United States deficits, and
had that country applied the discipline that the Prime Minister spoke about and actually
balanced its external account, as presumably the Prime Minister suggests it should have,
then the simple fact of the matter is that trade would have dried up completely. That is how it
is financed-surely the Prime Minister is not suggesting or advocating that. If the United
States had a surplus it would withdraw trading money from circulation and, under the
present system, world trade would simply collapse. That is why the system must keep going.
I want to know what the Prime Minister is driving at, because it is certainly not clear
from the Budget. International conferences will not solve the international financial
problem, which is at the root of our trading problem. We must help ourselves in conjunction
with the many other countries that can no longer afford to borrow. The Social Credit system
is not one of crude barter, as one or two people are determined to believe, simply because
they will not keep their ears open. The Minister of Education said that the Social Credit
trade system is comparable to exchanging a sheep for a dozen pair of sandals. Money is
necessary to facilitate modern trade, because it measures value exchange and also allows
freedom of choice. I shall enlighten the Minister of Education. If a sheep is worth $12 and a
pair of sandals is worth $1, then Social Credit sees that only one pair of sandals will be
wanted, leaving $11 over. The $11 can be spent on anything-a tie, a litre or two of petrol, or
perhaps some urgently needed text books. The goods or services that can be bought for the
$12 sheep under Social Credit are worth $12. The books will balance equal to the production
available; this is the fundamental principle of barter and the more sophisticated trade with
money derived from the principles of barter. I have said that before and I repeat it.
The difference between the Social Credit system and the present system is that money
available for trade will be adjusted to the value of goods and services available. At present,
the value of goods and services available is adjusted to the money available--the other way
round. Because of the Bretton Woods Agreement, world trade is still regulated by the
availability of American dollars, which are created with almost no relationship to the supply
of goods and the needs of the people. Two-thirds of the people of the world are suffering
from malnutrition. They do not eat, not because they do not want to, but because their
propensity to trade is regulated by the availability of reserve dollars, which in turn are
regulated by the amount the United States is prepared to import above what it exports.
Bilateral trade agreements have their problems and disadvantages-I concede that. The
freedom to purchase on the world market is restricted by the availability of goods and
services within the two countries involved. I repeat that a fairer, more moral, and more just
trading system, that adjusts the monetary system to the needs of the people and their
capacity to produce, must be introduced. New Zealand has no reasonable trading future
under the present system, nor do most of the Third World countries. The process can be
started with bilateral arrangements leading to multilateral arrangements. The advantages of
multilateral trade will become apparent as the system I am advocating extends and grows
and replaces the present system. A multilateral system giving wider freedom of choice in the
exchange of value and trade will come when three or more willing countries are prepared to
exchange and pool their own money equal to the value of what they have to trade.

Earlier this year, with the aid of the leaders of the Northland sub-province Federated
Farmers, we took steps to ensure that the special farming problems in our region were fully
understood at official level. The worst farming problems are first experienced in Northland,
and we felt a special responsibility to present the needs of the region as the framework for
budgetary measures designed to keep the smaller and most vulnerable farmers in business. It
is a matter of some pride to us that at a meeting with the Government arranged by us before
the Budget, one of the items suggested was none other than the supplementary minimum
price scheme.
Because of the region's special dependence on fertiliser, and the consequent higher
expenditure on this item, we in Northland are grateful that the fertiliser subsidy has been
increased. Northland farmers need that cash grant as much as any other farmers in the
country. We are pleased also with the other miscellaneous features in the package, such as
the encouragement of new horticultural crops. I believe that, because of its climatic
advantage, Northland has a great future with new crops. One parting thought on this
farmers' Budget, which has transferred more than $100 million to the farming community:
the Labour Party would not and Social Credit could not produce such a Budget, but the
National Government-and I think farmers would do well to remember this-was both
willing and able to provide that money.
With so much talk in the last few weeks about the restructuring of the tax system, it is, I
believe, timely to swing some attention back to expenditure. I am not referring to the
Government's conspicuous success in cutting back on overall expenditure, as this is already
familiar to anyone who follows political development. However, I believe it is fair to say that
expenditure in many areas of State activity has been cut to the bone, and waste has been
reduced as far as it is practicable to do so.
At a time when State department spending is being ruthlessly cut back, even in the more
desirable and important activities, it is inevitable that questions should be asked about the
giant State trading entities. Many people are aware that such departments present significant
problems for the economy. In a recent article in the New Zealand Listener of 20 May, Mr
Brian Easton pointed out that the rate of return on investment is, in his words “a crucial
measure of the wealth of the economy". He sought reasons why the return on investment in
New Zealand is so low. One reason is undoubtedly the way in which the State trading entities
are run. There is no escaping the fact that, generally, they are not profitably using the
substantial investment sunk into them, and, because of the size of these organisations, their
low profitability has been a significant factor in the relatively poor growth of our economy
since World War II. The extent to which these loss-makers are a drain on public revenue is
significant. For example, in the final financial year of the last Labour Government there was
a drain of $131 million for major State trading entities, including subsidies and deferred
interest payments.
Inevitably, this affects the space a Government has in which to manoeuvre when
altering rates of taxation. In fact, the Labour Party's attitude to State trading entities is one
of the reasons it has been, and will remain, a high-taxation party, no matter what assurances
to the contrary Opposition speakers may give. If the listed major State trading entities had
earned, say, a 10 percent rate of return in 1975-76, their profits would have been $320 million
higher than the recorded aggregations of profits and losses, or roughly the equivalent of the
total sum of sales tax receipts in that year. Furthermore, there would have been a saving of
an additional $121 million on subsidies and non-payment of interest.
What about return on capital? The major State trading entities, with assets exceeding $5
billion worth, represent an investment of between 60 percent and 80 percent of the entire
asset value of all public companies in New Zealand. Between 1970 and 1976 the value of
their assets nearly doubled. Yet the rate of return on this massive investment remained the
same, at less than 3.5 percent of the book value of the assets, or about one-third of the 10.2
percent earned by public companies in 1975-76. These figures are, to say the least,
disturbing. We should ask what can be done to make the State trading entities less of a
millstone around the neck of the economy. It would be possible to run them on commercial
lines, or, should I say, as commercially as it is possible to run any monopoly. Unprofitable
services could be dropped, or charges could be raised to cover their costs. Investment
priorities could be made to follow profitable demand, annual profit targets could be set,
emphasis could be placed on usage-sensitive pricing and effective use of capital equipment.
Such an approach certainly has considerable appeal for me, as the political head of a
large trading department concerned to provide post and telecommunication services, as and

Securities Advertising Bill-Supplementary Order Paper 9
THURSDAY, 8 JUNE 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SECURITIES ADVERTISING BILL-SUPPLEMENTARY ORDER PAPER 9
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That Supplementary Order
Paper 9 on the Securities Advertising Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee, the
proceedings of the committee during the hearing of evidence to be open to accredited
representatives of the news media. When moving the introduction of the Securities
Advertising Bill, I said that in a Bill of such wide application it had been necessary to vest in
the Registrar of Companies wide discretions and powers, and that I was aware that many had
suggested that an independent commission should exercise those wide discretions and
powers. I said that I would welcome submissions to the Statutes Revision Committee on the
need for such a commission and on its functions.
From the many submissions received on the Securities Advertising Bill, the weight of
opinion came down strongly on the side of establishing such a commission, and I should like
to refer briefly to three of those submissions, which were made in public. The New Zealand
Law Society considered that the Securities Advertising Bill should be drafted in more
general terms, and that a commission should be set up to define and redefine the disclosure
requirements to deal with the different and ever-changing circumstances of the commercial
world. The New Zealand Society of Accountants considered that such wide discretionary
powers should not be vested in a public servant but in a commission, which, they stressed,
would be in the best position to keep under continual review the law relating to securities
advertising and the securities industry. And the Stock Exchange Association of New
Zealand considered that a commission was the best way of administering such general
legislation, having the flexibility to deal speedily with new schemes for issuing securities
when such schemes were objectionable or had undesirable features.
Having regard to the weight of opinion for the establishment of an independent
commission, the Government has decided to establish a Securities Commission, and this
Supplementary Order Paper gives effect to that decision by making the necessary
consequential amendments to the Securities Advertising Bill.
I wish to emphasise that the Supplementary Order Paper is confined to setting up the
Securities Commission, and does not anticipate any other changes to the Bill that might be
made by the Statutes Revision Committee. To take account of the additional purpose of the
Bill, its title is to be changed from the Securities Advertising Bill to the Securities Bill.
The functions and discretionary powers of the Securities Commission are to be as
follows: first, to exempt any person or class or persons from compliance with any of the
provisions of the Securities Advertising Bill upon such terms and conditions, if any, as
thought fit-I envisage that this power will be exercised when less disclosure than that
required by the Bill is considered adequate; secondly, to cancel the registration of
prospectuses, and, at its discretion before so doing, to hold hearings and summon witnesses
for examination on oath; thirdly, to hear appeals from decisions of the Registrar of
Companies made under the Bill; fourthly, to keep under review and make recommendations
for amendments to the law relating to bodies corporate, securities, and unincorporated
issuers of securities; and fifthly, to perform such functions as are conferred on it by other
enactments. This function recognises that the commission may well have further
responsibilities arising from any future review of the law relating to the securities industry.
The Securities Commission is to take over the functions of the Company Law Advisory
Committee under the Companies Act 1955 and the Companies Special Investigation Act
1958. It is proposed that the commission will comprise five part-time members, whose
chairman will be a barrister and solicitor of not less than 7 years' standing. With part-time
members, it is more than likely that a member may find, from time to time, that his
commercial interests conflict with his duties as a member of the Securities Commission. For
such cases, and for cases in which a member is incapacitated from performing his duties as a
member, provision is made for the appointment of alternate members.
The commission is to have power to appoint such officers and employees as are


## p. 704 (#712) ############################################

704
8 June
Securities Advertising Bill-Supplementary Order Paper 9
necessary for the efficient carrying out of its functions and powers. The number of
appointments is subject to determination by the Minister of Justice. It is envisaged that the
Securities Commission will employ a small staff, probably five or six initially.
I propose to refer this Supplementary Order Paper to the Statutes Revision Committee,
and to ask that committee to circulate it to all those who made submissions on the Securities
Advertising Bill, so that they may make further submissions on the nature and scope of the
Securities Commission as conceived in this Supplementary Order Paper.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I must confess at the outset to be taken a little by
surprise with the motion coming on. It is my fault, I know, but I do not have the

ANIMALS PROTECTION AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Animals Protection
Amendment Bill be introduced. I propose to recommend that the Bill be referred to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee. The Bill contains four clauses, three of which are of a
machinery nature, but the one exception will bring about a quite significant change in the
law. Clause 2 confers upon the court discretionary power to order the forfeiture to the
Crown of an animal that has been found by the court to be a victim of cruelty.
For many years the Royal Federation of New Zealand Societies for the Prevention of
Cruelty to Animals has advocated three changes in the law. It wanted the penalties
increased, disqualification made possible upon the first conviction, and the animal
concerned to be taken away from the offender. Federated Farmers of New Zealand,
although not entirely opposed to the proposal, nevertheless considered it too harsh a penalty
for a first offence, especially for people whose livelihood was associated with animals.
In view of this divergence of thinking between the Royal Federation of New Zealand
Societies for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals and Federated Farmers, it is believed that
the forfeiture provision contained in clause 2 of the Bill is a satisfactory alternative.
To comment briefly on the Bill clause by clause, clause 1 contains the title of the Bill;
clause 2 has two subclauses, the first providing for the forfeiture to the Crown and disposal of
the ill-treated animal as the Minister thinks best, and the second providing for the animal
concerned to be held by an inspector until the court has dealt with the alleged offence.
Clause 2(2) is simply a consequential amendment to section 10(4) as a result of the
amendment empowering a court to order forfeiture of an animal.
Previously an inspector could hold an animal only until a magistrate had dealt with a
prosecution under the Act by ordering the return of the animal concerned either to the
owner or the person charged with an offence. But, with the amendment relating to
forfeiture, an inspector's power will be extended to hold covering the forfeiture situation
also.
Clause 3 provides for the increasing of fines specified in nine sections of the principal
Act. The monetary penalties have remained unchanged since the principal Act was passed in
1960, and, with the effect of inflation over the years, the fines are now considered
inadequate deterrents. All things considered, it is believed that the revised penalties in the
Bill are in keeping with present-day criteria, in the context of punishment of offences triable
under the Summary Proceedings Act 1967, by which most offences under the Animals
Protection Act are dealt with.
Clause 4 amends section 18 of the principal Act by providing for a monetary fine for the
offence of obstructing an inspector. At present the only penalty for such an offence is
imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 months, and this penalty has never been imposed.
It is considered that the amendment, in providing for a monetary fine, will give the courts


## p. 707 (#715) ############################################

8 June
707
Animals Protection Amendment Bill
some latitude to deal with, say, first offenders for whom imprisonment is too harsh a
punishment. It is a logical amendment, bringing the provision into line with that existing for
the same offence in the Animals Act 1967.

He asked why the Bill does not provide for prohibition of gin traps. The fine for

interested people can give their evidence on it. If they can make any helpful suggestions to
improve the Bill I shall be very happy to accept them.

FAMILY BENEFITS (HOME OWNERSHIP) AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That the Family Benefits
(Home Ownership) Amendment Bill be introduced. Members will be aware of the Budget
announcement that there is to be a substantial upgrading of the family benefit capitalisation
scheme. This Bill provides the necessary legislative authority.


## p. 708 (#716) ############################################

708
8 June
Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Amendment Bill
Family benefit capitalisation is available to assist families to buy a house, to build a
house, or to make alterations to their own home. The scheme is designed to direct assistance
to those who cannot reasonably be expected fully to finance their particular housing
proposition without capitalising their family benefit.
Three separate measures have been approved to upgrade the scheme. The first, which
does not involve any amendment to the Act, is a substantial increase in the income limits.
With effect from 2 June 1978 the income limit is increased from $95 to $125 a week for a one-
child family, and increased by $5 a week for each additional child. The increase will enable
many more families to take advantage of the capitalisation scheme.
Apart from the income limit, the other changes approved relate to the maximum
amount that may be capitalised and the amount of the family benefit that is available to be
capitalised. Clause 2 will increase the upper limit of capitalised advances from $2,000 to
$3,000. This will provide families with a more substantial contribution towards any particular
housing proposition. Clause 3 will increase the actual amount of family benefit that may be
available for capitalisation from $1.50 a week to $3 a week. This means that the full benefit
may be capitalised, and will assist more families to capitalise up to the new maximum
amount of $3,000.
The Government has recognised the need to help families who wish to provide suitable
housing for themselves, and the substantial upgrading of the capitalisation scheme will be a
major help to those families.
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St Kilda): I listened with interest to the Minister's introductory
comments. The Bill proposes to give effect to the statement on page 35 of the Budget. In the
ordinary course of events, a measure of this nature would naturally be welcomed, but I point
out to the Minister that, more than at any time since the inception of the family benefit
capitalisation scheme, low-income families in particular now need that money to help them
to exist.
Having said that, I add that any crumbs for the home seeker are welcome under the
National Administration. The low average loan available through the Housing Corporation,
and the low eligibility level, which has been frozen for far too long, have meant that many
people have been unable to acquire their own homes. For families with two or more children
the amendment Bill may be of some assistance to purchase an existing home, although even
that is very doubtful if the families live in higher-cost housing areas, because the loan
limitation for existing homes is only $17,500. The upgrading of the family benefit
capitalisation scheme is unlikely to assist those who prefer to build a new home.
The chairman of the major home builders group in New Zealand recently pointed out in
a very cogent statement that his firm and others can no longer cater for clients earning less
than $125 a week. How will the Bill help them? It may help them to add half a room to their
house, but I cannot see it doing much more. The revised scheme will not help many, and the
major reason is the cost of mortgage finance. That is the stumbling block.

QUESTIONS ORAL
Gasfitters
1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Labour: What proposals does the
Government have for increasing the number of gasfitters, the shortage of whom is stated to
be seriously restricting the reticulation of natural gas and the conversion of oil-burning
equipment to gas?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The number of vacancies for gasfitters
recorded in the October 1977 occupational vacancy survey was 24. In the short term the
immigration division of the Department of Labour may grant entry permits to gasfitters
recruited overseas when the employer can establish that he cannot fill the vacancy from
within New Zealand. For the longer term the Plumbing, Gas and Drainlaying Industry
Training Board has commissioned an investigation of the future requirements of the gas
industry for specialist labour, including gasfitters, and the extent to which these
requirements can already be met. Once the future requirements have been established, the
Government would expect to receive early recommendations from the training board
through the Vocational Training Council on what additional training schemes may need to
be introduced in order to train New Zealanders to meet the gas industry's requirements.
Hon. F. M. Colman: How long will it take to train the required numbers to fill expected
shortages, and what is the position expected to be when Maui comes on stream next year?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: My quick reply is that registered plumbers can take a very short
course and become qualified gasfitters if there is a surge of shortages. It is not expected that
there will be any major trouble when Maui comes on.

Maui B Construction
5. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Energy: Has he been correctly

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): It is correct that investigations showed that a

delay of a year or more. Comparative studies of the costs and timing of construction of both

Mining Co. Ltd, the Government-owned company in the Maui field development. Mr A. G.
Stirrat, chief civil engineer of the Ministry of Works and Development, along with Shell
International Petroleum Co., provided advice to the joint venture on both the technical and
economic feasibility of a concrete platform, while Offshore Mining engaged a firm of United
Kingdom consultants well experienced in offshore construction in the North Sea. The

consultants.

concrete structure?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I do not have a summary of the costs with me. However, I do know

into consideration?

manufactured in New Zealand, and this will create job opportunities.

TAUPO BOROUGH GEOTHERMAL ENERGY EMPOWERING BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Taupo Borough Geothermal Energy
Empowering Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be not allowed to proceed. I
move, That the report do lie upon the table.
It might be useful to the House if I give a brief background to the Bill and the reasons
for the committee's decision. The Bill would have provided the Taupo Borough Council with
the power to regulate and impose conditions on the development and use of geothermal
energy within the borough, and allow it to enter into contracts for the development of
geothermal energy either inside or outside the borough for the use of the inhabitants of or
occupiers of property in the borough. In other words, the powers would have been the same
as those conferred on Rotorua City by its Geothermal Energy Empowering Act 1967. I shall
not traverse the history of that legislation; I am sure, Mr Speaker, you would not allow me to
even if I wanted to. Suffice it to say that the right to develop energy, or contract to buy
energy for use by the Rotorua City Council, was also incorporated in that Act.
However, there are significant differences between the situations in Rotorua and
Taupo. In addition to the Tauhara field, only a small part of which underlies the Taupo
Borough, there are also the Wairakei field and the Rotokawa field nearby. There is now also
a defined policy on geothermal energy within the framework of the Government's general
energy policy. Thus times have changed dramatically in recent years. In addition, the
location of Taupo in a geothermal energy area is of even more significance when considering
the transfer of control to the Taupo Borough Council.
The three geothermal fields within the area proclaimed a geothermal energy area—


## p. 719 (#727) ############################################

8 June
719
Taupo Borough Geothermal Energy Empowering Bill
Wairakei, Tauhara, and Rotokawa-could all be subject to development or use by the
Taupo Borough under the powers that could have been conferred by the Bill. Wairakei is at
present being extensively exploited, and there is evidence of a connection between the
Wairakei and Tauhara fields. Rotokawa is, however, clearly separate from the other two.
The probability of a connection between Tauhara and Wairakei has been evident for some
time, and, because of this, it was decided that any drawoff from the Tauhara field would be
limited to a small fraction of its potential.
Several people have expressed interest in using geothermal energy from the Tauhara
field, and this is to be encouraged. However, all other considerations apart, the need to
protect the Government's investment in Wairakei means that the Crown must have full
control over the development of the Tauhara field. Added to this, the Tauhara field is in part
in the borough and in part in the county. If the borough is to have legislation controlling its
area of the field, it would seem logical for the county to have similar legislation. I should add
that we have not been made aware of any such request from the adjoining local authority.
It was obvious to the committee that the borough needed the power to control the
exploitation of geothermal energy for reasons of safety and to prevent pollution. I do not
believe that that is arguable. It is, however, a question of implementation. The Town and
Country Planning Act allows a local authority to deal with the zoned use of land, and the
Municipal Corporations Act 1954 deals with drainage control. It is claimed that hydrogen
sulphide levels in the borough are increasing, and, therefore, authority to control the use of
geothermal energy derived from bores shallower than the prescribed 61 m (200 ft) is
necessary to ensure that safety aspects are closely watched.
The Municipal Corporations Act 1954 allows bylaws to be made for "conserving public
health, safety, and convenience, and preventing and abating nuisances". The council
originally thought that this existing provision would enable it to make bylaws to control the
use of geothermal energy. However, its legal advisers considered this power to be
inadequate, and this is a view supported by the Department of Internal Affairs and the
Ministry of Works and Development. Accordingly, included in the Local Government
Amendment Bill will be a new and specific provision enabling bylaws to be made
"prohibiting or controlling the use of energy derived from any geothermal bore within the
district". It is clear that all the provisions sought by the Taupo Borough Council in the Bill
are either already provided for in general legislation or will be included in the local
government amendment legislation. In these circumstances, the committee does not see any
need for the Taupo Borough Geothermal Energy Empowering Bill to be allowed to proceed.

TUAKAU BOROUGH (RATES VALIDATION) BILL
Second Reading
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. On 1 April 1976
the Tuakau Borough Council made and levied a library rate of 0.4c in the dollar of the land
value. The council wrongly publicised the new library rate as 0.004c in the dollar. The
difference between the amount levied and the advertised amount was challenged by the
ratepayers, and the assistance of the district auditor was requested. He found that not only
had the library rate struck by the council exceeded the maximum rate specified in section 104
of the Municipal Corporations Act 1954, but the general consolidated rate for the past 3
years had also exceeded the maximum rate specified in section 90 of the Act. It would have
been better if the council had struck separate rates for the various amenities it provides in the
borough. However, that was not done. The general consolidated rate exceeded the
maximum statutory levels laid down by the Act, and the local Bill was introduced to validate
the matter.
Bill read a second time.

It is my intention to discuss the effects of the three National Government Budgets on

awareness. We have the classic example of the member for Hutt. He talked loud and long
about bursaries. Members opposite are always vocal. When Labour was the Government it
did nothing. That is the difference. We hear a lot of talk from Labour members when they
are in Opposition, but we see no action when they are the Government.
One classic example of the thinking of today's Labour Party was shown at the recent
Labour Party conference. The party claims it has a glorious past. It may be that Labour Party

Health expenditure for 1978-79 represents 5.7 percent of the gross national product-
the same as for 1977-78. Looking at the Health vote we find that in real terms it is down 1
percent, allowing for an inflation rate of 12 percent a year. This means that the Health vote

Dr Shearer: It is more realistic.
Mr HUNT: Is it realistic to have 10 000 people on the Auckland Hospital waiting list? Of

the health administrators. The doctor-health administrator team is a powerful one-the
former having control of health technology and the latter a monopoly of policy and planning
skills. The effect is to create an ever-widening gap between health users and health
providers. It is not surprising that there is little community participation in planning and
decision making, because there is no effective communication at the local level to allow two-
way exchange. Mechanisms need to be established through which lay people can identify
local needs and priorities, and health professionals can communicate their ideas.
As a first step, a Labour Government would begin a series of health care conferences in
1979-80. These conferences would be held for health professionals, health service
administrators, and health users; and regional meetings would be convened to hear opinions
of health service users. It is essential, in planning for a reform of health care, that the voice
of the consumer is heard, listened to, and noticed. The day is long past when professionals
made all the decisions. A health service that does not involve those it serves cannot be
effective.

I shall now speak about private medical insurance schemes. People who have private
medical insurance can receive attention more quickly for less acute conditions. I do not know
of an acute or serious case that has not been treated in the public hospitals, which are still, by
and large, the finest in the world. People receive attention more quickly for less acute
conditions, but the rapid growth of such schemes has aggravated difficulties in the public
sector. It is worth noting in the annual report of the Auckland-based Southern Cross Medical
Care Society the chairman said that business was again buoyant, with a record influx of new
members bringing the total enrolment to 472 691, and that membership was likely to pass the
half-million mark in a few months.
Despite its braying, the Government is becoming worried about the growth of private
medical insurance schemes. The Prime Minister is reported on page 4 of the Evening Post,
dated 17 May 1978, as having said that medical care societies must take care to ensure that
their increasing growth does not create “a grave imbalance" in the demand on specialists and
the apportionment of their time between public and private hospitals. We must consider
health priorities. When defining priorities, it is wise to remember that real health is more
than a dependence on the availability of medicine in hospitals, or on the provision of
professional health services.
Real health depends first, on people having ready access to an education system that
promotes the development of the individual's potential; secondly, jobs for those who can
work; thirdly, adequate income, so that one wage can maintain a family; fourthly, a realistic
and humanely operated system of income maintenance for those who cannot work; and,
fifthly, well-planned housing to cater for physical and social needs. The contribution that
health professionals make towards promoting a healthy society must be considered against
several factors. Emphasis needs to be placed on the need to move on thinking, planning, and
activities away from hospitals and technological medicine and provide instead adequate
front-line community care and active programmes of health promotion. To do this it is
necessary to redistribute resources.
In recent years it has been recognised that hospitals play too large a part in our health
system. More than 70 percent of the 1976-77 vote was spent on the hospital system. Each
New Zealander paid $220 in taxes for health services, of which $155 went into the hospital
system. Hospitals are a major industry, using considerable resources, including buildings,
manpower, and equipment. Are people getting value for their 70 percent investment in
health? The evidence suggests they are not. Four of the five principal killers in 1900 remain
unconquered. Tuberculosis has been removed from the list, not because of medicine and
hospitals, but because of improved sanitation and housing. If overseas patterns are reflected
in New Zealand it is probable that 70 percent of the Health vote already mentioned will be
expended on from 5 to 10 percent of people with health problems.
It is significant that studies of New Zealanders at work, at play, and at school indicate
that we are not a healthy nation. Child health is a good example. I am concerned that the
mortality rate in pre-schoolers is twice as high as in Sweden, and high by world standards
among countries similarly developed. Building children's hospitals is not the answer. Four
out of every 10 infant deaths in New Zealand are caused by accidents or violence. Of the 77
deaths from accident and violence in 1976, 36 percent involved motor vehicles, and 29
percent of infant deaths were caused by drowning. If the education system provided that
every 5-year-old learned to swim it would be a step forward in preventing the use of some
hospital services. Of much concern are reports of children suffering from malnutrition and
the prevalence of eye and ear disorders and respiratory and skin diseases. It is a poor record
for an affluent society. I hope that in the future hospitals will have a less dominant role to
fulfil.
A number of other questions need to be answered. Should we have more
decentralisation of hospitals-a move from the larger urban-based hospitals to smaller
community hospitals? Recently I visited the small hospital in Kaikohe. It is a beautiful
hospital, with 5 obstetric beds and 18 geriatric beds. The hospital is not threatened with

Government has imposed balanced management, and is seeing a falling off in the volume

more positive. I am concerned at the threat to break up the good relationship the National
Government has established in the past 2 years between consumers and traders. Members
opposite talk about a new bureau and Ministry of Consumer Affairs, whereas the National
Government has promised to improve the present system, which has worked well.
The Government has undertaken an entirely new approach to business-consumer
relations, which I call a co-operative approach. Since we took office, various working parties
have undertaken important studies in the interests of both consumers and the commercial
community. In 1976 a joint working party consisting of the New Zealand Manufacturers
Federation, the New Zealand Retailers Federation, the New Zealand Chambers of
Commerce, and the Consumers Institute was set up to fulfil the National Party's 1975
proposed review of the Commerce Act. This was described by Mr Dick Smithies, the chief
officer of the Consumers Institute, who is highly respected throughout New Zealand. He
said it was the first time his organisation-which is the senior independent organisation
dealing with consumer service and protection outside the Department of Trade and
Industry-had been invited to join the trade associations to work as a team. That working
party produced a unanimous report, accepted by me, and implemented by Government
legislation passed in 1976 in the interests of consumers and the commercial community.
The important point is that, as amended by the National Government, and as
administered by my department and the Commerce Commission, the Commerce Act forms
the basis of our consumer protection legislation today, as well as providing for the effective
maintenance and development of commerce in New Zealand. In February 1977 we set up a
joint working party, also consisting of representatives of the Consumers Institute, the
Manufacturers Federation, and the Retailers Federation, to review the proposed Consumer
Protection Bill, which had been drafted mainly to deal with the question of children's
flammable night attire. The working party recommended the substitution of that Bill by
another dealing exclusively with children's night attire-the Safety of Children's Night
Clothes Act, which was passed last session. The working party recommended that the other
matters proposed in the legislation should be placed in a new Product Safety Bill. These
recommendations are now being considered by the Government.
Mr MacDonell: When is the Bill coming in?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The honourable member should not become
excited. The promises we made in 1975 have been fulfilled to the letter. The working party's
recommendations will be considered seriously by the Minister of Labour and myself. I
established a joint working party of the Consumers Institute, the Manufacturers Federation,
the Retailers Federation, and the advertising industry to consider the Trading Coupons Act
1931. The working party is currently studying this to determine whether the legislation is still
required, and, if so, whether it should be amended.
The Government has set up a joint working party to examine all consumer legislation
administered by my department. The legislation to be examined includes the Merchandise
Marks Act 1954 and the Consumer Information Act 1969. The terms of reference for the
working party are broad and specific: first, to study consumer needs in the areas of
information, advertising, sales and services practices, and the best means of obtaining
redress when necessary; secondly, to recommend legislative and administrative procedures
to provide better services for the consumer, and fairer workable arrangements for the
businessman; thirdly, to consider the advisability of consolidating and modifying the
Consumer Information Act 1969 and the Merchandise Marks Act 1954, taking into account
the form and operation of the United Kingdom Trade Description Act 1968; fourthly, to
review and report on any other matter concerning relations between the commercial
community and consumers that the working party considers may require legislative,
administrative, or other action.
I am pleased to announce that the chairman of the working party is to be Mr H. E. J.
Martin of the New Zealand Manufacturers Federation. The other members are Mr J. K.
Iles, business consultant; Mr B. I. Purdie, New Zealand Retailers Federation; Mr R. J.
Smithies, Consumers Institute; and Mr M. J. Thompson, Newspaper Publishers Association
of New Zealand. Although I have stated the names and the organisations with which the
members are associated, they are not required to adhere to the specific policies of their
organisations. That consideration has been fundamental to each of the working parties in

I turn now to farming. The Leader of the Opposition said, "The Budget contains

on farming in the last few Budgets. In 1975, in the last Budget of the last Labour
Government, 2 pages were devoted to farming, mainly stating that the Government would
continue the subsidies on this and that. The 1975 Budget had no new policies, even though
farmers were in a state of despair beyond words. The farming community had lost its
confidence. The 1975 Budget stated that farming was at a low ebb, but all the former Labour
Government could muster was 2 pages devoted to continuing policies. In 1976 the first
National Government Budget devoted six pages to new policies for farming, the 1977 Budget
devoted 4 pages, and the 1978 Budget devotes eight pages.
One policy in particular captured my imagination, because it is forward looking and
innovative. It is headed “Commercial trials of new horticultural crops". Unfortunately, it
has been ignored by the press, but it is worth discussing. The Budget states: "In order to
encourage the establishment of commercial-size trial blocks of new crops the Government
proposes to make available interest-free suspensory loans towards the cost of planting and


## p. 743 (#751) ############################################

8 June
743
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
growing such blocks. . . . This scheme will commence next year, when supplies of planting
material for some of the new crops will become available." New crops are under research
and will be included in the scheme. The new crops have a promising export potential. The
scheme is designed to reduce the time lag between the research and the establishment of a
crop by offering selected growers in certain regions suspensory loans to cover the cost of
planting and growing the crops. The programme must be monitored for results and for the
potential of the crop. It is necessary to assess production, the cost of production, and the
market potential. It is also necessary to obtain a foothold in new markets. The new
horticultural crops envisaged include blueberries, sour cherries, macadamia nuts,
persimmons, cherrimoya, and certain types of guava. The crops are a new venture and are
slowly being established. I trust that this policy will take on with the farming community and
that it will seek further research into commercial crops.
One of the most amazing pieces of information to come my way in recent years is that
soya beans are the largest single earner of foreign exchange in the United States of America.
New Zealand cannot grow that type of bean, but there is no reason why, with a little
scientific knowledge, trial, and technology, we could not find a type suitable to New
Zealand. We would then be able to develop a market for the production and export of soya
beans.
I was also interested to learn, when investigating this new policy, that the Minister of
Agriculture, having decided that something needed to be done in horticulture, had set up
two export symposia. One was held in December of last year, and one in April of this year.
As a result of these symposia, a horticulture export development committee has been
established which has as its thrust and terms of reference the development of new export
fields and technology and attitudes in marketing and research. I commend the Minister for
this and trust that the committee will go from strength to strength and come up with enough
ideas, policies, and recommendations for export promotion. It has long been recognised that
New Zealand has to diversify, not only in its markets but also in its products. This new policy
is a very practical step towards that end. When one is selling one focuses on the needs of the
seller, but when one is marketing, one must focus on the needs of the buyer. Until the last
few years we have always been sellers. Now we are faced with the fact and the realisation
that we are marketers, and we have to learn the techniques of marketing amd marketing
promotion. The new policy is a very worth-while step along those lines, because it
emphasises exports.

Another aspect of the Budget that has been welcomed in New Plymouth is the regional
investment allowance for New Plymouth and Bell Block, which was increased from 5 percent
to 15 percent. The move has been greeted warmly by the people in my electorate. Curiously,
the investment allowances were first introduced at a higher rate in 1973-74 and maintained
by the Labour Government when the city of New Plymouth was booming. At that stage the
city was creaking under the weight of two of the largest capital works programmes ever
embarked on in New Zealand-Maui and the New Plymouth thermal power station.
Physical resources were stretched to the limit, and there was a shortage of houses and rental
accommodation. Builders could not cope with the demand and business activity was hectic.
At that stage the Labour Government introduced a regional investment allowance for New
Plymouth and Bell Block to encourage growth. At the time when the growing pains were at
their worst, the Labour Government added fuel to the fire. Builders from outside the region
arrived to share in the bonanza. Solicitors, accountants, estate agents and businessmen
established construction companies to get in on the act. New businesses based on growth
sprang up-businesses based on the unsustainable growth that the Labour Government had
helped to create.
On taking office the National Government was faced with the inevitable task of
dampening down activity to a sustainable level. One of the measures taken was a reduction
of the regional investment allowance to 5 percent. This, combined with the winding down of
the power station and on-shore Maui projects, has seen a reduction in building activity.
Business activity has also slowed down. The withdrawal pains of this unavoidable
readjustment have been unpleasant, and no one in the region would like to see them
repeated.
During that winding down operation I kept a close watch on the state of the building
industry. On a number of occasions I sought, and was granted, early introduction of
Government construction projects to help cushion the downturn. The co-operation I
received from a number of Ministers was greatly appreciated. I am concerned that, because
of the present level of building activity in New Plymouth, the industry is suffering through
lack of work. This lack of work for a sector of the industry is apparent, despite the fact that
the level of housing activity in the New Plymouth urban area is at present greater than in any
other comparable provincial city, other than Whangarei. The provisional figures for the 12
months to November 1977, which are the latest figures available, show that, on a population
basis the rate of house and flat construction in the New Plymouth urban area is 35 percent
above Wanganui and 130 percent about Napier, to name only two other cities. Furthermore,
our building industry is now operating at a level in excess of that achieved in Wanganui and
Gisborne at the peak of the building boom, and is equalling that reached in Hamilton and
Rotorua at the peak of that boom.
By the standards of any other comparable city, the New Plymouth building industry is
operating at a very healthy level, but is still feeling the pain of reduced activity. The obvious
question is, why? It is evident, when compared with other districts, that housing activity in

Before I leave housing, it is interesting to note in the Opposition's alternative budget
the statement about the introduction of variable mortgage repayments. A variable mortgage
repayment system exists now. Obviously, Labour members think it is a good idea, and that
they should keep it. That is a most sincere form of flattery. The alternative budget states that
mortgage lending will be based on the principle of 1 day's pay for 1 week's mortgage. That is
a high-sounding and impressive approach. To my mind it is really an exercise in deceptive
packaging-something of a con job.
Members opposite are saying that charges will remain about the same, because they
know, or should know, that Housing Corporation charges vary according to income and
family size. Let us take the example of a family with two children and with a first mortgage of
$20,000 from the Housing Corporation. If the breadwinner earns $95 a week, the interest
rate is 3 percent; at $130 a week it is 5 percent; at $170 a week it is 7.5 percent; and at $175 a
week it is 8.5 percent. If we look at the charges we find that a person with a 3 percent loan
pays $22 a week, which works out at 23 percent of his income, or almost 1 day's pay. A
person with a 5 percent loan pays 21.5 percent of his income, or about 1 day's pay. A person
with the 6.5 percent loan pays 19.5 percent of his income; therefore, having read the Labour
Party's recent announcements, I imagine that that person's charges would be increased
because he is at present paying less than 1 day's pay. For the person on $175 a week with an
8.5 percent loan the charges are $35 a week-20 percent, or 1 day's pay. All the Opposition
is saying is that it will continue what the National Government has shown to be a sound and
sensible housing policy, but it will dress it up with all sorts of bows and call it by other names.
Why does the Labour Party not just endorse the present policy? Why must it put on
embellishments and say it has a bold new policy with new ideas? When we look into the
policy we find the ideas are not new. Nothing is new; what is suggested is being done now.
We introduced the variable mortgage repayment system, which members opposite claim as
the cornerstone of their housing policy.

Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment Bill
FRIDAY, 9 JUNE 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Usual business, including the Budget
debate, will continue next week, except on Wednesday afternoon, when private members'
notices of motion will be discussed.
PRIVATE INVESTIGATORS AND SECURITY GUARDS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Private Investigators
and Security Guards Amendment Bill be introduced. The Private Investigators and Security
Guards Act 1974 provides for the control by a licensing and disciplinary authority of both
private investigators and security guards, together with their employees.
Under the Act, the Registrar of Private Investigators and Security Guards controls
those who undertake any class of business that falls within the definition of a private
investigator or security guard. Experience from the working of the Act has disclosed that
although its basic purpose has been effected, some matters of a mainly procedural nature
require legislative attention. The Bill amends both the substantive and procedural provisions
of the Act in a number of ways. The most significant substantive changes relate to the
definition of “private investigator" and to the form of a security guard's licence. With
respect to the definition of private investigator, the Bill provides that a person is not to be
considered to be carrying on the business of a private investigator if he does something only
as a necessary, usual, or reasonable incident of any undertaking that is not covered by the
defintion of private investigator.
At present, a person whose activities could not be considered to be those of a private
investigator but nevertheless fall within the scope of the present definition, must be excluded
from the ambit of the Act by an Order in Council. The new definition will obviate the need
for such a procedure without extending the definition to those who are currently specifically
excluded from the definition of private investigator.
The amendment to the provision dealing with a security guard's licence will allow the
registrar to issue a licence limited to a specified class of business. Under the present
provisions of the Act, a person who is issued with a licence may have sought that licence to
allow him to carry on the business of guarding property. However, there is nothing to
prevent him from carrying on the business of offering electronic surveillance assistance
although he may not be a suitable person to carry on such a business. Under the provisions of
the Bill, the registrar is empowered to issue a licence in those circumstances with respect
only to the guarding business. The procedural amendments relate in the main to the renewal
of licences and certificates of approval for employees.
Much of the need for change has arisen from the practice of issuing a new licence or
certificate of approval, rather than endorsing the fact of renewal on the original document,
and this in turn has become necessary having regard to the need to issue a licence or
certificate together with a photograph in a sealed tamper-proof plastic envelope. Although it
is mainly procedural I will be proposing that the Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision
Committee.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I did not hear whether the Minister said he intended
to send the Bill to a committee.
Hon. David Thomson: Yes.
Mr PREBBLE: And it will be open to the news media?
Hon. David Thomson: Yes.
Mr PREBBLE: I am pleased to hear that, because Bills of this sort should go to a
committee. Bills having anything to do with security guards or private investigators should
be considered carefully by Parliament to make sure that we are not, by licensing, giving the


## p. 756 (#764) ############################################

756
9 June
Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment Bill
stamp of approval to private police forces. Looking through the Bill I am a little concerned
that, although we may think we are controlling security guards, we may as a Parliament be
setting up private police forces. That would be very wrong, because it is the prerogative of
the Crown-the duty of the State-to provide security; it is not for other people to have their
own private police forces. That is the sort of society most of us are opposed to. Probably the
Government itself is officially opposed to it. I just draw attention to the fact that we have yet
another Bill of this sort, and we should look at it extremely carefully.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I repeat that the Bill will be sent to the
Statutes Revision Committee and that the committee will be open to the press, as is normal.
In fact, I recall that last year, with every Bill that went to a select committee, the proceedings
were open to the press. I would be surprised if the press was present and showed any
curiosity about the Bill. It is mainly procedural. What the member for Auckland Central is
concerned about was available under the Labour Government's Act, which was too wide.
The Bill proposes to confine the licence to certain classes of business only, so that there
cannot be a licence that could allow for what he called a private police force, or something
like that. Under the Labour Government's Act that could have been possible. We propose
to confine it to specific classes of business that the applicant proposes to carry out.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I move, That the Private Investigators and Security Guards
Amendment Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee, and that the proceedings of the
committee during the hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news

QUESTIONS-ORAL
General Election-Informal Votes
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: What were the major reasons
for the number of informal votes cast at the 1975 general election, does the Electoral Office
intend to conduct an advertising campaign about the correct and necessary procedures for
enrolment and voting, and, if so, will he give details?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): An informal vote is one in which the
intention of the elector is not clear. The total number of informal votes in 1975 was 8287. No
information is recorded about the reasons for informal votes. Indeed, it would be impossible
under our system to get such reasons. Arrangements have been made to mount an
advertising campaign through newspapers, radio, and television during June and July,
explaining the procedures and encouraging enrolment. After the rolls have been printed and
distributed early in September the same facilities will be used to encourage electors to check
the printed rolls and ensure that they are enrolled. This will continue into October. In the
period immediately preceding the poll, arrangements are being made to explain special
voting facilities and encourage electors to vote on polling day.

percentage increase in exports for the 1976, 1977 and 1978 export years?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): The
percentage increase in total exports for the year ended June 1976 was 47 percent, and, for

Food-Exporting Countries-Price-Fixing Cartel
3. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he seen the
report in the Evening Post of 1 June 1978 in which it is claimed that the world's four major
food-exporting countries are moving closer to the formation of an OPEC-type price-fixing
cartel, and, if so, has New Zealand been consulted by the nations concerned and is the


## p. 757 (#765) ############################################

9 June
757
Questions-Oral
Government in support of the proposal involving Canada, the United States, Argentina, and
Australia?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): Unhappily, I
am not able to be as brief with this one as with the previous question. It is rather complex. I
did see the report in the Evening Post of 1 June 1978. I also read the report in that same
newspaper on 2 June 1978, which reported the strong denial of the United States that it
would back any world food price-fixing cartel. New Zealand has not been approached by the
Government of any of the four countries mentioned to support any OPEC-type price-fixing
arrangement, and I do not think that we would support such a proposal if one were received.
We have, however, been concerned at the effects of subsidised exports of dairy products on
world prices, and we are currently members of agreements on minimum price levels for some
dairy products. We hope that these arrangements will be extended in the current GATT
multilateral trade negotiations. The intention is simply to allow a reasonable return to
efficient producers, in the face of heavily subsidised exports. It is not to set prices at any
unreasonable level, which would obviously be impossible when the international market has
in fact a surplus of such products. We have not made any such proposals on beef. Generally,
I would regard OPEC-type proposals on beef or dairy products as impractical, given the
international market situation.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Could the Minister tell the House whether the Government has
made an approach to any or all of the four countries mentioned in the question on direct
action against subsidised agricultural exports?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: As far as I know, we have not recently made any
direct approach on this specific subject, although our attitude is made well known to those
countries in international forums when we have discussions with them, including, of course,
GATT.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can I take it then from the Minister's reply that the Government will
still rely purely on any success it may achieve in the current GATT negotiations, rather than
try to arrange direct mutual action with these countries?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Our main thrust is in GATT-first, in the GATT
dairy subgroup, in which New Zealand is pressing for improvements in the current minimum
price arrangements for dairy products. The existing arrangements are the GATT minimum
price agreement on skim milk powder and the OECD agreement on whole milk powder. We
would like to see that extended to cover dairy products such as butter. Those are the
agencies with which we are working, as well as in the context of the MTN talks that are
currently proceeding, and which we trust the Minister will be able to attend.

Lake Rotorua-Preservation
11. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Works and Development: In
view of the National Party's manifesto promise to undertake "positive and co-ordinated
programmes for the preservation of rivers and lakes under threat of eutrophication", can he
state what positive progress has been made with the preservation of Lake Rotorua?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): Progress has been made on
lake level control structures for both Lake Rotorua and Lake Rotoiti, on the Utuhina
Stream flood control works, on the design of upper catchment soil conservation works, and
on negotiations with landholders affected by the works. Water rights have been obtained by
the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission for the lake level control structures, and detailed
design is proceeding. Approval of the Utuhina Stream flood control works has been given,
and works are about to begin. Soil conservation works to reduce erosion by retiring stream
edges and tree planting have been designed for some of the tributaries, and negotiations with
the farmers concerned have started. Discussions have been held with the Tauranga County
over likely offset works required in the Lower Kaituna River as a result of the upper
catchment works. Future progress in implementing the comprehensive scheme will depend
very largely on the availability of favourable rates of grants for the works, and that, in turn,
depends upon local authorities demonstrating their practical acceptance of the whole
scheme. So far, Rotorua City has shown no positive indication that it will accept and
promote works to remove its sewage discharge from the lake. The discharge contributes a
significant and growing proportion of nutrient material to the lake, and its removal is a vital
part of the comprehensive scheme.

17. Mr WETERE (Western Maori), on behalf of Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori), to the
Minister of Maori Affairs: Can he indicate how many wardens are registered under the
provisions of the Maori Welfare Act 1962, and how many of these wardens are registered in
each of the nine Maori district councils of New Zealand?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): There are 686 wardens registered
under the Maori Welfare Act 1962, and they are registered in each of the nine Maori district
councils of New Zealand as follows: Taitokerau, 112; Auckland, 33; Waikato-Maniapoto,
110; Waiariki, 87; Tairawhiti, 127; Aotea, 105; Ikaroa, 68; Wellington 21; and Te
Waipounamu, 23.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: Are the wardens' expenses, partially or totally,
being met from the Maori Affairs vote, or from any other Government source?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: They are not being met totally, but I understand that some
expenses are met from time to time.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: How many of the wardens are Pacific Island
Polynesians or Fijians?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I have not that information at the moment. I can get it if the
honourable member cares to ask a separate question.

Information Classification, Government Departments
20. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Prime Minister: Has the committee which the
Government established to look at the classification of information by Government
departments and agencies as reported in the New Zealand Herald of 6 May 1978 been
meeting regularly, will its report be made available to Parliament, and, if so, when?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The committee has not yet met.
Membership has been settled and an executive officer appointed. The executive officer is
preparing agenda papers for the first meeting, which will be held shortly. I expect the
committee to present its report to me early in 1979. As to whether it will be a report to
Parliament, this will depend to some extent on the contents, because part of the order of
reference is the question of highly secret information. It may be that the report to Parliament
would not be the total amount of the report to the Minister and to the Government, but
really that is a matter for decision in the future.
Mr Hunt: Can the Prime Minister indicate who the executive officer is, and when a press
statement will be released to show the membership of this group?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, I do not know who the executive officer is. He will be
from the State Services Commission, I imagine. The chairman of the committee will be Sir
Alan Danks, and one member is Professor Keith, Dean of the Law Faculty at Victoria
University. The other members are from the State Services Commission, the Prime
Minister's Department, the Department of Justice, the Ministry of Defence, and the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs, but frankly I do not know who the individuals are.
Mr Prebble: Will this committee to look into open government have any sessions open
to the news media, or is it to be a secret committee on open government?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The question is rather naive, because I cannot visualise any
Government having open meetings of a committee dealing with secret information. The
honourable member should have a look at the Powles report and then he will get a better
idea than he has at the moment.
Mr Hunt: In view of the fact that the Powles report was commissioned by the Labour

concerned the State Services Commission, the Prime Minister's Department, which is

responsible for security, the Department of Justice, the Ministry of Defence, and the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs-are all involved with security, particularly security of

Coal Production
21. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone), to
the Minister of Energy: Is it a fact, as indicated in the report of the International Energy
Agency recently released, "that the Mines Department will not expand production until a 70
percent extraction rate for coal is reached"?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The Minister of Energy replies: "The
recent International Energy Agency report on New Zealand's energy programme does not
say 'that the Mines Department will not expand production until a 70 percent extraction rate
for coal is reached, and in fact that is not so. The mines division of the Ministry of Energy
will very soon have the capacity to expand production greatly. This will be provided by new
mines at Huntly and later on at Ohai. It is true, however, that the mines division is looking
into the development of improved technology for future underground coal mines and has
adopted a recovery rate of 70 percent as its target."
Family Planning Teaching in the Schools
22. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the Minister of
Education: Has he seen the article in the Press of 2 June headed "Family planning in
Christchurch moves into a new era", wherein it is stated that "A recent circular from the
Department of Education warned teachers that prosecution could result from their even
mentioning contraception in primary schools"; can he confirm that such a letter was sent;
and, if so, can he explain why?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I have seen the article in the Press of 2
June headed "Family planning in Christchurch moves into a new era", and noted the
reference to a circular dated 17 April 1978 dealing with section 3 of the Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977, which I sent to all schools. The circular was prepared
because section 3 refers to principals, school committees, boards of governors, and
integrated schools and I decided that, because there might be difficulties with interpretation,
guidelines should be provided for these groups. Misinterpretation of the intent of the Act by
a teacher could result in serious consequences.

Bridge Standards
25. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Works and Development: How
many bridges in New Zealand are below the classified standard of the highways they are built
on, and how many require attention to bring them up to a high standard?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): On State highways
throughout the country there are 66 bridges with statutory loading limitations below those
applying to the highway on which they are built. Of these, 44 are included in the current
3-year bridging programme. In addition, other bridges are being strengthened as necessary
to provide for the highest possible loading standards.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Can the Minister tell us how much money has been set aside for this
3-year programme?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I cannot tell the member the amount that has been set aside, but I
can tell him that, because of Government grants and new arrangements that give the
National Roads Board a record income of $160 million this year, the bridging programme is
on a scale that was not possible with the amounts made available by the Labour
Government.
Mr Schultz: The Minister has said that 66 bridges are substandard. Can he say how
many substandard bridges there were during the Labour Government's term of office, and
whether any of them were included in a replacement programme?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: At the end of 1975, there were 83 substandard bridges.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Can the Minister say how many bridges were upgraded during the
term of the Labour Government?
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Not many.
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: I repeat the comment of the Prime Minister that not many were
upgraded. The Waiau Bridge was given no attention. It is a critical link in the South Island,
and is costing $3 million to upgrade.
Redwood-Proposed Secondary School
26. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: What progress has been
made on a proposal to establish a high school at Redwood in Christchurch?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): A site has been acquired in Tuckers
Road for the establishment of a new high school. The Ministry of Works and Development
has been asked to prepare preliminary layout plans and costs to enable consideration to be
given to seeking the Government's approval for the establishment of the school.
Mr Marshall: Is it possible for the Minister to give any idea of timing if the normal
processes are followed?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It was originally thought that the school would be needed in
about 1980. However, a recent review shows that rolls in the district are static or even
declining, so the date has been put back to 1983 at the earliest. The date will be kept under
review, and could be postponed even further, because it would be ridiculous to build a school
if existing high schools have diminishing rolls.
Mr Quigley: Is this because of growth in other parts of Christchurch, which assume

To all intents and purposes, our way of life depends upon the strength of the farming
sector. The capacity of our farmers to convert grass into feed, which they do more efficiently
that their counterparts anywhere else in the world, is the basis upon which all the things we
have been talking about rest. It is the bulwark of our welfare State, and it is the bastion of
our living standards. The budget acknowledges and recognises our continuing dependence,
as a people and as a total community, upon agricultural productivity. In particular, it
recognises that, as a result of a unique combination of circumstances that beset the industry
in the past season-natural problems such as flooding and drought, and marketing problems,
and in particular static prices-a response from the Government was needed.
The Government has provided a two-pronged response-first, a capital injection, and,
secondly, a major raft of production-related measures, of which the creation of a new
minimum price is the key. In short, the Budget says that the agricultural measures will
provide an assured and realistic base for forward planning. Farmers will benefit-of course
they will-but it is more complex than that. The total New Zealand community will benefit.
To say that farmers alone will benefit is to take a simplistic view. The fortunes of us all are
inextricably linked with the efforts of our primary producers. I believe there is now a better
understanding of and inter-relation between primary producers and other sectors of the
community. Much of the credit for that and other things lies with the Prime Minister, who
has explained to group after group throughout the country the facts of economic life in
simple terms and plain language.
Because the strength of the farming community is a matter of absolute importance for
all of us, I should have thought that Labour members would say of the farming sections of
the Budget, "Well, fair enough." But no, they are not doing that. Instead Opposition
members are subjecting us to their usual carping criticism, which can probably best be
summed up in the constantly recurring suggestion that the Budget is a "rural seats retention
scheme". No wonder the member for Sydenham, who is trying to interject, is not interested
in the farmers. No wonder that, when the Labour Party was last put to the test at the ballot
box, it came third in a rural seat. I have no doubt that it will continue to come third in future
elections.
The 1978 Budget concentrates on the basics-productivity, the farming sector, the
fishing industry, which has had a further boost, and tourism, which has also had another
boost. The measures in the Budget also provide more than $300 million worth of tax relief,
and demonstrate the Government's continuing attention to the needs of the family and
practical concern for the less fortunate.

If this principle applied at the moment, members of the Maori Battalion would not have
had to pay the 10 percent tax when they visited the graves of their fallen colleagues on Crete.
The Government is hated by the travelling citizens of New Zealand. It is unfair that a New

The Government talks about making New Zealand a better country and supporting the
