It has been suggested that I should rule out on two grounds the notice of motion given
by the honourable member for New Plymouth. The first ground was that the notice of
motion seeks to link Opposition members with the Communist Party, with Trotskyites, and,
I suppose, with stirrers. Those are the three different categories of people mentioned in the
notice of motion-communists, Trotskyites, and stirrers. The second ground was based on
whether it is in order for members in the House to use the references made about people
outside the House, and I have been referred to Speaker's ruling 82/1, which provides that
temperate and decorous language should be used with regard to persons outside Parliament.
That is true. Nevertheless, it does not prevent us, as members, from making references that
are not decorous or temperate about people outside Parliament if we believe it is necessary
to do so.
I believe that the right of free speech should be uninhibited in Parliament, so long as it is
used responsibly-and that is a matter not for me to judge in this instance, but for
honourable members to judge themselves when they refer to people outside the House. Of
course, it is quite beyond the scope of my jurisdiction to say whether a member is sheltering
behind the rules of the House if he makes such an accusation, because that is his business,
not mine. The main point at issue is really whether the notice of motion links members of the
Opposition-members of Parliament-with the Communist Party and Trotskyites, as some
members have claimed that it does.
The notice of motion was referred to me, and I looked at it very carefully because I
knew there would be some suggestion that this had happened. It seems to me that the main
reference is to two Labour Party candidates, one a Ms Shields and the other a Mr Pickering,
and it asks whether the Leader of the Opposition would explain their presence in the
company of the other people mentioned. I am not sure whether the Leader of the
Opposition is responsible for their presence, but I suppose that is a matter for debate.
Certainly whether he can explain their presence on a march or in any other situation is a
matter for debate.
The other question is whether those candidates should refuse to recognise the rule of
law. That again is not within my jurisdiction, but it is a matter for debate. As I see it, it is
really a matter of my having to decide whether the notice of motion issues a charge against
members of the Parliamentary Labour Party, as members of Parliament, of being associated
directly with the Communist Party or with the Trotskyites, to which they have taken
exception; and I have said that I would rule against any reference linking them in that way.
My jurisdiction is only within the Chamber, within the House, so it makes it somewhat
difficult for me to say it is impossible for members of the Labour Party, members of the
National Party, or members of the Social Credit Political League outside of Parliament to be
within my jurisdiction, and I do not think I can. There is, of course, the insinuation-there is
no charge-that the people are members of the Communist Party. The advertisement
referred to in the notice of motion simply asks why those people had asked all
Wellingtonians to join them in a protest march, and then the list of people was given
underneath.
I think the notice of motion is fairly close to the borderline, but as it does not involve
members of Parliament I thought it was only reasonable to allow it to come forward. I
reiterate that if it had involved members of Parliament in a way I think is undesirable I would
certainly not have allowed it to come forward as a notice of motion. I think perhaps we can
decide whether the wording of notices of motion is a matter of taste or of judgment. As
things stand at the moment, I do not think it is within my jurisdiction to rule them out. Some
members may regret that they have been put in, as much as some members may dislike the

QUESTIONS-ORAL
Electoral Boundaries
1. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Justice: In view of the confusion
about electoral boundaries that exists both inside and outside his department will he, as a
matter of urgency, arrange for the compilation of the Index of Places and Streets Showing
Electorates and No-licence Districts for the present new electorates, as has been done with
every Representation Commission report since 1952?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): There is no confusion within my
department about electoral boundaries. Electoral offices are becoming familiar with the
changes and have information available to answer questions and clarify situations as they
arise. The Index of Places and Streets is prepared for electorates by electorate officers during
the process of reallocating electorates to electors following the boundary changes. In the past
it has been printed and available for use at the poll, when its prime purpose is to assist
electors seeking special votes to ensure that their vote is cast for the correct electorate. On
this occasion the index will be prepared by using a computer, and it is planned to have it
available by October, in ample time for the conduct of the poll.
Mr Prebble: How can the Minister claim that there is no confusion within his
department when, in my own electorate of Auckland Central, the people in No. 4 Home
Street have been advised that they are in Auckland Central, those at No. 2 in Mt. Albert,
and those at No. 8 in Auckland Central? In fact, they are all in the Mt. Albert electorate.
The people in Kiwi Street have been told that they are in Waiheke, which is in Auckland
Central, when, in fact, they are in Mt. Albert. People in Park Road have been told that they
are in Auckland Central, when, in fact, they are in Remuera, but the electoral officer, when
challenged, said they were in Mt. Eden.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: If the member has difficulty in finding the answer from the
electoral officers he should certainly put the matter to me, and I shall inquire from the head
office of the department.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: What is the Minister's explanation for the delay in compiling the
index of streets for new electorates until October? The index could be prepared at once,
because, obviously, the boundaries are now fixed.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: As I told the House in my original answer, the purpose of the
index is to assist electors seeking special votes to ensure that their vote is cast in the correct
electorate. Therefore, plans have been made for this index to be available by October, in
ample time for the conduct of the poll.
Mr Hunt: Why does the Minister's original answer mention October when a week or
two ago I was told by the Chief Electoral Officer, in answer to a telephone inquiry, that the
publication would be released in late June or early July?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I must accept the honourable member's word that he was
told "late June or early July”, but in my original answer I gave the information supplied by
the Chief Electoral Officer.
Mr Rogers: Can the Minister explain why some electoral officers do not have a new
map or any map-showing the electoral boundaries?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: If the member would indicate to me which electoral officer
lacks this information, I shall certainly see that the omission is corrected.
Mr Prebble: Is it correct that the index could be produced immediately from the
information now available?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, I can give the member no such assurance.

Shipment of Meat-Cost
6. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Transport: Has he read the statement
of Mr Gerdelan, Secretary of the Harbour Board Employees Union, as reported in the
Gisborne Herald of Tuesday, 9 May 1978, that “it costs $17 per tonne to ship meat overseas
from Gisborne as opposed to $65 per tonne for railing it to Wellington and putting the meat
on a container ship to Europe", and can he tell the House (a) whether the quoted figures are
correct; and (b) who pays?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I have read the statement made
by the secretary of the Harbour Board Employees Union on the cost of shipping meat to
Europe from Gisborne and from Wellington. I am not aware how Mr Gerdelan derived his
figures, nor am I aware of any freight rate existing for meat shipments from Gisborne as, in
fact, no such service exists. The comparison is merely hypothetical and assumes that there is
a conventional shipping service operating with the required frequency to move the relatively
small quantities of meat that would be exported through the port of Gisborne. In drawing
any comparisons it must be realised that it is not economic to maintain a large fleet of
conventional ships that are both time and labour intensive to uplift relatively small
quantities. The principle behind New Zealand's entry into containerisation has always been
to reduce the number of vessels servicing our trade. On the question of who pays in Mr
Gerdelan's example, under the scheme aggregating meat cargoes to the container ports the
meat trade as a whole, through the freight rate, pays.
Mr Bell: Could the Minister confirm that he was referring to the shipping of
containerised meat out of the port of Gisborne as opposed to the port of Wellington, and
that considerable quantities of meat are still shipped out of Gisborne in traditional vessels?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: My information is that the shipping of meat for export
out of Gisborne stopped in 1974.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: In view of the Minister's comment that there is no such service,
what ideas does he have to encourage the use of the port of Gisborne?
Mr SPEAKER: That is outside the scope of the original question. The member may ask
such a question later, but not now.
Prescriptions and Medicines-Charge on Patients
7. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Health: How many medicines
formerly on the free list to patients at 1 January 1976 have now become the subject of either
a part charge or full charge on patients, and what prescriptions have been so affected?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Sixty-six medicines formerly on the free list to
patients on 1 January 1976 have now become the subject of either a part charge or full charge
to patients. This action was taken on the recommendation of an expert committee
comprising doctors in active practice who considered that there was a sufficient range of
cheaper products available free of charge. There are also 17 individual brands of certain
medicines for which there are identical drugs available at a lower price. There are also five


## p. 799 (#807) ############################################

13 June
799
Questions-Oral
medicines that have become a full charge on the patient because clinical judgment is now
that they are no longer suitable therapy. I would add that, since 1 January 1976, 56 items
have been added to the drug tariff and qualify under the pharmaceutical benefit scheme.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Was the main consideration in removing items from the free list the
cost of the product, or was it an attempt by the Government to reduce the cost of
prescriptions generally?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The whole programme tends to hold down the price of prescriptions.
The fact that an eye is kept on what is happening also tends to lower the price. Apart from
the five medicines that have been removed because the clinical judgment is that they are no
longer suitable therapy, the main consideration was that a similar drug, perhaps under a
different brand name, was available considerably more cheaply. In such an instance, a part
charge that is the difference between the lower and the higher price is introduced. When a
patient is wedded to a particular brand-perhaps having a psychological belief in it-a
doctor may apply to the Department of Health and seek approval for that patient to receive
that drug free.
Mr W. R. Austin: Can the Minister confirm that, because of the implementation of this
policy, more patients are being adequately treated for the same amount of money?
Mr SPEAKER: That is an interesting question, but it is unrelated to either the original
or the supplementary questions.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: As patients pay for the prescription, but do not write it, has the
medical profession been advised of the position outlined in the Minister's original answer?
Hon. T. F. GILL: If the member means policy, I think that is widely understood. If he
means individual cases, clinical newsletters every month advise the medical profession and
chemists of changes.

Road Safety Advertising on Television
9. Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of Transport:
How much has been expended on television advertising for road safety purposes in the last
12 months, and how much was expended on such television advertising immediately before
this year's Queen's Birthday weekend, aimed specifically at warnings about holiday road
travel?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): A total of $77,000 has been spent
by the Ministry of Transport on television advertising for road safety purposes in the last 12
months. Of this amount, $26,000 was spent on the television advertising part of a $61,000
follow-up campaign on the new traffic regulations in October and November last year. The
remaining $51,000 was spent on the recent seat belt campaign. Although the seat belt
publicity continued right through Queen's Birthday weekend, there was no television
advertising aimed at holiday road travel as such. However, as is common practice before and
during any holiday weekend, local media statements were made by Ministry of Transport
officers, and these contained holiday travel advice.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Was any of the money expended aimed specifically at the
hazards of drinking and driving?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: It is true that the Ministry of Transport and the
Government consider that programmes should be aimed at a particular cause that is
prominent in road accidents. It is also considered that publicity is more effective if limited to
the type of advertisement seen on television. This year the ministry's road safety advertising
will concentrate on seat belts, drinking and driving, and further publicity on the new
transport regulations if the department feels that is required.

Maui-Effect on Imported Fuels
10. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) to the Minister of Energy: What is the estimated saving in

field when it comes on stream?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The Minister of Energy replies:

accelerated production from the Kapuni field. Over the next 2 to 3 years, therefore, oil
import levels can be stabilised, with reductions in oil use by power stations and some large
industries being offset by possible growth from the transport sector. At an equivalent import
value of around $2/GJ, the Maui-Kapuni field production is estimated to be worth about

Tourist Numbers and Accommodation
14. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Tourism: What are the projected
figures for increase in tourist numbers over the next 5 years, and how much additional
accommodation will be required to cope with this increase?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): Provisional projections which are now
being considered by the Tourism Advisory Council envisage an increase in overseas visitors
from 390 940 in 1977-78 to 489 500 in 1981-82. Based on earlier surveys of overseas visitor
requirements, it is likely that up to half of the accommodation for these additional visitors
will be provided in private homes. There is also some unused capacity in commercial
accommodation in many centres. More hotel rooms will, however, be required in some
areas. Provisional estimates for the 3 years from 1977 to 1980 indicate a need for 925 new
hotel rooms in nine key areas that account for more than 80 percent of the hotel
accommodation required by overseas visitors.

The Opposition's tourism policy has never been laid so bare as in the speech of the member
for Sydenham. It is a skinny policy. The member for Sydenham contributed nothing to the
debate, on tourism or anything else. His concern for tourism would have been much more
apparent if he had apologised for the disastrous 3 years, from 1972 to 1975, of Labour's
administration of tourism, led by his colleague the member for Southern Maori, who
bungled and interfered her way through the 3 years by stifling and interfering with the efforts

The member for Sydenham spoke of National's 1975 tourist policy, to which I shall rerer
in some detail. He also said that in this year's Budget only 12 lines were devoted to tourism.
He did not tell the House and the country that in the last year of Labour's rule-and I mean
the last year-only six lines were devoted in the Budget to tourism, and that the 1974 Budget
had not one word. If that is not a non-event, I do not know what it is. What is the anti-
achievement Labour Party endeavouring to do? One sometimes wonders. It appears that
Labour members are trying to whip up some sort of emotional doubt on any matter one likes
to mention, with no concern for the sound development of the economy, whether it is
tourism or anything else.
Labour's spokesman on tourism has become known as a specialist in innuendo and
rumour, and he has clearly disclosed the party to be an anti-Air New Zealand party. In fact,
it appears to have a bad attack of "anti-Air New Zealanditis". If its criticism was
constructive, fair enough, but it is destructive. Not one word has been mentioned about the
massive savings in cost with the merger of the airlines or about the new administration that
will give better service domestically and internationally. The airline will be geared to
transporting a maximum number of passengers and a maximum quantity of freight for our
growing tourist markets and our trading partners. Air New Zealand has accepted the task,
and the National Government is supporting it; it is not interfering with the working of the
airline, as Labour would. Throughout the debate it has become evident that Labour is an
anti-development, anti-achievement party. In my 12 years in the House I have never heard
so much hollow, destructive, anti-New Zealand criticism, and so little constructive criticism,
as I have during the past 2½ years. During the past 3 weeks this has been particularly so, and
the Labour spokesman on tourism is a prime example.
Let us look briefly at Labour's so-called alternative budget. It contains an amazing
proposal for a surcharge on foreign exchange. Labour says that all New Zealanders taking
overseas trips more than once every 5 years and using foreign exchange will pay a 10 percent
surcharge. At the same time, the foreign travel tax will be abolished. At first glance this may
look attractive, but at second glance it looks like the old put-and-take trick. When one looks

is going overseas more and more, and the travel industry generally has the message once and
for all on Labour's hollow tourism credibility. Labour's foreign exchange proposal would
completely reverse the trend throughout the world of extensive and regular travel by people
of an increasing number of nations.
There are international signs that tourism is taking on a new importance in international
politics. New technology and economic efficiency in aviation are providing the catalyst and
rapidly making tourism the world's No. 1 industry. It is imperative that New Zealand should
be in on the deal. The present travel boom is looking so attractive to many nations that they
are moving the emphasis from political factors and becoming more concerned with trade and
economics. It is imperative that New Zealand should take part in this move, and the
National Government has taken a big step in that direction. The Tourist and Publicity
Department has been strengthened both at home and abroad. The Ministry of Foreign
Affairs has accepted responsibility for overseas information and publicity, strengthening our
involvement through our diplomatic representatives overseas. New aviation technology is
resulting in a move to low fares being introduced by many international airlines. Air New
Zealand is considering its own position in these new and dramatic moves. If the present
trend continues, the growth of tourism around the world could be as great in the next few
years as in the 1960s, when a great increase occurred.
Through the Government's policies and actions, we are gearing our tourist industry,
which includes our international airline, to cash in on this possible new era of growth that is
not very far away. Future movements of people may be so large that they will raise the
political and social aspirations of the world-and the main impact in future may be at a social
and political level-and be responsible for breaking down many existing barriers. In the time
scale of human history, mass travel and tourism have been in existence for the equivalent of
only a split second. With tourists now beginning to move away from beaten tourist tracks,
out into local indigenous populations and into their natural environments, the new
international, political, and social impact of this will be considerable. This dramatic
development is now coming to a head, with lower international air fares and more people,
both young and old, becoming involved. Of considerable international importance is the
proposal by the 100-member World Travel Association for a bill of rights for tourists and a
code of conduct covering the travel industry and governments worldwide. These may appear
to be futuristic proposals, but they will be considered in detail at the conference of the world
travel organisations in Manila in 1980.
In New Zealand, the tourist industry is keen to respond to both domestic and
international demands. The Government has developed a first-tier industry, recognised in its
budgetary plan as a major source of overseas exchange earnings. Tourism in New Zealand is
a priority industry, but one would not have thought so when listening to the Opposition
spokesman on tourism. I wish to tell the House and the country of some of the achievements,
progress, thrust, and development taking place in this first-tier industry. The Government
has built up a liaison in partnership with the New Zealand tourist industry that is second to
none in any sector.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Who wrote that?
Mr TALBOT: Realistic incentives are being given to the National Travel Association.

on tourist travel. In the same period, Reserve Bank travel receipts rose from $107 million to

million, and that challenge must be accepted by the tourist industry. I believe it will be

of people between countries, with lower fares on airlines, and people of all ages are moving
throughout the world, will have an effect on the development of international understanding
in the coming years.
Steps are now being taken to reverse the downturn in the number of visitors from

through a new promotional campaign being undertaken by Air New Zealand and the Tourist
and Publicity Department. Most encouraging is the growth of tourists from new markets
such as Japan, with an increase of 30.9 percent in the 1977 calendar year, and from Western
Europe, with an increase of 23.4 percent in the same period. In this year's Budget, the

accommodation industry. The TADCO scheme collapsed during the Labour Administra-

essential hotel development in key areas. An example is that the guarantee provided in 1977
for a 120-room town-house hotel in Auckland, which is now being built. It is clear that the
reintroduction of the scheme has stimulated an interest in hotel development, and the latest
proposals, announced in the Budget, will activate the TADCO scheme further.
Domestic tourism, which the Opposition members mention occasionally, has not been
forgotten. More New Zealanders than ever before are travelling within New Zealand. We
have built up a network of motels that is second to none in the world. That accommodation is
being used mainly by the average New Zealander. Camping grounds and facilities are being
expanded, and statistics disclose that the number of caravans owned by New Zealanders has
grown dramatically year by year. The average New Zealander's requirements are being
catered for and extended, with camping grounds, caravans, motel accommodation, and
more sophisticated tourist hotels. The increase in the grant for tourist promotion in the
Budget is of great significance to our tourist industry. Notwithstanding the need for
economic restraint in the public sector, the tourist promotion budget has been increased
from $1.49 million in 1975-76 to $2.298 million in 1978-79. This is in accordance with the
Government's determination to promote tourism actively as a first-tier industry and as a
significant earner of foreign exchange.
Overseas tourist promotion is continuing in close co-operation with the private sector,
and the number and strength of the Government's tourist promotion offices in the major

source of tourists to this country, the Minister of Tourism recently opened in Toronto a new
office. That brings the number of the department's overseas offices to 10 in six countries.
New Zealand's tourist promotion record is quite outstanding when compared with that of
countries such as the United States, which has a budget for foreign tourist promotion of $8.7
million. At present the United States travel service has only six branches overseas-three in

people, is indeed on the job promoting tourism in the major markets. We must do more. We
shall have to open offices in cities such as Chicago, the hub of the United States. However,

in July this year. Our ambassador to GATT and the Secretary-General of that organisation
told me in Geneva earlier this year that it was hoped tariffs could be reduced by an average
of 40 percent on a world-wide basis. These multilateral trade negotiations have received
support from Labour and National Governments since 1974. Against that background the
Labour Party proposes to introduce a tariff of 10 percent on most imported goods, with some
exceptions. Such a proposal would be decried by our trading partners as an unfair and

unacceptable imposition. Years of negotiation for improved trade terms would be swept
aside overnight.
A foreign exchange surcharge would provide the EEC, Japan, Australia, and the
United States with the perfect excuse to raise tariffs against us, reduce quotas, and close
their markets. Although I have no fear that a Labour Government would be elected to

It is one thing for the whiz-kid, the member for Manukau, to dream up absurd domestic
policies such as the baby bonus and the MRP scheme, but it is another thing for the Labour
Party to make off-the-cuff proposals that would endanger our international reputation and
trading prospects. New Zealand has mounted a sustained attack on trade protectionism, and
Opposition members have joined Government members in opposing trade protectionism at
every level. That attack has been undermined by the Labour Party's proposal to suppress
international trade unilaterally. I turn, now, to our international obligations and treaties.
These facile attempts to subvert and repress world trade were foreseen and prohibited by
agreements enforceable by international law. New Zealand is a contracting party to GATT,
and maintains a schedule of tariff concessions on imports from other parties.
The concessions are safeguarded by article 2b and article 2c, which require that products
described in the schedule "shall be exempt from all other duties or charges of any kind
imposed on, or in connection with, importation in excess of those imposed on the date of this
agreement." With even more precision, article 2(3) provides that "no contracting party shall
alter its method of converting currencies so as to impair the value of any of the concessions
provided for in the appropriate schedule." Should even these be too general for members of
the Opposition, I refer to article 8(1)(a), which states that fees or charges imposed in
connection with importation shall be “limited in amount to the approximate cost of services
rendered, and shall not represent an indirect protection to domestic products or taxation of
imports for fiscal purposes."
The limitation is then specifically related, in article 8(4)(2), to charges "imposed by
governmental authorities in connection with exchange control." The prohibition could not
be stated any more clearly. It is a total and absolute prohibition in a document signed by
New Zealand, and observed by New Zealand Governments. The provisions in the
agreement aim directly at the objective of the Labour Party's surcharge, which aims at—and
I quote from page 5 of the document-"curtailing the importing of luxury items and finished
consumer goods . . . while at the same time attacking the problem of excessive importing."
It should not be thought that GATT is a toothless animal to be ignored by New
Zealand. New Zealand is heavily reliant upon the GATT proviso of a 20 percent tariff on our
sheep meats, ensuring that there is a limit to any detrimental effect on New Zealand by the
adoption of EEC sheep meats regulations. Article 23 of GATT expressly provides for action
by countries that feel New Zealand may be nullifying or impairing benefits accruing from the
agreement. That article also provides in unequivocal terms for retaliatory action in
appropriate circumstances. In the existing world trading climate there can be no doubt that
such retaliatory action would be taken, and would be taken joyfully.
Now I turn to the International Monetary Fund. As a member of the IMF New Zealand
is entitled to apply "restrictions on payments and transfers for current international
transactions." However, we are obliged "to remove restrictions as soon as the balance of
payments will allow." The IMF asks annually for justification for the continuation of any
such restrictions. The Labour Party would not apply the surcharge to improve the balance of
payments, but intends to spend the money to reduce taxation. I should be obliged if the next
Opposition speaker would tell me what could happen if the IMF were to say that the balance
of payments no longer justified such a restriction. The IMF could remove that restriction
within a few months of a surcharge being imposed. If that were to happen, would the Labour
Government apply a massive tax bite of $400 million to finance the removal of the currency
tax?
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: You'll frighten yourself into a stupor.
Mr BRILL: The member for Timaru should be expressing concern that the financial and

or will receive more than $250,000 from the stock grant scheme. Some farmers need this
assistance, and the taxpayers have not objected to helping them.
In 1976, the Budget produced by the present Minister of Finance reduced the fertiliser
subsidy by $10 a tonne, which amounted to a reduced subsidy payment of $20 million. In the
1977 Budget, the same Minister of Finance reduced the subsidy yet again by $2.50 a tonne,
which amounted to a total reduction of $5 million, to which must be added the $20 million
from the first year. In election year the Government wants the farmers to vote for the
National Party, so the subsidy is increased by $9.50 a tonne. What has happened? The
subsidy was reduced for 2 years, taking a total of $45 million from the farmers who were
receiving assistance for fertiliser; then they are given back $19 million in election year, and
expected to support the Government and to agree that the Budget is good. Not only that, but
the Government has built in a camouflage as well, because the Budget states that it will
amount to only $7 million this year-not $19 million.
One might ask why, and it is obvious that the Government has cut out the bounty
system, the fertiliser-spreading subsidy. One might wonder why, and I shall tell the member
for Pahiatua, who is trying to interject. Members such as he, and other members sitting
opposite, have no feeling at all for the sharemilkers or the rural transport operators, whom
the bounty subsidy helped. The spreading of fertiliser on dairy farms is in the main done by
the sharemilkers. The Government scrubbed the bounty system, saying, "To hell with the
sharemilker; he does the work. Let the farmer who owns the property get the increase in
fertiliser subsidy." That is the Government's attitude, indicated in the Budget.
What about the transport operator in a rural community, who has spent $30,000,
$40,000, or $50,000 buying expensive machinery to spread the fertiliser? What does the
farmer do when the bounty is cut? He says, "Oh well, I will think about spreading it myself."
The Government does not consider the transport operator who has done the spreading for
many years. It is the farmers' vote that the Government is after, not the votes of those who
service the farmers. The Government does not want the votes of the share milkers, only
those of one class of person in the rural communities-the farmers. Those are the votes the
Government is trying to buy.
I support the minimum price scheme in principle, but I am a little surprised to find that
the Government accepts the socialistic ideas of the Labour Party. I welcome it, because 2
months ago, in a release outlining the Labour Party's agricultural policy, I expressed my
party's belief in the need to ensure an adequate return to efficient farmers. National
members sitting opposite accused me of being socialistic, and sneered at me across the
House. The member for Awarua did that in the Address in Reply debate.

In 1975 there was a downturn in farm incomes. In February the nation stood with bated
breath, because the Labour Prime Minister was to make a great announcement. He said that
$50 million would to to the farmers-$35 million to meat, $15 million to wool, and $1 for

Members opposite obviously have not grasped the significance of the Government's
Budget. In his Budget speech, the Leader of the Opposition complained bitterly that we had
done away with the trigger price. He thought it was bad that there was no further skimming
off in a boom to enable producers to stabilise their own prices. He does not seem to
understand that the stabilisation regulations and administration that we brought in provide
for that. Only the Labour Party would complain about good years, in which New Zealand
goes forward. The supplementary minimum prices operate between the official stabilisation
floor price and the trigger price.
Last week at Massey University, the Leader of the Opposition complained about the
large payment necessary to keep the supplementary minimum price up. He has not realised
that the proposed prices are those estimated, on the best information available, as the
average prices for 1978 and 1979. They have been guaranteed for 2 years. We have allowed
talks to begin forthwith for fine tuning the system, and for further fine tuning with
experience, enabling farmers to plan for production-not only for themselves, but for the
country. The same formula is used for the meat floor price and the meat trigger price: last
year's prices; this year's prices, which are an estimate, and next year's prices, which are a
guestimate.
In the Labour Party's budget we see talk of the abandonment of the wool stabilisation
scheme. I cannot understand the reasoning of Opposition members. In the wool boom the
stabilisation scheme creamed off $27 million in individual accounts, and at the same time
took 3 percent off every kilogram of wool sold. All that money went into the stabilisation
fund, which now stands at about $40 million. When there was a downturn because of the
drought, the drop in prices, and the increase in costs, the farmers were very pleased to have
$26 million given back to them. Much of that money would not have been available had it
been in their hands beforehand.

the Wool Board and the Minister of Agriculture. We have not abandoned the stabilisation

Amendment Bill that I had hoped to introduce last session. In all, the implementation of 12

In the field of family law, the revision of the law on divorce, separation, maintenance,
and custody that I referred to last year will be introduced as soon as possible after the Royal
Commission on the Courts has reported and its views on domestic jurisdiction have been
examined. In addition, the problem of trans-Tasman abduction of children will receive
attention. This question has been of great interest to many people for some time.
Regrettably, the measures contained in the Matrimonial Property Act 1976 are still the
subject of misunderstanding. Although the social justice of the legislation has been widely
recognised, criticism of its operation has attracted much more public attention. As often
happens, the criticism is not always well informed as it is male in origin. A common
misapprehension about the Act is that it requires a couple to sell all their matrimonial
property and split the proceeds down the middle. Honourable members know, of course,
that this is not so. In the large majority of cases the rule is that the value of the home and
chattels is divided equally, with the implementation of the division being a matter for the
parties, or for the court in the absence of agreement. The court has broad powers to do what
is best in all circumstances. Where there are young children the best way might well be for
the party not having custody to be given a charge over the matrimonial home, but, if the
children have left home, the best way may well be to sell the house. In the absence of
agreement between the parties, this kind of decision must be made by the courts after
considering all the circumstances.
Another common misapprehension is that farms and businesses will inevitably have to
be sold as a consequence of court orders under the Act. Equal division of a farm or business
would be rather less common than equal division of the home and chattels, because a farm
business is not shared equally if one party satisfies the court that he or she has clearly made a
greater contribution to the marriage partnership. In deciding on the method of division, the
court must bear in mind the desirability of preserving an existing economic unit, on the one
hand, and, on the other, the need to ensure that the other party, who is usually the wife,
does not have to wait indefinitely for her share. The sale of a going concern will always be
avoided if any other means of financing the departing spouse's share can be found. However,
if social justice requires that a property be sold, as occurred in one case I know of involving a
farm, the courts will not shrink, I believe, from doing what is right. I cannot say that the
implementation of division under the Matrimonial Property Act will always be
straightforward. In some cases it may not be easy to devise another suitable method of
division if cash is not available to pay the share that rightfully belongs to the other party.
I would be the first to concede that there are problems in implementing the legislation in
times of economic difficulty. The same would have applied if the 1963 Act had continued in
force, but critics of last year's Act should not let these problems blind them to its essential
fairness and equity. I think a sensible and sympathetic approach to the new Act should
ensure that in the future fair shares for both husband and wife become the rule and not the
exception.
The report of the Royal Commission on the Courts is taking a little longer than
expected, and members of the next Parliament will no doubt have the opportunity to settle a
court structure that will serve the needs of the country into the twenty-first century. I am well
aware of the great pressure there is from people in the major cities of Auckland, Wellington,
and Christchurch for replacements for their courts. The experiment with small claims courts
appears to have been a success, and the Government is at present considering their extension
to other centres, but further study needs to be done first before we can start planning for the
resources necessary.
This first Parliament of the third National Government's administration will, therefore,
have dealt with all the undertakings of its manifesto policy, and it will have been to a
remarkable degree, I believe, creative in the development of more humane and just law. For
that, I must express my appreciation not only to the Secretary for Justice and his officers, but
also to the members of the Statutes Revision Committee-its chairman, the member for
Birkenhead, and those other able and hard-working members who regularly comprise the
committee.

Standing Orders will need review, but there is no substantial evidence to suggest an urgent
need for major reform of the rules by which we conduct parliamentary Government. We can
have a vigorous debate on the Financial Statement-or the positive Budget, as I regard it—
as we have had tonight and since its presentation by our Prime Minister, the Minister of
Finance. I am quite certain that this Parliament will be a hard-working one, undoubtedly
well controlled by yourself, Mr Speaker, with the assistance of the Leader of the House, and,
I expect, the Leader of the Opposition.
The Budget is a good one, and has been greatly welcomed in my province of Taranaki. I

I thank the Minister. The Budget is a good one, a positive one, and typical of what we can
expect from our present Prime Minister.

Speaker's Ruling-Personal Explanations
WEDNESDAY, 14 JUNE 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SPEAKER'S RULING—PERSONAL EXPLANATIONS
Mr SPEAKER: As some members are apparently confused about procedures for
personal explanations and correcting misrepresentations it might be helpful if I took a
moment or two to explain them.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: What happens if we don't agree?
Mr SPEAKER: A procedure is open to the honourable member. Two of the Standing
Orders deal with explanations by members of their conduct or of words used by them.
Standing Order 169, the so-called misrepresentation Standing Order, states: "Member may
explain his words. A member who has spoken to a question may again be heard to explain
himself in regard to some material part of his speech which has been misquoted or
misunderstood, but he shall not introduce any new matter or interrupt any member
addressing the Chair, and no debatable matter shall be brought forward or debate arise upon
such explanation."
The points to emphasise here are these. It applies to words that a member used in a
debate and that he claims were incorrectly quoted by another member later in the same
debate. The member simply states what the other member quoted him as having said and
then states what in fact he did say. The member has the absolute right to correct the
misrepresentation or misquotation. He should make the correction at the first opportunity-
that is, at the end of the offending speech-but he may defer his correction until he receives
his unrevised Hansard report. He must be brief. He must not introduce new or debatable
.material, and he must confine himself strictly to the correction of the misquotation or
misunderstanding of his own words.
The second Standing Order is 167, which states: "Personal explanation. By the
indulgence of the House a member may explain matters of a personal nature whether or not
there is a question before the House; but such matters may not be debated." The points to
emphasise here are these. Under the Standing Order, the member rises to a point of order
and seeks the leave of the House to make his personal explanation. He has no absolute right,
as he has to correct words used by him in the same debate that he considers to have been
misunderstood or misquoted, and so he rises to a point of order and seeks the leave of the
House. When he has not spoken in the debate, it should be pointed out to him that the
appropriate time to make his personal explanation is when he is called upon to speak; in
other words, if he has an opportunity to speak during the debate, that is the correct time for
him to make his personal explanation.
However, there are exceptions to that. These are when the member considers that his
honour has been impugned. Under those circumstances, normally, the House will grant him
leave to make his personal explanation then and there, although he may still have the
opportunity to speak. When the words were used by him outside the debate that is under
discussion at the time, but not a debate of the same session, or were used by him outside the
House and misquoted or misinterpreted during the current debate in the House, then leave
is not normally granted to him if he still has the opportunity to speak in that debate,
although, of course, the House may take into consideration the lapse of time there may be
before he has the opportunity to explain himself.
The third point arises with the correction of something he has said in the House that he
subsequently finds to be incorrect. Occasionally, we find a member makes a statement, or a
Minister answers a question, and finds later the information he gave was incorrect. It is then
proper for him to seek the leave of the House to make his personal explanation, and,
normally, the House will do that then and there, although there is no question before the
House.
In the first case, that of misrepresentation, the member has the absolute right to correct
the words used by him and misquoted by another member. In the other case, explaining
himself is done with the leave of the House, and that is a matter that needs to be borne in
mind very carefully by members, so that they do not confuse the two procedures, and do not


## p. 845 (#853) ############################################

14 June
845
Speaker's Ruling-Personal Explanations
misuse the second, that of seeking the leave of the House. I hope that this explanation has
made the procedure somewhat clearer to honourable members. I am quite happy to send
them a copy for their guidance.

Unemployment Statistics
14. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Labour: Can he confirm that
the method used to measure unemployment in most OECD countries, such as Australia and
the United States, is by a sample survey technique, while that used by New Zealand relies on
registration, and so no real comparisons can be made?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Labour replies:
"Unemployment statistics are available from household sample surveys in most member
OECD countries. Almost all member countries also collect employment service registration
or unemployment insurance statistics on a monthly or more frequent basis. The number of
registered unemployed in New Zealand can be compared with the registration statistics.
available for other countries. For instance, registered unemployed expressed as a percentage
of the labour force stood at 6.4 percent in Australia and 6 percent in Great Britain at the end
of March 1978. This compares with a corresponding rate of 1.7 percent for New Zealand. At
the end of March 1978 the registered unemployed seeking full-time work in Australia
numbered 409 994, whereas the household survey of registered unemployed also seeking
full-time work numbered 345 300-a difference of 64 694."
Mr Prebble: Can the Minister confirm that if a similar sample survey were used in New
Zealand, our unemployment rate would be about 6 percent, which would be higher than in
countries such as Australia, Great Britain, and the United States?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I cannot confirm that, because the measurement systems
used in producing these figures are the same in Australia and New Zealand. The systems
ascertain the number registered as unemployed, and, having the same yardstick, they can be
properly compared.

Farm Vendor Mortgage Scheme
19. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) to the Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and
Finance Corporation: How many farms have changed hands since the farm vendor mortgage
scheme was introduced?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): The farm vendor finance settlement scheme applied to sale and purchase
agreements entered into on or after 28 July 1977, but which had a date of settlement not
earlier than 1 April 1978. As at 30 May 1978 the bank had approved the following
resettlements under the scheme: bond option, 8 settlements valued at $683,400; guarantee
option, 21 settlements valued at $1,236,760; making a total of 29 settlements valued at $1.9
million.
Mr Cooper: Can the Minister give a brief precis of the difference between a bond option
and a guarantee option?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Briefly, the Rural Bank accepts the role of mortgagee and the
investment of the on-going farmer is satisfied by the issue of the farm vendor finance bond.
Under the guarantee option the vendor takes either a first or subsequent mortgage at the
Rural Bank standard interest rate, and this is guaranteed by the Rural Bank on 50 percent of
the interest earned. The guaranteed mortgage is exempt from income tax.
Immigrants-Knowledge of English
20. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei), on behalf of Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay), to the
Minister of Immigration: How long has it been an essential requirement for intending
immigrants that they should have a knowledge of English; what section of the Immigration


## p. 852 (#860) ############################################

852
14 June
Questions-Oral
Act requires this; and what are the criteria for adjudging adequacy of English, and who
applies them?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): As early as 1899 New Zealand's
immigration legislation included a provision that some prospective immigrants be required
to pass an English language test. Entry to New Zealand is now governed by the Immigration
Act 1964, and there is now no such requirement in the Act, but this requirement has been
accepted as part of entry policy for some years. The Act does not prescribe details of
immigration policy, but directs that entry permits may be granted subject to any conditions
which may be prescribed by regulations under the Act, or which may be imposed by the
Minister of Immigration. The Act itself accordingly does not require immigrants to have an
adequate knowledge of English. Current policy for permanent entry to New Zealand accepts
that one factor that facilitates successful settlement in New Zealand is fluency in English.
Where possible, applicants for permanent entry are interviewed by an officer of the nearest
New Zealand overseas post, to assess this and other factors. If an interview is not possible
the assessment is made on the basis of the applicant's educational attainments and previous
employment history.

Squid
23. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Fisheries: What is the value of squid

Zealand waters have increased each year, and in the last season some 70 000 tonnes were
taken. The actual potential is not precisely known, but catches at this level do not appear to
damage the resource. As squid is an annual species, it is possible there will be variations in

become involved in this industry?

amount of the catch brings substantially less. The New Zealand Government does not own a
fishing fleet, and does not intend to. It does give the fishing industry incentives and support
to allow it to expand and to continue its efforts in catching squid. It does not intend to give
the resource away. The amount now being caught by New Zealand fishermen is far greater
than ever before.
DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Economic Policy
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): I move, That this House notes with satisfaction that for the sixth
successive month the value of exports has exceeded the value of imports and that the figures of
$99.8 million is the best surplus achieved in any 1 month during the past 22 months and
congratulates the Government on the outstanding success of its policies for restructuring of the
economy in face of international recession.
The prime promise of the National Party in the 1975 election campaign was to restore
New Zealand's shattered economy. The key to achieving that was to bring the country back
to living within its income, either by increasing the income or by reducing the internal
standard of living. In its first few months of office the Government moved in various ways to
reduce the internal demand and the standard of living within New Zealand. Much has been
made of that by the Opposition. It believed that the economy could be brought into balance
by merely continuing to borrow to cover the deficit and hoping something would turn up.
But, on the other hand, the more important and more long-term aspect of Government
policy was to improve our balance of trade and to increase the wealth from abroad that flows
into the country-the only source of improving and increasing the standard of living of New
Zealanders and the only long-term method of overcoming unemployment and all our
economic problems.
This motion particularly draws attention to the outstanding success the Government has
achieved to date. It has to be borne in mind that throughout the 24 years of the Government
we have had continually adverse terms of trade, and indeed each of the last three quarters
was worse than the quarter before. I am speaking in terms of trade in price terms-prices
over which we have no control. We have been unable to purchase as much in the way of
imports for a given quantity of exports as previously. We cannot control prices, but we can
control volumes. That is a matter of economic management, and there is a sharp distinction
between the attitude of the Labour Government when in power and the attitude of the
present Government.
If we look at the record, the volume of imports fixed on a 1971 index moved to a sharp
peak in 1975 from a base of 1000 to 1468. Under the last 2 years of Labour management


## p. 854 (#862) ############################################

854
14 June
Discussion of Motions
volumes of imports were up 34.4 percent. Compare that with the last 2 years of the
Government and we find that the volume of imports is down 18.5 percent, which is a sharp
turnround from the spending spree that took place under the previous Government. It had
gone from an increase of 34.4 percent in 2 years to a decrease of 18.5 percent in 2 years. The
other side of the same ledger is the volume of exports. In the last 2 years of the Labour
Government it decreased by 13.8 percent; in the 2 years of the National Government it is up
by 29.6 percent. In all the indicators, including import and export volumes, there has been a
sharp turnround since the advent of the National Government, and that turnround is the
very heart of the restructuring and restoration that were needed, and were promised in 1975.
Those are the causative factors, and they have led to an overseas exchange transaction
surplus for March of $103 million. That is an all-time record.
If we turn to the other method of measuring our export trade-the balance of payments
figure we have a figure for April of $99.8 million, the highest since the boom year of 1974.
These records have been set not because prices have improved, which is not within the
control of the New Zealand Government, but because the volumes have been managed-a
matter that is within the control of the Government, which has now developed a sense of
direction and a sense of purpose.
Let us turn to something closer to home-the NAFTA agreement. It covers our trade
with only one country, Australia. For entirely obscure reasons, the Opposition on occasion
suggests that some factors in our trade with Australia are open to criticism. When we look at
the position at the change of the Government in 1975, we find that for every $100 worth of
goods we sold to Australia, Australia sold us $301 worth. Now, 2 years later, for every $100
worth we sell to Australia we buy $170 worth from Australia. That is a significant
achievement for the Minister of Overseas Trade and the Minister of Trade and Industry,
who have had regular negotiations with the Australians within the framework of NAFTA in
the last 2 years. If we consider the figures for NAFTA, which are the latest figures; the
figures for the overseas exchange transactions, which are the latest figures and an all-time
record surplus; and the balance of payments, which is the best since the boom year of 1974,
we can then look at the inflation figure.
The latest inflation figure we have is 2 percent for the quarter, the best since under the
National Government in 1972. The Opposition is fond of telling the Government that it
should not be seeing lights at the end of tunnels, that it prefers us to deal with the facts as

## p. 860 (#868) ############################################

860
14 June
Discussion of Motions
under the Labour Government. We well remember the year ended March 1972, when the
deficit stood at the relatively low level of $72 million. The following year, the first year under
Labour, it rose to $206 million.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: How much?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: This reads like a horror story. You have not heard the worst
yet. In 1974 it had risen to $241 million and in 1975 to $390 million, compared with $72
million 3 years earlier. That represents an increase from about 1.12 percent of the gross
national product to about 4.13 percent. It has been reiterated time and time again that, when
we took office, it appeared that the deficit for the year to 31 March 1976 would reach a figure
of about $1,200 million. That estimate was made only a few weeks before the end of the
financial year, and one can understand why we were worried. A deficit of $1,200 million
would have represented about 10 percent of the gross national product, or an increase from
1.2 percent in the last year of the previous National Government to almost 10 percent at the
time we regained office. Is it any wonder that we were worried and that the Ministers saw
disaster looming unless some action was taken immediately?
However, we moved quickly. We got rid of the unnecessary and unwanted subsidies,
and a large amount of excess Government expenditure. We took measures that could have
brought immediate unpopularity for the sake of improvements we knew would take some
time to come to fruition. As a result, we were able to hold the deficit before borrowing to
$1,000 million at the end of the March year, compared with the $1,200 million deficit
expected. Soon after that I made the statement that is the subject of the motion we are
debating today. Frankly, I believe that no Government could have brought the deficit back
to less than $1,000 million in a few short weeks. Short of actually derailing the runaway train,
there was no way of applying the brakes and getting the train to stop quickly. We believed it
was courting disaster to leave the deficit at $1,000 million under the conditions prevailing at
the time; but remember that that was 2 years ago, and a lot has happened since then. The
economy then was barely under control because of the conditions we had inherited from the
Labour Government.
I do not retract one word or syllable from the statement I made in June 1976. At that
time we certainly could not have afforded to leave the deficit at $1,000 million, and, of
course, we did not. By the end of the 1977 financial year we had halved the deficit to $506
million, and by the end of the 1978 financial year it was still well down at $694 million. It was
slightly higher at that time, but by then the economy was far more under control, and our
financial standing in the world was slowly being restored.
Financial control is, of course, at the heart of the whole question under debate. It
should be obvious that if an economy like ours is under control and is seen to be under
control by the world's financial institutions, we can afford a higher deficit before borrowing
than we could afford if it was out of control or, as was the case early in 1976, barely in
control.
Another point that should be made is seen in the light of our experience between March
1977 and March 1978, when the deficit was halved in the short space of 12 months. That
showed that, with effective and determined economic management, it is possible to bring
control mechanisms to bear on the internal deficit quite quickly if they are needed. That
might mean unpopular and tough measures, but it can be done, and early in 1976 the
National Government showed that it could be done. For this financial year we have an
estimated deficit before borrowing of slightly more than $1,000 million. That is only 6.4
percent of the gross national product compared with 9.18 percent represented by the $1,000
million deficit for the 1976 year, because, of course, the gross national product has grown.
I have noticed that, from the time my statement was first quoted by the Deputy Leader
of the Opposition the other night, not one member of the Labour Opposition has brought it
down to meaningful terms and expressed the comparisons as a percentage of the gross
national product. They have not done so, either because they know that it would blow their
case sky high or because, more seriously, they do not know any better. Either way it is
extremely serious, and either way they stand condemned. Not only does the $1,000 million
deficit now mean considerably less in terms of an overall debt burden; it can also be far
better sustained because the economy is once again healthy and in full control. In addition to
those considerations, the experience of the 1977 and 1978 financial years has shown that
quick and effective action could be taken to reduce the deficit, if that became necessary next
year.
If Opposition members feel that the present budgetary deficit is unjustified on economic

knows who cut down the first tree in New Zealand, but history will record that the present

The Government has borrowed more in 2 years than the former Labour Government
borrowed in 3 years. The Auditor-General's report clearly demonstrates this. The total net
sum officially borrowed by the Labour Government was $665 million, but in 2 years the
National Government has borrowed $709 million. During the 3 years of the former Labour
Government the external debt increased by $900 million, whereas during the first 2 years of
the National Government it increased by $983 million. The total gross sum officially
borrowed by the Labour Government during its 3 years in office was $923 million, but in 2
years under the National Government the figure reached a mammoth $1,450 million. These
figures are taken directly from the Auditor-General's report. I have no doubt at all that the
Prime Minister could come up with some other figures to prove his point, but I know whom I
would believe. I would believe the Auditor-General every time.
This unprecedented level of overseas borrowing by the National Government has
resulted in New Zealand becoming widely known as the beggar of the Western World. In
spite of having approximately $1,750 million more by way of export income this financial
year than Labour had in its last year in office, National has still recorded a record overseas
deficit of around $900 million. In other words, the Government continues to insist on
spending approximately 4 years of overseas income every 3 years, despite record overseas
export receipts. The Government has been going cap in hand on its knees around every
lending agency in the world to make up the difference between what it is spending each year
and what it is earning. Apparently, the Deputy Prime Minister is again off on one of his
overseas jaunts to raise some extra money somewhere. We all know that the Prime Minister
makes at least three of four trips a year to do just that—to beg, to borrow and hope, to
borrow without purpose, and, in fact, to borrow just to pay the grocers.
Until now, New Zealand has not been an impoverished country. It has not been a
country that has had to rely on handouts to provide a reasonable standard of living for its

known as the beggars of the Western World? Up until the time the Government took office,

destroyed every time the Prime Minister goes overseas to raise another loan. Today,
overseas financiers are not far from the point at which they will say they have had enough
involvement with New Zealand. They will shortly say, "Enough is enough; stop squandering
your record income receipts; we will lend you no more."
New Zealand is going broke. It will take at least 10 years to put right what the National
Government has done in the last 3 years. Its policy of borrow and hope has been a total
failure. Do we really need all the imports that keep flooding in? Do we need all the imported
typewriters, calculators, shoes, cameras, and furniture, and even lollies for the lolly
scramble, as well as the bananas that keep pouring in in ever-increasing quantities? I should
like the next Government speaker to tell me what the National Party has done to implement
the Prime Minister's promises and policies of 1975 to control the situation by selectively
limiting imports.
Sometimes, when the National Government is in a more optimistic frame of mind, it will
admit that it really borrowed quite a lot overseas. It sometimes admits borrowing more in 2
years than the Labour Government did in 3 years; but National members say that they have
been smarter, because they borrowed the money at a lower interest rate. They point to the
fact that they got a Japanese yen loan at 6.8 percent and a Swiss franc loan at 3.75 percent.
Members opposite say that they are smarter, brighter, and cleverer than the Labour
Government was, and that it had to borrow at much higher interest rates. Interest rates have
dropped on a worldwide basis, but there is another factor. New Zealand currency has been
declining in value against the Japanese yen and the Swiss franc. The real interest rate is no
longer 6.8 percent on the Japanese yen. The effective rate-and that is what is important
when considering the depreciation of the New Zealand dollar over the last 2 years—is not 6.8
percent, but 19.4 percent. How clever was the Government there? The Swiss franc loan
interest rate of 3.75 percent, which Government members gloat about, has now become a
17.3 percent effective interest rate. That takes into consideration the depreciation that has
taken place in the New Zealand currency, and what we will have to repay.
Today's New Zealand Herald editorial says, "New Zealand is living on tick." It would

To illustrate my point, the claim is made in the Budget that output per man is rising. I
should have thought that, with the economy being run down and plant and machinery being

recently, counsel for the Minister of Finance and the Secretary to the Treasury argue that

accurate where the real nitty-gritty takes place, in the Arbitration Court. One of the many

the first quarter, the inflation rate was 2.6 percent. That compounds to an annual inflation

and for 1977 an annual inflation rate not of 10.8 percent, but 15.3 percent. It appears that
this is selective compounding of figures; you do it when it suits you, but not when it does not
suit you. But that is par for the course. In 1975 members opposite were choosing, not a
quarter, but our worst month, multiplying that by 12, and saying it was the annual inflation
rate then.

in 1975? When it took office in 1975 the National Government said it would control inflation

their first year they had some small success. The inflation rate of 15.7 percent was brought
down all the way to 15.6 percent-a 57-year programme, a spectacular success. A little more
spectacular was bringing the inflation rate down from 15.6 percent to 15.3 percent the next
year.
Mr Birch: The trend was being reversed.

of the world recession that developed in 1974. On page 1 the Budget states, "A world
recession developed in 1974, partly as a result of the increase in oil prices at the end of 1973."

1974 or 1975-nor even, for that matter, in 1976-but now, in 1978, when all else has failed,

We also find that it has been with us, not for just a couple of years, but since 1974. We on this
side have been trying to tell the Minister of Finance for some time that it was a problem over
which we had limited control, although, to be fair, the Labour Government did much in 1974
and 1975 to overcome this imported problem. In 1974, the proportion of imported inflation
was about 11 percent of the 15 percent inflation rate; in other words, about two-thirds to
three-quarters of our inflation rate in the Labour Government's last year was imported.
In 1976, with subsidies lifted, food prices going mad, and service charges escalating
rapidly, the proportions were roughly reversed, and about two-thirds to three-quarters of the

I turn now to the Budget. The introductory passage to most Budgets is boring in the
extreme. The long and dry run-up to what turns out to be either the good or bad news at the
end is full of padding and platitudes. This one is no exception, it is just as boring as any
Budget I have ever heard. But it is also curiously revealing, and its revelation appears on the

as a result of the increase in oil prices at the end of 1973." However, the world was in an
economic crisis in 1972, when Labour came into office, not 1974. At first, the Labour
Government treated it as just another recession in the manner that the Minister of Finance
now calls it—one of the cyclical imbalances of forces to which the capitalist world is prone.
We applied the Keynesian expansionist remedies that have proved reasonably successful in
the past.
Hon. H. C. Templeton: Nonsense.

successful in the past. If the Minister's memory goes back, that is exactly what happened in
the 1930s. These remedies succeeded in controlling unemployment, which has always been a
feature of earlier cyclical depressions. However, in the past most of these have normally
been accompanied by deflated economies. This time the disease of the Western World was
inflation, and most countries suffered both depreciated currencies and diminished work
forces, adding up to stagnating economies. I believe we handled the problems of 1973 as well
as anyone, and indeed better than most, although, I will concede, not with complete success.

Many people lose sight of the fact that tourism is one of the world's major industries; it is
second only to the oil industry. Valuable growth has taken place in tourism and in New
Zealand it contributes significantly to our overseas exchange, without imposing strain on the
quality of life or on legitimate environmental objectives.
Competition for financial resources limits the scope for private investment in higher-risk
areas such as accommodation and services, and a judicious blend of support assistance and
direct participation by the Government will continue to enable tourism to develop to its full
potential consistent with overall economic growth objectives. Revenue from overseas
tourists has increased by more than 1,000 percent in the past 10 years.
The National Government established the Tourism Advisory Council last year. The last
major review of all aspects of tourism was in 1969, when a successful Tourism Development
Conference was held. The Government felt that a further review was needed to ensure that,
as far as possible, there would be no serious obstacles that might impede the continued
development of both overseas and domestic tourism, and that adequate supporting facilities
would be available. The Tourism Advisory Council was established in 1977 to carry out a
major review of tourism and to make recommendations to the Government on future
policies and planning requirements. The council will be assisted by specialist committees
representing a wide cross-section of public and private sector interests.
Following a conference of tourist interests to be held in August 1978, the council will
submit what it is hoped will be a comprehensive report for consideration by the
Government. The council's terms of reference will provide for a review of tourism policy,
but in some respects the council will not be able to reach a final conclusion. Some of the
topics already being studied are of an evolutionary nature. It is, therefore, envisaged that the
council will remain in being and that the Tourist and Publicity Department will continue to
provide the secretarial and support services. The National Government feels that tourist
promotion in overseas markets should continue in close co-operation with the private sector.
In the main markets the number and the strength of the Government's tourist promotion
offices will be kept under review to ensure that the promotional services offered to the
industry as a whole are thorough and up to expectations. We have 10 offices that are
compatible with the needs of the industry and its reasonable growth.

On a recent overseas tour I was most impressed with the calibre of the New Zealand
representatives in the private sector in the North American market, and was also by Air New
Zealand's representatives and those in authority in Government travel commissions. The
Tourist Hotel Corporation has evolved as a main element in the provision of tourist hotel
accommodation, and has acquired considerable skill and experience in the development and
management of hotels. The department has observed a growing tendency among hotel
developers to utilise the Tourist Hotel Corporation in a leasing or managing capacity. The
role of the Tourist Hotel Corporation could be further investigated.
Members may be interested to know that the new premises of the National Film Unit at

efficient workshops and encouraging it to work even more proficiently. The information and
press section will continue to carry out the function of informing the public, directly or
through the media, of what the Government and its departments and agencies are doing to
ensure that policy decisions are widely disseminated and understood.
In the present Budget, $2.3 million, virtually double the amount allocated 3 years ago,
has been set aside for tourist promotion overseas. There is a continuing need for
Government support for the promotion of New Zealand as a tourist destination. This would
involve an intensification of activity in Australia to arrest the decline in the number of
Australian tourists, and to continue expansion of activities in areas showing potential
growth, notably the United States, Canada, Japan, South-east Asia, and Western Europe.
The private sector looks to Government services to provide initiative and to assist in
promotiong markets.
Next week the National Travel Association is celebrating the twenty-fifth anniversary of
its inauguration. It is an association of entrepreneurs in which the Government has every
confidence, and to which the Government looks for guidance in the tourist industry. The
importance of this association, representing many diverse elements of tourism, has been
recognised by the substantial increases in subsidies granted by the Government in each of the
last 3 years; and $50,000 has been allocated to the National Travel Association in this
financial year. The need is foreseen to continue to provide this grant to assist the association
to develop further its promotional and other activities. The association would have received
nothing had the Labour Government been returned to office in 1975.
Combined promotions in Australia are a credit to the Government and to private
enterprise. Publicity campaigns in Australia have been operating 25 years, and involve 47
members who benefit from the tourist promotion tax incentive scheme. The campaign is led
by the Tourist and Publicity Department, and has been extremely successful in co-ordinating
the resources of the Government and of private enterprise in promoting New Zealand in the
Australian market, a market from which New Zealand receives 55.5 percent of its visitors.
This year's audio-visual campaign is entitled "The New Zealand Experience". It is a
low-key, elaborate, consumer-orientated presentation using 8 screens and 16 projectors.
Thirty-five thousand dollars has been spent on the presentation, which is a continuing
promotion using slides that can be changed as required. To date, it has been shown at the
Moomba Festival in Melbourne and at the Royal Sydney Easter Show. Future screenings are
scheduled for Brisbane, Newcastle, Wollongong, Adelaide, Canberra, Perth, and smaller
centres. Audience reaction has been extremely favourable, and repeat screenings are
scheduled for Sydney and Melbourne.
Tourism in its fullest sense also embraces the travel activities of New Zealanders within
New Zealand. Support for this sector of the tourist industry, while overlapping international
tourism and its particular requirements, has been given in a number of ways, including
comprehensive travel and booking services by Government tourist bureaus. In addition to
contributing to New Zealand's ability to promote tourism overseas, these bureaus provide
valuable services to the travelling public, and are an effective marketing outlet for hundreds
of accommodation, transport, and sightseeing operators. This important role needs to
continue. In its latest Budget the Government recognises the need to encourage investment
in the accommodation sector, especially in the provision of first-class hotels in key areas able
to cater for increasing numbers of overseas visitors in large groups.
It is proposed to make the tourist accommodation development scheme more effective.
The Development Finance Corporation can now provide loans for the building of much-
needed accommodation, and the Tourist and Publicity Department can still give guarantees
under the TADCO scheme. Other tax incentives are mentioned in the Budget. With the
growth of tourism and the development of other facilities and plant, the need arises to keep

under review existing and additional incentives and to provide finance for the tourist

Industry training is very important, and the success of tourism will depend on the calibre
