The Tourist and Publicity Department undertakes research and provides data to assist
the Government and the private sector in planning and investment decisions and in
promoting and marketing tourism. Major projects to be undertaken as soon as possible
include domestic travel survey and an updated study of accommodation use by overseas
visitors. The recommendations of the review committee on tourism shall be implemented,
and full consideration given to the Tourist Advisory Council's recommendations on research
and statistics. I want to mention the Opposition's proposals on a foreign exchange surcharge.
Its spokesman on tourism has said that if a Labour Government is elected it would abolish
the travel tax. However, it would impose a foreign exchange tax, which would distort the
industry.
The present travel tax on a New Zealand-London return air fare costing $1,200 is $120.
Labour would abolish this tax and introduce a 10 percent foreign exchange surcharge, which,
at a conservative estimate of $2,500 spending money, would mean that a traveller would pay
$250 tax, not $120, on sightseeing, meals, drinks, souvenirs, and so on. At present a traveller
to Fiji or to other Pacific Islands pays no travel tax. Under Labour all his overseas allowance
would be taxable.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Rubbish.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: All his overseas allowance would be taxable. The exception
would be those who had not travelled in the previous 5 years. Labour intends penalising the
frequent business traveller who seeks and services export markets. It intends to exempt
persons who have not travelled overseas during the previous 5 years-a regulation open to
all kinds of abuse. Importers will pay a surcharge on funds used when importing goods. As
that has to be somehow recouped, the tax would be compounded as it passed from importer,
to wholesaler, to retailer, and, finally, to the consumer.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: What happens to customs duty?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The member, with his great powers for mental arithmetic and
his cash-register psychology, will know that anybody who has to pay a 10 percent penalty on
the purchase of overseas exchange will have a right to his profit, as will the wholesaler and
the retailer; and the consumer will, of course, have to pay more. It is a vicious tax on the
consumer, and I am appalled that these so-called friends of the people could suggest that this
tax might in the long run benefit New Zealanders. The 10 percent surcharge on foreign
exchange is estimated by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition to yield $400 million each
year, and would be a one-sided devaluation. If imposed, it could contravene many of our
trading agreements, and do untold damage to our trading relations with other countries.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Name one.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The Leader of the Opposition knows jolly well that that is a
fact. The National Government tourist policy is devised in the interest of New Zealand's
economy. We shall continue to encourage the building of more accommodation, and
promote New Zealand as a tourist attraction. The March statistics show that the number of
overseas visitors is increasing-in the March year by almost 3 percent. We are receiving
almost 1100 overseas visitors a day, and it is estimated that by 1981-82 we shall be catering
for approximately 500 000 visitors. Tourism is a most valuable business. It has earned almost
$162 million in foreign exchange in the past year, and will continue to grow. It behoves all
New Zealanders to assist in that growth.
Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua): It is a great pleasure to follow the Minister of Tourism after
his last Budget speech in the House.
Mr Prebble: Again!
Mr FALLOON: I wish the member for Auckland Central would give other members a

896
14 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement.
chance to speak. He was very loud of voice and very low in content this afternoon. The
Minister of Tourism has served the House and the country very well. Recently, I spent some
time at Taupo and at Rotorua, inspecting tourist resorts and enterprises. One, in particular,
had had 300 000 visitors in a year.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Not in the lake; it's polluted.
Mr FALLOON: It was Rainbow Springs. There are others. People have been
encouraged by the Government to develop enterprises and to attract tourists, and there are
many facilities of which people in New Zealand are unaware. The Government is prepared
to foster private enterprise. Indeed, that is what the Budget is all about. It is a Budget for
people who are prepared to work if they can get a job. I say "if they can get a job", because
I, like other Government members and many Opposition members, am well aware that
many New Zealanders are not working. If those who have a job are prepared to work
overtime their tax rate will not rise because of the extra dollar or two that they earn.
Mr Prebble: Oh yes, it will.
Mr FALLOON: No, not unless it takes their incomes over the plateau at $10,000, or one
of the other plateaus mentioned in the Budget. At least those on the average wage will have
an opportunity to work extra hours without feeling they are being discriminated against, as
they have been in the past when they have worked a little harder and a little longer. Recently
one of the comments made in a freezing works in the Wairarapa was that some absenteeism
occurred because workers felt that they were being discriminated against when working
overtime. I hope they will stay at work in the coming season. No matter what the
Government does in its Budget, and no matter what we do in the House, the work must be
done.
99
A problem during the last 2 or 3 years, or perhaps even longer, has been that the service
industries have not kept pace with technology in the farming industry. That has caused a
great break in the New Zealand economy, and it is a problem faced by many people. If one
looks carefully at a particular industry one usually finds that a problem is caused by lack of
communication. In the meat industry tremendous changes in hygiene regulations have
overtaken the workers. An employee may now find that he has to wash his hands, or change
technique, or he may have someone standing over him telling him what to do, even though
he has been doing the job for 20 years. The worker probably thinks he is doing a good job,
and no doubt he is by old standards. No wonder he cannot understand it when someone says
to him, "You are not doing a good enough job, because you have left a hair on a carcass.'
New Zealand has been served well by the National Government in the past 3 years.
Unemployment statistics show that the problem here is not as great as it is in other countries.
In that giant manufacturing democracy, West Germany, the unemployment rate is 4.4
percent. In Holland it is 5.1 percent, in Japan it is 2.1 percent, and in Socialist Denmark it is
11 percent. In the United States of America it is 6 percent, and under a socialist Government
in the United Kingdom it is 5.8 percent. One of the reasons the level of unemployment in
New Zealand is not as high as it is in other countries, and one of the reasons we have not had
the growth in real gross national product experienced by some of those countries, is that the
economy is based on farming. If you grow something, you must process and manufacture it.
Grass will grow, and sheep will not cease to grow wool.
The economy has been well served by the farming industry, and the Government
recognises that it is the only industry that can extract the country from the hole it is in. The
only answer given by Opposition members in the little pink budget they have produced is the
suggestion that they would consult the farmers, and that would solve the whole problem.
They have been criticising the $60 million granted to the farming industry in stock money.
Apparently they forget that in the middle of the 1975 season they gave farmers $50 million
when sheep farmers' incomes fell by 72 percent. The incomes of those farmers have fallen by
40 percent in the past 12 months, but they continue to spread fertiliser and lime. The farmers
have faith in the National Government, and the Government believes in the future of the
farming industry. The Budget has allayed farmers' fears for their incomes, and I am sure
there will be a great drive in the farming industry to increase production-providing, of
course, the service industries can stay abreast of technological advances in farming. As I said
before, the document we are debating is a people's Budget, and it is of particular help to the
farmers.
The Budget also recognises the problems of single-income families. The member for
Southern Maori, who persists in interjecting, should know that the tax for those earning an
average wage-even where the wife is working and earning less than $1,000-has been more


## p. 897 (#905) ############################################

14 June
897
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
than halved, if he was earning the same income in 1975. I believe the member for Southern
Maori knows that quite well. If she would desist from interjecting, I could continue with my
speech.
The farming industry is being paid on performance, an important change from past
policies. Like most farmers, I do not wish to be subsidised by the community. In the past, the
most efficient New Zealand industry has had to be subsidised by the taxpayer. You could call
it redistribution. One wonders why that has been necessary when the New Zealand economy
earns about 72 percent of its overseas funds from farming. It has been necessary, because in
New Zealand many industries are cost plus. These industries have been protected from
overseas markets, and have not had to live in the real world. The National Government has
changed that by encouraging people to export, and in the last 2 years we have seen an
increase of 30 percent in the volume of trade. Under the Labour Government, exports
decreased by 9 percent in volume terms.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: That is an index term.
Mr FALLOON: If the Leader of the Opposition reads the Planning Council's report, he
I will see the facts there. At the same time, under the Labour Government, the volume of
imports increased by 40 percent, mainly because of Labour's incredible monetary policy.
During the last 3 years we have seen a significant change because of the National
Government's policies. People have been encouraged to save money so that it can be used
for investment by others. In 1975, New Zealanders were encouraged to spend on consumer
goods, on excessively priced land, on houses which often they did not need-
Hon. W. A. Fraser: And at lower rates of interest.
Mr FALLOON: The member for St. Kilda knows that at that time people often bought
houses they did not need. When the Labour Government was in office 80 000 houses were
empty, and the prices of houses increased by 88 percent in 3 years. The member for St. Kilda
does not understand a monetary policy. People must save money so that it can be invested
for use by others.
Hon. Members: Oh!
Mr Prebble: It that official policy?
Mr FALLOON: If the Opposition rabble wants to make a speech, could Opposition
members all do so together. I repeat that people must be encouraged to save, so that other
people can use that money. If everybody spent their money on consumer goods, on sections,
houses and farms, and on other things that they may not need, or perhaps buy just to beat
inflation, nobody would save. If interest rates are kept at artificially low levels, it creates a
problem, as the Leader of the Opposition knows. Members opposite have referred to their
housing policy, but we know that it put the opportunity to buy a house beyond the reach of
many New Zealanders. The Budget makes significant changes in interest rates, and in the
level of income allowable to qualify for loans at low interest rates. The member for St. Kilda
should realise that. The role of the Reserve Bank has been changed. The Government has
provided the Bank with an opportunity to enter the market to finance transactions, and this
has controlled the money supply. Very importantly, the Government has kept its finger on
increases in the supply of money which often cause inflation if allowed to rise above the
inflation rate to an excessive level.
The Labour Party, in its alternative budget, said it would control the money supply, but
last year the Leader of the Opposition said that the money supply in New Zealand could not
be controlled because we were a major exporting country. Now he has changed his tune. The
Labour Party's alternative budget sets out an export surcharge. I wonder what the effect
would have been on the export industries of this country. It would have been a one-sided
devaluation. The members opposite had a policy of consultation for farming. It would have
probably been promises and nothing else, because they are not sufficiently courageous in
their statement to suggest that the farming industry really needs assistance. The suggested
export surcharge would have cost enough. What would have been the cost of fertiliser, or the
cost of oil and other staple goods needed by farmers? What about the machinery required by
the servicing industries and the aerial topdressing industry?
I should like to talk about what has happened in my electorate in the past year in
relation to export incentives. It is significant to note that three major industries have
expanded their operations. That has been done outside any of the Labour Government's
regional development areas, and has been done with assistance from this Government. One
industry has expanded its operations by using an export suspensory loan of $100,000.
Norsewear Industries has expanded its operation by building more factory space, thus


## p. 898 (#906) ############################################

898
14 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
providing more jobs for people. It is significant to note that the building industry is in good
shape because the opportunities are there. The member for Southern Maori, who is trying to
interject, would be interested to know that the Peter Pan factory-even though it is a small
business, and albeit shaky-is surviving and processing raw materials. I invite the member
for Southern Maori, when next she visits that part of the electorate, to see it.
During the past year one of the major things which has concerned me about the
economy is the wastage of our resources. At times the local bylaws are causing a tremendous
waste of public money. In public buildings, in educational buildings, in university buildings,
and in playing fields, facilities are provided which are far beyond our means. Many were
built in the time of the Labour Government. We have the position in which a university
lecturer has an office twice the size of that occupied by a member of Parliament. We have a
situation where $9,000 has been spent to provide a playing field for a country school, when
the local people would have been quite prepared to help, and when there is a sandpit 3 ft
deep so that the kindergarten children are lost if they burrow in it too deeply. We are wasting
public resources in that way.
The Government is unable to police this sort of thing, and it is up to the people in local
government to exercise control. How many of us who examine what we achieve in our
electorates believe it is good to spend such amounts of money? I have heard many
Opposition members talk like that. If the money had been spent more carefully it could have
been spread around the electorate to help people in State houses that are not heated, while
we sit in a hot-house with a temperature higher than necessary. New fire regulations are
introduced for buildings that have been sound and safe for 100 years. These regulations cost
local communities thousands of dollars. Country halls that have stood for 100 years have to
put in special doorways and fire-fighting hose-reels.
When the Labour Government was in office, it introduced legislation banning cats from
shops. I wonder how many Opposition members realise that the cats are now back in the
shops. This is the sort of proliferation of ridiculous bylaws that must be avoided. Millions of
dollars of taxpayers' and ratepayers' money is being wasted. It is up to county councils and
local authorities to do something about this waste. I have seen two-lane bridges on side roads
when a one-lane bridge would do, and when the road leading up to the bridge is metal it
causes a risk to drivers who might skid off the road and into the bridge. I believe it would be
better to have the road sealed and a one-lane bridge built. To me it seems extraordinary that
this type of thing happens merely to advertise the money we spend and to publicise what has
been done for the people we represent. We must put a stop to it.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
